Department of Justice
28 CFR Part 106
[JMD Docket No. 157; A.G. Order No. 7256-2026]
RIN 1105-AB71
AGENCY:
Department of Justice.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
On April 19, 2024, the Department of Justice published an interim final rule to implement the HAVANA Act of 2021. No comments were received on the interim final rule. The HAVANA Act authorizes agency heads to provide payments to certain individuals who have incurred qualifying injuries to the brain. This
(
printed page 67477)
final rule adopts the interim final rule with minor, non-substantive changes to the titles of certain officials involved in the payment review process and the earliest eligibility date for claims in accordance with statutory changes occurring after issuance of the interim final rule. This rule covers current and former Department of Justice employees and their dependents.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on November 27, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Gordon R. Jimison, Assistant General Counsel, Justice Management Division; email:
Gordon.R.Jimison@usdoj.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Department of Justice (“Department”) published an interim final rule titled “Implementation of HAVANA Act of 2021,” which appeared in the
Federal Register
on April 19, 2024 (
89 FR 28633
). A technical correction to that interim final rule was published in the
Federal Register
on May 3, 2024 (
89 FR 36671
). That correction was effective on May 20, 2024.
The interim final rule implemented the HAVANA Act of 2021,
Public Law 117-46
, 135 Stat. 391 (2021) (codified at
22 U.S.C. 2680b(i)
). The HAVANA Act authorizes agency heads to provide payments to certain individuals who have incurred qualifying injuries to the brain. The interim final rule covers current and former Department of Justice employees and their dependents. The comment period on the interim final rule closed June 18, 2024.
The Department received no written or electronic comments on the interim final rule during the comment period. Although the Department received no comments about the commenting process, the Department was concerned that the public may have been hindered from submitting electronic comments through the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov
because of a technical problem that was discovered after the comment period closed. Accordingly, on October 8, 2024, the Department reopened the comment period until November 18, 2024. The Department received no written or electronic comments during the reopened comment period.
After conclusion of the comment period, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Justice Management Division (JMD) conducted reorganizations of their respective components, resulting in changes to the titles of certain officials involved in the process set forth in the rule. Specifically, in the FBI, the interim final rule referred to the “Executive Assistant Director, Human Resources Branch;” this official is now identified as the “Operations Director, Human Capital Branch.” In the Justice Management Division, the “Deputy Assistant Attorney General, Human Resources and Administration” is now known as the “Deputy Assistant Attorney General for Human Capital.”
This rule implements the HAVANA Act of 2021,
Public Law 117-46
, 135 Stat. 391 (2021) (codified at
22 U.S.C. 2680b(i)
).
Background and Authority—§ 106.1
In 2016, Department of State employees stationed in Havana, Cuba, began reporting a sudden onset of symptoms, including headaches, pain, nausea, disequilibrium, and hearing loss, in conjunction with sensory events. Federal agencies have called such incidents Anomalous Health Incidents (“AHIs”). Since 2016, Federal employees in numerous countries reported suspected AHIs. On December 20, 2019, Congress authorized the Department of State to pay benefits to employees and their dependents for injuries suffered after January 1, 2016, in the Republic of Cuba, the People's Republic of China, or other foreign countries designated by the Secretary of State, in connection with war, insurgency, hostile acts, or terrorist activity, or in connection with other incidents designated by the Secretary of State.
See
Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2020,
Public Law 116-94
, div. J, title IX, § 901, 133 Stat. 2534, 3079-81 (2019) (codified as amended at
22 U.S.C. 2680b
). These benefits were limited to State Department employees only (
i.e.,
not other employees under Chief of Mission (“COM”) authority).
On January 1, 2021, Congress amended this law to authorize other Federal Government agencies to provide benefits to their own employees under COM authority if they suffered similar injuries. National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021,
Public Law 116-283
,  1110, 134 Stat. 3388, 3892-93 (2021).
On October 8, 2021, Congress passed the Helping American Victims Afflicted by Neurological Attacks or the HAVANA Act of 2021,
Public Law 117-46
, 135 Stat. 391 (2021) (“HAVANA Act”). In the HAVANA Act, Congress authorized Federal Government agencies to compensate affected current employees, former employees, and their dependents for qualifying injuries to the brain. The HAVANA Act also omitted the previous law's requirement that the qualifying injury must occur in the Republic of Cuba, the People's Republic of China, or another foreign country designated by the Secretary of State. The scope of coverage now includes a qualifying injury that occurs in any foreign or domestic location. The HAVANA Act requires Federal agencies who make payments under the HAVANA Act to prescribe implementing regulations not later than 180 days after the effective date of the Act. Section 9216 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023,
Public Law 117-263
, 136 Stat. 2395, 3877 (2022) (codified at
22 U.S.C. 2680b(j)
), provided agencies with authority to designate incidents affecting employees or dependents who are not under the security responsibility of the Secretary of State.
This rule implements section 3 of the HAVANA Act as it applies to the Department of Justice (the “Department”). This rule only applies to current and former employees of the Department and their dependents, as defined in § 106.2 of this rule.
On June 30, 2022, the Department of State published an interim final rule to implement its requirements under the HAVANA Act, with an effective date of August 15, 2022.
87 FR 38981
(June 30, 2022) (codified at
22 CFR pt. 135
). The Department of State subsequently published a final rule that became effective on January 25, 2023.
88 FR 4722
(Jan. 25, 2023) (codified at
22 CFR pt. 135
). The Department of Justice has independently reviewed the approach implemented by the Department of State in these rules and has determined that its approach is reasonable and well considered. Accordingly, the Department of Justice plans to adopt that approach as appropriate in its regulations to ensure consistency of benefits among Federal employees and their dependents. In particular, the Department based its final rule on the Department of State's definitions and process for the payment of benefits.
On December 18, 2025, Congress amended the HAVANA Act to cover qualifying injuries dating back to September 11, 2001, rather than January 1, 2016 (
Pub. L. 119-60
, Sec. 5604).
Definitions—§ 106.2
The rule defines those who are eligible to receive payments: covered employees (including current and former employees) and covered dependents who on or after September 11, 2001, experience a qualifying brain injury. A “covered employee” includes all Department employees, including employees on Limited Non-Career Appointments, employees on Temporary Appointments, personnel hired on Personal Services Contracts,
(
printed page 67478)
and students providing volunteer services under
5 U.S.C. 3111
.
An employee's family member is a covered dependent if, on or after September 11, 2001, the family member experiences a qualifying injury. The rule defines the family members who are eligible as certain dependent children, parents residing with the employee sponsor, dependent siblings, or spouses.
For the purposes of this rule, the Department also adopts the Department of State's definition of “qualifying injury to the brain.”
22 CFR 135.2
. The Department has determined that the Department of State definition is reasonable and well considered. The Department of State consulted with the chief medical officers at other Federal agencies and experts at civilian medical centers of excellence. There is no diagnostic code or criteria for AHIs in the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM). Because of the varied symptoms and still nascent understanding of how to test or otherwise screen for AHI impacts, the standard adopted is broadly inclusive of the types of injuries that have been reported to date.
The definition of “qualifying injury to the brain” is based on current medical practices related to brain injuries. The individual must have: (1) an acute injury to the brain such as a concussion, a penetrating injury, or an injury as the consequence of an event that leads to permanent alterations in brain function as demonstrated by confirming correlative findings on imaging studies; (2) a medical diagnosis of a traumatic brain injury that required active medical treatment for 12 months or more; or (3) the acute onset of new, persistent, disabling neurologic symptoms, as demonstrated by confirming correlative findings on imaging studies or a physical exam or other appropriate testing, that required active medical treatment for 12 months or more.
The first component of the definition of “qualifying injury to the brain” set forth in § 106.2(d)(2)(i) accounts for a variety of observable impacts to an individual, including a concussion or a penetrating injury or, absent either of those, permanent alterations in brain function as confirmed by a board-certified physician's review of a variety of forms of medical imaging evidence. The goal with this standard is to ensure there is some documented evidence of impact to the brain, while minimally circumscribing what that impact entails. The second and third components of the definition (paragraphs (d)(2)(ii)-(iii) of the definition) are intended to provide alternative avenues for demonstrating sustained, long-term impact to the individual. This benefit is intended for individuals who experience long-term consequences, potentially including an inability to gainfully work, as a result of a reported AHI.
The standard is consistent with that employed by other agencies, including the Department of State. A 12-month threshold of active medical treatment is indicative of a long-term injury. For example, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (“CDC”) broadly defines chronic diseases “as conditions that last 1 year or more and require ongoing medical attention or limit activities of daily living or both.” CDC,
About Chronic Diseases,
https://www.cdc.gov/​chronic-disease/​about/​index.html
(last reviewed October 8, 2026). The Department notes that applicants who have suffered kinetic or external, physically caused injuries to the brain such as the head striking an object, the brain undergoing an acceleration or deceleration movement, or brain injuries from events such as a blast or explosion, including penetrating injuries, may be eligible if the injuries satisfy the other requirements of this rule.
Under the HAVANA Act, the injury must have occurred “in connection with war, insurgency, hostile act, terrorist activity, or other incidents designated by the Secretary of State,” and cannot have been “the result of the willful misconduct” of the covered individual.
22 U.S.C. 2680b(e)(4)(A)(ii)-(iii)
, (e)(4)(B)(ii)-(iii), (i)(1)(D). The Department will work with an applicant upon the applicant's submission of the DS-4316, “Eligibility Questionnaire for HAVANA Act Payments,” to determine whether his or her alleged incident qualifies.
The definition of “other incident” is a new onset of physical manifestations that cannot otherwise be readily explained and that is designated under
22 U.S.C. 2680b
. The Department will review available information on the reported incident. If a physician does not indicate that there is a credible alternative explanation for the individual's symptoms, and if the information the Department has regarding the incident does not provide a credible alternative explanation for the incident, that incident will be recommended for designation. Incidents for which an alternative explanation has been identified will not be recommended for designation. For incidents affecting employees or dependents who are not under the security responsibility of the Secretary of State, the Department will determine whether to designate such incidents.
Eligibility for Payments—§ 106.3
The Department will make available to its workforce information on the regulations and the process to apply for HAVANA Act payments. Current employees, former employees, and covered dependents (as defined in this rule) can apply for consideration. Applicants will be required to provide the necessary documentation so the Department may determine whether they qualify for payment. The DS-4316, “Eligibility Questionnaire for HAVANA Act Payments,” is the form associated with developing the necessary evidence to submit a claim, and it will be available upon request with instructions on how to apply for a HAVANA Act payment. A portion of the form must be filled out by a qualified physician; the rule specifies certain board certification requirements for physicians who can evaluate a qualifying injury to the brain.
The Department has determined that the payment scheme set forth in the Department of State's HAVANA Act regulations,
22 CFR 135.3
, is well reasoned and provides an effective means of compensating covered employees. Accordingly, the Department has adopted it for purposes of this rulemaking. Pursuant to this final rule, the Department, in its discretion, may authorize a one-time, non-taxable, lump sum payment based on, and may not exceed, Level III of the Executive Schedule.
See
5 U.S.C. 5311
et seq.
The payment is non-taxable pursuant to
22 U.S.C. 2680b(g)
. Payment eligibility and the amount of the payment will be at the Department's discretion. The maximum should be awarded only where a condition has a consistent, sustained, and exceptionally severe impact on a victim's quality of life or prevents a victim from successfully performing his or her work-related duties. The purpose is to compensate individuals only for qualifying brain injuries that meet the criteria set forth in this rule. The following factors will be taken into account to determine the amount of the payment to be authorized: (1) the applicant's responses on the eligibility form; and (2) whether the Department of Labor (Office of Workers' Compensation Programs) has determined that the applicant has no reemployment potential for the indefinite future, the Social Security Administration (“SSA”) has approved the applicant for Social Security Disability Insurance or Supplemental Security Income benefits, or the applicant's board-certified physician has certified that the individual requires a full-time caregiver for activities of daily living, as defined
(
printed page 67479)
by the Katz Index of Independence in Activities of Daily Living.
The award thresholds are based on, and may not exceed, Level III of the Executive Schedule. A Base payment will be 75 percent of Level III pay, and a Base+ payment will be 100 percent of Level III pay. The specific use of Level III of the Executive Schedule sets the compensation at the maximum annual salary potentially available to most of the Federal workforce. The Department believes this amount is the most it can reasonably compensate each applicant while ensuring funds for the total number of applicants it believes will likely receive payments. If the applicant meets any of the criteria for severe impacts, the applicant will be eligible to receive a Base+ payment. Applicants whose board-certified physician confirms that the definition of qualifying injury to the brain has been met, but who have not met any of the criteria for severe impacts, will be eligible to receive a Base payment.
The criteria established for severe impacts are reflective of the Department's objective of ensuring that the individuals most severely affected by AHIs (as indicated by a lack of reemployment potential, an inability to engage in substantial gainful activity, or the need for a full-time caregiver) receive additional payment. The use of the Department of Labor's or the SSA's determination is to ensure that both Federal employees as well as their dependents have access to a mechanism for this determination. The Department recognizes that the criteria the Department of Labor and SSA use in their determinations are distinct, as well as the fact that the procedural timelines for seeking and receiving approval may be different between these agencies. The third option, that a board-certified physician certify that the individual requires a full-time caregiver for activities of daily living, provides an alternative mechanism for all individuals. Finally, the Department notes that if an applicant who received a Base payment later meets any of the criteria listed for severe impacts, the applicant may apply for an additional payment that will be the difference between the Base and Base+ payment. As the payments are tied to the Executive Schedule payment levels, the amounts will change over time based on changes to the Federal salary schedule. Payments will be based on the Executive Schedule in effect at the time the payment was approved.
While payments under the HAVANA Act may be in addition to other leave benefits, disability benefits, or workers' compensation payments that the applicant may be receiving or may be entitled to receive that also help augment any loss of income, the Department believes this is an appropriate additional payment. This payment scheme is also consistent with what is being offered by other Federal agencies and will ensure consistency of benefits among affected individuals.
The Department notes that payments may only be made using amounts appropriated in advance specifically for this purpose in the relevant fiscal year, unless Congress specifies otherwise. Therefore, payments are contingent on appropriated funds, and all payments will be paid out on a first-come, first-served basis.
Consultations With the Department of State—§ 106.4
Under the rule, the Department's procedures for determining whether an incident has been designated under
22 U.S.C. 2680b
include, where appropriate, consultation with the Secretary of State.
See
22 U.S.C. 2680b(i)(1)(D)
(cross-referencing subparagraph 2680b(e)(4)).
Procedures—§ 106.5
Each Federal agency is responsible for (1) processing applications for the HAVANA Act payments; (2) determining or, as necessary, consulting with the Secretary of State to determine, whether the incident causing the injury may be deemed a designated incident under the statute,
see
22 U.S.C. 2680b(j)
;
id.
2680b(i)(1)(D) (cross-referencing subparagraph 2680b(e)(4)); (3) determining eligibility for the benefit, determining the amount of the benefit, and processing payment of the benefit; and (4) notifying applicants upon receipt of their applications and when a decision has been made whether to authorize payment.
The Operations Director, Human Capital Branch, Federal Bureau of Investigation (“FBI”), is authorized to approve HAVANA Act payments to FBI employees or their covered dependents. The Deputy Assistant Attorney General for Human Capital, Justice Management Division (“JMD”), is authorized to approve HAVANA Act payments for all other Department employees or their covered dependents. If payment is denied by the designated FBI or JMD official, the applicant may direct an appeal to the Assistant Attorney General for Administration within 60 days of the notification of denial, but decisions on the amount of payment are not appealable.
Regulatory Analysis
In developing this final rule, the Department considered numerous statutes and executive orders applicable to rulemaking. The Department's analysis of the applicability of those statutes and executive orders to this rule is summarized below.
Congressional Review Act

5 U.S.C. 804
for the purposes of congressional review of agency rulemaking under the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996,

.

This rule will not result in the expenditure by State, local, or Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million in any year, and it will not significantly or uniquely affect small governments. Therefore, no actions were deemed necessary under the provisions of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995,
2 U.S.C. 1501
et seq.
Executive Order 13175
—Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments
The Department has determined that this rulemaking will not have Tribal implications, will not impose substantial direct compliance costs on Indian Tribal governments, and will not preempt Tribal law. Accordingly, the requirements of
Executive Order 13175
do not apply to this rulemaking.
Regulatory Flexibility Act: Small Business
A regulatory flexibility analysis is not required under the Regulatory Flexibility Act,
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.,
because the Department was not required to issue a notice of proposed rulemaking.
Executive Order 12866
,
Executive Order 13563
, and
Executive Order 14192
The Department provided this final rule to the Office of Management and Budget for its review. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs has designated this rule as “significant” under
Executive Order 12866
. The Department has also reviewed the rule to ensure its consistency with the regulatory philosophy and principles set forth in
Executive Order 12866
and finds that the benefits of the rule (in providing mechanisms for individuals to obtain compensation for certain injuries) outweigh any costs to the public, which are limited, given the anticipated small number of individuals with qualifying injuries. The
(

AGENCY:
Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
PHMSA proposes to update the Hazardous Materials Regulations to adopt certain international regulations and standards related to proper shipping names, hazard classes, packing groups, special provisions, packaging authorizations, air transport quantity limitations, and vessel stowage requirements. These proposed amendments are intended to maintain consistency with the latest international regulations and standards, to reduce costs to entities or individuals within the United States, and to lower the cost of regulations on the U.S. economy.

I. Executive Summary
The Federal Hazardous Materials Transportation Law directs the Secretary of Transportation to ensure domestic regulations for the transportation of hazardous materials are generally consistent with the latest international regulations and standards, unless they are unnecessary or unsafe, or a more stringent safety standard is in the public interest.
[
1
]
Consistent with this statutory requirement, the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) proposes to amend the Hazardous Materials Regulations (HMR;
49 CFR parts 171 to 180
) to adopt certain international regulations and standards. The amendments in this notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) include changes to material incorporated by reference, hazardous materials descriptions and proper shipping names (PSN), hazard classes, packing groups (PG), special provisions (SP), packaging authorizations, air transport quantity limitations, and vessel stowage requirements.
The proposed amendments will maintain the current levels of safety achieved under the HMR. Harmonizing the HMR with international regulations and standards will reduce delays and interruptions in the transportation of hazardous materials and promote the free flow of commerce by eliminating unnecessary and outdated regulatory requirements. Overall, the proposed amendments will reduce costs to entities or individuals within the U.S. or otherwise lower the cost of regulations on the U.S. economy.
[
2
]
PHMSA anticipates the NPRM will benefit safety by harmonizing domestic and international regulations. PHMSA
(
printed page 67721)
solicits comments on the need, benefits, and costs of the proposed HMR revisions; impact on safety and the environment; and any other relevant information. PHMSA also solicits comments regarding approaches to reducing the costs of the proposed HMR revisions while maintaining or increasing safety benefits and on any other specific changes (
e.g.
, greater flexibility regarding a particular proposal) that might improve the rulemaking. As further explained in the Preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis (PRIA), PHMSA expects the aggregate benefits of the NPRM will justify the aggregate costs for U.S. entities or individuals.
II. Background
PHMSA participates in the development of international standards for the transportation of hazardous materials and promotes the adoption of standards consistent with the HMR. When considering whether to adopt new or amended international regulations and standards, PHMSA reviews each provision, assesses its overall impact on transportation safety, and analyzes the economic impacts of its adoption. The goal of PHMSA is to harmonize the HMR without reducing safety or imposing undue burdens on the regulated community.
The United Nations Sub-Committee of Experts (UNSCOE) on the Transport of Dangerous Goods (TDG) and on the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) issues the UN Model Regulations (UNMR). The UNMR are amended and updated biennially by the UNSCOE and serve as the basis for national, regional, and international modal regulations, including the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Technical Instructions and IMDG Code. PHMSA routinely updates the HMR to incorporate by reference these biennial amendments.
PHMSA has evaluated the latest biennial updates and proposes to revise the HMR to adopt changes consistent with revisions to the 2027-28 edition of the ICAO Technical Instructions, Amendment 43-26 to the IMDG Code, the 2024 updates to the Transport Canada's TDG, and the 24th revised edition of the UNMR. These biennial updates will be published by or in effect on January 1, 2027.
[
3
]
PHMSA also proposes to incorporate by reference certain revised international regulations and standards, as well as several new or updated International Organization of Standardization (ISO) standards, which are referenced in these international frameworks. The regulations and standards incorporated by reference are authorized for use for domestic and international transportation under specific conditions in
49 CFR part 171, subpart C
of the HMR.
III. Incorporation by Reference Discussion Under
1 CFR Part 51
PHMSA currently incorporates by reference into the HMR all or parts of numerous standards and specifications developed and published by standard development organizations (SDO). In general, SDOs update and revise their published standards every two to five years to reflect modern technology and best technical practices. The National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995 (NTTAA;
Pub. L. 104-113
) directs Federal agencies to use standards developed by voluntary consensus standards bodies in lieu of government-written standards whenever possible. Voluntary consensus standards bodies develop, establish, or coordinate technical standards using agreed-upon procedures. The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) issued Circular A-119 (
Federal Participation in the Development and Use of Voluntary Consensus Standards and in Conformity Assessment Activities
) to implement the obligations imposed on Federal agencies under the NTTAA. OMB Circular A-119 provides guidance for agencies participating in voluntary consensus standards bodies and describes procedures for satisfying the reporting requirements in the NTTAA.
PHMSA is responsible for determining which standards currently referenced in the HMR should be updated, revised, or removed, and which new standards should be added to the HMR, under the NTTAA and OMB Circular A-119. PHMSA proposes revisions to materials incorporated by reference in the HMR via the notice-and-comment rulemaking process. PHMSA must obtain approval from the Office of the Federal Register to incorporate by reference any new materials during that process. The Office of the Federal Register issued a rulemaking that revised
1 CFR 51.5
to require that an agency detail in the preamble of an NPRM the ways the materials it proposes to incorporate by reference are reasonably available to interested parties, or how the agency worked to make those materials reasonably available to interested parties.
[
4
]
Proposed changes to the material incorporated by reference in the HMR are discussed in detail in the Section 171.7 discussion (
see Section V. Section-by-Section Review of NPRM Proposals
).
The regulations and standards addressed in this NPRM are reasonably available to interested parties in several ways. The UNMR and its supporting United Nations Manual of Tests and Criteria (UN Manual of Tests and Criteria) are free and easily accessible to the public on the internet (links are provided in footnotes as part of the Section 171.7 discussion (
see Section V. Section-by-Section Review of NPRM Proposals
)).
[
5
]
The Transport Canada Transportation of Dangerous Goods regulations are also available for free online.
[
6
]
The ICAO Technical Instructions, the IMDG Code, and all ISO standard references are available for interested parties to purchase, either in print or electronic versions through the organizations' websites. In addition, all standards that PHMSA proposes to incorporate by reference in the NPRM will be available for review at the DOT docket office during the comment period, free of charge, at PHMSA Headquarters, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
IV. Amendments Not Proposed for Adoption
PHMSA has determined that certain elements of updated international regulations and standards should not be adopted into the HMR and thus is not including them in this proposed rule.
[
7
]
PHMSA has also determined that certain transport requirements should be considered for authorization on a case-by-case basis through special permits rather than proposed for adoption for general applicability in the HMR. Additional information about these topics is provided below.
A. Revised Cylinder Definitions
The 24th revised edition of the UNMR contains updated definitions for “cylinder,” “bundle of cylinders,” “salvage pressure receptacle,” “tube,”
(
printed page 67722)
“usable water capacity,” and “pressure-volume product.” The cylinder definition includes a test-pressure cap expressed in volumetric-pressure units (
e.g.
, 1.5 million bar-litres). Additional information about these revisions is available in the UNSCOE TDG working paper.
[
8
]
PHMSA is declining to propose to adopt these revised definitions. PHMSA has not identified sufficient safety or performance data indicating that the revised definitions would produce measurable safety benefits beyond the current HMR requirements. Adopting these definitions could also disrupt domestic industry practices without a clear compensating safety advantage. Accordingly, PHMSA will retain the current HMR definitions to preserve regulatory clarity, to minimize disruption to U.S. stakeholders, and to maintain the high safety standards already in place.
B. Infectious Substances (Indicative List)
The 24th revised edition of the UNMR adopted an updated version of the indicative list of Category A infectious substances. PHMSA previously determined that adopting the UNMR indicative list of infectious substances into
49 CFR 173.134
would introduce redundancies with existing U.S. public health frameworks and create unnecessary compliance complexities. PHMSA's criteria-based classification system in
49 CFR 173.134
, developed in consultation with experts from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), ensures rigorous oversight of substances capable of causing life-threatening or fatal diseases in humans or animals. This approach provides flexibility to address emerging pathogens (
e.g.
, novel viruses) without reliance on a static list, while maintaining consistency with domestic enforcement protocols, stakeholder expectations, and packaging requirements tailored to U.S. healthcare and research logistics. PHMSA concludes that retaining its current criteria-driven framework for Category A infectious substances in
49 CFR 173.134
, rather than adopting the UNMR indicative list, best serves the public interest by balancing global harmonization objectives with the need for adaptable, risk-proportionate regulations.
In addition, the UNMR adopted language stating that an infectious substance not meeting the criteria for inclusion in Category A is assigned to Category B (UN3373). Because PHMSA is not proposing to adopt the Category A indicative list, a clarifying amendment to the HMR for Category B infectious substances is not necessary.
C. Exceptions for Medical Devices as Infectious Substances
The 24th revised edition of the UNMR adopted exceptions for medical devices that may be contaminated with an infectious substance. The HMR already contains provisions for the transportation of medical devices containing an infectious substance in
49 CFR 173.134
. Therefore, a clarifying amendment to address the new exceptions in the UNMR is not necessary.
D. Environmentally Hazardous Paint
The 24th revised edition of the UNMR adopted a new special packing provision (PP99) for PSN “UN3082, Environmentally Hazardous Substance.” As discussed in the UNSCOE TDG working paper, this new provision applies to packaging of mixtures assigned to UN3082 containing less than one percent of substances of highly toxic ingredients with an M-factor of 10, 100, or 1000.
[
9
]
PHMSA is not proposing to adopt this provision because these mixtures are already excepted from regulation under the HMR. The definition of a “marine pollutant” in
49 CFR 171.8
includes mixtures or solutions packaged in a concentration which equals or exceeds one percent by weight of the solution or mixture for materials that are identified as severe marine pollutants in Appendix B to 49 CFR 172.101, or 10 percent by weight of the solution or mixture for non-severe marine pollutant materials listed in the appendix. The exception provided in the international standards applies only if the total concentration of highly toxic ingredients (
e.g.
, the constituents that are marine pollutants) do not exceed one percent. All mixtures covered by this exception are already excepted under the HMR.
E. UN Fiber Reinforced Plastic (FRP) Portable Tanks and Service Equipment
The 24th revised edition of the UNMR added standards for UN FRP portable tank service equipment. In the HM-215Q NPRM, PHMSA concluded that further research on UN FRP portable tanks is necessary in areas covering material fatigue, suitability of the pool fire test and impact testing as packaging qualification methods, and in the identification of the most appropriate non-destructive test methodology to qualify UN FRP portable tanks.
[
10
]
Since PHMSA did not adopt the requirements for UN FRP portable tanks, there is no justification to adopt the provision for UN FRP portable tank service equipment.
PHMSA is proposing an amendment to
49 CFR 171.25
—Additional requirements for the use of the IMDG Code—that would allow limited import and export of UN FRP portable tanks and service equipment within a single port area.
See Section IV. Section-by-Section Review of NPRM Proposals
for a discussion of
49 CFR 171.25
changes.
F. Net Explosive Weight (NEW)
The 24th revised edition of the UNMR and the associated UNSCOE TDG working paper revises the term “NEW” to “net explosive mass” (NEM) to align with scientific precision, as mass (measured in kilograms) and weight (a force measured in newtons) are distinct physical concepts.
[
11
]
Although PHMSA acknowledges this technical distinction, adopting the UNMR terminology would introduce inconsistency with longstanding HMR terminology and industry practice. Accordingly, PHMSA is not proposing to adopt the new terminology.
G. Regulatory Clarification for Labels
The 24th revised edition of the UNMR adopted language permitting the use of labels with minor variations to the symbols used in various modal and regional regulations, provided such variations do not alter the clear meaning of the label. The HMR already authorizes the use of labels conforming to the UNMR, the IMDG Code, the ICAO Technical Instructions, and the TC TDG in
49 CFR 172.407(f)
. Consequently, the wording from the UNMR does not need to be adopted in the HMR.
H. Use of Recycled Plastics
The 24th revised edition of the UNMR adopts provisions for the use of recycled plastics in the manufacturing of intermediate bulk containers (IBCs). In the HM-215Q NPRM, PHMSA determined that oversight for the use of recycled plastics is still needed in areas such as batch testing to ensure the quality of recycled plastics used in the
(
printed page 67723)
construction of rigid plastic IBCs. PHMSA continues to believe that oversight is needed for the approval of IBCs that are manufactured from recycled plastics to ensure safety of their use in hazardous materials transportation. PHMSA is evaluating the stakeholder feedback received in response to a previous request for information on the recycled plastics policy and expects to address that issue in a future rulemaking.
[
12
]
For these reasons, PHMSA is not proposing to adopt the revised provisions in the UN Model Regulations at this time.
I. Periodic Leakproofness Testing
The 24th revised edition of the UNMR clarifies that the periodic leakproofness test for IBCs, required every two and a half years, may be performed at the design type test level rather than under full retesting conditions. A UNSCOE TDG working paper identifies perceived ambiguity in the current language and seeks to standardize interpretation across jurisdictions.
[
13
]
PHMSA does not believe that this clarification needs to be adopted. The HMR already requires that IBCs undergo periodic leakproofness testing in accordance with
49 CFR 180.352(d)
.
[
14
]
Specifically,
49 CFR 180.352(d)(1)(i)
requires that repaired or remanufactured IBCs comply with the original design type specifications. This linkage ensures that leakproofness testing is inherently aligned with the design type's validated performance standards, eliminating the need for additional language to specify “design type-level” testing. The HMR framework emphasizes functional equivalence and safety by tying periodic testing to the design type's integrity, as demonstrated during initial design qualification.
J. Regulatory Clarification for Definition of Class 1 Explosives as Articles
The 24th revised edition of the UNMR clarifies that explosive substances deemed “too dangerous to transport” are explicitly prohibited for transportation. The UNSCOE TDG adopted this clarification to address a gap in the existing framework. While prohibiting transport of overly sensitive substances, the UNMR did not similarly restrict overly sensitive articles. The UNSCOE TDG determined that this omission could create ambiguity regarding whether overly sensitive explosive articles are similarly forbidden under the UNMR.
PHMSA does not believe that this clarification needs to be adopted. The HMR already addresses the concern that UNSCOE TDG identified with the UNMR. Class 1 explosives explicitly encompass both substances and articles under
49 CFR 173.50
. Section 173.54(k) also prohibits the transportation of any Class 1 explosive, substance, or article that fails to meet the acceptance criteria outlined in
49 CFR 173.57
. In addition,
49 CFR 173.57(b)
explicitly prohibits articles that are thermally unstable or impact-sensitive. For these reasons, the regulatory gap in the UNMR never existed in the HMR.
K. ISO 11515:2022, (Gas Cylinders—Refillable Composite Reinforced Tubes of Water Capacity Between 450 l and 3000 l—Design, Construction and Testing)
The 24th edition of the UNMR adopted ISO 11515:2022. PHMSA is not proposing to incorporate by reference ISO 11515:2022 in this NPRM. Incorporating ISO 11515:2022 would require extensive exceptions to maintain the HMR's current level of safety. The standard contains a significant typographical error regarding testing thresholds for Type 4 liner thickness modifications greater than 105 percent instead of greater than 10 percent. In addition, the new gunfire test does not apply to civilian Type 2 designs, and its five-minute bonfire test falls short of the 15-minute duration required by PHMSA special permits to allow for first responder arrival. For these reasons, PHMSA declines to propose to incorporate this edition pending future ISO corrections.

B. Part 172
Section 172.101 Hazardous Materials Table (HMT)
The HMT designates listed materials as hazardous materials and summarizes terms and conditions governing their transportation under the HMR. For each entry, the HMT identifies basic information, such as the PSN, UN identification number, and hazard class and hazard label. The HMT specifies additional information or references requirements in the HMR, such as hazard communication, assigned special provisions, packaging reference citations, and modal requirements, like quantity limits aboard aircraft, and vessel stowage restriction of hazardous materials aboard vessels. PHMSA proposes several changes to the HMT as discussed below. For purposes of the U.S. Government Publishing Office's typesetting procedures, proposed changes to the HMT appear under three sections of the HMT: “remove,” “add,” and “revise.” Certain entries in the HMT, such as those with revisions to the PSNs, appear as a “remove” and “add.” Proposed amendments to the HMT include the following:
New HMT Entries
Butyl Acrylates, Stabilized (UN 2348)
PHMSA proposes to add a PG II entry for the PSN “UN2348, Butyl acrylates, stabilized, 3” to the HMT. Butyl acrylates are a group of chemicals that are flammable and liable to polymerize without stabilization. This group includes the substance tert-butyl
(
printed page 67726)
acrylate. Currently, the HMT only provides for a Class 3, PG III designation for this material. According to data listed in the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) database, the flash point for tert-butyl acrylate is 14 °C (57 °F). Flammable liquids with a flash point below 23 °C (73 °F) are assigned to PG II or PG I depending on the boiling point. PHMSA is proposing to add a line to the current entry to allow for assignment of “Butyl Acrylates, Stabilized” as a PG II material. This amendment will ensure appropriate packaging use, hazard communication, and accurate information for emergency responders.
Vanadium Pentoxide (UN2862)
PHMSA proposes to add a PG II entry for the PSN “UN2862, Vanadium pentoxide, 6.1” to the HMT. Vanadium pentoxide is commonly transported in flake or powder form and is primarily used as a catalyst in industrial processes such as sulfuric acid production and as a steel additive. Currently, the HMT only lists a PG III designation for this material. Data indicates that vanadium pentoxide in a respirable particle size range meets the criteria for GHS Category 2 acute inhalation toxicity, which aligns with assignment of PG II under the UNMR.
[
37
]
For transport purposes, a solid substance is considered respirable if it contains particles 10 micrometers (μm) or smaller and must be tested if at least 10 percent of its total mass is likely to be dust in a respirable range. Vanadium pentoxide powder with a particle size under 45 μm is commercially available, but the minimum size is not specified, raising concerns that a portion of the material may fall within the less than 10 μm respirable range. Given this uncertainty and the toxicological data, the UNSCOE TDG supported adding a PG II entry while retaining the existing PG III entry, citing a long record of safe transport under PG III without known health incidents. This is consistent with the precedent used when adding the Division 6.1, PG I entry for “UN3550, Cobalt dihydroxide powder,” which is a solid substance similarly classified due to inhalation risks when packaged containing 10 percent or more respirable particles. PHMSA proposes that vanadium pentoxide (in non-fused form) containing 10 percent or more respirable particles be assigned to PG II. When containing less than 10 percent respirable particles, the existing PG III entry for vanadium pentoxide is assigned. This new entry will be added with italics that may be used in addition to the PSN, “UN2862, Vanadium pentoxide,
non-fused form, containing not less than 10 percent respirable particles.”
In addition, PHMSA is proposing to revise the PSN for the PG III vanadium pentoxide entry to account for the 10 percent threshold as “UN2862, Vanadium pentoxide,
non-fused form containing less than 10 percent respirable particles.
” PHMSA expects these provisions will facilitate the continued safe transport of this material as a PG III material when appropriate and maintain the HMR's safety standard for transportation of Division 6.1 solid materials.
Chlorophenols (UN3561 and UN3562)
Chlorophenols are currently transported under “UN2020, Chlorophenols, solid, 6.1, PG III” or “UN2021, Chlorophenols, liquid, 6.1, PG III,” along with a separate entry for “UN3155, Pentachlorophenol, 6.1, PG II.” A review of the 19 total chlorophenols (phenols with only chlorine substituents) presented to the UNSCOE TDG found that individual chlorophenols within the chemical group include: (1) those that do not meet the definition of a hazardous material; (2) those that meet the classification criteria for Division 6.1, PG III consist with the existing HMT entries for liquids and solids; (3) solids that meet the Class 8, PG II classification criteria; (4) solids that meet the Class 8 and Division 6.1, PG II classification criteria, and; (5) for pentachlorophenol, a solid meeting the classification criteria for Division 6.1, PG II, assigned to UN3155.
[
38
]
To address the findings described in items (3) and (4) above and to ensure appropriate classification of chlorophenols not addressed by the current UN2020, UN2021, and UN3155 entries, PHMSA proposes to add two new corrosive entries, “UN3561, Chlorophenols, corrosive, toxic, solid, n.o.s., 8 (6.1), II” and “UN3562, Chlorophenols, corrosive, solid, n.o.s., 8, II.” Consequently, the existing UN2020 and UN2021 entries would be amended by adding the symbol “G” in column one of the HMT, which signifies that a technical name must be included with the basic description. In addition, the proper shipping names in column two would be modified to include the text “toxic” and “n.o.s.” for consistency with the new entries proposed to differentiate between toxic and corrosive hazards. Together, these amendments will ensure appropriate classification, packaging use, hazard communication, and accurate information for emergency responders for all chlorophenols meeting the definition of a hazardous material.
Lithium Metal Batteries, Lithium Ion Batteries, and Sodium Ion Batteries Transported in Cargo Transport Units (UN3563, UN3536 and UN3564)
PHMSA proposes to add two new entries for cargo transport units (CTU) containing batteries: “UN3563, Lithium metal batteries installed in cargo transport unit” and “UN3564, Sodium ion batteries installed in cargo transport unit.” Lithium batteries installed in a CTU and designed only to provide power external to the CTU are presently assigned to the HMT entry “UN3536, Lithium batteries installed in cargo transport unit
lithium ion batteries or lithium metal batteries.
” Although most energy storage systems offered for transport in accordance with the provisions for UN3536 are lithium ion, there are currently three possible battery chemistries (lithium ion, lithium metal, and sodium ion) used for battery energy storage systems. Further, lithium ion and lithium metal batteries are both assigned UN3536 without indicating the battery chemistry, which impacts the manner of emergency response should they become involved in a fire.
In 2024, near Baker, California, an overturned truck transporting lithium batteries classified and described as UN3536 was involved in a fire.
[
39
]
Emergency responders on the scene were initially unable to determine whether the CTU contained lithium ion or lithium metal batteries. The uncertainty over the battery chemistry negatively impacted the emergency response. An indication of the type of batteries being transported allows for appropriate differentiation of transport provisions and for application of appropriate emergency response actions based on the types of batteries installed in the CTU.
PHMSA proposes splitting the single entry for UN3536 into three separate entries with separate UN numbers, consistent with revisions in the UNMR. This will more precisely communicate the battery chemistries being
(
printed page 67727)
transported in CTUs and allow transport provisions and emergency response measures tailored to each chemistry. To minimize impacts to shippers, PHMSA proposes to keep CTUs containing lithium ion batteries assigned to UN3536 and to establish two new entries for CTUs containing lithium metal batteries and sodium ion batteries; specifically, “UN3563, Lithium metal batteries installed in cargo transport unit” and “UN3564, Sodium ion batteries installed in cargo transport unit.” In addition, the existing entry UN3536 PSN would be revised to reference lithium ion only.
Finally, PHMSA proposes a conforming revision to Special Provision 389, which is assigned to UN3536 and will be assigned to the new entries. In Special Provision 389, PHMSA proposes to clarify that the PSN selected should reflect the primary battery chemistry type used in the CTU and that the use of multiple chemistries must be identified for emergency response purposes. These amendments will enhance safety and emergency response effectiveness by clearly distinguishing battery chemistries through separate UN numbers and additional information, ensuring responders have accurate information during incidents.

By combining the high energy density of lithium ion batteries with the low temperature adaptability of sodium ion batteries, hybrids are anticipated to see widespread use in the automotive and energy storage industries. Due to their intermediate energy density and the inability of the lithium ion cells to be discharged fully, hybrid batteries present a hazard profile similar to lithium ion batteries.
To facilitate safe transport, PHMSA proposes to require hybrid batteries to be tested and to be packaged in accordance with the provisions for lithium ion batteries. Specifically, each component lithium ion and sodium ion cell within the hybrid battery must be of the type proven to meet the criteria in part III, subsection 38.3 of the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria. PHMSA also proposes that hybrid batteries must be classified and described under the lithium ion battery entries, UN3480, UN3481, or UN3536, as appropriate. For UN 3556, see the proposed language in 172.102, Special Provision 135. Special Provision 410 would also clarify that when hybrid batteries are transported under the small battery provisions prescribed in
49 CFR 173.185(c)
, the Wh rating must not exceed 100 Wh and must be marked on the outer casing.
Special Provision 411
PHMSA proposes a new Special Provision 411 to facilitate the transportation of a recently developed type of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner. This new type of MRI scanner includes the use of new, superconductive magnets. These magnets contain helium that must be cooled to near absolute zero to achieve superconductivity of the coils. Traditional MRI scanners typically contain between 125 and 250 kg of refrigerated liquid helium and are classified and described as “UN1963, Helium, refrigerated liquid.” In contrast, the new MRI scanners use significantly less helium (1.5 kg). Due to this difference, UNSCOE determined that the UN1963 identification number is not the most appropriate description for these devices. In addition, since these MRI scanners contain components designed for cooling purposes, PHMSA proposes to provide the same exception currently applicable to refrigerating machines containing less than 12 kg of a non-flammable, non-toxic gas to include these devices. Specifically, Special Provision 411 will be assigned to the current HMT entry “UN3538, Articles containing non-flammable, non-toxic gas, n.o.s,” and would except MRI scanners with less than 12 kg of such gas from the requirements of the HMR when designed and constructed to prevent the risk of bursting or cracking of the components containing gas under normal conditions of transport. This special provision will support the safe global transport of MRI scanners, while applying a level of regulation appropriate to the hazard.
Special Provision 412
PHMSA proposes to adopt and to assign new Special Provision 412 to HMT entries “UN1075, Petroleum gases, liquefied
or
Liquefied petroleum gas” and “UN1965, Hydrocarbon gas mixture, liquefied, n.o.s.” to authorize the use of these entries for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) containing up to 12 percent by mass of “UN1033, Dimethyl ether.” The LPG industry is transitioning to more sustainable sources like bio/renewable/recycled materials. This includes blending LPG with renewable or recycled dimethyl ether (DME), a clean-burning, low-carbon fuel compatible with existing LPG infrastructure. DME shares similar properties with LPG, making it feasible to blend up to 12 percent by mass without altering transport, filling, or hazard communication requirements. The flow capacity for pressure relief valves shows that if the valves are sized for LPG, they will also have the correct flow capacity for DME/LPG blends. Testing with blends of 20 percent DME (by mass in the liquid phase) with LPG shows that the materials used in the transport and storage chain are still suitable, affording the proposed 12 percent a safety factor.
Special Provision 413
PHMSA proposes to adopt and to assign new Special Provision 413 to HMT entry “UN3082, Environmentally hazardous substance, liquid, n.o.s.” This special provision would establish a quantity limit for physically dissolved hydrogen in liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHCs) to ensure safe transport conditions.
Hydrogen can be transported in several forms, including as a compressed gas under high pressure, as a refrigerated liquefied gas, or as chemically bound to liquid carrier substances known as LOHCs. For a substance to be an LOHC, it must be capable of chemically binding hydrogen. Depending on the degree of hydrogenation, one liter of LOHC can hold several hundred liters of hydrogen. The hydrogen can be released through a reversible chemical process, which requires a dedicated dehydrogenation catalyst and high temperatures (>250°C). The spontaneous release of chemically bound hydrogen during transport is not possible. During the process of binding hydrogen to the carrier, very small amounts may remain physically dissolved, not chemically bound, in the LOHC. These physically dissolved traces can potentially be released during transport due to changes in temperature or pressure, creating the risk of an explosive atmosphere. One of the substances that hydrogen can be chemically bound to is benzyltoluene, which is commonly classified and described for transport under UN3082.
To address the absence of a defined limit for the amount of physically dissolved hydrogen allowed in LOHCs, testing was conducted under extreme conditions to evaluate the potential for
(
printed page 67732)
an explosive atmosphere formation.
[
44
]
The test results demonstrated that only untreated samples under extreme conditions showed a minor risk of ignition; in all other cases, no ignition occurred. The tests showed the effectiveness of treatment procedures such as inertization with nitrogen. Using the definition for Division 4.3 materials as a reference—substances that emit flammable gas at a rate exceeding one L/kg per hour when in contact with water—a more conservative limit of 0.5 L/kg per hour was adopted. Proposed Special Provision 413 would require that LOHCs classified and described under UN3082 may only be transported if the amount of physically dissolved hydrogen does not exceed 0.5 L of hydrogen/kg of LOHC. Transporting hydrogen using LOHCs offers a potentially safer alternative to conventional methods.

Section 173.62
Section 173.62 provides specific packaging requirements for explosives. PHMSA proposes to revise Table 2 to paragraph (c)(5) “Table of Packing Methods” by updating Packing Instruction (PI) 130. The revision would clarify that cartridges classified and described under “UN0012, cartridges, small arms” and “UN0014, Cartridges, small arms, blank” may be packed in metal containers without inner packaging. PI 130 is currently assigned to “UN0012, cartridges, small arms” and to “UN0014, Cartridges, small arms, blank” which consist of metal components. PI 130 does not require inner or intermediate packaging and authorizes outer packagings, including boxes and drums made of aluminum, steel, and other metals. But
49 CFR 173.60(b)(3)
, which corresponds to a Class 1 special packing provision in the UNMR, creates an inconsistency in the regulations by requiring that metallic components of articles, such as small arms cartridges, must be prevented from making contact with metal packagings.
Two sessions of the Explosives Working Group of the UNSCOE TDG discussed this topic. The group evaluated the potential for the buildup of static electricity between metals posing an ignition risk and concluded the risk is negligible. Acknowledging that preventing metal-to-metal contact represents best practices in packaging explosives for transport, several experts recognized that transporting bulk ammunition in metal containers without inner packaging has been standard military practice for decades. No incidents related to this packing method have been reported by explosives experts. This is further supported by extensive experience in the United States, where small arms cartridges are often transported loose in metal outer packaging, allowing metal-to-metal contact. The proposed revision will resolve the inconsistency and clarify a widely accepted and historically safe packaging method for cartridges under UN0012 and UN0014.

Section 173.224 outlines the packaging and control and emergency temperatures for self-reactive materials. PHMSA proposes to clarify paragraph (a) to emphasize that, “[t]o avoid the unnecessary confinement
of liquids,

Furthermore, paragraph (c) of this section prescribes requirements for new self-reactive materials, formulations, and samples. PHMSA proposes to add a new paragraph (c)(5) with provisions addressing transportation of samples of potentially explosive or self-reactive substances in quantities of up to 200 grams for solids or 200 mL for liquids per outer package when supporting data for classification is unknown. These substances usually consist of organic molecules that are active ingredients, building blocks, or intermediates for pharmaceutical or agricultural chemicals. The molecules of the substances often possess chemical functional groups listed in Tables A6.1 and/or A6.3 in Annex 6 (Screening Procedures) of the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria, which would indicate explosive or self-reactive properties, though these substances are not designed with explosive intent.
This amendment is necessary to facilitate transport of these materials during research and development because often there is not enough material available for classification testing or the cost of testing is otherwise prohibitive. Typical quantities of material handled in this phase are small, ranging from 10 to 100 grams. The existing provisions for samples of self-reactive materials do not necessarily satisfy the quantity needs or require classification test data that is unavailable. The International Group of Experts for Unstable Substances: Energetic and Oxidizing Substances (IGUS EOS Working Group) and the Explosives Working Group of the UNSCOE TDG reviewed the proposed criteria. Decomposition energy and the onset of decomposition can be determined by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), a thermal analysis method using very small amounts of a material. The results of decomposition energy analysis show that salts and complexes of organic compounds with energies of less than 1,500 J/g, or other organic substances with energies of less than 2,000 J/g, would not be more dangerous than a self-reactive material of Type B. Therefore, no further testing is required. For energy thresholds more than 1,500 J/g or 2,000 J/g, respectively, additional testing is prescribed. In addition to criteria for applicability and eligibility, the proposed new paragraph (c)(5) would authorize transport of samples up to 200 grams for solids or 200 mL for liquids per outer package in accordance with existing provisions in paragraphs (c)(3) and (c)(4)(i)-(iii).

A submission to the UNSCOE TDG explained that the originally specified foam is no longer readily available and presented test data demonstrating that a functionally equivalent foam with a density of 24 plus or minus 2.4 g/L provides comparable protection.

Section 176.905
Section 176.905 prescribes transportation requirements and exceptions for vessel transportation of motor vehicles (“vehicle”). PHMSA proposes to replace the existing text of
49 CFR 176.905
to adopt updated transport provisions and exceptions for vessel shipments of these vehicles consistent with changes made in the IMDG Code. In response to multiple roll-on/roll-off vessel (“Ro-Ro vessel”) fire incidents resulting in crew member deaths and injuries and hundreds of millions of dollars in loss to cargo and vessels, the International Maritime Organization Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers established a correspondence group to review existing international transport standards and safety of transport of motor vehicles and to make recommendations for changes to prevent future incidents or mitigate impacts. The resulting recommendations were adopted in the IMDG Code and, in this NPRM, PHMSA proposes to adopt these amendments in the HMR.
Specifically, PHMSA proposes a new paragraph (a) that requires the shipper(s) of all vehicles offered for transport by vessel, except for those driven on board Ro-Ro passenger vessels under their own power by a passenger, to assess the safety condition of the vehicle prior to offering it for transport. If a vehicle has or shows signs of damage to electrical equipment (
e.g.,
batteries) or to supplemental restraint systems (
e.g.,
airbags or seatbelt pretensioners) or has been impacted by extreme weather or natural events (
e.g.,
flooding, wildfire), the vehicle may not be offered for transport unless corrective action can be implemented to address the identified hazard from damage prior to offering for transportation. Similar inspection criteria prior to loading a vessel are in
49 CFR 176.905(a)(1)

49 CFR 176.905(i)
, which includes all vehicles offered for transport on Ro-Ro vessels (and, thus, most vehicle vessel shipments).
PHMSA believes an increased assessment prior to offering a vehicle for transport and clearly outlining conditions under which a vehicle is not allowed to be transported will help prevent future incidents by ensuring unsafe vehicles (for transport) are not offered for vessel transportation. In response to a fire aboard the Ro-Ro vessel, Höegh Xiamen, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) issued safety recommendation M-21-014 to PHMSA to remove the exceptions in
49 CFR 176.905(i)
for used and damaged flammable liquid-powered vehicles transported by Ro-Ro vessels.

E.O. 13132

The Federal Hazardous Materials Transportation Law contains a provision at
49 U.S.C. 5125(b)
that expressly preempts State, local, and Tribal requirements on certain covered subjects, unless the non-Federal requirements are “substantively the same” as the Federal requirements, including the following:
(1) The designation, description, and classification of hazardous material;
(2) The packing, repacking, handling, labeling, marking, and placarding of hazardous material;
(3) The preparation, execution, and use of shipping documents related to hazardous material and requirements related to the number, contents, and placement of those documents;
(4) The written notification, recording, and reporting of the unintentional release in transportation of hazardous material; and
(5) The design, manufacture, fabrication, inspection, marking, maintenance, recondition, repair, or testing of a packaging or container represented, marked, certified, or sold as qualified for use in transporting hazardous material in commerce.
This proposed rule addresses covered subject items (1), (2), (3), (4), and (5) above and would preempt State, local, and Tribal requirements not meeting the “substantively the same” standard. In this instance, the preemptive effect of the proposed rule is limited to the minimum level necessary to achieve the objectives of the hazardous materials transportation law under which the final rule is promulgated.

3.
In § 171.8, revise the definitions of “Large packaging,” “Large salvage packaging,” and “Single packaging” to read as follows:
§ 171.8
Definitions and abbreviations.
*
*
*
*
*
Large packaging
means a packaging that—
(1) Consists of an outer packaging that contains articles or inner packagings;
(2) Is designated for mechanical handling;
(3) Exceeds a net mass of 400 kg (882 pounds) or a capacity of 450 liters (119 gallons);
(4) Has an internal volume of not more than 3 cubic meters (m
3
) (106 cubic feet) (
see
§ 178.801(i) of this subchapter); and
(5) Conforms to the requirements for the construction, testing and marking of Large Packagings as specified in subparts P and Q of Part 178 of this subchapter.
*
*
*
*
*
Large salvage packaging
means a special packaging into which damaged, defective, leaking, or non-conforming hazardous materials packages, or hazardous materials that have spilled or leaked are placed for the purpose of transport for recovery or disposal, that—
(1) Is designed for mechanical handling; and
(2) Exceeds a net mass of 400 kg (882 pounds) or a capacity of 450 L (119 gallons) but has an internal volume of not more than 3 cubic meters (m
3
) (106 cubic feet).
*
*
*
*
*
Single packaging
means a non-bulk packaging other than a combination packaging (
i.e.,
a packaging which does not require any inner packaging to perform its containment function during transport).

7.
In § 172.102:
a.
In paragraph (c)(1), revise special provisions 135, 136, 160, 196, 360, 379, and 388, 389, 401, and add new special provisions 75, 410, 411, 412, 413, and 601 in numerical order;
b.

c.

The additions and revisions read as follows:
§ 172.102
Special provisions.
*
*
*
*
*
(c) * * *
(1) * * *
75 Refrigerating machines include air conditioning units and machines or other appliances which have been designed for the specific purpose of keeping food or other items at low temperature in an internal compartment. Heating machines include machines or other appliances which have been designed for the specific purpose of heating. Machines that are used to perform heating and cooling functions may be transported either under “Refrigerating machines” or “Heating machines.”
*
*
*
*
*
135 Internal combustion engines installed in a vehicle must be described using “Vehicle, flammable gas powered” or “Vehicle, flammable liquid powered,” as appropriate. If a vehicle is powered by a flammable liquid and a flammable gas internal combustion engine, it must be described using “Vehicle, flammable gas powered.” This includes hybrid electric vehicles powered by both an internal combustion engine and wet, nickel-metal hydride, lithium metal, lithium ion, metallic sodium, sodium alloy, or sodium ion batteries installed. If a fuel cell engine is installed in a vehicle, the vehicle must be described using “Vehicle, fuel cell, flammable gas powered” or “Vehicle, fuel cell, flammable liquid powered,” as appropriate. This includes hybrid electric vehicles powered by a fuel cell, an internal combustion engine, and wet, nickel-metal hydride, lithium metal, lithium ion, metallic sodium, sodium alloy, or sodium ion batteries installed. Electric vehicles must be described as “Vehicle, lithium ion battery powered,” “Vehicle, lithium metal battery powered,” and “Vehicle, sodium ion battery powered” as appropriate, for vehicles powered solely by lithium ion, lithium metal or sodium ion batteries transported with the batteries installed. Electric vehicles powered solely by hybrid batteries containing both lithium ion cells and sodium ion cells must be described as “Vehicle, lithium ion battery powered.” Further, for the purpose of this special provision, vehicles are self-propelled apparatus designed to carry one or more persons or goods. Examples of such vehicles are cars, motorcycles, trucks, locomotives, scooters, three-wheeled and four-wheeled vehicles or motorcycles, lawn tractors, self-propelled farming and construction equipment, boats, and aircraft. Lithium batteries or sodium ion batteries installed in a cargo transport unit, designed only to provide power external to the cargo transport unit must be described using the proper shipping name “Lithium ion batteries installed in cargo transport unit,” “Lithium metal batteries installed in cargo transport unit,” or “Sodium ion batteries installed in cargo transport unit,” as appropriate.

(6) When transported in a cargo transport unit the cargo transport unit must be placarded on each side and each end regardless of whether the vehicle is packaged or unpackaged.
(7) All equipment used for handling vehicles must be designed so that the fuel tank and the fuel system of the vehicle are protected from stress that might cause rupture or other damage incident to handling.
(8) Two hand-held, portable, dry chemical fire extinguishers of at least 4.5 kg (10 pounds) capacity each must be separately located in an accessible location in each hold or compartment in which any vehicle is stowed.
(9) “NO SMOKING” signs must be conspicuously posted at each access opening to the hold or compartment.
(10) Each portable electrical light, including a flashlight, used in the stowage area must be an approved, explosion-proof type. All electrical connections for any light must be made to outlets outside the space in which any vehicle is stowed.
(11) Each hold or compartment must be ventilated and fitted with an overhead water sprinkler system or fixed fire extinguisher system.
(12) Each hold or compartment must be equipped with a smoke or fire detection system capable of alerting personnel on the bridge.
(13) All electrical equipment in the hold or compartment other than fixed explosion-proof lighting must be disconnected from its power source at a location outside the hold or compartment during the handling and transportation of any vehicle. Where the disconnecting means is a switch or circuit breaker, it must be locked in the open position until all vehicles have been removed.
