II. Background
A. Legislative Overview
The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (
Pub. L. 111-148
) was enacted on March 23, 2010. The Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 (
Pub. L. 111-152
), which amended and revised several provisions of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, was enacted on March 30, 2010. In this proposed rule, these statutes are collectively referred to as the Affordable Care Act.
Section 1311(b) and (c)(6) of the Affordable Care Act outlines provisions for the establishment of Exchanges that facilitate the purchase of insurance coverage by qualified individuals through QHPs during an annual OEP or SEP. Section 1401 of the Affordable Care Act created section 36B of the Internal Revenue Code (Code), which provides for a premium tax credit (PTC) for eligible individuals who enroll in a QHP through an Exchange. Section 1402 of the Affordable Care Act establishes provisions to reduce the cost-sharing obligations of certain eligible individuals enrolled in a QHP offered through an Exchange through the provision of CSRs.
Under section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act, the Secretary of HHS is directed to establish a program for determining whether an individual meets the eligibility standards for enrollment in a QHP through an Exchange, APTC, and CSRs. Section 1411(b) of the Affordable Care Act specifies the information to be provided by applicants for enrollment in QHPs offered through an Exchange, including what is required for applicants seeking APTC and CSRs. This applicant information may include names, addresses, dates of birth, and Social Security Numbers; information about citizenship and immigration status; and, for individuals applying for APTC and CSRs, information about household income, family size, and offers of health coverage from employers. Section 1411(c) of the Affordable Care Act requires Exchanges to submit certain applicant information to specified data sources for verification of its accuracy. Section 1411(c)(4) of the Affordable Care Act generally requires verifications of certain applicant information to be performed electronically using online systems. However, section 1411(c)(4)(B) of the Affordable Care Act grants HHS flexibility to modify the methods of such verifications to reduce administrative costs and burden on applicants, and section 1411(d) of the Affordable Care Act delegates to HHS responsibility for the manner in which certain other verifications are completed.
Consistent with the requirements of section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act, when an applicant applies through an Exchange, they attest to information on the application, such as their citizenship or immigration status, and their household's expected annual income. As part of the application process, Exchanges check trusted data sources to determine if application information is reasonably compatible with information from those data sources. In cases where the information is not reasonably compatible or data is unavailable, generally the applicant will receive notification of a data matching issue (DMI). Consistent with additional requirements of section 1411(e) described below, the applicant will have 90 or 95 days to resolve the DMI by submitting requested documentation. The applicant will be provided 95 days for document submission for DMIs related to the verification of citizenship or immigration status. Throughout this proposed rule, we refer to this 90/95-day period as an “inconsistency period,” and we refer to instances where an applicant has an inconsistency as the applicant having a DMI.
Section 1411(e)(2)(A) of the Affordable Care Act establishes that when certain information has been verified, an applicant becomes eligible to enroll in a QHP through an Exchange, and for APTC and CSRs, as applicable. Section 1411(e)(3) of the Affordable Care Act specifies the process Exchanges must follow when applicants have a DMI related to citizenship or immigration status by referencing section 1902(ee) of the Social Security Act. In the March 27, 2012
Federal Register
(
77 FR 18310
) (Exchange Establishment Rule), we interpreted this to require the Exchange to notify applicants of their DMI and provide them an opportunity to submit evidence to verify their information within 95 days from the date the notice is received. In the Exchange Establishment Rule, we also interpreted section 1411(e)(3) of the Affordable Care Act as requiring Exchanges to make eligibility determinations on the basis of information provided on the application during an inconsistency period related to citizenship or immigration status.
Similarly, section 1411(e)(4)(B)(i) of the Affordable Care Act requires that Exchanges make eligibility determinations on the basis of information provided on the application during an inconsistency period related to information other than citizenship or immigration status. This means that applicants with a DMI may be able to enroll in a QHP and receive APTC and CSRs during an inconsistency period, if eligible based on the information provided on their application. Section 1411(e)(4) specifies the process Exchanges must follow when applicants have DMIs, other than those related to citizenship or immigration status, including notifying applicants and providing them an opportunity to submit evidence to verify their information within 90-day inconsistency periods.
Under section 36B of the Code, a taxpayer is only allowed a PTC for months that are coverage months for the taxpayer or other individuals in the taxpayer's family (a taxpayer's family consists of the taxpayer, the taxpayer's spouse if filing a joint tax return, and the taxpayer's tax dependents). Section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation amends section 36B of the Code to provide additional requirements before a month can be a coverage month, effective for tax years beginning after
(
printed page 67659)
December 31, 2027.

Effective January 1, 2028, section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code provides that a month is generally not a coverage month for an enrollee in a QHP unless an Exchange “verifies”, “using applicable enrollment information that shall be provided or verified by the applicant,” the enrollee's eligibility to enroll in a QHP through an Exchange and, to the extent relevant, for APTC for the coverage for that month. In this proposed rule, we use the term “confirm” as a synonym to “verify” when referring to the requirement in section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code that information shall be “verified by the applicant.” We reserve the term “verify” to describe the section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code requirement for Exchanges to verify eligibility. This terminology avoids confusion throughout this proposed rule about which subject of the statute (that is, “the Exchange” or “the applicant”) is the subject of the term “verify.” Section 36B(c)(5)(B) of the Code provides, “applicable enrollment information” referenced in subsection (c)(5)(A) includes, to the extent relevant: (i) household income and family size of the enrollee, (ii) whether the enrollee is an eligible alien, (iii) any health coverage status or eligibility for coverage, (iv) the enrollee's place of residence, and (v) such other information as may be determined by the Secretary of the Treasury (in consultation with the Secretary of HHS) as necessary to the verification prescribed under section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code.
Section 36B(c)(5)(C) of the Code allows months that begin before the verification required by section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code to be considered coverage months if an Exchange completes the required verification for those months. Section 36B(c)(5)(D) of the Code provides that a consumer must not be treated as ineligible to enroll in a QHP solely for failing to meet the requirements of section 36B(c)(5) of the Code for a month. Section 36B(c)(5)(E) of the Code delegates to the Secretary of the Treasury authority to waive the verification requirements of section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code for individuals who enroll in a QHP during an SEP granted due to a change in family size.
Section 71303(b) of the WFTC legislation added new section 36B(c)(3)(A)(ii) of the Code. This change modifies the definition of QHP for the purpose of section 36B of the Code. Specifically, it excludes from the definition of QHP any plan that is enrolled in through an Exchange that does not provide a process through which any consumer may verify their household income and eligibility for QHP enrollment for the following plan year. This process must be in place no later than August 1, 2027 (and by August 1 for each subsequent year) to ensure applicants and current enrollees in QHP coverage who are seeking QHP coverage with APTC for plan year (PY) 2028 and subsequent years remain eligible for PTC and APTC, if otherwise eligible.
Section 71305 of the WFTC legislation removed section 36B(f)(2)(B) of the Code. This change eliminated the limitation on repayment of excess APTC for tax years after December 31, 2025.
III. Provisions of the Proposed Regulations
A. Part 155—Exchange Establishment Standards and Other Related Standards Under the Affordable Care Act
1. Election To Operate an Exchange After 2014 (§ 155.106)
We propose to amend § 155.106(a)(2) to require an Exchange submitting a Blueprint application to do so at least 15 months prior to the date on which it proposes to begin its pre-OE verification period instead of at least 15 months prior to the date on which it proposes to begin its OEP. In section III.A.9.c. of this proposed rule, we are proposing to add §  155.410(h) to require that all Exchanges permit consumers to provide eligibility information to Exchanges for the upcoming plan year prior to the beginning of the OEP each year, beginning on August 1, 2027, for PY 2028 and August 1 of each subsequent year. Accordingly, we have considered the implication of the new proposed pre-OE verification period on our current requirements and process for approval of States currently utilizing the Federal platform, as an FFE or SBE-FP, that wish to establish a State Exchange.
As part of the State Exchange establishment process under 45 CFR Part 155, subpart B, we currently require at § 155.106(a)(2) that any State on the Federal platform that intends to establish and operate a State Exchange must submit its Exchange Blueprint application to HHS for review and approval 15 months prior to when the State intends to begin OEP operations as a State Exchange. The State Exchange Blueprint continues to serve as a vehicle for a State to document its progress toward implementing its intended Exchange operational model. HHS approves a State's Exchange Blueprint Application and subsequently provides approval for a State to operate a State Exchange, based upon a State meeting the State Exchange implementation requirements noted in the Blueprint Application.
Under the proposed pre-OE verification period requirement, the proposed pre-OE verification period would immediately precede the OEP. Accordingly, an Exchange would not only need to be responsible for its OEP activities but would also need to be responsible for the proposed pre-OE verification period activities. We are of the view that a State that is in the process of establishing a State Exchange should be responsible for its pre-OE verification activities as well as its OEP activities, since eligibility determinations made during the pre-OE period also would relate to eligibility for enrollment in the following plan year. We therefore determined that a State that is in the process of establishing a State Exchange should be ready to do so by the beginning of the pre-OE verification period, instead of by OEP, as currently required. As such, in HHS' State Exchange Blueprint application review and State Exchange approval process, we would need to account for assessing the readiness of a transitioning State Exchange to conduct the proposed pre-OE verification period functions for the August 1 timeframe. HHS' existing review and approval timeline has been oriented around the first OEP for a transitioning State Exchange. This is when a new State Exchange becomes operational (that is, “goes live”) and accordingly, HHS notifies a transitioning State Exchange of its decision prior to the OEP start date. HHS' decision is based on a 15-month period of time that HHS needs to sufficiently assess the readiness of a transitioning State Exchange to operate its own Exchange platform and perform the essential functions of an Exchange and allow for a sufficient period of time for HHS to then remove the transitioning State Exchange and its State Medicaid agency from the Federal Exchange platform. Due to the August 1 timeframe associated with this new proposal that needs to be included into the State Exchange readiness assessment, the overall timeline for HHS' review and assessment of State Exchange functionality would need to be moved up so that notification to a transitioning State Exchange of HHS' decision occurs earlier than August 1, rather than prior to the start of the OEP, since the start of the pre-OE verification period would be the new date for when an approved transitioning State Exchange first becomes operational.
Accordingly, in conjunction with the proposed addition of § 155.410(h), we are proposing to modify § 155.106 to
(
printed page 67660)
provide that a State seeking to operate as a State Exchange would be required to submit its Blueprint application 15 months before the date it proposes to begin its pre-OE verification period, rather than the date it proposes to begin its OEP. We are of the view that this rule, if finalized, would not materially burden States, as any State offering an FFE or SBE-FP that is considering establishing a State Exchange, and that has not yet submitted a State Exchange Blueprint application to HHS, would have sufficient time after the release of the final rule to include the new pre-OE verification period requirements into their planning and decision-making leading up to submitting a State Exchange Blueprint application and establishing a State Exchange. Building the pre-OE verification period in tandem with the initial OEP may require some more start-up effort for a State newly establishing a State Exchange, in comparison to an initial OEP only, but we are of the view that this would be minimal and less burdensome overall than if a State were to first establish an OEP as a State Exchange and then subsequently build out the pre-OE verification period as a State Exchange.
We seek comment on this proposal.

4. Verification Process Related to Eligibility for Enrollment in a QHP Through the Exchange (§ 155.315)
a. Verification of Residency
We are not proposing any changes to the existing regulatory requirements in § 155.315(d) related to verification of residency for the reasons described further in this section. However, we are considering the feasibility of new residency verification requirements and are seeking comment on whether the existing requirements to verify residency should be updated in the final rule or in future rulemaking to reflect advancements in technology and the availability of new data sources or alternative verification methods. We acknowledge that historically, verifying residency has been challenging for Exchanges due to a variety of reasons that we discuss in this section, however, we are seeking comment on whether there are ways to overcome these past challenges to allow Exchanges to begin to transition from primarily accepting an applicant's self-attestation of residency without verification, except in limited circumstances where an Exchange has no other option.
Since the establishment of the Exchanges in 2014, the landscape has changed significantly, and, due to challenges Exchanges have faced over time, we have reevaluated our position that permitting Exchanges to accept an applicant's attestation of residency without further verification may no longer be appropriate and a risk to Exchange program integrity. We hold this view because of the increased number of unauthorized enrollments of consumers in Exchange coverage by agents, brokers, and web-brokers, achieved in part through inaccurate residency attestations. Therefore, we seek comment on how (1) Exchanges can move away from primarily accepting self-attestation of residency without further electronic or manual verification to an alternative verification method or procedure; (2) how Exchanges can potentially strengthen requirements to verify residency, including new methods that Exchanges might employ in the short and long term to improve program integrity; and (3) whether the final rule should require Exchanges to adopt such methods so that accepting self-attestation of residency is limited to circumstances where there is truly no other option for an Exchange to electronically or manually verify residency. We may finalize one or more of the approaches discussed in this section rather than retaining the existing requirements at § 155.315(d), or consider alternative approaches suggested by commenters for future rulemaking, if necessary. We acknowledge that any residency verification method discussed in this section would require a period of implementation that is likely not feasible to complete in time for PY 2028. Thus, we additionally solicit comment, particularly from State Exchanges, on the anticipated time that would be needed to implement any such residency verification methods. When providing comments, we also welcome robust solutions that take into consideration ongoing operational costs for States, the Federal Government, and Exchanges.
To be eligible for enrollment in a QHP, an applicant or enrollee must reside in the State where an Exchange is established per section 1312(f) of the Affordable Care Act, and § 155.305(a)(3) specifies the residency requirements an applicant or enrollee must meet to be eligible for enrollment in a QHP. Generally, with some exceptions, an applicant or enrollee who is age 21 or over and not living in an institution meets the residency requirements if the applicant or enrollee (1) is living and intends to reside in the service area of the Exchange; or (2) is living and has entered into a job commitment or is
(
printed page 67661)
seeking employment in the service area of the Exchange. An applicant or enrollee under age 21 and not living in an institution generally meets the residency requirements if they (1) reside in the service area of the Exchange; or (2) reside with a parent or caretaker who has met the residency standard for the service area of the Exchange. In addition, applicants or enrollees are not required to have a fixed address to meet the residency requirements; however, they must live in the State where they are applying for coverage with the intent to reside in that State. This is a critical protection for individuals experiencing homelessness or housing instability.
Section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act does not specify the data source or verification method that the Exchanges must use to verify residency. Therefore, under section 1411(d) of the Affordable Care Act, the Secretary of HHS has broad authority to specify any appropriate manner of verification for Exchanges to verify the residency requirements so long as it is accurate and appropriate. Generally, as outlined in § 155.315(d), if information provided by an applicant regarding residency is reasonably compatible with other information provided by the individual or in the records of the Exchange, an Exchange may either verify information with an electronic data source that is sufficiently current and accurate and minimizes administrative costs and burdens, or by accepting the applicant or enrollee's attestation without further electronic or manual verification. If the information provided by the applicant or the enrollee regarding residency is not reasonably compatible with other information provided by the individual or in the records of the Exchange, the Exchange is required to verify information with an electronic data source that is sufficiently current and accurate and minimizes administrative costs and burdens. If the information provided by the applicant or enrollee does not match the information returned via the approved data source, then a DMI is created in accordance with § 155.315(f).
Currently, we have not identified any single data source to verify residency for the FFE and SBE-FPs that is current, accurate, and minimizes administrative costs and burdens. Using the flexibility provided in section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act, we have implemented operations for the FFE and SBE-FPs to validate that the address provided by an Exchange applicant or enrollee is a real address, but it does not validate that the applicant or enrollee actually resides at that address. This validation process requires the applicant or enrollee to provide a home address on their Exchange application. Once the address is provided, the FFE or SBE-FP confirms whether the home address is within the service area of the Exchange where the applicant or enrollee is applying for coverage. The FFE or SBE-FP then attempts to validate the home address to ensure it exists by checking United States Postal Service (USPS) records, and the applicant or enrollee is prompted to either agree with their provided home address or accept a corrected address from USPS records. Address validation provides HHS with benefits such as better data quality and assurance that mail is delivered to a real address, which reduces downstream administrative costs associated with incorrect addresses. However, because it does not validate that an applicant lives at a specified address and given our ongoing concerns regarding unauthorized or potentially fraudulent enrollments, we are of the view that address validation is not enough and relying on self-attestation without further verification, is a program integrity risk and should only be reserved for instances where Exchanges have no other option to verify residency.
Over the years, we have explored options to successfully verify residency for applicants or enrollees applying for Exchange coverage and identified several challenges. The first challenge relates to the lack of available data sources that are current, accurate, and would minimize administrative burden. Historically, we have considered data sources such as a single database that an Exchange could directly query to verify information, similar to how Exchanges connect with Social Security Administration (SSA) to verify Social Security Numbers (SSNs). We have also considered verification services provided by third-party companies that generally use multiple data sources or have their own proprietary verification product or method to verify residency. This is similar to the optional Verify Current Income Hub (or “Hub”) service Exchanges may use to verify a consumer's projected household income. As we noted earlier in this section, there is no data source or other verification method mentioned in the statute for the verification of residency, although the Secretary of HHS may specify one as needed. This means that to implement a stronger process for residency verification, we would need to identify a suitable data source (or multiple ones), verification service, or another process to meaningfully verify a consumer's residency, as well as create a DMI process to resolve verifications for any consumers for whom we cannot verify residency through either a data source or a verification service.
We are of the view that States and State Exchanges generally are better positioned to verify residency for insurance affordability programs such as Medicaid and CHIP and for QHP coverage because they have access to a variety of State data that could be leveraged to verify residency. For example, States and State Exchanges likely have access to data sources specific to their State, such as the State Directory of New Hires or quarterly wage and unemployment insurance data from State workforce agencies (the underlying data that is reported in the National Directory of New Hires (NDNH)), which are currently unavailable to Exchanges on the Federal platform, in addition to casework conducted in their State at the local level.
Another challenge to verifying residency is that we would need to determine which document(s) would be acceptable to successfully verify an applicant or enrollee's residency in accordance with § 155.315(f), when any approved data source could not do so. Certain populations may be harder than others to verify through documentation, such as consumers living with roommates, consumers who sublease, or consumers who move frequently. If we require a new residency verification process, and we continue to be unable to electronically verify residency for many applicants or enrollees, Exchanges would have to establish a DMI process for residency to manually verify residency through document submission for many applicants or enrollees. As a result, total DMI volumes would increase, and could lead to increasing operational costs for Exchanges.
After exploring the challenges related to implementing residency verification, we considered several potential approaches to adjust residency verification for applicants or enrollees applying for Exchange coverage with APTC and CSRs. The first approach we considered was imposing additional residency verification for all Exchange consumers. In 2024, we conducted an address matching pilot with LexisNexis to determine the feasibility and accuracy of using that verification service for residency verification. This pilot was limited to Exchanges on the Federal platform. During the pilot, we found that data was only available for about half of the pilot population, likely due to consumers who move frequently or do not update their addresses in a
(
printed page 67662)
timely manner after a move. Based on the pilot and past experience with DMIs, we estimate that about half of all Exchange applicants or enrollees would receive a DMI and be required to submit documentation to verify their residency, due to the lack of data available for verifying residency. Ultimately, we determined that the low rate of data matching combined with the potential costs of using the LexisNexis service did not meet the regulatory standard for using LexisNexis as a data source.
Another approach we considered to verify residency for all Exchange applicants was contracting with the IRS, a data broker, or both, to develop a Hub service that could verify residency. From our research, we determined that, like our pilot with LexisNexis, any of the available data brokers or government agencies that could create a Hub service to verify residency would likely encounter similar coverage rates and result in a large portion of consumers receiving residency DMIs.
A third approach we considered was a risk-based approach to target applications with a higher risk of insurance fraud. Based on our own experience, residency fraud on the FFE is largely driven by instances of residential health care providers, frequently associated with sober living facilities, working with unlicensed agents (known as “body brokers”) to direct consumers to misrepresent their State of residence so that the provider receives greater compensation from a plan with more generous out-of-network benefits. This type of residency fraud typically occurs in States where QHP issuers offer more generous out-of-network benefits, usually in States that are large geographically but have a small population. This fraud has been identified when QHP issuers have requested QHP rescissions
[
4
]
due to the applicant's or enrollee's misrepresentation of their State of residence. We have also identified other factors that could signal an application has a higher fraud risk including mailing addresses outside of the State in which an applicant or enrollee is applying for coverage, or applications in States with high rates of fraud. However, we cannot identify enrollments resulting from transactions with “body broker” agents directly and efficiently. We estimate that to be able to adequately identify such enrollments, we would need to use a broad sampling methodology that casts a very wide net, such as verifying the enrollments of entire States to uncover instances of fraudulent activity. This would be costly and does not solve the challenges Exchanges would still face regarding lack of reliable data sources to use in a risk-based verification approach, or the challenges consumers might face to secure suitable documentation to prove their residency, examples of which are discussed above. Therefore, we concluded that a risk-based approach may not be the best approach either, but we welcome comment from interested parties, in particular States and State Exchanges to share their experiences, if they have tried implementing risk-based approaches.
We are of the view that there may be additional solutions, such as leveraging federated identity (ID) verification sources, that can reasonably verify a consumer's provided address. Such solutions provide Exchanges with a higher degree of assurance as addresses are associated with applicants who have verified their identities through standards-based identity proofing mechanisms. Similar to how other Federal agencies use federated ID verification sources to link a claimed identity with a real individual, we are of the view that Exchanges could leverage such verification methods to verify both identity and residency at once and may alleviate many of the challenges Exchanges have faced in the past with limited coverage or out-of-date data sources. Furthermore, because federated ID verification sources create a unique digital identity tied to a specific individual, we are of the view that this could reduce potential fraudulent activities and create more trust in the self-attestations of residency that applicants with verified identities provide on their applications. We are also of the view that this verification method would deter bad actors from pursuing some insurance fraud schemes. This solution could operate in addition to the address validation checks that the FFE and SBE-FPs conduct today to ensure that the provided address is standardized and deliverable. We are considering requiring Exchanges to use federated ID verification and invite comments on its use as a residency verification source.
Additionally, recognizing that availability of data between States and Exchanges is a challenge, we are also interested in exploring the idea of mutual data sharing between States and Exchanges, to the extent permitted under applicable law, to alleviate the challenges States and Exchanges all face regarding residency verification. One avenue to achieve such mutual data exchange could be through the Hub, whereby States and State Exchanges could make available State data sources through the Hub for all requestors, namely the FFE, SBE-FPs, other State Exchanges, and State Medicaid Agencies, to access. We are of the view that access to more data streams could further mitigate unauthorized enrollments and residency fraud. Therefore, we also seek comment on whether States are able to share their residency data with HHS to facilitate verifications for their State's consumers, as well as any barriers that could prevent States from sharing data with HHS, such as State law, and whether statutory or regulatory changes in their respective State laws would be necessary for them to be able to do so. We also invite comment on any data quality standards that we should consider to ensure that these data are current, accurate, and minimize administrative costs and burdens. Finally, we seek comment from State Exchanges and State Medicaid agencies about their experiences with verifying residency and any challenges they currently face.
Based on all the considerations laid out in this section, we are of the view that without a more robust residency verification process, the risk of applicants or enrollees, and potentially agent, broker, or web-broker bad actors inappropriately attesting to residing in a State or at a particular address to receive Exchange coverage remains. We want to emphasize that it is imperative, to the extent practical, that Exchanges exercise program integrity measures to discourage potentially fraudulent behavior in this area and that is why we are considering options for requiring new methods of residency verification, such as by using federated ID verification and are seeking comment from interested parties on other potential data sources that might be more economical for States and/or the Federal Government to procure.
At this time, we do not propose changes to the current regulatory requirements regarding verification of residency as outlined in § 155.315(d); however, we may instead require new methods of residency verification and are exploring options for Exchanges to strengthen residency verification using these new methods or through improving historically difficult to use data sources. We are using this proposed rule to solicit additional ideas for consideration to inform the final rule and potentially future policy and regulatory changes. We also seek comment on any additional Exchange operational updates that could be done in the near term for residency verification that could ultimately
(

strengthen program integrity while protecting Exchange risk pools.
We seek comment on these proposed plans and invite interested parties to share their experiences with residency verification, including challenges, risk for residency fraud, feasibility of other verification approaches or methods such as risk-based approaches, and cost/budget impacts.
b. DMIs
We propose to amend § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) to state that Exchanges would generally not be permitted to authorize payment for APTC and CSRs for applicants who have DMIs described in § 155.315(c) for citizenship status or lawful presence status; § 155.315(d) for residency; § 155.320(b) for eligibility for MEC other than through an employer sponsored plan; § 155.320(c)(3) for annual household income, family size, and eligible noncitizen status; and § 155.320(d) for enrollment in an eligible employer-sponsored plan and eligibility for qualifying coverage in an eligible employer-sponsored plan, until such DMIs are adjudicated and applicants are determined eligible for APTC and CSRs, as applicable. We also propose in § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) to exempt those who qualify for an SEP due to a change in family size as described under § 155.420(d)(2) from the verification requirements described in proposed new § 155.315(f)(4)(ii), which is described in section III.A.4.c. of this proposed rule.
Additionally, we propose to add § 155.315(f)(4)(iii) to establish the requirements related to providing APTC and CSRs during inconsistency periods described in § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) created from an eligibility redetermination when the information related to the DMIs described in § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) was previously verified for the plan year. This is described in section III.A.4.d. of this proposed rule. We also propose to add new § 155.315(f)(4)(iv) to establish that Exchanges would be required to determine eligibility for APTC and CSRs on behalf of an applicant following successful verification of information as described in proposed new § 155.315(f)(4)(ii), and to establish new effective dates of those eligibility determinations or redeterminations. We additionally propose to add § 155.315(f)(4)(v) specifying that applicants with DMIs other than those described in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) are able to receive APTC and CSRs during the inconsistency period if eligible based on the information provided on their application. Finally, we propose to amend § 155.315(f)(4)(i) to remove language around proceeding with all other elements of eligibility determination to align with proposed changes to § 155.315(f)(4)(ii).
(i) Statutory and Regulatory Overview
(A) Applicable enrollment information
As described in section II.A. of this proposed rule, under section 36B(c) of the Code, a taxpayer is only allowed PTC for months that are considered coverage months for the taxpayer or other individuals in the taxpayer's family. Section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation added section 36B(c)(5) of the Code to provide that, starting in 2028, a month is generally not a coverage month for an enrollee in a QHP for any month that an Exchange fails to verify specific criteria related to the enrollee's eligibility to enroll in a QHP through an Exchange and, to the extent relevant, for APTC for the coverage for that month, referred to as “applicable enrollment information”. The specific criteria include household income and family size, whether the individual is an eligible alien, any health coverage status or eligibility for coverage, place of residence, and other information determined by the Secretary of the Treasury in consultation with the Secretary of HHS. As outlined in the Department of Treasury's Premium Tax Credit proposed rule (PTC proposed rule), “any health coverage status or eligibility for coverage” refers to “minimum essential coverage” as interpreted by the Department of Treasury (
91 FR 65499
), which aligns with § 155.20 which says the term MEC has the meaning given in section 5000A(f) of the Code. Additionally, as explained later in this section, the Secretary of the Treasury has proposed regulatory changes to include lawful presence status and citizenship in addition to the explicitly referenced criteria.
(B) Application to APTC and CSRs
Section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act outlines the requirements for establishing eligibility for QHP

and APTC. We interpret section 1411(a)(2)(A) of the Affordable Care Act as requiring Exchanges to make APTC eligibility determinations consistent with the PTC eligibility requirements of 36B of the Code,

including for whether an applicant has met the requirements for a month to be considered a coverage month. Therefore, we read section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation as requiring verification of specified information before APTC can be paid.
Additionally, section 1402 of the Affordable Care Act outlines requirements for CSRs. Specifically, section 1402(g)(2) states that CSRs cannot be allowed for months that are not coverage months for PTCs as defined under section 36(B) of the Code. Given this, we have also interpreted section 1402(g)(2) of the Affordable Care Act to require that an Exchange only provide CSRs for months that qualify as coverage months under section 36B of the Code, and therefore we find the new eligibility limitations on APTC also apply to Exchange determinations of eligibility for CSRs. As discussed later in this rule, there is an exception for CSRs for American Indians and Alaska Natives (AI/AN) that are not income based.
Therefore, given the changes outlined under section 36B of the Code as amended by section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation as discussed above, we propose that Exchanges can no longer provide APTC and CSRs for any month before an Exchange “verifies, using applicable enrollment information that shall be provided or verified by the applicant” the individual's eligibility to enroll in a QHP through an Exchange and for APTC. Throughout this rule, “DMI(s) related to applicable enrollment information” means a DMI for at least one of the specific criteria set forth in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii), as described in section III.A.4.b.i.A. of this proposed rule. For an applicant who is not eligible for the family size SEP waiver as described in section III.A.4.c. of this proposed rule, or for an eligibility redetermination during the plan year as described in section III.A.4.d. of this proposed rule, such a DMI prevents an Exchange from providing or increasing any APTC and CSR amounts during the inconsistency period. The term therefore excludes DMI for one of the specific criteria set forth in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) when the family size SEP waiver applies, as discussed in section III.A.4.c. of this proposed rule, as well as during an eligibility redetermination during the plan year, as discussed in section III.A.4.d.of this proposed rule.

Therefore, we read section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation to prohibit payment of APTC and CSRs for any month before an Exchange verifies residency, enrollment in an eligible employer-sponsored plan and eligibility for qualifying coverage in an eligible employer-sponsored plan, eligibility for MEC other than through an eligible employer-sponsored plan, and family size—however verification is required under section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act, its implementing regulations, and any successor or other applicable regulations as may be issued, and we are exploring further updates to residency and family size verification as outlined further in sections III.A.4.a. and III.A.4.c. of this proposed rule. Additionally, we emphasize that some State Exchanges may have data available to them that are sufficiently current, accurate, minimizes administrative burden, and approved by the Secretary of HHS for usage and therefore may already be setting DMIs for criteria that the Federal Exchange currently does not, and this proposed rule does not limit State Exchanges from setting DMIs in those instances. In summary, when attestations about such information must be verified through a trusted data source or documentation, we read section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation to prohibit payment of APTC and CSRs until such verification is complete.

One could read these provisions together as permitting Exchanges to verify an applicant's eligibility using only the applicant's provided affirmation (or attestation) of the enumerated eligibility criteria, rather than using an external data source or submitted documentation. However, as explored further below, we are of the view that this reading of section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation is implausible.
As discussed previously in this proposed rule, given that the term “verifies” is ambiguous in section 71303 of the WFTC legislation, the statutory language is best read to mean that an Exchange verifies the specified criteria in accordance with the verification procedures articulated in section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act, its implementing regulations, and any successor or other applicable regulations as may be issued.

These successor applicable regulations include potential future updates to perform further verification of residency beyond accepting attestation, as described in section III.A.4.a. of this proposed rule. This is supported by the language in section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation stating that an Exchange must verify eligibility for enrollment in a QHP and for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, using the specified information “provided” or “verified” by the applicant. We read that the terms “provided” and “verified” to refer to the verification procedures under section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act and implementing regulations which, as explained previously in this proposed rule, allow Exchanges to verify some eligibility criteria using an attestation provided by the applicant and which require further verification from a trusted data source or documentation in the case of other eligibility criteria. Given that the WFTC legislation does not prescribe any new specific methods of verification, we read it as permitting existing verification processes to continue, except that generally a month may not be a coverage month, and therefore no APTC or CSRs can be provided, until verification under section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act, its implementing regulations, and any successor or other applicable regulations as may be issued, is complete. As previously stated, we are requesting comments on whether updates should be made to the verification of residency as defined under § 155.315(d), which is discussed further in section III.A.4.a. of this proposed rule, and the verification of family size as defined under § 155.320(c)(3), which is discussed further in section III.A.5. of this proposed rule.
Additionally, we are of the view that reading section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation to permit Exchanges to treat all attested information as verified would, effectively, render the changes under section 71303(a) meaningless as, under current rules, that reading would result in a month likely being considered a coverage month based on just an applicant's attestation of eligibility criteria. Therefore, we are of the view that the intention of the WFTC legislation is to rely on existing verification procedures in section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act, its implementing regulations, and any successor or other applicable regulations as may be issued for purposes of verification under section 71303 of the WFTC legislation.
In summary, due to the new requirements in section 71303 of the WFTC legislation, we are of the view that APTC and CSRs cannot be provided to consumers when eligibility for enrollment in a QHP and for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, have not been verified using the specified criteria in accordance with section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act and implementing regulations—which allows certain information to be verified through attestation and which requires certain other information to be verified by either a trusted data source or documentation provided by the applicant during an inconsistency period. Therefore, we have determined that significant changes to the verification procedures in § 155.315(f)(4) related to providing APTC and CSRs during an inconsistency period are required. These changes are described below.
(ii) APTC and CSRs During Certain Inconsistency Periods (§ 155.315(f)(4)(ii))
As described in section II.A. of this proposed rule, section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation describes the specific criteria that must be verified before a month is considered a coverage month. One important clarification is that the special cost-sharing rule specific to AI/AN applicants specifically for items and services provided through the Indian Health Service, an Indian Tribe, Tribal Organization, an Urban Indian Organization, or through referrals under contracted health services (hereinafter “Indian health providers”) under section 1402(d)(2) of the Affordable Care Act, and implemented in § 155.350(b), is not impacted by new requirements in section 71303 of the WFTC legislation because it is not conditioned on being eligible for APTC. (iii) Eligibility Redeterminations During the Plan Year (§ 155.315(f)(4)(iii))
As previously stated, we propose to amend § 155.315(f)(4)(ii), which would prohibit Exchanges from providing APTC and CSRs based on application information during inconsistency periods for DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information. Exchanges would, therefore, be prohibited from providing APTC and CSRs during inconsistency periods as they currently do, including for the entire application household in cases of household-level DMIs such as those related to annual income and family size. However, for applicants who submit an application and receive new DMIs after they had previously verified all of the eligibility criteria specified in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) for the current plan year, we propose to add § 155.315(f)(4)(iii) to permit Exchanges to provide APTC and CSRs during an inconsistency period. This is discussed in detail in section III.A.4.d. of this proposed rule.
(iv) Resolution of DMIs (§ 155.315(f)(4)(iv))
We also propose to add new § 155.315(f)(4)(iv) to establish that Exchanges would be required to determine eligibility for APTC and CSRs on behalf of an applicant following a successful verification of the information described in § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) and to provide effective dates for the eligibility determination. Specifically, these proposed effective dates rules would apply to determinations and redeterminations in two circumstances. First, they would apply to determinations resulting from resolution of DMIs related to applicable enrollment information. Second, they would apply to redeterminations resulting from an applicant resolving all DMIs when the applicant would qualify for a greater amount of APTC than they were receiving during their inconsistency period upon DMI resolution—that is, DMIs described in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(A). These rules would apply to the DMIs described in § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) and (iii)(A) because resolution of these DMIs would generally result in changes to a consumer's APTC and CSR eligibility. In contrast, when a DMI described in § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(B) is resolved, such resolution would instead confirm the consumer's eligibility for the APTC and CSRs, as applicable, that they were already authorized to receive during their inconsistency period based on their attestation, and the amount of APTC and CSRs would remain the same.
We propose in § 155.315(f)(4)(iv)(A) that, if a consumer is already enrolled in a QHP when such DMIs are resolved by an Exchange, an Exchange would generally be required to implement the resulting APTC and CSR eligibility determination effective the first day of the first month in which all the following criteria are met: (1) an Exchange determined all eligibility criteria described in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) to be verified for that month, (2) the consumer was enrolled in a QHP on the first day of that month, and (3) the consumer's DMI was generated prior to the first of that month. This would allow APTC and CSRs to be paid prospectively, as well as retroactively, subject to the conditions described. We propose one exception to these rules, for cases where these rules would otherwise result in Exchanges being required to provide APTC for months in the prior coverage year. In these cases, we propose that Exchanges would not provide APTC for months in the prior coverage year, and consumers would instead claim any PTC for which they were eligible on their Federal income tax return.
This proposal would implement section 36B(c)(5)(C) of the Code, which was added by section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation. Section 36B(c)(5)(C) of the Code provides that a month that begins before completion of the verification prescribed by section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code must be treated as a coverage month for an individual if the Exchange verifies (using applicable enrollment information) that the individual is eligible to enroll in a QHP and for APTC. This provision effectively requires an Exchange to provide APTC and CSRs, as applicable, retroactively after verification of applicable enrollment information.

This exception is intended to mitigate tax administration issues and consumer burden that would result if Exchanges provided APTC for a month after the Exchange had already generated a consumer's Form 1095-A for the coverage year.
Consider the following example. A consumer submits an application to the Exchange on November 15, 2028, and qualifies for an SEP due to a November 30, 2028, loss of MEC. The consumer selects a plan on November 15, 2028, and in accordance with § 155.420(b)(2)(iv), qualifies for a coverage effective date of December 1, 2028. The consumer has a DMI related to their annual household income for 2028. The consumer chooses to enroll in a QHP effective December 1, 2028, without APTC or CSRs. Subsequently, the consumer submits documents to the Exchange, and the Exchange verifies the consumer's annual household income for 2028 and resolves their DMI on February 1, 2029. Were an exception not applied, under the rules proposed at § 155.315(f)(4)(iv)(A)(

This proposed exception is necessary to avoid significant tax administration issues. Exchanges generate Form 1095-A for enrollees in January following the applicable coverage year, which includes information about any APTC paid for each month in the coverage year. If, in the scenario described above, the consumer's Form 1095-A is generated prior to the Exchange's determination on February 1 that the consumer qualifies for APTC for December, the consumer's Form 1095-A would reflect that they were enrolled in a QHP but no APTC was paid for the month of December. Assume the consumer used this Form 1095-A to file their Federal income tax return and claim PTC for the month of December. If, in February, the Exchange then provided APTC for the month of December, the Exchange would need to issue a corrected Form 1095-A, a process that generally takes multiple months. Then, upon receipt of the corrected Form 1095-A, the consumer would have to file an amended 2028 tax return, reduce the December PTC the consumer claimed by the amount of APTC paid for the consumer's December coverage, and include a tax payment equal to the December APTC, plus interest and perhaps penalties, with the 2028 amended return. Instead, if there is no retroactive payment of APTC for December, the consumer would, on the consumer's 2028 tax return, lower his or her tax liability or receive a tax refund for the amount of the December PTC for which the consumer is eligible.
Thus, to alleviate these burdens on Exchanges, consumers, and the IRS, we propose that Exchanges would not provide or increase APTC for months in prior coverage years. We acknowledge that there are limited additional situations in which Exchanges may already be providing or increasing APTC for months in a prior coverage year, including if a consumer qualifies for an SEP with a retroactive effective date, or in the case of certain appeals. At the FFE, consumers are only able to receive prior year APTC through manual processes, by calling the Marketplace Call Center and having their case reviewed on an individual basis. As a result, we have determined that the current volume of cases where prior-year APTC is permitted is quite low. In contrast, the consumers to whom the effective date rules proposed in this section would apply would be able to use an online, automated process to enroll and to resolve their DMIs, and we therefore expect that the volume of consumers who may qualify for prior year APTC as a result could be quite significant by comparison. Therefore, we are only proposing to prevent Exchanges from providing prior-year APTC in this specific situation, but we seek comment regarding whether this principle should apply in other cases as well.
Regarding the rules proposed at § 155.315(f)(4)(iv)(A), we seek comment from issuers and other interested parties on operational considerations regarding retroactive provision of APTC and CSRs for eligible consumers. Specifically, we understand that providing CSRs for weeks or months prior to DMI resolution may be operationally challenging for issuers and consumers. We understand that, today, correctly re-processing claims that a consumer incurred during a period prior to an Exchange's determination of CSR eligibility often requires a consumer to manually submit, and an issuer to manually process and reimburse, costs incurred by consumers in the past. We seek comment on these and any other operational considerations.

Proposed effective date rules for such plan selections are described in section III.A.9. of this proposed rule for individuals who make a plan selection during the annual OEP, and in section III.A.10. of this proposed rule for individuals who select a plan during an SEP. This proposal would ensure that, for consumers who elect that their plan only become effective once verification requirements are met, enrollment and APTC would start on the same date, resulting in a clear process for consumers and streamlined communications for Exchanges, as well as ensuring that the consumer does not have a period of unsubsidized coverage.

(v) APTC and CSRs during Other Inconsistency Periods (§ 155.315(f)(4)(v))
We also propose new § 155.315(f)(4)(v) to specify that applicants with DMIs not related to applicable enrollment information would be provided APTC and CSRs based on attested application information, if otherwise eligible, during an inconsistency period. Section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation provides that no month shall be considered a coverage month until an Exchange verifies, using applicable enrollment information, an individual's eligibility to enroll in a QHP and for APTC. We read this to mean that if an Exchange has failed to verify information that is
not
applicable enrollment information, then section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation does not apply. Therefore, we propose that if an individual has a DMI not related to the applicable enrollment information, an Exchange would be required to follow the existing process established in section 1411 of the Affordable Care Act and implementing regulations and provide APTC and CSRs, as applicable, during the inconsistency period. If finalized, this exception would allow a consumer who qualifies for a change in family size SEP to be determined eligible for APTC and CSRs (if otherwise eligible) based on attested application information during an inconsistency period, as they are under current rules. As explained previously, we interpret section 1411(a)(2)(A) of the Affordable Care Act as requiring Exchanges to make APTC and CSR eligibility determinations consistent with the PTC eligibility requirements of section 36B of the Code. Therefore, it is necessary for HHS to also adopt the Secretary of Treasury's waiver of the verification requirements of section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code to ensure that Exchanges make APTC and CSR eligibility determinations consistent with PTC eligibility determinations. Additionally, by aligning our requirements with those proposed by the Secretary of Treasury in the rule described above, HHS can ensure timely and continuous coverage for enrollees who qualify for SEPs due to a change in family size, particularly consumers who are adding newborns or dependents to their families. There are several situations where, without this exception, consumers could potentially lose APTC and CSRs at critical junctures of needing medical care, including the newborn and postpartum periods.
The requirements specified in section 1411(c) and (d) of the Affordable Care Act and the implementing regulations at §§ 155.315 and 155.320, which are the basis for Exchange verification processes, require verification of information provided by applicants, including citizenship or immigration status, household income and family size, and eligibility for or enrollment in employer-sponsored coverage. If a consumer, either new or current, is eligible to enroll or re-enroll during a family size SEP, generates DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information, and then is unsuccessful at resolving those DMIs and loses their APTC, the consumer may still be allowed PTC for the months during the inconsistency period when filing their
(
printed page 67672)
tax return and reconciling their APTC with their actual allowed PTC.
Section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation allows a waiver of the verification requirement in section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code for an individual who enrolls in a QHP during a SEP based on “a change in the family size of the individual.” We read this as referring to the following current SEPs: gaining a dependent through marriage, birth, adoption, placement for adoption, placement in foster care, or through child support or another court order in § 155.420(d)(2)(i); and loss of a dependent or consideration as a dependent through divorce, legal separation, or death in § 155.420(d)(2)(ii) (if offered by an Exchange). To qualify for the SEP at § 155.420(d)(2)(i) through marriage, one or both spouses need to demonstrate having one or more days of MEC in the prior 60 days preceding the date of marriage under § 155.420(d)(2)(i)(A). Exchanges on the Federal platform do not currently offer the SEP at § 155.420(d)(2)(ii), as generally the consumer who is losing or is no longer considered a dependent qualifies for a loss of MEC SEP, thereby preventing a loss of coverage.
We are requesting comment specifically on whether Exchanges should be required to offer the loss of dependent or consideration as a dependent SEP offered at § 155.420(d)(2)(ii) so that consumers who are eligible to enroll during this SEP may continue to qualify for APTC and CSRs based on their attestation during an inconsistency period that occurs due to updating their eligibility information to the Exchange. While consumers are already required to promptly report any changes that may affect their APTC or CSR eligibility, we are of the view that doing so is more important than it has been previously, in light of the change that removes APTC repayment caps in section 71305 of the WFTC legislation. For consumers that have been determined eligible to enroll during a family size SEP as described at § 155.420(d)(2) and otherwise have a DMI due to the new information on their application, this statutorily allowed exception ensures that consumers receive the APTC and CSRs that most closely reflect their attested-to situation, thereby minimizing the potential for larger tax liabilities. Requiring Exchanges to offer the loss of dependent or dependent status SEP would also prevent individuals who lose dependent status—for example, due to divorce or death of the primary policyholder—from losing potential APTC and CSRs until they newly meet pre-verification requirements.
For these reasons, we are proposing to amend § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) and add new § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(C) to require all Exchanges to determine eligibility for APTC and CSRs based on the attested application information during an applicant's inconsistency period for DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information if the applicant's household is eligible to enroll during a family size SEP in accordance with § 155.420(d)(2)(i) and (ii). The proposed change would ensure that both new applicants and enrollees who have previously verified their information under § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) and (iii) are eligible for APTC and CSRs based on the attested application information if they are eligible to enroll during a change in family size SEP.
We seek comment on this proposal. We understand State Exchanges may find it challenging to implement these requirements for PY 2028. Therefore, we are considering providing flexibility for State Exchanges to delay implementation of the change in family size SEP exception until PY 2029. We seek comment, in particular from State Exchanges, about whether the availability of this flexibility would be useful to ease the burden of implementing the requirements in this proposed rule.
d. Eligibility Redeterminations During the Plan Year
Consistent with the PTC proposed rule (
91 FR 65499
), we propose the addition of new § 155.315(f)(4)(iii) to describe the requirements for providing APTC and CSRs for enrollees who have reported a change to eligibility criteria during the plan year after an Exchange has completed verification of those same criteria using the enrollee's information from their immediately preceding eligibility determination. As outlined in section II.A. of this proposed rule, section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation provides additional criteria for a month to be considered a coverage month. Specifically, a month generally may not be a coverage month for an enrollee in a QHP for any month that an Exchange fails to verify specific criteria related to the enrollee's eligibility to enroll in a QHP through an Exchange and, to the extent relevant, for APTC for the coverage for that month using certain criteria. More specifically, beginning with PY 2028, an Exchange must verify eligibility for enrollment in a QHP and APTC using the following information before a month is considered a coverage month and PTC may be paid: (1) household income and family size; (2) eligible noncitizen status; (3) any health coverage status or eligibility for coverage; (4) residency; and (5) other information as determined by the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of HHS.
In proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(A) and (B), we propose Exchange procedures regarding the provision of APTC and CSRs when an enrollee reports a change that generates one or more DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information. If the reported change results in an amount of APTC or CSRs that is in excess of or equal to the amount of APTC or CSRs previously determined for the individual, we propose that Exchanges would be required to continue providing APTC and CSRs (as applicable) during inconsistency periods at the same amount as previously determined. If the reported change results in an amount of APTC or CSRs that is lower than the amount previously determined for the individual, then we propose that Exchanges would lower APTC and CSRs based on the information provided by the applicant during an inconsistency period.
Section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation amends the definition of “coverage month” and conditions PTC eligibility on successful verification of applicable enrollment information (that is, the criteria described in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii)) listed above. We construe this change as a requirement that Exchanges must comply with
in addition to
(not in place of) existing verification requirements prescribed by sections 1411 and 1412 of the Affordable Care Act. Importantly, while section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation requires that information be verified prior to treating a month as a coverage month (that is, before PTC can be allowed for an applicant's coverage), we propose this process would not immediately supersede all prior verifications or require automatic termination of APTC and CSRs at the point that an enrollee reports a change within the plan year. Instead, we read section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation to mean that any verification of applicable enrollment information must remain effective for the duration of the plan year, but, if an enrollee reports a change resulting in a DMI related to the applicable enrollment information, additional verification is required only before any
additional
APTC may be paid. For example, consider an enrollee receiving $250 per month in APTC. The enrollee reports a decrease in projected annual household income during the plan year that would make the enrollee eligible for $300 per month in APTC.
(

The enrollee's income cannot be verified with IRS, resulting in a DMI. Section 71303(a) of the WFTC would prohibit an Exchange from providing the enrollee with the additional $50 per month in APTC until the enrollee's income was verified, but it would not permit the Exchange to end APTC during the DMI period entirely (unless otherwise permitted).
Additionally, even if 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation did not compel this outcome, the Exchange may continue to draw authority from section 1412(b) of the Affordable Care Act for changes reported during the benefit year. Specifically, section 1412(b)(2) of the Affordable Care Act allows the Secretary of HHS to establish procedures to determine APTC on the basis of information other than an enrollee's prior tax return data when an enrollee's application form demonstrates substantial changes in circumstances, such as changes in income, family size, or other significant changes affecting eligibility.
