Accordingly, we propose a framework that would require an Exchange to maintain or decrease an enrollee's previously determined APTC or CSR amount (where applicable) if a reported change generates a DMI related to the applicable enrollment information after the enrollee was determined eligible for APTC or CSR for a given plan year. The maintained or decreased APTC amount would be applicable until an Exchange either resolves the DMI, the consumer reports another change in circumstance, or until the end of the inconsistency period during which the updated information remains unverified.
Throughout this paragraph, we use “previously verified” or “previously determined” to reference the enrollee's most recent verification or determination conducted by the Exchange. We propose in § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(A) that when an individual reports a change that results in an amount of APTC or CSRs greater than or equal to the amount of APTC or CSRs previously determined for the individual, an Exchange would be required to maintain APTC or CSRs at the previously verified amount during an inconsistency period. If the DMI is not resolved, under section 1411(e)(4)(B)(ii) of the Affordable Care Act and regulations at §§ 155.315(f)(5) and 155.320(c)(3)(vi)(F) through (G), an Exchange would be required to redetermine eligibility for enrollment in a QHP and for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, on the basis of records maintained by specific Federal officials as outlined in section 1411(c) of the Affordable Care Act, which may include termination of enrollment in a QHP and/or of APTC and CSRs. We propose the approach in § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(A) because until new information is verified, maintaining an enrollee's prior verified eligibility preserves program integrity and eases burden on enrollees related to reporting changes to the Exchanges, as stated later in this section. This is particularly relevant as it is reasonable for an individual to experience changes that significantly impact their eligibility, resulting in DMIs.
For example, consider a scenario where an enrollee reports a decrease in income from 350 percent of the FPL to 150 percent of the FPL, corresponding with an
increase
in APTC and new eligibility for CSRs, and resulting in a household income DMI. Under proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(A), Exchanges would be required to maintain the previously determined lower amount of APTC and CSRs based on previously verified information during the inconsistency period. Once the household income DMI is successfully resolved, an Exchange would be required to redetermine eligibility and adjust the amount of APTC or CSRs upwards based on the consumer's verified income attestation, with an effective date consistent with proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(iv) and other proposed changes regarding effective dates following resolution of DMIs outlined in section III.A.6.b. of this proposed rule. As noted previously, if the DMI is not resolved, the Exchange would be required to redetermine QHP and APTC and CSR eligibility, as applicable, on the basis of records maintained by a trusted data source, which may include removal of QHP and/or APTC and CSR eligibility.
By maintaining the lower amount of APTC and CSRs based on the previously verified information during the inconsistency period, Exchanges would ensure that APTC and CSRs are only ever provided to enrollees during an inconsistency period at a level that does not exceed the amount provided based on previously verified information. Additionally, this proposed policy supports program integrity by ensuring that accurate amounts of APTC and CSRs are being provided on behalf of enrollees.
We acknowledge that this proposal would result in many consumers receiving less APTC and CSRs during an inconsistency period than they are ultimately determined eligible for when their DMIs are resolved. For APTC, consumers could be made whole during the tax filing and reconciliation process. We acknowledge that this may present a gap for some enrollees regarding CSRs when compared to APTC, because enrollees with APTC less than their PTC may claim the difference as a tax credit on their tax return for the year of coverage whereas there is no similar process for CSRs. However, we are of the view that this proposed policy strikes a balance between ensuring responsible Exchange operations regarding the provision of APTC and CSRs and encouraging enrollees to report changes.
In contrast, consider the opposite scenario, where an enrollee reports an increase in income from 150 percent of the FPL to 350 percent of the FPL, corresponding with a
decrease
in APTC and ineligibility for CSRs, and resulting in a household income DMI. We propose in § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(B) that Exchanges would be required to adjust APTC or CSRs downward immediately after application submission based on the information provided by the enrollee on the application. Under this proposal, since the enrollee was previously verified for a higher amount of APTC or CSRs, the enrollee would be determined eligible for a lower amount of APTC or CSRs during the inconsistency period based on their newly attested applicable enrollment information. By requiring the Exchange to decrease APTC or CSRs in this manner, this proposal would help ensure that the Exchange does not pay out more APTC than that for which the consumer may be eligible based on the consumer's reported increase in income.
We are of the view that the policies described in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(A) and (B) are permitted under section 1412(b)(2) of the Affordable Care Act, which affords discretion to the Secretary to modify procedures for making advanced determinations as circumstances warrant. In other words, this broad authority allows the Secretary to structure Exchange rules for determining an enrollee's APTC or CSRs when the enrollee reports a change during the benefit year. We are of the view that this interpretation allows an Exchange to maintain or adjust APTC or
(
printed page 67674)
CSRs downwards for instances described in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(A) and (B). We are of the view that this proposed framework—maintaining or reducing APTC or CSRs during the inconsistency period for an enrollee following a mid-year change that results in a change to the amount of, or eligibility for, APTC or CSRs—best achieves Congressional intent of section 71303 of the WFTC legislation. Under both proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(A) and (B), enrollees would continue to receive APTC and CSRs during the 90/95-day DMI period as long as they are otherwise eligible for APTC.
Under this proposed framework, Exchange determinations would always utilize verified information. In the first instance where an enrollee's reported change would result in an increase of APTC and CSRs, the Exchange would maintain APTC and CSRs at the previously verified level during the inconsistency period while verification of reported changes is pending at the Exchange. In the second instance, when the enrollee's reported change would result in a decrease in APTC and CSRs, the Exchange would base their determination on the enrollee's newly reported information. This determination would not occur in the absence of verified information. Rather, this determination (and the resulting provision of APTC and CSRs during the inconsistency period) would reflect both the enrollee's newly reported information and the fact that the Exchange previously verified the enrollee eligible for a higher amount of APTC and CSRs. We are of the view that this approach is critical, as the only alternative would be to disregard an enrollee's attestation that supports eligibility for less APTC and CSRs than previously verified. Importantly, the downward adjustment of APTC and CSRs based on the enrollee's attestation simply adjusts the verified baseline amount of APTC and CSRs downward to limit the enrollee's exposure to tax liability. We considered that an enrollee would have less incentive to report a change that results in a decrease in APTC or CSRs if they were not aware of the tax implications and did not wish to limit their tax liability.
In contrast, some enrollees may be inclined to report a change that results in an increase of APTC and CSRs because they are unaware of the tax implications or are focused on the short-term benefit of doing so (that is, lower monthly premiums). For these reasons, we believe the proposed approach best balances the interests of protecting consumers from increased tax liability and program integrity. Ultimately, the provision of APTC and CSRs during the inconsistency period while verification of reported changes is pending at the Exchange would use previously verified information as a foundational element for determinations. This two-pronged approach would ensure that enrollees and households do not receive more APTC and CSRs than they are verified for.
We considered alternatives to this proposal. We considered an approach in which Exchanges would be required to maintain an enrollee's current APTC or CSRs (that is, maintain a higher amount of APTC despite the enrollee's attested increased income) during an inconsistency period described in § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) when the enrollee reports a change that would result in a decrease in APTC or CSRs. However, since section 71305 of the WFTC legislation eliminates the limitation on repayment of excess APTC for tax years after December 31, 2025 (as set forth in section 36B(f)(2) of the Code), this approach could result in a consumer incurring a large tax liability despite correctly reporting a change. Therefore, our proposed policy serves as a key consumer protective measure by helping to safeguard consumers from large APTC repayments. We also considered requiring Exchanges to provide the higher amount of APTC or CSRs when an enrollee reports a change that results in an increase of APTC or CSRs, but encouraging consumers to take less APTC—specifically the amount they were receiving prior to reporting a change in circumstances—to avoid the risk of incurring a significant tax liability if their attestation was not verified. However, we determined that this would create consumer confusion and may not be effective as consumers would need to take additional actions to manually adjust the amount of APTC applied to their monthly premium if desired.
This alternative operational approach could result in consumer confusion and friction, which may inadvertently disincentivize consumers from reporting changes. Importantly, we are of the view that structuring Exchange operations in the manner proposed would ensure accurate APTC determinations to the extent possible. Such a posture would enhance program integrity by ensuring that enrollees receive no more APTC than they have been determined eligible for after verification of their applicable enrollment information. Ultimately, such an approach reduces unnecessary Federal APTC outlays in the event attestations are inaccurate while safeguarding consumers from large tax liabilities, preventing an unnecessary cycle of APTC payment and repayment.
We considered another alternative approach, which would require Exchanges to remove APTC or CSRs during inconsistency periods. This approach would require individuals to pay the full premium to maintain coverage, which could be unaffordable for many individuals and result in them terminating coverage. That outcome could have a destabilizing impact on risk pools due to increases in adverse selection, as individuals with greater health needs would be more likely to maintain coverage (whether by quickly resolving DMIs or paying the full cost of premiums) than healthy individuals. Furthermore, we are of the view that it is important to structure the Exchange rules such that enrollees are motivated to report changes as required. Requiring Exchanges to terminate APTC or CSRs for consumers who report a change that results in a DMI related to the applicable enrollment information would likely discourage consumers from reporting changes.
We acknowledge that this proposal may require Exchanges to modify application and enrollment processes to accommodate scenarios where APTC and CSRs are maintained and those where APTC and CSRs are decreased. We especially acknowledge the burden that this change may impose on State Exchanges and the operational costs that may be incurred to implement these changes. However, given the high likelihood that individuals may experience significant changes during the benefit year after their applicable enrollment information has been verified, it is critical that Exchanges implement these new requirements to motivate individuals to report changes that accurately represent their circumstances. Exchanges may leverage existing infrastructure to implement these changes, such as current functionality that enables Exchanges to maintain APTC and CSRs during an inconsistency period, or functionality that adjusts or removes APTC as required by section 1411(e)(4)(B)(ii) of the Affordable Care Act as described above.
We also acknowledge that this proposal would require changes to existing enrollee communication procedures and associated infrastructure. In particular, enrollees may find it difficult to distinguish between scenarios where their APTC or CSRs would be maintained compared to those where APTC or CSRs would be reduced. Importantly, while alternative approaches such as removing APTC or CSRs altogether or requiring enrollees to
(
printed page 67675)
manually adjust APTC may appear simpler on their face, such approaches would simply shift complexity on to the enrollee at a later moment in the enrollment process, such as at the point of plan selection or enrollment where an enrollee (or an agent or broker applying on their behalf) must manually adjust their APTC or at tax reconciliation, where the enrollee may incur tax liabilities. Such approaches would likely deter enrollees from reporting changes during the benefit year.
We expect Exchanges to identify communication strategies that are tailored to their enrollee populations, such as updated eligibility determination notices that describe APTC or CSR changes following a mid-benefit year change, text message alerts to enrollees when APTC or CSRs are reduced, dynamic messaging for consumers after application submission and so on. We note that State Exchanges have successfully absorbed comparable operational changes, such as changes resulting from Medicaid unwinding from 2023-2024, suggesting that system changes such as these are likely within existing institutional capacity and would not impose a burden once integrated into normal operations. We anticipate that enrollee familiarity (as well as that of assisters, agents, and brokers that assist enrollees) will increase across enrollment cycles as their application better reflects the enrollee's most recent applicable enrollment information.
To summarize, we propose the addition of § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(A) and (B) to describe the requirements for providing APTC and CSRs for enrollees who have reported a change during the plan year that results in a DMI related to applicable enrollment information (such as household income), after an Exchange has completed verification of those same criteria for the same plan year using the enrollee's information from their immediately preceding eligibility determination. We propose that Exchanges would be required to maintain the amount of APTC or CSRs if a reported change results in an amount of APTC or CSRs that is in excess of or equal to the amount of APTC or CSRs previously determined for the individual. We propose that Exchanges would be required to reduce APTC or CSRs based on the individual's attested income if a reported change results in an amount of APTC or CSRs that is lower than the amount previously determined for the individual.
We seek comment on this proposal. We understand State Exchanges may find it challenging to implement these requirements for PY 2028. Therefore, we are considering providing flexibility for State Exchanges to delay implementation of this proposal for enrollees who have reported a change during the plan year until PY 2029. We seek comment, in particular from State Exchanges, about whether the availability of this flexibility would be useful to ease the burden of implementing the requirements in this proposed rule.
5. Verification Process Related to Eligibility for Insurance Affordability Programs (§ 155.320(c))
We do not propose any changes to the existing regulatory requirements at § 155.320(c) related to verification of family size as described further in this section. However, we seek comment on how we might strengthen requirements for Exchanges to verify family size in the future. We also seek comment on how Exchanges could verify family size using data sources, and which data sources we should consider making available for Exchanges, with the ultimate goal of increasing program integrity, while minimizing burden for Exchanges and consumers, and limiting the cost for Exchanges to procure new data sources.
As background, to be eligible to receive APTC or CSRs, applicants or enrollees must provide certain information regarding the individuals that make up their tax household, including their relationship to the tax filer (the tax anchor on the application) and tax filing status, according to section 1411(b)(3)(A) of the Affordable Care Act. Under section 1411(c)(3) of the Affordable Care Act, the Secretary of HHS must submit the family size information collected by Exchange applications to the Secretary of the Treasury for verification of both household income and family size.
Per current § 155.320(c)(3)(i)(A), an Exchange must require an applicant or enrollee applying for coverage with financial assistance, such as APTC and CSRs, to attest to information about the individuals that comprise the tax filer's family. If an applicant or enrollee attests that a change in circumstance has occurred or is likely to occur that would result in an inaccurate projection of their family size for the year for which they are applying for coverage, and so it is not representative of the family size for the plan year, an Exchange may accept the applicant or enrollee's attestation without further verification, per § 155.320(c)(3)(i)(C), as long as the data provided by the applicant is reasonably compatible with other information provided about their family. If the data provided by the applicant or enrollee is not reasonably compatible with other information provided by the application filer for the family, an Exchange generally must utilize data obtained through other electronic data sources to verify the attestation. If such data sources are unavailable or information in such data sources is not reasonably compatible with the applicant or enrollee's attestation, an Exchange must request additional documentation to support the attestation, consistent with current § 155.315(f).
Currently, the FFE application prompts the applicant or enrollee to provide information about their tax filing status and the current makeup of their household, including any dependents they plan to claim on their Federal income tax return. However, the FFE application does not allow the applicant or enrollee to provide a specific number of family members in their household. Rather, the FFE's eligibility logic works to calculate the applicant's family size based upon the information the applicant or enrollee has provided in their application regarding tax filing status and any dependents they listed.
In light of the new requirements in the WFTC legislation, we wish to revisit family size verification and solicit comment from interested parties on possible alternatives, new data sources, or other enhancements that Exchanges could implement to strengthen family size verification. We explored additional ways Exchanges could strengthen or enhance their verification procedures for family size, but discovered some important challenges Exchanges would likely face, which we discuss in more detail in the remainder of this section.
First, we are not aware of any existing external data source currently used by any Federal agency to verify an applicant or enrollee's current or future family size, other than Federal income tax return data that Exchanges access through the IRS Hub service. Exchanges could potentially use this data to verify family size by calculating the number of dependents an applicant or enrollee claimed on their tax return and comparing with the number of dependents attested to on the coverage application; however, any such estimate is likely to often be incorrect, since IRS displays tax data for the most recent tax year for which data is available, which is typically 1 to 3 years prior to the current coverage year, due to the time delay between a tax return being filed and the time period the tax data represents, and the consumer's family
(
printed page 67676)
size may have changed during that timeframe. Furthermore, the operational process to determine the number of dependents a tax filer plans to claim on their tax return is difficult for both an Exchange and consumers because changes to family size during the plan year may cause inconsistencies when trying to match against IRS data. For example, an applicant or enrollee who gains a dependent via a birth in October 2026 and applies for coverage during the OEP in November 2026, would not be able to electronically verify his or her family size using IRS data. This is because that new dependent was not included on the applicant's most recent Federal income tax return and, therefore, IRS data will not have any record of that new dependent until the applicant or enrollee claims them on their 2026 tax return filed in 2027. A relative dearth of data available to prove changes in a consumer's tax household size is a major challenge with verifying family size through IRS tax data.
A second challenge for Exchanges verifying family size is navigating the complicated rules relating to who qualifies as a tax filer's dependent on their tax return. In general, a consumer is able to claim an individual as a dependent if (1) the individual is a U.S. citizen, a U.S. national, U.S. resident, or a resident of Canada or Mexico, (2) the individual, if married, does not file a joint return with his or her spouse except in limited situations, and (3) the individual is a qualifying child or a qualifying relative of the consumer. Additional tests must be met for an individual to qualify as a qualifying child or qualifying relative of a consumer. In addition, it is possible for an individual to be a qualifying child of more than one tax filer, and in those situations, there are tiebreaker rules to determine which tax filer can claim the individual as a dependent. Because of these complex rules, it may be difficult for tax filers to provide documentation supporting the attested family size provided on their application.
While considering the current challenges that Exchanges face regarding family size verification discussed previously and the new requirements in section 71303 of the WFTC legislation, we also considered two potential approaches to strengthen or enhance family size verification for applicants or enrollees applying for Exchange coverage with APTC/CSRs. The first approach involved setting a family size DMI for all applicants or enrollees whose reported household size did not match their household size in IRS tax data. Based on our analysis of FFE data that looked at IRS response codes from consumers for PY 2024 and PY 2025, we found that household size data from IRS could not be returned for 13,423,627 applications, out of a total of 30,328,781, which is roughly 44 percent. While many reasons may have contributed to a lack of available IRS data for these consumers, this approach could result in almost half of all applicants receiving a family size DMI, which would require significant technical and operational updates for all Exchanges. Additionally, we expect that the percentage of applicants or enrollees who successfully resolve their family size DMI would be low, given the lack of available documentation types for an applicant to prove tax family size. Moreover, there is a high likelihood of inaccurate DMI processing, due to the complexities in tax rules for claiming dependents. A notable concern with this approach is that if an applicant's or enrollee's family size DMI could not be resolved, then APTC would be removed for the entire household. Finally, this approach may have negative impacts on the risk pool as it may lower overall participation in Exchanges due to the increased burden to resolve DMIs, thus increasing the risk of adverse selection as certain populations, such as younger individuals, would choose to forego Exchange coverage.
A second option we explored was a targeted, risk-based approach to modifying the family size verification process. We explored if an Exchange could either randomly verify a specific percentage of households, verify family size changes greater than two when compared to IRS tax data, verify family sizes greater than a certain amount of people, or verify non-applicant dependents without an SSN. This option would require the same technical and operational updates as the first option but would result in fewer DMIs. However, similar to the first option, we anticipate the percentage of applicants who would successfully resolve their family size DMI would be low due to the lack of available documentation options to prove tax family size. This option would likely have less of a negative impact on the risk pool as compared to the first option as a smaller subset of applicants would receive a DMI.
Given that Exchanges face such extensive challenges and costs associated with enhancing family size verification operations, we propose to retain the current regulatory requirements regarding verification of family size as outlined in § 155.320(c). We are of the view that the current regulatory requirements and Exchange operations to verify family size are sufficient given the challenges we discussed earlier in this section. We note that historically, we have seen very limited cases of fraud as it relates to family size, however, we are still interested in ways to potentially strengthen or enhance family size verification, in a way that is both cost-efficient for Exchanges and minimally burdensome on consumers.
We seek comment on alternatives and invite interested parties to share their experiences with family size verification, including challenges, risk for family size fraud, feasibility of other verification approaches such as risk-based verification, and cost/budget impacts.
6. Eligibility Redetermination During a Plan Year (§ 155.330)
a. Effective Dates for Enrollee-Reported Changes (§ 155.330(f)(1))
(i) Summary of Proposed Effective Dates for Enrollee-Reported Changes
In § 155.330(f)(1), we propose that if an Exchange redetermines an enrollee's eligibility to enroll in a QHP, for APTC, or for CSRs because the enrollee has provided updated information to the Exchange, such redetermination of eligibility would become effective on the first of the month following an Exchange's eligibility redetermination. We clarify that, throughout this section, when we refer to a redetermination of APTC or CSR eligibility, we are referring to both redeterminations that result in a consumer becoming eligible for a different amount or level of APTC or CSR, as applicable, and redeterminations that result in a consumer becoming newly eligible or ineligible for APTC or CSRs.
The proposal in § 155.330(f)(1) would maintain the general rule currently in § 155.330(f)(1)(i) that eligibility updates resulting from enrollee-reported changes must be effective on the first of the month following an Exchange's eligibility redetermination. Currently, § 155.330(f)(1)(i) provides that eligibility changes “resulting from a determination under this section” must be effective on the first of the month following the date of the consumer's eligibility determination notice, subject to certain exceptions enumerated in § 155.330(f)(2) through (5). Determinations “under this section” include both enrollee-reported changes as described in § 155.330(e)(1), as well as determinations made as part of the periodic data matching process described in § 155.330(e)(2). We propose effective dates for determinations made as part of the periodic data matching process in proposed § 155.330(f)(3),

discussed in section III.A.6.c. of this proposed rule.
Proposed § 155.330(f)(1) would apply to eligibility redeterminations when an enrollee provides updated information to an Exchange and the Exchange determines the enrollee has an inconsistency. For example, § 155.330(f)(1) would apply if an Exchange determines that an enrollee's APTC or CSRs, as applicable, needs to be reduced during their inconsistency period because they have a DMI as described in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(B). In these cases, the redetermination of the enrollee's APTC or CSRs eligibility would be effective on the first of the month following the Exchange's eligibility redetermination.
At § 155.330(f)(1)(i), we propose an exception such that, if the Exchange redetermines an enrollee's eligibility because the enrollee has provided updated information to the Exchange, and the Exchange also determines that the enrollee qualifies for certain SEPs described in § 155.420(b)(2)(i) or (b)(2)(iii), then the Exchange would implement the enrollee's eligibility redetermination on the coverage effective dates described in § 155.420(b)(2)(i) or (b)(2)(iii), respectively.
Current § 155.330(f)(1)(iii) specifies that eligibility changes “affecting enrollment or premiums only” must be effective on the first day of the month following the date “the Exchange is notified of the change.” Under our proposed restructure of § 155.330(f), we propose that all enrollee-reported changes, including those affecting enrollment or premiums only, would be subject to the effective dates under proposed § 155.330(f)(1) and therefore would generally be effective on the first of the next month following the eligibility determination. For Exchanges on the Federal platform, we clarify that even if a reported change only affects enrollment or premiums, an Exchange generally also redetermines an enrollee's eligibility for enrollment in a QHP and for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, before sending an updated transaction to the enrollee's issuer. We request comment from State Exchanges regarding whether State Exchanges also redetermine enrollees' eligibility in cases in which a reported change only affects enrollment or premiums, such that proposed § 155.330(f)(1) would apply. We also note that § 155.400(b)(1) requires Exchanges to send all eligibility and enrollment information, which includes updates on eligibility and enrollment, to issuers “promptly and without undue delay.”
(ii) Proposal to No Longer Allow Exchanges To Delay Effective Dates for Enrollee-Reported Changes
Current § 155.330(f)(2) provides an exception to current § 155.330(f)(1), permitting Exchanges to delay the effective dates of eligibility redeterminations by one month if they occur on or after the 15th of a month. For example, if an enrollee reported a change in income to an Exchange and an Exchange redetermined the enrollee's eligibility for APTC and CSRs on May 20, an Exchange could delay the effective date of the resulting APTC and CSR change from June 1, as prescribed under the general rule at current § 155.330(f)(1), to July 1, as permitted in current § 155.330(f)(2). In proposed § 155.330(f)(1), we propose that Exchanges would no longer be permitted to delay the effective dates for eligibility redeterminations resulting from enrollee-reported changes in the manner allowed by current § 155.330(f)(2). As proposed at § 155.330(f)(1), all eligibility redeterminations resulting from enrollee-reported changes would be effective the first of the month following an Exchange's redetermination, with limited exceptions for scenarios where the enrollee also qualifies for certain SEPs. As a result, in the example described previously, a change in eligibility for APTC and CSRs resulting from an enrollee reporting a change to their income on May 20 would be effective on June 1, and Exchanges would not be permitted to delay the effective date for such changes to July 1.
We propose to no longer allow the exception currently at § 155.330(f)(2) for eligibility redeterminations following enrollee-reported changes for several reasons. First, the redeterminations discussed in proposed § 155.330(f)(1) would be limited to enrollee-reported changes, where the enrollee is actively engaging with the Exchange. They would not apply to determinations as part of the periodic data matching process or following the expiration of an inconsistency period, where the Exchange is redetermining eligibility without the enrollee's active engagement. When an enrollee reports a change to the Exchange, the enrollee is typically informed of the results of their redetermination in real-time, and there is therefore no compelling need to delay the effective date of the redetermination to ensure that an Exchange is able to communicate with the enrollee regarding the change before it takes effect.
Second, the elimination of the limitations on repayment of excess APTC starting in PY 2026, required by section 71305 of the WFTC legislation, makes it even more important that Exchanges apply the changes that enrollees report without delay, to reduce the risk that consumers who accurately report changes to the Exchanges are faced with increased tax liability despite their efforts to proactively report changes. We seek comment on the proposal to remove the exception currently at § 155.330(f)(2) regarding eligibility redeterminations following enrollee-reported changes.
Similarly, for redeterminations resulting from enrollee-reported changes, we are proposing to remove § 155.330(f)(3), which provides that if a change results in decreased APTC or a change in CSR eligibility, and the redetermination occurs after the 15th of a month, Exchanges are required to delay the effective date of such eligibility redeterminations by one month. For example, if an enrollee reports an increase in income to an Exchange and the Exchange determines on May 20 that the enrollee is eligible for less APTC, an Exchange is required to delay the effective date of the resulting decrease in APTC from June 1, as prescribed under the general rule at current § 155.330(f)(1), to July 1, as required by the exception in current § 155.330(f)(3). For enrollee-reported changes, we are proposing to remove the required delay at § 155.330(f)(3) for the same reasons we are proposing to remove the option for Exchanges to delay under § 155.330(f)(2). For redeterminations not resulting from enrollee-reported changes—specifically, those resulting from the expiration of an inconsistency period or periodic data matching—we propose to maintain the required delay for redeterminations that result in a decreased amount of APTC or decreased level of CSR. This proposal is discussed in detail in section III.A.6.c. of this proposed rule.
We considered proposing an alternative under which Exchanges would be required or permitted to immediately implement eligibility redeterminations resulting from enrollee-reported changes. However, we determined that immediate, mid-month adjustment of APTC and CSRs would be more difficult for Exchanges and issuers to implement. Changes to APTC and CSR amounts in the middle of a month would require Exchanges and issuers to prorate both APTC and premium amounts and would require issuers to retroactively re-bill consumers for the month in which the change was reported. For these reasons, we are proposing at § 155.330(f)(1) that eligibility redeterminations resulting

(iii) Enrollee-Reported Changes Resulting in an SEP
Current § 155.330(f)(4) provides another exception to current § 155.330(f)(1), requiring that eligibility redeterminations associated with an SEP due to gaining or becoming a dependent through birth, adoption, foster care, child support, or court order, as described at § 155.420(b)(2)(i), become effective on the SEP effective dates prescribed in § 155.420(b)(2)(i). We are proposing to maintain this exception at proposed § 155.330(f)(1)(i). This exception ensures that if, for example, an enrollee adds a newborn to their application, the resulting redetermination of the enrollee's eligibility due to their change in family size is effective retroactive to the newborn's date of birth.
Current § 155.330(f)(4) further provides that eligibility redeterminations associated with an SEP due to marriage become effective on the SEP effective dates prescribed in § 155.420(b)(2)(ii). We are not proposing to maintain this exception in proposed § 155.330(f)(1)(i), because § 155.420(b)(2)(ii) requires that coverage selected in accordance with an SEP due to marriage becomes effective on the first of the month following plan selection. Therefore, for consumers with a marriage SEP, their coverage effective date already generally aligns with the effective dates for eligibility redeterminations proposed at § 155.330(f)(1).
Current § 155.330(f)(5) provides an exception to current § 155.330(f)(1) such that eligibility changes associated with an SEP described in § 155.420(d)(4), (d)(5), and (d)(9) may be effective “based on the specific circumstances of each situation.” The SEP at § 155.420(d)(4) is for qualified individuals who experience an error of the Exchange; the SEP at § 155.420(d)(5) is for enrollees whose QHP violates a material provision of its contract with the enrollee; and the SEP at § 155.420(d)(9) is for qualified individuals who experience an exceptional circumstance. In proposed § 155.330(f)(1)(i), we are proposing that if an Exchange determines that an enrollee qualifies for any of the SEPs enumerated in § 155.420(b)(2)(iii)—which include the SEPs described at § 155.420(d)(4), (d)(5), and (d)(9)—then the enrollee's eligibility redetermination would be effective on the coverage effective date prescribed by § 155.420(b)(2)(iii). Section 155.420(b)(2)(iii) provides that the Exchange “must ensure that coverage is effective on an appropriate date based on the circumstances of the special enrollment period.” Therefore, we are proposing to maintain the flexibility currently permitted under § 155.330(f)(5) for Exchanges to establish appropriate eligibility redetermination effective dates for enrollees who qualify for these SEPs.
We are newly proposing that an Exchange follow the same eligibility redetermination effective date rules for an individual eligible for the three other SEPs enumerated in § 155.420(b)(2)(iii): the SEP at § 155.420(d)(11) for qualified individuals who are determined ineligible for Medicaid or CHIP after their enrollment period has ended; the SEP at § 155.420(d)(12) for enrollees whose enrollment was influenced by a material error regarding certain plan characteristics; and the optional SEP at § 155.420(d)(13) for individuals who resolve an inconsistency after their QHP has been terminated. We do not see a compelling reason to impose different eligibility redetermination effective date rules for enrollees with these SEPs as compared to the SEPs at § 155.420(d)(4), (d)(5), and (d)(9), given that Exchanges have the discretion to establish appropriate coverage effective dates for all of these SEPs under § 155.420(b)(2)(iii). Because § 155.330(f)(5) was finalized prior to these SEPs being established, we are of the view that the lack of reference to these SEPs at § 155.330(f)(5) is merely an oversight.
We seek comment on this proposal. Specifically, we seek comment from State Exchanges and other interested parties regarding any operational burden these proposed changes to current effective date policies would create, and whether a 1-year delay in implementation would mitigate any expected risk of State Exchanges having insufficient time to make necessary updates to their IT systems.

c. Effective Dates for Redeterminations Following Expiration of Inconsistency Period or Periodic Data Matching (§ 155.330(f)(3))
In § 155.330(f)(3), we propose effective date rules for eligibility redeterminations following the expiration of an inconsistency period or as part of the periodic data matching process described at § 155.330(e)(2). Currently, these rules are primarily enumerated in § 155.330(f)(3), which covers redeterminations that result in a decreased amount of APTC, or a change in the level of CSRs. We clarify that current § 155.330(f)(3) also applies in cases where an enrollee is redetermined newly ineligible for QHP, APTC, or CSRs. While current § 155.330(f)(3) does not explicitly refer to the end of an inconsistency period or periodic data matching processes, these situations are covered under § 155.330(f)(3) because they generally result in the removal or reduction of APTC.
Current regulations at § 155.330(f)(3) provide that such decreases in amount of APTC or in the level of CSRs must be effective the first of the month following the redetermination, unless the redetermination occurs after the 15th of the month, in which case the Exchange must delay the effective date by one month. At § 155.330(f)(3)(i), we are proposing to maintain these effective date rules in cases where an eligibility redetermination is the result of an inconsistency period expiring or a periodic data matching process ending, and such redetermination results in a decreased amount of APTC or decreased level of CSRs.
Consider an example in which an enrollee is found, through the periodic data matching process described in § 155.330(e)(2), to be enrolled in other MEC, and in which an Exchange notifies the enrollee regarding this updated information on May 20. In accordance with § 155.330(e)(2)(i)(B), an Exchange provides the enrollee with 30 days, or until June 19, to respond to their notice. If the enrollee has not responded by the end of this 30-day period, an Exchange must redetermine the enrollee's eligibility, in which case the enrollee would be determined ineligible for APTC because they are enrolled in other MEC. Under current § 155.330(f)(3), because this eligibility redetermination results in a decrease in APTC and occurs on June 19, the eligibility redetermination must be effective on August 1. Under proposed § 155.330(f)(3)(i), this rule would be maintained, and the eligibility determination would also be effective on August 1.
We also propose to maintain the rules currently at § 155.330(f)(3) for eligibility redeterminations following the end of an inconsistency period, where the redetermination results in decreased APTC or a decreased level of APTC or CSRs. In a similar example where an enrollee's 90-day inconsistency period expires on June 19, the resulting eligibility determination would continue to be effective on August 1.
We are proposing to keep these rules for several reasons. First, unlike cases where a consumer is reporting updated information to the Exchange, consumers whose APTC or CSRs are redetermined following the end of an inconsistency period or as part of the periodic data matching process are not actively engaged with the Exchange. Therefore, a delay between any reduction to the consumer's APTC or level of CSRs and the effective date of that redetermination is appropriate to give the Exchange sufficient time to communicate the upcoming change in eligibility to the consumer. Second, section 71303 of the WFTC legislation does not require Exchanges to update existing effective date rules for inconsistency period expiration or periodic data matching processes or to implement such redeterminations as soon as possible.
Finally, we have determined that maintaining these existing rules is operationally simpler for Exchanges than requiring a change to existing policy and operations. We acknowledge that the proposals in this rule would require Exchanges to make significant changes to their systems on a short timeline to meet statutory deadlines. To increase the likelihood that Exchanges can successfully implement the many changes already required by the WFTC legislation and that would be required by this proposed rule, and for the other reasons stated above, we propose to maintain the existing effective date policy with regard to periodic data matching and DMI expirations that result in a reduction in APTC or CSRs.
There are cases in which the expiration of an inconsistency period may instead result in the Exchange determining a consumer eligible for the same or an increased amount of APTC, or the same or a more generous level of CSRs. In accordance with § 155.315(f)(5), at the end of an inconsistency period, if an Exchange remains unable to verify an attestation, an Exchange must determine a consumer's eligibility based on information available from trusted data sources. In the case that the Exchange obtains income data from the Department of Treasury, as described in § 155.320(c)(1)(i) and (ii), but such data does not verify the consumer's attestation of their income, the Exchange must determine eligibility based on this data at the end of the consumer's inconsistency period. Depending on the consumer's income attestation and the data available to the
(
printed page 67680)
Exchange from the Department of Treasury, this could result in the Exchange determining the consumer eligible for more APTC or a more generous level of CSRs than provided during their inconsistency period. Currently, such redeterminations are subject to the effective date rules in § 155.330(f)(1)(i) and (f)(2). These current rules give Exchanges the option to either consider such redeterminations effective the first of the month following the date of the redetermination notice, or to delay the effective date by a month, if the redetermination occurred after the 15th of the month.
Additionally, given the proposals enumerated in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) and (iii), the end of an inconsistency period may result in no change to a consumer's APTC or CSR eligibility. For example, if a consumer has a DMI related to their enrollment in other MEC, and the Exchange determines in accordance with the requirements in § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) and (iii) that the enrollee cannot be provided with APTC or CSRs during their inconsistency period, then the expiration of such inconsistency period simply confirms the consumer's ineligibility for APTC or CSRs and does not result in an increase or decrease.
At § 155.330(f)(3)(ii), we propose that, for redeterminations following the expiration of an inconsistency period or periodic data matching that result in the same or an increased amount or level of APTC or CSRs, the Exchange be required to implement such redeterminations on the first of the month following the redetermination. This maintains the general requirement currently enumerated at § 155.330(f)(1) but removes the flexibility for Exchanges to delay such effective dates until the first of the following month afforded under § 155.330(f)(2).
We propose these rules regarding redeterminations following the expiration of an inconsistency period or periodic data matching that result in an increased amount or level of APTC or CSRs for several reasons. First, eliminating the flexibility currently permitted under § 155.330(f)(2) better ensures timely access to APTC and CSRs for eligible consumers. While enrollees in this scenario are not actively engaged with the Exchange, we see no reason to delay implementing a change that results in the same or more APTC or CSRs. In contrast, for a change that results in a decrease of APTC or CSRs, we determined a delay would be justified to ensure consumers receive timely notice. In addition, proposing to remove the flexibility currently permitted under § 155.330(f)(2) for these eligibility redeterminations aligns with our proposed effective date rules for enrollee-reported changes, described in section III.A.6.a. of this proposed rule, thereby promoting a consistent set of rules.
We seek comment on this proposal.

7. Annual Eligibility Redetermination (§ 155.335)
We propose to modify the title of this section to “Annual eligibility redetermination and re-enrollment.” We propose to amend § 155.335 by revising § 155.335(a) and (b); removing § 155.335(c) through (i); redesignating § 155.335(j) as new § 155.335(c); and removing § 155.335(k) through (n). Current § 155.335(a) through (i) and (k) through (n) include procedures required for an Exchange to annually redetermine eligibility for APTC and CSRs using the information previously provided by an enrollee in a QHP for the current plan year, or an earlier plan year, along with updated information from trusted data sources, when the enrollee does not contact the Exchange during the annual OEP to update their eligibility information. We are proposing to no longer permit these procedures.
Proposed § 155.335(a) would require Exchanges to redetermine the eligibility of an enrollee for enrollment in a QHP and for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, on an annual basis in accordance with § 155.305 and adhere to the existing notification standard for eligibility determinations under § 155.310(g). Proposed § 155.335(a)(1) would newly specify that for an Exchange to redetermine an enrollee eligible for APTC and CSRs for the subsequent plan year, the enrollee or the enrollee's application filer would be required to provide or confirm household income and family size; U.S. citizenship or status as a lawfully present eligible non-citizen, as applicable; eligibility for or enrollment in other MEC; and place of residence for the subsequent plan year on or after August 1 and no later than December 31 of the year preceding the applicable plan year, and the Exchange would verify the specified eligibility information using the processes in §§ 155.315 and 155.320, including the relevant provisions in those sections regarding DMIs.
We propose to modify § 155.335(b) to specify that the annual eligibility redetermination of QHP and for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, would be effective on the first day of the applicable plan year. We propose an exception to this effective date for the redetermination of APTC and CSRs in instances where an enrollee has an unresolved DMI under § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) as of December 31 of the year preceding the plan year and for whom APTC and CSRs are not provided during the inconsistency period. In these instances, we propose that the redetermination of APTC and CSRs under this part take effect in accordance with §§ 155.315(f)(4)(iv)(A) or 155.330(f)(3), as applicable.
Proposed § 155.335(c) would retain the QHP re-enrollment standards currently at § 155.335(j). We also clarify that under § 155.1200(b)(2), State Exchanges would still be required to submit information annually to HHS for HHS oversight on operations regarding § 155.335.
Section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation specifically states that the applicable enrollment information must be “provided or verified” by the individual and that, generally, the term coverage month does not include months “before the Exchange verifies” that information. As described previously, PTC is allowed only for months that are coverage months. Eligibility for PTC is determined after the end of each tax year, based on information, such as household income and family size, relating to the year of coverage. As a result, section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code, as added by section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation, applies to a tax year and contemplates that an Exchange must verify an individual's eligibility at least once every plan year before a month in the year can be a coverage month and any APTC or CSRs can be paid for that month. The statutory text further reinforces the year-by-year concept by utilizing the term “any individual” covered by a QHP, rather than limiting it to new enrollees. Further, by specifying that information be provided or verified by the “applicant” in the clause following the Exchange verification requirement, the text indicates that all applicants must

provide or confirm

the applicable enrollment information that is the basis of Exchange verifications at minimum as frequently as the Exchange must verify that information. Therefore, requiring individuals seeking to re-enroll in a QHP with APTC and CSRs to provide or confirm the applicable enrollment information pertaining to the subsequent plan year is consistent with the section 71303(a) amendment to section 36B(c).
Additionally, even if section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation did not require enrollees who are re-enrolling with APTC or CSRs to provide or confirm their information for each plan year, we would still propose this requirement under our authority in section 1411(f)(1)(B) of the Affordable Care Act, which directs the Secretary to establish procedures for redetermining eligibility on a periodic basis in appropriate circumstances, and section 1412(b)(1)(A) of the Affordable Care Act, which directs the Secretary to establish a program to make advance eligibility determinations for PTC. We have determined that annual redetermination of APTC and CSRs without an enrollee providing updated eligibility information or confirming existing information to the Exchange is no longer appropriate. We have determined that an enrollee should be required to provide or confirm their eligibility information for each plan year to be redetermined eligible for APTC and CSRs to improve the accuracy of APTC and CSR payments, mitigate the risk that enrollees receive APTC or CSRs for which they are no longer eligible, and protect enrollees from potential tax liability, as described in more detail later in this section.

Under § 155.335(a)(2)(iii), Exchanges may conduct annual redetermination in accordance with procedures approved by the Secretary of HHS based on a showing of the following: that the alternative procedures would facilitate continued enrollment in coverage for which the enrollee remains eligible, provide clear information about the process to the qualified individual or enrollee (including regarding any action by the qualified individual or enrollee necessary to obtain the most accurate redetermination of eligibility), and provide adequate program integrity protections.
Under § 155.335(a)(2)(ii) through (iii), all Exchanges have procedures in place that enable them to redetermine an enrollee's eligibility for enrollment in a QHP and APTC and CSRs, as applicable, for the subsequent plan year when an enrollee does not provide updated eligibility information to the Exchange for the subsequent plan year. Therefore, in all Exchanges, such an enrollee who is eligible for APTC or CSRs in a plan year may remain eligible for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, for the following plan year based on data available to the Exchange without providing any updated eligibility information. These current procedures result in redeterminations for APTC or CSRs based on information that may be considerably outdated. When Exchanges rely on prior plan year information or data obtained from trusted data sources only, it means the enrollee has not confirmed that such information remains accurate for purposes of redetermining their eligibility for the subsequent plan year. Given that eligibility for APTC and CSRs is highly sensitive to changes in income, family size, and other applicable eligibility criteria, reliance on information provided for a past plan year increases the likelihood of inaccurate eligibility determinations.
For example, consider an enrollee who provided a projected annual household income for PY 2026 in November 2025 and enrolled in PY 2026 coverage, but did not contact the Exchange during Open Enrollment for PY 2027. While Exchanges can produce an estimated PY 2027 annual household income derived from the PY 2026 income amount, or currently available data sources, an enrollee-provided projection for PY 2027 annual household income is more likely to accurately reflect the enrollee's anticipated financial and family circumstances. Unlike income estimates derived from prior-year information or currently available data sources, an enrollee-provided projection includes the enrollee's current knowledge of their financial situation for the subsequent plan year. Requiring enrollees to project their household income for the applicable benefit year and requiring Exchanges to verify the enrollee's projection reduces the likelihood of significant discrepancies between projected and actual income, thereby minimizing the risk of inaccurate APTC or CSR amounts being applied to the upcoming benefit year.
We have determined that requiring an enrollee to provide updated specified information for the applicable plan year or confirm that the specified eligibility information remains accurate to be redetermined eligible for APTC and CSRs would strengthen program integrity for the Exchanges. While section 71305 of the WFTC legislation removes the limitation on repayments of excess APTC, there are cost burdens to the IRS associated with recovering excess APTC. For example, there are enrollees who do not comply with the requirement to file a Federal income tax return and reconcile APTC. While the IRS has procedures to address non-compliance with tax filing requirements, the IRS must utilize resources to initiate these procedures and assess tax liability from excess APTC. These concerns are especially true when a current Exchange enrollment is improper or unauthorized and carried over into the next coverage year. Therefore, there is a significant program integrity benefit to the Federal Government by ensuring that all Exchange enrollees seeking financial assistance provide updated information or confirm their information remains an accurate basis upon which the Exchange can redetermine APTC or CSRs for the plan year.
Given the removal of the limitations on repayment of excess APTC under section 71305 of the WFTC legislation, we have also determined this annual requirement is critical to protecting enrollees from large potential tax liabilities. We expect that requiring enrollees to minimally confirm the
(
printed page 67682)
applicable eligibility information, or otherwise update the information, annually to be redetermined eligible for APTC and CSRs would help ensure that an enrollee's projected household income and other applicable eligibility criteria more accurately reflect the enrollee's expected circumstances for the subsequent plan year than current procedures. As a result, eligibility determinations would be based on more current information. In turn, APTC payments would be more closely aligned with the PTC that enrollees ultimately qualify for based on their actual household income for the plan year. We anticipate that more accurate APTC determinations would reduce the likelihood that consumers receive excess APTC and incur associated tax liability at reconciliation.
In addition, we previously finalized the requirements for enrollees to report changes that may affect their eligibility during the benefit year under § 155.330(b) in the Exchange Establishment Rule (
77 FR 18374
). Current § 155.330(b)(1) through (3) indicates that enrollees must report any changes relevant to the eligibility standards specified in § 155.305 within 30 days; however, enrollees who did not seek a determination for insurance affordability programs are not required to report changes affecting those programs, and the Exchange may set an income change threshold below which reporting is not required.
While the existing requirements under § 155.330(b) continue to apply, our proposed policy further strengthens our approach by requiring enrollees to provide or confirm specified eligibility information on an annual basis, and the Exchange to verify that information, to receive APTC and CSRs. Requiring this action on at least an annual basis ensures eligibility information is actively reviewed, rather than passively assumed to remain unchanged. Conditioning an enrollee's annual eligibility redetermination for APTC and CSRs on their affirmative provision or confirmation of eligibility information, and Exchange verification of that information, represents a more robust program integrity measure than the existing requirement under § 155.330(b) to report changes in circumstances within 30 days, which lacks an inherent enforcement mechanism to ensure enrollee compliance.
We are not proposing any changes to annual re-enrollment in QHPs because, as provided in section 36B(c)(5)(D) of the Code, which was added by section 71303 of the WFTC legislation, the new verification rules in section 36B(c)(5) of the Code do not affect an individual's ability to enroll in a QHP through an Exchange. We also have determined that it is appropriate under section 1411(f)(1)(B) of the Affordable Care Act to maintain this process. Annual automatic re-enrollment in health insurance plans continues to be an industry standard in the off-Exchange, unsubsidized individual and small-group markets. Continuing this practice in the Exchanges promotes continuous coverage. Exchanges would continue to be required to automatically re-enroll eligible individuals who do not make an active plan selection into a QHP under proposed § 155.335(c). This includes automatically re-enrolling individuals into a full-price QHP without APTC and CSRs, as well as re-enrolling individuals into a QHP with APTC and CSRs, if applicable, if the enrollee provided updated eligibility information pertaining to the subsequent plan year or confirmed that the prior plan year information remains accurate for the subsequent plan year and the Exchange verified that information, consistent with the requirements proposed under § 155.335(a)(1)(i) and (ii) of this subpart.
To be re-enrolled in a QHP through the Exchange with APTC and CSR, we propose that enrollees would be required to provide or confirm, and an Exchange would be required to verify, the specified eligibility criteria on or after August 1 preceding the coverage year. First, we propose the timing of this requirement to align with the start date of the proposed pre-OE verification period described in section III.A.9.c. of this proposed rule. In that section, we propose that Exchanges would be required to make available a verification period before the OEP to support applicants and enrollees in verifying certain eligibility information for the subsequent plan year. Aligning the start date for when enrollees would be required to verify certain information to be redetermined eligible for APTC and CSRs for the subsequent plan year with the start of the annual period intended to support verifications for the subsequent year would promote operational clarity and consistency for Exchanges, consumers, and other interested parties. In other words, we have determined that it would be clearest to consumers, agents, brokers, and other assisters that August 1 is the first day consumers, especially current enrollees, may begin providing information to the Exchange for purposes of verifying eligibility information for the subsequent plan year. We emphasize that enrollees would not be required to utilize the pre-OE verification period described in section III.A.9.c of the proposed rule and may instead provide or confirm their information during the OEP or until December 31 and have it verified by the Exchange to satisfy the requirement proposed in this section.
Second, we propose August 1 because it would increase the likelihood of accurate future year attestations by current enrollees and accurate verifications by Exchanges as compared to verification on an earlier date. For example, we are of the view that consumers are less likely to be able to reliably estimate their annual household income for the subsequent plan year earlier than August of the preceding year. Permitting Exchanges to conduct annual verifications earlier than August of the preceding year would also result in the use of older data than if verifications occur in August or later. For example, if an Exchange were to conduct verification procedures in May 2027 for purposes of determining eligibility for PY 2028, a data source available in May for coverage to begin in January, would make the data at least 8 months old.
Additionally, the IRS provides tax return data for the most recent tax year for which data is available to Exchanges once it becomes available. As a result, IRS tax return data accessed earlier in the year is more likely to reflect older income information compared to data accessed later in the year. We are concerned that permitting an earlier start date would decrease both the reliability of individuals' projected eligibility information and the accuracy of the Exchange's verification procedures, both of which this proposal is intended to improve. For example, for an enrollee who filed their Federal income tax return in March and reconciled past APTC, that latest income information is likely to be returned to an Exchange starting in May. However, for an enrollee who filed their Federal income tax return and reconciled past APTC near the April deadline or filed late, that latest income information is not likely to be returned to an Exchange starting in May or even June or July, depending on IRS processing. By August, we expect most tax filers without an extension are likely to have their latest tax data returned to the Exchange. Finally, a start date later than August 1 would mean enrollees have less time to provide or confirm their information and that there would be less time for Exchanges to verify it in time for January of the applicable plan year. Therefore, we are proposing on or after August 1 to reasonably balance all of these considerations.

However, we propose an exception to redeterminations of APTC and CSRs for instances when an enrollee has an unresolved DMI related to the applicable enrollment information and for whom APTC and CSRs cannot be provided during the inconsistency period as of December 31 of the year preceding the plan year. We propose that the effective date for the APTC and CSRs redeterminations in these instances where the redetermination occurs in the applicable benefit year, rather than before, follow the rules established in §§ 155.315(f)(4)(iv) or 155.330(f)(3), as applicable.

For example, consider an enrollee who confirms their information for plan year 2028 on October 1, 2027. The Exchange verifies their applicable enrollment information in real-time except for income and therefore, generates an income DMI under proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) that prevents APTC and CSRs from being provided during the inconsistency period. On December 31, 2027, the income DMI expires. The Exchange would redetermine eligibility for APTC and CSRs after the income DMI expires by relying on trusted data source information. In this scenario, IRS data indicates that the enrollee is eligible for APTC and CSRs, which is effective January 1 in accordance with proposed § 155.335(b). Now consider the same enrollee except they confirm their information for plan year 2028 on November 1, 2027. The enrollee's income DMI remains open as of December 31 and then expires on January 31, 2027. We recognize that Exchanges have invested in their enrollee communication infrastructure and eligibility and enrollment systems to operationalize and support the current annual redetermination policy. We acknowledge that implementation of this proposal would require Exchanges to modify existing enrollee communication and eligibility redetermination and re-enrollment processes. Specifically, Exchanges would likely need to make substantial system changes to update eligibility

We also anticipate that Exchanges would need to conduct system testing and validation activities after completing updates to ensure compliance with the requirements of this proposal.
Exchanges could choose to develop and implement processes designed to streamline the collection of applicable enrollment information for re-enrollees with APTC or CSRs. We anticipate that, over time, Exchanges would refine their processes and identify more efficient approaches to facilitate compliance, thus minimizing administrative burden on enrollees. For example, Exchanges could utilize the single streamlined application with pre-populated information from the enrollee's most recent application; design and implement a simplified application review mechanism that would make it easier for enrollees to review and confirm application information; provide previously submitted application information through alternative means, like a notice, that an enrollee would be required to respond to; or adopt a combination of these or other approaches, as appropriate, to best service their enrollee populations in meeting the proposed requirement. For strategies available to Exchanges for collecting the applicable enrollment information provided or confirmed by the enrollee, or their application filer, during the pre-OE verification period, see section III.A.9.c.vi. of this proposed rule.
We recognize that this proposal, if finalized, would require updates to issuers' enrollment projections and associated business procedures. We anticipate that issuers would need to modify operational and administrative processes, including coordinating more closely with Exchanges to reconcile enrollment transactions, process terminations and re-enrollments, and update enrollee communications. We also acknowledge that issuers may experience changes in enrollment patterns, including increased enrollee churn, which could affect risk pool predictability, particularly during the initial years of implementation.
Because of the longstanding policy of automatic re-enrollment with APTC or CSRs without required action by enrollees, many enrollees may continue to expect that their coverage with financial assistance will continue from year to year with no action required on their part. Enrollees who otherwise would have taken no action but must do so to remain eligible for APTC or CSRs under this proposed policy would have additional burden to provide or confirm their eligibility information, which may result in DMIs that require the submission of documents so the Exchange can verify information that could not be verified through a trusted data source. Some of these enrollees may not provide or confirm their information at all due to a lack of knowledge about this change in policy, which would result in a loss of APTC or CSRs. Enrollees who are automatically re-enrolled into QHP without APTC or CSRs would have the opportunity to update or confirm their eligibility determination during the plan year, in which case the Exchange would redetermine eligibility for APTC and CSRs in accordance with § 155.330(a). However, some portion of these enrollees would not be able to pay the full cost of enrollment which would prompt them to disenroll or be disenrolled for nonpayment of premiums, under the termination rules in § 155.430(b)(2)(ii). In this instance, such individuals would need a qualifying life event to re-enroll in a QHP outside of the yearly OEP through an SEP. With this in mind, we expect that the required notification under § 155.410(h), Exchange outreach, and extensive training for those assisting individuals with Exchange coverage, such as agents, brokers, and assisters, would be essential to minimizing the population of enrollees who do not provide or confirm their eligibility information with the Exchange at all and therefore lose financial assistance.
Similarly, we assume that many agents, brokers, and web-brokers have structured their staffing, outreach, client management practices, and operational workflows around existing automatic eligibility redetermination and re-enrollment practices. Changes to these procedures may necessitate adjustments to how agents, brokers, and web-brokers engage with clients, including increased efforts to prompt all of their enrollees to provide or confirm information for the subsequent plan year, which may impact their staffing needs and business costs. For example, some agents, brokers, and web-brokers who have historically adopted a staffing model focused on increasing seasonal support during the OEP may deem it necessary to expand the period of time during which they employ workers to include the pre-OE verification period to support all their clients. We expect the availability of the pre-OE verification period would support agents, brokers, and web-brokers in assisting their clients with meeting the proposed Exchange requirements for annual re-enrollment with APTC and CSRs. This is because the pre-OE verification period would give agents, brokers, and web-brokers three additional months to submit eligibility information to the Exchange on behalf of their clients and help their clients resolve DMIs, if they have them, for an applicable plan year. We also expect that agents, brokers, and web-brokers would identify opportunities to improve the services they provide within the shifting landscape to set themselves apart from their competitors.
Despite the costs associated with these groups making necessary modifications for this proposal, we have determined that the proposed change is critical to ensuring the integrity and accuracy of Exchange redeterminations and authorization of APTC and CSRs across plan years. As described in this section, we have determined that requiring enrollees to annually provide or confirm their eligibility information strengthens Exchange program integrity and better aligns APTC determinations with PTC determinations. Additionally, it would help protect enrollees from potentially significant tax liabilities at reconciliation, particularly given the removal of repayment limitations. In addition, this proposal would bring Exchange operations into closer alignment with the statutory framework established under the WFTC legislation. We seek comment on these proposals.

As background, HHS' regulations currently require that, on FFEs and SBE-FPs, and in State Exchanges that adopt a binder payment policy, the deadline for making the binder payment must be within a specified range:
(1) For enrollments with regular coverage effective dates, the deadline must be no earlier than the coverage effective date, and no later than 30 calendar days from the coverage effective date;
(2) For enrollments with special effective dates,

the deadline must be no earlier than the coverage effective date and no later than 30 calendar days from the date the issuer receives the enrollment transaction or the coverage effective date, whichever is later; and
(3) For enrollments with retroactive effective dates, the deadline must be no earlier than 30 calendar days from the date the issuer receives the enrollment transaction. In addition, effectuation of retroactive coverage requires payment of premium for all retroactive months of coverage through the first prospective month, and if only one month's premium is paid, coverage is effectuated prospectively.
In the 2015 Payment Notice (
79 FR 30240
), HHS established in § 155.400(e) that Exchanges may, and the FFE and SBE-FPs must, require payment of the first month's premium to effectuate an enrollment. In the 2016 Payment Notice (
80 FR 10750
), HHS established the initial requirements regarding deadlines for making the binder payment under regular coverage effective dates (no earlier than the coverage effective date, and no later than 30 calendar days from the coverage effective date), and special effective dates (30 days from the date the issuer received the enrollment transaction). These rules were updated in the 2017 Payment Notice (
81 FR 12204
), to provide that, for making the binder payment under special effective date rules, the deadline may be no earlier than the coverage effective date and no later than 30 calendar days from the date the issuer receives the enrollment transaction or the coverage effective date, whichever is later. HHS also established the rules regarding making the binder payment for retroactive enrollments.
HHS established the binder payment rules to ensure a consistent process on the FFE for collection of the first month's premium by issuers. HHS further established specific deadlines for issuers to collect binder payments to balance the interests of flexibility for issuers in collecting premiums (traditionally a business decision made by issuers), and consumer protection. The rules that we established balanced these needs by ensuring that issuers could not require payment of the first month's premium earlier than the coverage effective date, but also that they must require payment within 30 days. For retroactive enrollments, which may require payment of multiple months of premiums, the rule ensured that consumers would have at least 30 days from the date the issuer received the enrollment transaction to pay the binder payment, while also providing flexibility to issuers to set a later payment due date.
