b. Plan Selection in the Case of Certain DMIs (§ 155.400(i))
We are proposing to add new § 155.400(i) to require that Exchanges permit applicants and enrollees to “pend” their plan selection until the information for DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information is verified.
As described in section III.A.4.b. of this proposed rule, we propose that Exchanges may not be permitted to authorize payment for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, for applicants and enrollees who have DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information until that information is verified. While applicants and enrollees with these DMIs may choose to enroll in full-cost coverage through an Exchange according to the effective date rules described at §§ 155.410 and 155.420 while the DMI is pending, some may be unable to afford to do so. Therefore, we propose to require Exchanges to permit applicants and enrollees to “pend” their plan selection during their inconsistency period such that the plan selection is only sent to the issuer, and QHP coverage only becomes effective, after the Exchange determines the applicant or enrollee eligible for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, as described by § 155.315(f)(4)(iv) or § 155.315(f)(5). For a discussion of when an applicant's or enrollee's pended plan selection (PPS) would become effective, refer to section III.A.9. of this proposed rule.
As background, a PPS is an option provided to applicants utilizing the FFE and SBE-FPs today while their SEP pre-enrollment verification, referred to as SEP Verification, is in progress. Currently, new applicants enrolling through the FFE and SBE-FPs can pend a plan selection after submitting an application that requires SEP Verification in accordance with § 155.420(g). New applicants subject to SEP Verification generate a special enrollment period verification issue (SEP verification issue) and are required to provide documentation to an Exchange demonstrating that they have experienced an SEP qualifying event before they can enroll in QHP coverage. New applicants are permitted to select and “pend” the QHP they would like to be enrolled in upon resolution of their SEP verification issue so they do not have to return to the Exchange to select a plan and enroll after their SEP verification issue is resolved. These PPSs are stored within an Exchange's records only and are released to the issuer upon successful resolution of the applicant's SEP verification issue. We have determined that a similar process is needed to allow applicants to pend QHP enrollments when they are not eligible to receive APTC or CSRs during an inconsistency period for DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information because applicants may be unwilling or unable to enroll in a full price QHP during that period. Therefore, we propose that an Exchange would be required to allow applicants and enrollees to elect to pend a plan selection that would be released to the issuer if and when the Exchange determines the applicant or enrollee eligible for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, as described by § 155.315(f)(4)(iv) or § 155.315(f)(5). This would streamline the enrollment process for applicants and enrollees who elect not to enroll in a full-price QHP during their inconsistency period
(
printed page 67688)
because it would remove the burden of them returning to an Exchange to enroll in a plan once the relevant DMIs are resolved. Under our proposed rule, applicants and enrollees would also have the option to enroll in a full-price QHP during the inconsistency period, which, as of today, could be selected in a single session along with the application submission.
We note that this policy is particularly important for individuals who enroll using an SEP. As described in section III.A.4.b. of this proposed rule, applicants and enrollees with a DMI related to the applicable enrollment information would have a 90-day window to resolve their DMI. Upon resolution of their DMIs by an Exchange, as described in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii), such applicants or enrollees could start receiving APTC and CSRs, if otherwise eligible. In contrast, individuals enrolling through an SEP generally have only 60 days from the triggering event to select a plan. For example, if an applicant becomes newly eligible to enroll in a QHP on March 1, they would generally have until April 30, which is 60 days from the date they became eligible to enroll in a QHP, to select a QHP using that SEP. If, on April 30, this applicant submits an application to enroll through the SEP and also generates a DMI related to the applicable enrollment information, then this applicant would have a 90-day inconsistency period until July 29 to provide documentation to an Exchange to resolve their DMI. In this scenario, if the applicant used any of the 90-day period to resolve their DMI and did not have the opportunity to pend their enrollment, they would be unable to enroll in a plan after an Exchange resolved their DMI because the 90-day inconsistency period would begin after the 60-day SEP window to select a plan ended.
We have similar concerns regarding the mismatch between inconsistency period timelines and enrollment period timelines for applications submitted during the OEP. Based on policies proposed elsewhere in this rule, starting with the PY 2028, applicants and enrollees seeking to enroll with APTC and CSRs would miss the opportunity to enroll during OEP if an Exchange does not resolve their DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information before the end of the OEP, unless they are permitted to pend their plan selections. For example, suppose on December 15 an applicant applies for QHP coverage and financial assistance which generates a DMI related to the applicable enrollment information, the applicant provides documentation to resolve the DMI on January 5, and it takes an Exchange 15 days to resolve the DMI which occurs January 20. If the applicant waits until their DMI is resolved to enroll in a QHP, then (absent an SEP) they would be unable to enroll because OEP would have already ended if the Exchange has a January 15 OEP end date. Despite Exchanges' best efforts to create efficient processes for DMI resolution, the potential for Exchange backlogs and delays in processing documents creates a risk that many DMIs generated during the OEP will not be resolved before the end of the OEP for reasons beyond the applicant or enrollee's control. Therefore, permitting PPSs is crucial for applicants and enrollees who cannot, or do not want to, enroll in an unsubsidized QHP during an inconsistency period when APTC and CSRs cannot be paid.
To address these concerns, we are proposing to add new § 155.400(i), so that an Exchange would be required to: (1) accept a QHP selection from applicants and enrollees with DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information; and (2) at the option of the applicant or enrollee, transmit to a QHP issuer the enrollment information necessary to enable the QHP issuer to enroll the consumer only upon the Exchange determining the applicant or enrollee eligible for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, as described by § 155.315(f)(4)(iv) or § 155.315(f)(5).
We are adding, “at the option of the consumer” language, to make it clear that an applicant also has the option to enroll in full price QHP coverage during the inconsistency period for a DMI related to the applicable enrollment information if they so choose. Additionally, we note that some households may have DMIs that only prevent APTC and CSRs for some household members and not others (such as those related to eligibility or enrollment in other coverage), in which case APTC would be payable but the total amount of APTC payable during the inconsistency period would be lower than if the information related to the DMI was verified. In this circumstance, all household members may want to enroll in a QHP during the inconsistency period as they would not be required to pay the full cost.
We seek comment on this proposal. We understand that State Exchanges may find it challenging to implement these requirements for PY 2028. Therefore, we are considering providing flexibility to State Exchanges to delay implementation of the proposed PPS requirements until PY 2029. In particular, we seek comment from State Exchanges and other interested parties on the operational burden these proposed requirements would create and whether flexibility is needed to provide sufficient time for State Exchanges to build appropriate IT systems. We additionally welcome suggestions on equivalent alternatives to PPS for State Exchanges that would accomplish the same goal.
Furthermore, we are also considering allowing the release of the PPS at the end of the inconsistency period when an applicant has failed to verify their attested information and an Exchange redetermines the applicant ineligible for APTC and CSRs based on trusted data sources as described in § 155.315(f)(5). We are concerned that applicants may not have alternate paths to coverage when their DMI is expired outside of the OEP and we want to preserve applicants' access to health insurance even without financial assistance. The applicant would still have the ability to cancel their plan if they do not wish to maintain the coverage without assistance.
We seek comment from State Exchanges and other interested parties on whether a PPS should also be released when applicants are redetermined ineligible for APTC and CSRs at the end of their inconsistency period or if applicants should be given an option at point of application to decide if they would like their PPS to be released without APTC or CSRs at the end of their inconsistency period. We also seek comment from State Exchanges and other interested parties on other situations where releasing a PPS before the end of the inconsistency period might be warranted and options for doing so.

If all DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information are resolved (and APTC and CSR eligibility, as applicable, is verified) after January 15, and between the 1st and 15th of the current month, the applicant's QHP would be effective the first of the month in which the resolution occurs. If the resolutions occur between January 1 and January 15, the applicant's pended plan selection would be effective starting January 1. If the DMIs are resolved by an Exchange between January 16 and January 31, the applicant's pended plan selection would be effective on February 1. For a resolution in February, if the DMIs are resolved by an Exchange between February 1 and February 15, the applicant's pended plan selection would be effective on February 1. We propose these rules for the following reasons. Under the proposed new DMI process described in section III.A.4.b. of this proposed rule, some applicants who newly apply or update their application during the annual OEP would receive DMIs that result in APTC and CSRs being withheld until the DMI is resolved by an Exchange. While some consumers may have their DMIs resolved by an Exchange during the pre-OE verification period described in section III.A.9.c. of this proposed rule, or during the annual OEP, there might be others who have DMIs resolved after the end of the annual OEP. This would mean that APTC and CSRs may not be available on the consumer's otherwise-permitted coverage effective date. As a result, and as described in section III.A.8.b. of this proposed rule, we propose that applicants would have the choice to pend their plan selection until all DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information are resolved by an Exchange if they prefer to only enroll once they are determined eligible for APTC and CSRs, as applicable. For such consumers, these proposed rules provide clarity regarding when their QHP coverage, APTC, and CSRs must become effective, once their DMIs are resolved.
The proposals in this section are intended to align with existing OEP effective date rules to the extent possible. We propose that coverage become effective in accordance with applicants' original coverage effective dates even if the applicant's DMIs are not resolved until 15 days later to prevent applicants' coverage from being delayed due to the time it takes for Exchanges to review and verify documentation. Given the large volume of applicants who apply for January 1 coverage during the annual OEP and the potential for Exchanges to have backlogs of documents to process, we want to ensure that if, for example, a consumer submits documents to verify their DMI related to the applicable enrollment information by the December 15 deadline for January 1 coverage, that their QHP coverage can begin on January 1, even if the Exchange cannot resolve the DMI until later in January—for example, because the Exchange needed to request different or additional documents from the consumer.
In instances where DMIs generated during OEP are not resolved by an Exchange until more than 15 days after their originally prescribed coverage effective date, this proposed policy attempts to balance the benefits of immediate coverage availability to a consumer with the potential harms imposed by requiring consumers to pay premiums for past periods of coverage, when the coverage could not have been meaningfully used by the consumer. We also carefully considered the potential impacts of this policy on adverse selection and market stability. If we permit coverage to extend too far retroactively, then consumers may have an incentive to wait and see whether they incur medical bills before submitting documents to resolve their DMIs, which would have a negative impact on the risk pool. By proposing to limit retroactive coverage to a maximum of 15 calendar days, we limit potential adverse selection as it would not be practical for consumers to wait until they incur medical bills to submit documents because consumers could not be assured that an Exchange would resolve their DMI within the same 15-day period. We seek comment regarding whether consumers should instead be permitted to enroll in a QHP and access APTC and CSRs on their originally prescribed coverage effective date regardless of when their DMIs are resolved, and if so, what strategies HHS should consider to mitigate adverse selection and promote market stability.
We also considered proposing that, in instances where an applicant pends a plan selection during the annual OEP and resolves their DMIs after their otherwise-prescribed effective date, plan selections would become effective on the day that all DMIs were resolved. Like our proposal, this approach would balance the benefits of immediate coverage availability with the harms imposed by requiring consumers to pay premiums for past periods of coverage
(
printed page 67691)
and would limit risks of adverse selection. However, we are of the view that requiring mid-month effective dates would be administratively challenging for issuers and Exchanges, given that it would require them to prorate APTC and premiums.
We have determined that this proposal minimizes administrative burdens on both Exchanges and issuers associated with providing retroactive coverage. If coverage effective dates for a pended plan selection made during the OEP were always extended back to the consumer's original coverage effective date, then issuers might struggle to collect multiple months of past premiums from new enrollees and may need to expend excessive resources to appropriately administer cost-sharing reductions for months of previous medical bills. We are of the view that these proposals balance the interests of consumers to have coverage start in a timely manner and not owe premiums for months of coverage they did not meaningfully utilize, and the interests of Exchanges and issuers to maintain a stable risk pool and limit administrative burden.
Finally, we considered whether section 36B(c) of the Code would require coverage effective dates retroactive to the consumer's original coverage effective date regardless of when an Exchange resolves their DMI. Sections 36B(c)(2) and (5) of the Code relate to when a month can be a coverage month for purposes of the PTC. Section 36B(c)(2)(A)(i) of the Code requires an individual to be enrolled in a QHP as of the first of a month before the month can be a coverage month. Section 36B(c)(5)(A) of the Code provides, in relevant part, that a coverage month does not include any month that begins before the Exchange verifies an individual's eligibility to enroll in a QHP and for APTC. Section 36B(c)(5)(D) provides that an individual shall not be treated as ineligible to enroll in a QHP for a month solely because of failing to meet the requirements of section 36B(c)(5) for the month. We read these requirements to mean that months prior to verification must be treated as coverage months if they would otherwise be considered coverage months under the requirements prescribed in section 36B(c) of the Code, including the requirement that an individual be enrolled in a QHP as of the first of the month. Section 36B does not relate to coverage effective dates and cannot reasonably be read to require HHS to prescribe specific coverage effective dates.
In section III.A.4.b. of this proposed rule, we describe our proposal to implement section 36B(c)(5)(C) of the Code by requiring Exchanges to provide APTC and CSRs, as applicable, for all months prior to verification that the applicant was enrolled in a QHP, as long as the Exchange verified all eligibility criteria described in proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) for such months. The authority to permit pended plan selections, and to prescribe reasonable effective dates for those pended plan selections, is drawn from the broad authority to offer enrollment periods and to operate Exchanges afforded to HHS in sections 1311(c)(6) and 1321(a) of the Affordable Care Act, and Exchange enrollment period and coverage effective date rules are not explicitly addressed in section 71303 of the WFTC legislation.
Under the authority afforded to HHS under sections 1311(c)(6) and 1321(a) of the Affordable Care Act, and for the reasons described in this section, we propose to add § 155.410(f)(5) to provide effective date rules for consumers who pend their plan selections during the annual OEP.
We seek comment on this proposal. We understand State Exchanges may find it challenging to implement these requirements for PY 2028. Therefore, we specifically seek comment from State Exchanges regarding any risks that State Exchanges will not be able to implement these proposed effective date rules by PY 2028, and whether there are alternative proposals that could achieve similar outcomes while alleviating operational burden.
c. Annual Pre-Open Enrollment Verification Period (§ 155.410(h))
(i) Overview
Section 71303(b) of the WFTC legislation adds section 36B(c)(3)(A)(ii) of the Code modifying the definition of “qualified health plan” to provide that, for purposes of PTC, the term will not include any plan enrolled through an Exchange that fails to provide a verification period that begins not later than August 1 prior to the beginning of the OEP each year. Absent the establishment of a verification period beginning not later than August 1 before the upcoming plan year, no PTC (and therefore no APTC or CSRs) would be allowed for the coverage of enrollees in plans offered by the Exchange for the plan year.
Because providing access to APTC and CSRs for enrollees is one of the fundamental purposes of an Exchange, we have determined that it is necessary that all Exchanges make a pre-OE verification process available. Thus, we are proposing to require that all Exchanges make this new pre-OE verification period available to applicants prior to the 2028 plan year on August 1, 2027. Also, it is important to note that neither the statute nor the regulatory changes we are proposing require consumers to participate in a pre-OE verification process, only that Exchanges make such a process available.
We propose to add new § 155.410(h), which would require Exchanges to make available a pre-OE verification period that begins on August 1 each year for purposes of verifying certain consumer eligibility criteria for the following plan year. The first pre-OE verification period would start on August 1, 2027, in advance of PY 2028. The pre-OE period would end the day before the OE period for the plan year begins. For example, the pre-OE period would end on October 31 for Exchanges where the OE period begins on November 1.
During the pre-OE verification period, we propose at § 155.410(h)(2) that Exchanges would be required to allow consumers to provide their information, including, at a minimum, their household income, citizenship or lawful presence, incarceration status, and place of residence. Added section 36(B)(c)(3)(A)(ii) of the Code requires Exchanges to provide a process through which applicants may “verify” eligibility information “with the Exchange.” In proposed § 155.410(h), we reserve the term “verify” for the role of the Exchange to avoid confusion about which subject of the statute (that is, “the Exchange” or “the applicant”) we are referring to when using the term “verify.” In proposed § 155.410(h)(2), we use the term “provide” to represent “the applicant's” role in the process to “verify with the Exchange.”

the pre-OE period the Exchange would be required to enable consumers to provide and confirm their eligibility information which may come in the form of attestations or documents including an attestation that previously provided information remains the same.
For consumers who choose to provide eligibility information to an Exchange during the pre-OE verification period, we propose in § 155.410(h)(3) that Exchanges would be required to follow the verification procedures in §§ 155.315 and 155.320 for verifying such information. Specifically, for information that is required to be verified using trusted data sources and, for which verification is unsuccessful, Exchanges would be required to follow the proposed DMI procedures in § 155.315(f) (see section III.A.4.b. of this proposed rule for more information).
(ii) Timing (§ 155.410(h)(1))
While section 71303(b) of the WFTC legislation specifies that the pre-OE verification period must start no later than August 1 of the year preceding the coverage year, we propose in § 155.410(h)(1) that all Exchanges start their annual pre-OE verification period on August 1 each year and no earlier. We are of the view that a start date prior to August 1 may be too early for consumers to make informed projections of their household income and family size for the following year. While the IRS generally makes updated tax data available on a rolling basis as it processes returns, the IRS' updated failure to file and reconcile codes for the previous tax year are not available until the last week of July. Exchanges may need to again use these codes to determine APTC eligibility for PY 2028 and beyond, given the changes to coverage month made by section 36B(c)(6) of the Code. Furthermore, limiting eligibility verification for the future year to August 1 or later would facilitate the use of more recent data for the verification process. Finally, we have determined that an August 1 start date for the pre-OE verification period would best accommodate the annual implementation timelines of plan-year specific policy changes required by legislation and regulations. For example, each year Exchanges make changes to eligibility logic in their systems for the following coverage year based on the annual publication of the final HHS Notice of Benefit and Payment Parameters (typically April of each year) and the annual publication of the IRS revenue procedure providing the indexing adjustment for the applicable percentage table and the required contribution percentage. (For PY 2026, the revenue procedure was released by the IRS on July 18, 2025). We request comment on whether Exchanges should be allowed to start pre-OE verification periods earlier, especially if State Exchanges have evidence that an earlier start date would work better for their markets.
Section 71303(b) of the WFTC legislation does not specify an end date for the pre-OE verification period. Thus, we propose in § 155.410(h)(1) that the pre-OE verification period ends as soon as an Exchange's OEP starts, to account for the fact that State Exchanges have varying OEP start dates that begin before November 1.
We seek comment on this proposal.
(iii) Collection of Information (§ 155.410(h)(2))
Section 71303(b) of the WFTC legislation specifies that during the pre-OE period, applicants must have the opportunity to verify household income and eligibility for enrollment in a QHP. We therefore propose that the minimum information that Exchanges would be required to allow consumers to provide or confirm prior to the OE period is limited to household income, as that is mentioned specifically in section 71303(b) of the WFTC legislation, and citizenship or lawful presence status, incarceration status, and residency, as those are the criteria pertinent to eligibility for enrollment in a QHP. Minimizing the information that Exchanges would accept during the pre-OE period is intended to give Exchanges flexibility to design this period in the manner most appropriate for their consumers and their operations. However, the proposed rule at § 155.410 does not reduce the amount of information that the Exchange would collect to adjudicate an applicant's eligibility for insurance affordability programs in accordance with § 155.305. Therefore, while we do not propose to require that Exchanges collect or verify information beyond what is specified in section 71303(b) of the WFTC legislation during the pre-OE period, an Exchange may find it more efficient to include additional information collection in their pre-OE process. For example, Exchanges may find value in collecting information during the pre-OE period about an applicant's expected tax filing status, eligibility for other MEC, and their compliance with tax reconciliation requirements to determine APTC and CSR eligibility. The Exchange may seek to collect AI/AN status for purposes of CSR eligibility.
For first-time applicants, the Exchange would also need to collect identifying information from the applicant—such as name, birthdate, and SSN (if the applicant has one)—for purposes of verifying eligibility using electronic data sources, as described in §§ 155.315 and 155.320. We have determined that because section 71303(b) of the WFTC legislation specifies that an Exchange provides a pre-enrollment verification process during which “any applicant” may verify their eligibility, an Exchange may not restrict the pre-OE verification period only to current enrollees.
While we do not construe section 71303(b) of the WFTC legislation to require Exchanges to permit consumers to provide all information that could impact their eligibility for insurance affordability programs, we expect that collecting information about all relevant eligibility criteria during pre-OE would reduce consumer burden and unnecessary operational steps for Exchanges. Note that if an Exchange chooses not to collect and verify information on consumer eligibility or enrollment in MEC during the pre-OE verification period, then the Exchange would not have sufficient information to make APTC or CSR eligibility determinations during the pre-OE period for any applicant or re-enrollee. As described in section III.A.4.b. of this proposed rule, starting in 2028, Exchanges would be required to verify eligibility for or enrollment in MEC prior to providing APTC and CSRs. As described in section III.A.7. of this proposed rule, a current enrollee would be required to provide or confirm their eligibility for, or enrollment in, other MEC annually as part of the annual redetermination process to be determined eligible for APTC and CSRs for a subsequent plan year. Therefore, for applicants or enrollees seeking an eligibility determination for insurance affordability programs during the pre-OE verification period, the Exchange would need to request additional information regarding eligibility for or enrollment in other MEC. This additional information would include not only an attestation and verification of whether the applicant is currently enrolled in other coverage, but also the collection of information related to potential Medicaid and CHIP eligibility (such as pregnancy and former foster care status) required to determine whether the consumer should be assessed or determined eligible for Medicaid or CHIP rather than for APTC

and CSRs. As noted in § 155.410(h)(3)(ii), we propose that when making an eligibility determination during the pre-OE period, an Exchange would be required to comply with the standards for eligibility determinations established at § 155.305, including paragraphs (c), (d), and (e), which require the Exchange to determine eligibility for Medicaid, CHIP and BHP.
For re-enrollees, Exchanges may be able to perform a full information collection in a streamlined format, such as by permitting a re-enrollee to attest that they have had no changes since the previous year. In this proposed rule, we propose to defer to Exchanges on the extent and method of information collection beyond the minimum criteria designated in the statute. We provide additional information on implementation strategies in subsection (vi) of this section.
We seek comment on whether the information collection requirements should be different for returning enrollees as compared to consumers new to an Exchange.
(iv) Verification and Determination (§ 155.410(h)(3))
In § 155.410(h)(3), we propose that Exchanges would be required to attempt to verify information collected during the pre-OE verification period using the verification procedures in §§ 155.315 and 155.320. If verification using a trusted data source is required and is unsuccessful, Exchanges would be required to follow the proposed DMI procedures in § 155.315(f), which, in most cases, require the Exchange to resolve the DMI prior to the consumer receiving APTC or CSRs. If a consumer generates a DMI during the pre-OE verification period, we note that an Exchange may extend the 90/95-day inconsistency period under existing authority described in § 155.315(f)(3) but recommend that Exchanges not provide extensions that would enable the inconsistency period to go beyond December 15 to align with the date that consumers using Exchanges on the Federal Platform must generally select a plan to begin coverage on January 1. However, we are still assessing the best date for these extensions and request comment, especially from State Exchanges, on this recommendation. Consumers who utilize the pre-OE verification period to verify their information prior to OE are likely demonstrating a good faith effort to obtain their documentation and verify their information, as they are doing so ahead of the beginning of the plan year, when they could instead wait until the annual OEP to provide information for the subsequent year.
Operationally, such extensions may facilitate a smoother enrollment process, specifically in cases where the DMI generated during the pre-OE period has a 90/95-day inconsistency period that ends either before or during the Open Enrollment period and before the deadline for a January 1st effective date in the future coverage year. If an Exchange successfully verifies information for the criteria described in proposed § 155.335(a)(1) through (4), then consumers may be eligible for APTC and CSRs, as applicable, upon their coverage effective date.
However, Exchanges maintain the authority to decide whether a consumer is demonstrating a good faith effort to obtain documentation. If an Exchange finds evidence that a consumer, or a non-Exchange entity or authorized representative assisting the consumer, is submitting suspicious or false documentation or attempting to manipulate the application to circumvent DMI document submission requirements, the Exchange may find that the consumer (or person or entity assisting the consumer) is not demonstrating a good faith effort to obtain documentation and therefore may rescind or refuse to provide an extension to the inconsistency period under this authority.
Allowing Exchanges to extend the inconsistency period for consumers who generate DMIs during the pre-OE verification period is necessary to reduce administrative burden on applicants and operational complexity for Exchanges because individuals who generate DMIs during the pre-OE verification period may have 90/95-day inconsistency periods that end before December 15, which is the date that consumers using Exchanges on the Federal Platform must generally select a plan by to receive coverage starting January 1. If an individual does not resolve their DMI by the end of the 90/95-day period, Exchanges would be required by § 155.315(f)(5) to redetermine eligibility based on trusted data sources, often resulting in the individual being redetermined ineligible for a QHP, and APTC and CSRs, as applicable. As a result, consumers would likely re-submit an application during the OEP, which would restart the entire DMI process, even though their attestation likely remained unchanged. This process would impose administrative burden on applicants, who would have to submit a new application to start another 90/95 DMI period, and operational complexity for Exchanges, who would have to process two DMIs based on the same attestation instead of one.
Furthermore, this optional extension for DMIs generated during the pre-OE verification period is distinct from the former 60-day extension for household annual income DMIs outlined in the 2025 Marketplace Integrity and Affordability final rule because the optional extension is for the specific population of consumers who generates DMIs during the pre-OE verification period rather than the entire population who generate an annual income DMI. Unlike the automatic 60-day extension for annual household income DMIs, the optional extension would not be granted for DMIs generated during the OEP or any SEP.
We read section 71303 of the WFTC legislation to require an Exchange to make an information collection and verification process available during the pre-OE verification period, but not to require an Exchange to make an eligibility determination. If an Exchange collects only the minimum information outlined in proposed § 155.410(h)(2)(i) during the pre-OE verification period, then the Exchange would have sufficient information to determine eligibility for enrollment in a QHP but would not have sufficient information to make an eligibility determination for insurance affordability programs. We expect that the most useful way for Exchanges to collect information during the pre-OE verification period would be to use the single streamlined application as described in proposed § 155.410(h)(2)(ii). We also expect that, for many Exchanges, the operational burden of creating a new pre-OE verification period would be reduced if the Exchange makes use of its existing application infrastructure rather than designing something new. In § 155.410(h)(3)(ii), we propose to require Exchanges to make an eligibility determination in accordance with §§ 155.305 and 155.310 during the pre-OE verification period if they collect and verify sufficient information to do so.
Thus, the proposed rule would require that, when making eligibility determinations during the pre-OE verification period, Exchanges adhere to the timeliness and notice standards at § 155.310(e) and (g) as well as the requirements in paragraph (d) of that section related to eligibility determinations for insurance affordability programs. This would include transmitting account transfers to the State Medicaid or CHIP agency in the case of an assessment or determination that an applicant is eligible for Medicaid or CHIP. Still, we
(
printed page 67694)
also seek to maintain flexibility for Exchanges that have a different view of how to make the pre-OE verification period most useful and efficient. We request comment on this proposed requirement, especially from State Exchanges.
We note that for many Exchanges, including those operating on the Federal platform, QHP data for the upcoming plan year would not be available during much or all of the pre-OE verification period. If future year plan data is unavailable when an Exchange verifies a consumer's information, an Exchange would not have the Second Lowest Cost Silver Plan (SLCSP) information required to determine any applicable amount of APTC. Therefore, when a consumer provides eligibility information to an Exchange during the pre-OE verification period, an Exchange would need to process and verify that information but may not have sufficient information available to determine the amount of APTC for which the consumer may be eligible. We acknowledge that there are drawbacks to communicating an APTC eligibility result to an applicant prior to calculating an APTC amount. For example, an individual may be determined eligible for APTC during the pre-OE verification period but, once SLCSP information is available, the amount of APTC for which they qualify is $0. In contrast, before plan data is available, an Exchange would be able to make a determination regarding an applicant's eligibility for CSRs and the level of CSRs for which they qualify as described in § 155.305(g). Unlike APTC, the available amount of CSRs is based on the household's projected annual income without regard to the cost of the SLCSP.
If an Exchange notifies a consumer of their eligibility determination without providing an APTC amount because plan data is not yet available, then the Exchange would need to communicate the APTC amount to the consumer once plan data becomes available. We are of the view that Exchanges must determine the best method for providing that amount in accordance with their operations and preferred communication channels, so long as consumers are entitled to appeal rights regarding the determination of their APTC amount once it is available.
We seek comment on this proposal.
(v) Plan Selection
If an Exchange does have certified plan data available during the pre-OE verification period, that Exchange could permit consumers to view plan information and indicate their preferred plan ahead of the OEP. The Exchange could store the consumer's plan selection and transmit it to the issuer once the OEP begins or confirm the consumer's preferred plan during the OEP prior to transmitting it to the issuer. This could reduce the burden on consumers, and on individuals assisting consumers with the application and enrollment process, because consumers who use the pre-OE verification period would not have to return to an Exchange website or call center during the OEP to select a plan and enroll for the upcoming plan year. A consumer would still be allowed to update their application and change plans during the OEP.
Under this proposal, if an Exchange allows an applicant to select a plan during the pre-OE verification period, that selection could be a full-price plan without APTC or CSRs (either because applicable enrollment information was not verified or because the applicant was not eligible for APTC or CSRs), a plan with verified APTC or CSRs applied, or a plan with APTC or CSRs for which enrollment would be pended until all DMIs described in § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) are resolved. We propose adding § 155.400(i) to describe the option for consumers to “pend” a plan selection such that it would only be transmitted to the issuer if and when applicable DMIs are resolved, as described in section III.A.8.b. of this proposed rule. We also note that we outline the proposed Exchanges' re-enrollment requirements for existing enrollees who do not select a plan for the upcoming year in proposed § 155.335.
We acknowledge the logistical and operational barriers to having certified plan data available prior to the OEP, including issuer rate-setting timelines, State Department of Insurance review timelines, and certification timelines. As noted previously, QHP data for the upcoming plan year would likely not be available at the start of the pre-OE verification period for Exchanges operating on the Federal platform.
We seek comment on this proposal.

10. Special Enrollment Periods (§ 155.420)
We propose to add § 155.420(b)(6) to provide the effective dates for coverage if a consumer qualifies for an SEP and elects to pend their enrollment until all DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information are resolved by an Exchange. Currently, § 155.420(b) describes the coverage effective dates that are applicable for consumers enrolling under an SEP based on the SEP type and the trigger date for the SEP. We propose that if an Exchange resolves a consumer's DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information prior to the effective date specified in § 155.420(b)(1) through (b)(3), then the consumer's coverage effective date would be the date specified in § 155.420(b)(1) through (b)(3). However, if the DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information are resolved by an Exchange after the applicable coverage effective date described in § 155.420(b)(1) through (3), then the new proposed rule at in § 155.420(b)(6) would apply. Under proposed § 155.420(b)(6), if such DMIs are resolved by an Exchange on or before the 15th of a month, then we propose an Exchange would make coverage effective the first of the same month. If such DMIs are resolved after the 15th of a month, then we propose that an Exchange would make coverage effective the first of the following month.
For example, consider a consumer who becomes newly eligible to enroll in a QHP on August 1, on August 30 submits an application to enroll through an SEP, and generates a DMI related to the applicable enrollment information. The consumer submits documents to verify their DMI on September 1, and the Exchange resolves their DMI on September 10. If this consumer pended their plan in accordance with proposed § 155.400(i), then, because the DMI was resolved before the 15th of the month, the effective date of the plan selection would be September 1. If instead an Exchange resolved the DMI on September 16, then the effective date of the plan selection would be October 1.
As described in section III.A.9.b. of this proposed rule, this effective date proposal would balance the benefits of continuous coverage promoted through the earliest possible effective dates with the need to minimize administration burdens associated with retroactive coverage and avoid the risks of adverse selection. If coverage effective dates for pended plan selections were always extended back to the original coverage effective date under § 155.420(b)(1) through (b)(3), then issuers may struggle to collect multiple months of past premiums from new enrollees and may need to expend excessive resources to appropriately administer CSRs to months of previous medical bills. In addition, the opportunity for an extended retroactive coverage period could promote adverse selection by incentivizing consumers to delay document submissions to an Exchange until they know their medical needs during the inconsistency period. We seek comment regarding whether consumers should instead be permitted to enroll in a QHP and access APTC and CSRs on their originally prescribed coverage effective date regardless of when their DMIs are resolved, and if so, what strategies HHS should consider to mitigate adverse selection and promote market stability.
As discussed in section III.A.9.b. of this proposed rule, we are not proposing that pended plan selections become effective on the day that all DMIs are resolved by an Exchange due to the administrative challenges associated with requiring mid-month effective dates. As further discussed in section III.A.9.b. of this proposed rule, we do not read section 36B(c)(5)(C) of the Code as prescribing any requirements related to coverage effective dates.
We also propose conforming changes to § 155.420(b)(1), (b)(2)(iii) through (vi) to cross-reference the new proposed effective date rules in § 155.420(b)(6).
We request comment on this proposal. We understand State Exchanges may find it challenging to implement these requirements for PY 2028. Therefore, we specifically seek comment from State Exchanges regarding any risks that State Exchanges will not be able to implement these proposed effective date rules by PY 2028, and whether there are alternative proposals that could achieve similar outcomes while alleviating operational burden.
In addition to requesting comment on this proposal, we also request comment on whether we should consider expanding the timeframe of the SEP at § 155.420(d)(11) in the final rule. Specifically, we are concerned with the application submission component of the SEP at § 155.420(d)(11), which is commonly referred to as the Medicaid/CHIP denial SEP. For this SEP, if a consumer applies for Medicaid or CHIP during the Open Enrollment period either indirectly through their Marketplace application or directly through their State's Medicaid or CHIP agency and is subsequently determined ineligible for Medicaid and CHIP that is MEC, then they are granted an SEP to enroll in Marketplace coverage. We request comment on whether we should include a minor revision to the Medicaid/CHIP denial SEP at § 155.420(d)(11) such that individuals who apply for Medicaid or CHIP either during the annual OEP or during the pre-OE verification period may be eligible for an SEP, if other otherwise eligible. This would ensure that consumers applying for coverage during the pre-OE verification period and during the annual OEP are treated similarly. Depending on how long a State Medicaid agency takes to process the consumer's Medicaid application and make a determination, as well as the length of the OEP in the future, a consumer may not receive a Medicaid

B. Severability
We generally intend this rule's provisions, if finalized, to be severable from each other. In this rule, we propose distinct policies regarding requirements for consumers to provide or confirm certain eligibility information annually, requirements that Exchanges provide a pre-OE verification period, requirements that Exchanges generally not provide APTC and CSRs during certain inconsistency periods, requirements that Exchanges provide APTC and CSRs during certain other inconsistency periods, and requirements that Exchanges permit applicants to pend plan selections. In addition to these major policies, we include proposals regarding effective dates and binder payments.
We are of the view that the policies proposed in this rule are well-supported in law and practice and must be upheld in any legal challenge. We also are of the view that this exercise of our statutory authority reflects sound policy. However, if any portion of a final rule is declared invalid, we have determined that these provisions are generally capable of functioning sensibly on an independent basis. It is our intent that if any provision of these proposed rules, if finalized, is held to be invalid or unenforceable by its terms, or as applied to any person or circumstance, the other provisions in the rule may be construed so as to continue to give maximum effect as permitted by law, unless the holding may be one of utter invalidity or unenforceability. In the event a provision as finalized is found to be utterly invalid or unenforceable, we intend that provision to be severable. We solicit comment on the severability of these provisions.

We propose to adopt an hourly value of time based on after-tax wages to quantify the opportunity cost of changes in time use for unpaid activities. This approach matches the default assumptions for valuing changes in time use for individuals undertaking administrative and other tasks on their own time, which are outlined in an Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE) report on “Valuing Time in U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Regulatory Impact Analyses: Conceptual Framework and Best Practices.”

We divide this weekly rate by 40 hours to calculate an hourly pre-tax wage rate of approximately $30.83. We adjust this hourly rate downwards by an estimate of the effective tax rate for median income households of about 17 percent, resulting in a post-tax hourly wage rate of approximately $25.58. We adopt this as our estimate of the hourly value of time for changes in time use for unpaid activities.

B. ICRs Regarding DMIs (§§ 155.315, 155.320, 155.330)
The following changes will be submitted for review under OMB Control Number 0938-1191.
We are proposing to modify § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) to state that Exchanges generally cannot provide APTC and CSRs to consumers who receive DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information. We also propose to exempt those who qualify for an SEP due to a change in family size from these new requirements to verify certain factors of eligibility before providing APTC within proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) and proposed § 155.315(f)(4)(iii)(A). We are also proposing to add § 155.315(f)(4)(iii) to describe that Exchanges would be required to continue to provide APTC and CSRs (as applicable) during inconsistency periods created due to reporting a change to eligibility criteria during the plan year after an Exchange has completed verification of those same criteria.
We also propose to add § 155.315(f)(4)(iv), which provides that Exchanges would be required to determine eligibility for APTC and CSRs on behalf of an applicant per new effective dates following successful verification of information as described in proposed new § 155.315(f)(4)(ii). We additionally propose to add § 155.315(f)(4)(v), clarifying that applicants with DMIs other than those related to the applicable enrollment information would be able to continue receiving APTC and CSRs if otherwise eligible during the inconsistency period.
We also propose to amend § 155.330(f)(1) such that if an Exchange redetermines an enrollee's eligibility to enroll in APTC or CSRs because the enrollee has provided updated information to the Exchange, then the redetermination of eligibility would become effective on the first of the month following an Exchange's eligibility redetermination, with an exception at § 155.330(f)(1)(i) for enrollees who qualify for certain SEPs.
We propose to amend § 155.330(f)(2) to state that if a consumer is already enrolled in a QHP when their DMI is resolved, an Exchange would be required to implement their APTC and CSR eligibility determination effective the first day of the first month in which an Exchange determined all relevant eligibility criteria to be verified, as long as the consumer was enrolled in a QHP as of the first of that month, and the consumer's DMI was generated prior to the first of that month.
Finally, we propose to amend § 155.330(f)(3) to provide effective date rules for an Exchange's redetermination of eligibility following the expiration of a DMI or the end of a periodic data matching period. This proposal maintains current effective date rules for such redeterminations, with the exception that, if the redetermination results in the consumer qualifying for the same or an increased amount or level of APTC or CSRs, then Exchanges are no longer permitted to delay the effective dates for such redeterminations beyond the first of the next month.
We clarify that the impacts of the proposed effective dates for consumers who choose to pend their plan selection during their inconsistency period as described at § 155.315(f)(4)(iv)(B), are addressed in sections IV.D. of this proposed rule. We further clarify that the proposal at § 155.330(f)(4) maintains current policy and therefore, is not expected to result in new information collection or regulatory impacts.
In this section, we have included the proposed policies at § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) regarding Exchange provision of APTC and CSRs during inconsistency periods and applicants who qualify for an SEP due to a change in family size; § 155.315(f)(4)(iii) regarding DMIs during the coverage year; and § 155.330(f)(1), (2), and (3) regarding effective dates. We are considering these policies together in our analysis in both this section and in the Regulatory Impact Analysis in section VI.C.1. of this proposed rule due to their related and overlapping impacts. It would be difficult to calculate the costs and burdens of these policies independently, as we anticipate Exchanges will make similar updates and changes across the same areas to implement these proposals. Attempting to calculate independently would likely result in overestimating costs, since many of the technical updates and burdens would be counted multiple times in cases where updates and changes would occur simultaneously for different policies. Given this, we have determined that the more accurate estimation is by estimating these policies together.

In total, the burden associated with all system updates would be 690,000 hours at a cost of $68,323,800 across Exchanges on the Federal platform and State Exchanges.
We do not anticipate that modifying the DMI process for these types of DMIs to block APTC and CSRs during the inconsistency period—including proposed changes related to exceptions for a family size SEP or an eligibility redetermination during the plan year, and effective date changes related to enrollee-reported changes and DMI resolution and expiration—would result in additional burden by consumers to complete application questions or submit supporting documentation. Currently, consumers are already required to answer application questions and submit documentation for the existing DMI process. As mentioned in this proposed rule, Exchanges can generally continue their existing processes around setting and processing DMIs, so we do not expect a notable difference in consumer burden. Additionally, the proposed changes to effective dates of coverage and APTC would not result in additional application questions or submitted documents.
We seek comment on these proposed burden estimates and assumptions.
C. ICRs Regarding Annual Eligibility Redetermination (§ 155.335)
The following changes would be submitted under OMB Control Number 0938-1191 (CMS-10440).
We propose to modify § 155.335(a) by specifying that for an Exchange to redetermine an enrollee eligible for APTC and CSRs for the subsequent plan year, the enrollee or the enrollee's application filer would be required to provide or confirm household income and family size; U.S. citizenship or status as a lawfully present eligible non-citizen; eligibility for or enrollment in other MEC; and place of residence for the subsequent plan year on or after August 1 and no later than December 31 of the year preceding the applicable plan year, and the Exchange must verify the specified eligibility information using the processes in §§ 155.315 and 155.320, including the relevant provisions in those sections regarding DMIs.
We also propose to amend § 155.335(b) to state the annual eligibility redetermination would be effective on the first day of the applicable plan year, and the Exchange would be required to adhere to the existing notification standard for eligibility determinations under § 155.310(g). We propose an exception in instances where an enrollee has an unresolved DMI under § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) as of December 31 of the year preceding the plan year and for whom APTC and CSRs are not provided during the inconsistency period. In these cases, we propose that the redetermination of APTC and CSRs under this part take effect in accordance with §§ 155.315(f)(4)(iv)(A) or 155.330(f)(3), as applicable. We propose to remove § 155.335(c) through (i); redesignate § 155.335(j) as new § 155.335(c); and remove § 155.335(k) through (n).
We estimate that implementing this proposed policy would require one-time costs to the Federal Government and each State Exchange. Based on preliminary analysis, we estimate that it would take the Federal Government and each State Exchange 22,000 hours in 2026 and 2027 to develop and implement system changes to their annual eligibility redetermination and re-enrollment logic. These changes would enable Exchanges to correctly evaluate whether enrollees have provided or confirmed the eligibility information described previously and to discontinue APTC and CSRs, as applicable. Of those 22,000 hours, we estimate it would take a database and network administrator and architect 5,500 hours at $106.52 per hour and a computer programmer 16,500 hours at $96.52 per hour. VI. Regulatory Impact Analysis
A. Statement of Need
This proposed rule includes proposed updates to provisions related to Exchange eligibility and verification consistent with new requirements specified under the WFTC legislation. This proposed rule also proposes related updates to provisions affecting inconsistency periods, reported modifications to eligibility criteria, verification procedures, and eligibility redeterminations. Additionally, this proposed rule proposes to remove annual eligibility redetermination and re-enrollment requirements for APTC and CSRs while continuing the same for QHP coverage, expand enrollment options during the verification process, and establish new effective dates.
B. Overall Impact
We have examined the impacts of this rule as required by
Executive Order 12866
, “Regulatory Planning and Review”;
Executive Order 13132
, “Federalism”;
Executive Order 13563
, “Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”;
Executive Order 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”; the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) (Pub. L. 96-354); section 1102(b) of the Social Security Act; and section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
Pub. L. 104-4
).
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select those regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety, and other advantages; distributive impacts). Section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
defines a “significant regulatory action” as any regulatory action that is likely to result in a rule that may: (1) have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or adversely affect in a material way the economy, a sector of the economy, productivity, competition, jobs, the environment, public health or safety, or State, local, territorial, or Tribal governments or communities; (2) create a serious inconsistency or otherwise interfere with an action taken or planned by another agency; (3) materially alter the budgetary impacts of entitlements, grants, user fees, or loan programs or the rights and obligations of recipients thereof; or (4) raise novel legal or policy issues arising out of legal mandates, or the President's priorities.
A regulatory impact analysis (RIA) was prepared for this rule in keeping with
Executive Order 12866

We have prepared an RIA that, to the best of our ability, presents the costs and benefits of the rulemaking.

Finally, we propose to add § 155.315(f)(4)(v) to clarify that applicants with DMIs other than those outlined in § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) would be able to continue receiving APTC and CSRs if otherwise eligible during the inconsistency period.
We also propose to amend § 155.330(f)(1) such that if an Exchange redetermines an enrollee's eligibility to enroll in APTC or CSRs because the enrollee has provided updated information to the Exchange, then the redetermination of eligibility would become effective on the first of the month following an Exchange's eligibility redetermination, with an exception at § 155.330(f)(1)(i) to allow APTC or CSR effective dates that align with SEP effective dates in cases of retroactive or case-by-case SEPs.
We propose to amend § 155.330(f)(2) to provide that if a consumer is already enrolled in a QHP when their DMI is resolved, an Exchange would be required to implement their APTC and CSR eligibility determination effective the first day of the first month in which an Exchange determined all relevant eligibility criteria to be verified, as long as the consumer was enrolled in a QHP as of the first of that month, and the consumer's DMI was generated prior to the first of that month.
Finally, we propose to amend § 155.330(f)(3) to provide effective date rules for an Exchange's redetermination of eligibility following the expiration of a DMI or the end of a periodic data matching period. This proposal maintains current effective date rules for such redeterminations, with the exception that, if the redetermination results in the consumer qualifying for the same or an increased amount or level of APTC or CSRs, then Exchanges are no longer permitted to delay the effective dates for such redeterminations beyond the first of the next month.

In section IV.B. of this proposed rule, we estimated that to implement all of these proposed changes, including withholding APTC during an inconsistency period; creating exceptions to that process for both a Family Size SEP waiver and a new DMI set during an eligibility redetermination during the plan year, and adding in rules for effective dates for enrollee-reported changes and the resolution and expiration of DMIs, it would result in a one-time burden cost of $2,970,600 to Exchanges on the Federal platform and a one-time burden cost of $65,353,200 for all State Exchanges across 2026 and 2027.
We anticipate that both Exchanges on the Federal platform and State Exchanges would each incur an ongoing, annual cost burden related to requiring a new Eligibility Determination Notice (EDN) be generated in relation to changes in § 155.315. This would result in an estimated annual increase of 1.5 million notices for each Exchange. Using the cost of $0.62 per notice, we estimate this will result in an annual ongoing burden cost of $930,000 for Exchanges on the Federal Exchange (1,500,000 notices × $0.62 cost per notice) and $20,460,000 for State Exchanges (1,500,000 notices × $0.62 cost per notice × 22) for a total of $21,390,000 annually, beginning in 2027.
In addition to the annual ongoing costs of generating additional EDNs, we also expect one-time costs related to updating notices. Currently, Exchanges on the Federal platform and State Exchanges send notices to consumers when their eligibility for coverage and financial assistance changes, as well as potentially in instances where a consumer submits an insufficient document to resolve a DMI, when a DMI expires, when a DMI is resolved, and other potential related scenarios. Given the significant changes included in these proposals, such as the requirement to resolve DMIs prior to determining eligibility for APTC, the exception to that requirement during a family size SEP and when a DMI generates during a mid-year change, and the associated effective dates for being determined eligible for APTC, we expect that all Exchanges will need to make significant updates to their noticing processes.
These processes will include language-related updates across these types of notices, as well as considering whether current noticing efforts must be changed to account for these significant proposed changes. Given this, using the median wage rates estimated in IV.A., we estimate that it would require Exchanges a total of 5,000 hours to update the associated notices, split between a technical writer and a management analyst. The median wages were doubled to account for overhead and fringe benefits (2,500 × $86.92 + 2,500 × $97.94). Therefore, we estimate that Exchanges on the Federal Platform may incur an estimated one-time cost of $462,150 and all State Exchanges may incur 110,000 hours for an estimated one-time cost of $10,167,300 (92,500 × $86.92 + 2,500 × $97.94] × 22 State Exchanges) to update associated notices in 2027, for a total of 115,000 hours at a cost of $10,629,450.
We estimate that our proposal to amend § 155.315(f)(4) to allow for Exchanges to provide APTC during an applicant's inconsistency period if the applicant's household is eligible for an SEP in accordance with § 155.420(d)(2), as well as our proposal to add § 155.315(f)(4)(iii) to require Exchanges to continue to provide APTC and CSRs during inconsistency periods created due to reporting a change to eligibility criteria during the plan year after an Exchange has completed verification of those same criteria, would not impose substantial ongoing burdens or costs on Exchanges, issuers, or consumers (besides the one-time implementation cost that was mentioned in section IV.B. of this proposed rule) beyond the ongoing costs that are already accounted for as part of the existing policy to allow APTC to be paid on behalf of consumers during their inconsistency period.
We also are of the view that requiring a consumer to adjudicate their DMI prior to receiving APTC may cause Exchanges to have increased operational needs to decrease the amount of time needed to review and approve documentation to ensure that consumers receive APTC in a timely fashion. Exchanges currently have a 90/95-day period to help consumers resolve DMIs while they receive APTC and CSRs, and current consumer behavior leads to consumers tending to submit the needed documentation near the end of this period. However, with our proposed changes, consumers will not be eligible for APTC or CSRs until after they have resolved their DMIs.
We have determined that this change would also result in a change in consumer behavior where a consumer is more likely to resolve a DMI towards the beginning of their inconsistency period versus delaying their efforts until closer to when their inconsistency period is ending. While consumers are generally shielded from the time that it takes an eligibility support worker to process their DMI in the current environment as there is no effect on their APTC eligibility (within their current 90/95-day period), consumers will be acutely aware of the delay in processing DMIs in this new regime due to their unresolved DMI impacting their APTC and CSR eligibility. If there are delays in determining a consumer eligible for APTC and CSRs, it could create consumer satisfaction pressure for Exchange operations to decrease the amount of time that it takes for an Exchange to process a DMI, especially at points in the year such as towards the end of Open Enrollment to ensure that consumers will be able to receive APTC and CSRs beginning in January if they are indeed eligible. Some Exchanges may find that it is necessary to increase seasonal staffing to help consumers resolve their DMIs and therefore receive APTC and CSRs. We seek comment on estimates from Exchanges as to the time that it takes to resolve different DMIs and whether Exchanges predict any staffing changes could be made in response to these proposed changes.
Additionally, these changes could help mitigate potentially fraudulent behavior done by agents, brokers, and web-brokers. As outlined in the 2025 Marketplace Program Integrity and Affordability Rule and the 2027 Payment Notice, many agents, brokers, and web-brokers may be incentivized to enroll consumers with potentially incorrect income amounts that result in maximum APTC amounts for the consumers. While this would typically result in at least an income DMI, under current regulations, those consumers would be enrolled for at least 90 days with that level of APTC before the income DMI would expire, allowing agents, brokers, and web-brokers to receive commissions for the time that consumers are enrolled.
With the proposed change to not determine APTC and CSR eligibility until all DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information are adjudicated, agents, brokers, and web-brokers that have historically participated in fraudulent behavior would no longer be able to have consumers receive APTC or CSRs until they work with those consumers to submit documents and resolve those DMIs. This is especially true for agents, brokers, and web-brokers who mislead consumers into believing they are eligible for more APTC than they may be eligible for. Given this, we anticipate that Exchanges may see a decrease in costs associated with combating fraud in relation to inaccurate application attestations and may see a decrease in agents, brokers, and web-brokers who have potentially
(
printed page 67703)
fraudulent motivations participating in Exchanges.
While potentially less significant than the proposals to generally disallow APTC and CSR during inconsistency periods, we expect that there will also be qualitative impacts of the proposals in § 155.330 related to APTC and CSR effective dates. We propose eliminating the exceptions currently at § 155.330(f)(2) and (3), and therefore no longer allowing Exchanges to delay effective dates for certain eligibility redeterminations. We anticipate this proposed change will benefit consumers insofar as it requires their updated eligibility redetermination to take effect sooner than it would under current rules, resulting in more accurate APTC determinations and reduced risk of consumer tax liability at reconciliation. This is particularly important given that section 71305 of the WFTC legislation removes caps on the amount of APTC a consumer may be liable to repay when filing their taxes and reconciling their APTC. However, we also expect that some consumers may find that the shorter time between eligibility redetermination and APTC and CSR effective date makes it more difficult to anticipate and plan for unexpected increases to their net premium or cost-sharing responsibilities.
Finally, we acknowledge that these proposed changes may result in one-time changes to issuer operations. Due to both the timing of DMIs and new use cases in which consumers may qualify for retroactive APTC and CSRs, we assume issuers would need to make updates to their notices to consumers. Specifically, because proposed effective date changes would allow for retroactive APTC and CSRs upon DMI adjudication in cases where an Exchange is able to verify APTC and CSR eligibility for previous months, issuers would likely see an increase in the number of consumers that are requesting the application of retroactive APTC and CSRs on their plans. We seek comment from issuers and other affected parties on what these cost burdens may look like for the proposed updates to effective dates upon DMI resolution.
We seek comment on these proposed impacts and assumptions.
2. Annual Eligibility Redetermination (§ 155.335)
We are proposing to modify § 155.335(a) to specify that for an Exchange to redetermine an enrollee eligible for APTC and CSRs for the subsequent plan year, the enrollee or the enrollee's application filer would be required to provide or confirm household income and family size; U.S. citizenship or status as a lawfully present eligible non-citizen; eligibility for or enrollment in other MEC; and place of residence for the subsequent plan year on or after August 1 and no later than December 31 of the year preceding the applicable plan year, and the Exchange would be required to verify the specified eligibility information using the processes in §§ 155.315 and 155.320, including the relevant provisions in those sections regarding DMIs.
We also propose to amend § 155.335(b) to state the annual eligibility redetermination would be effective on the first day of the applicable plan year, and the Exchange would be required to adhere to the existing notification standard for eligibility determinations under § 155.310(g). We propose an exception in instances where an enrollee has an unresolved DMI related to the applicable enrollment information as of December 31 of the year preceding the plan year and for whom APTC and CSRs are not provided during the inconsistency period. In these cases, we propose that the redetermination of APTC and CSRs under this part take effect in accordance with §§ 155.315(f)(4)(iv)(A) or 330(f)(3), as applicable. We propose to remove § 155.335(c) through (i); redesignate § 155.335(j) as new § 155.335(c); and remove § 155.335(k) through (n).

For the Federal Government, we estimate a burden between 2026 and 2027 of 22,000 hours at a cost of $2,178,440. For State Exchanges, we estimate a burden in 2026 and 2027 of 484,000 hours at a cost of $47,925,680 for completing the necessary updates to State Exchange systems. In aggregate, we estimate the total annual cost burden to all Federal Government and State Exchange consumers for the additional data collection beginning with the pre-OE verification period to be $72,556,353, beginning in 2027.
As further discussed in section IV.C. of this proposed rule, we estimate that the proposed policy would result in an increase of 1,749,325 DMIs generated and processed by Exchanges on the Federal platform. We estimate that the increase in cost for consumers from Exchanges on the Federal platform beginning with the pre-OE verification period for PY 2028 would be approximately $32,995,975 per year.
Additionally, we estimate that an increase in the number of DMIs that the Federal Government would generate and process would result in an increase in burden for Exchanges. In aggregate, we estimate the total annual cost burden to Exchanges on the Federal platform because of increase of DMIs would be $109,409,783 beginning with the pre-OE verification period for PY 2028, which is in 2027.
We also anticipate an increase in the number of transactions transmitted by the Federal Government to trusted data sources for the purpose of verifying consumer eligibility information. The costs associated with these transactions vary by data source and the type of information returned. State Exchanges currently employ varying operational approaches for utilizing trusted data sources to verify information. As a result, we anticipate that some State Exchanges may experience an increase in trusted data source transactions, while others may not. b. Benefits
Beyond these cost estimations, we expect that requiring consumers to provide or confirm specified eligibility information as a condition of re-enrollment with APTC and CSRs in the subsequent plan year and Exchanges verifying that information would mitigate the risk that individuals receive APTC or CSRs for which they are no longer eligible, thereby reducing incidences of improper or fraudulent enrollment. As discussed in the 2025 Marketplace Program Integrity and Affordability final rule (
90 FR 27074
) and the HHS Notice of Benefit and Payment Parameters for 2026 final rule (
90 FR 4424
), we have observed instances in which agents, brokers, and web-brokers enroll consumers using potentially inaccurate income information that results in the application of maximum APTC amounts for consumers. Improper payments are a fiscal risk to the Federal Government and undermine public trust in the integrity of the Exchanges. We are of the view that our proposed policy is likely to substantially reduce fraudulent or abusive practices by agents, brokers, and web-brokers by interrupting the perpetuation of inaccurate subsidy amounts across plan years. This verification requirement strengthens the overall credibility of the Exchanges, improves program integrity, and protects consumers from downstream financial and coverage consequences of enrollment fraud.
In addition, we anticipate that the proposed policy would improve APTC accuracy by aligning subsidy determinations more closely with a consumer's projected household income, for example, and other applicable eligibility criteria and circumstances for the upcoming plan year. More accurate APTC determinations on at least an annual basis would reduce the likelihood of excess APTC and the associated tax liability at reconciliation for consumers.
We seek comment on these proposed impact estimates and assumptions.

We anticipate that the proposed modifications to binder payment regulations at § 155.400(e)(1), which would update the rules for collection of binder by Exchange issuers under the new enrollment scenarios proposed in this rule, would have a minor but positive impact on the risk pool, and would result in minor costs to issuers associated with the potential need for system changes. 4. Pre-Open Enrollment Verification Period (§ 155.410(h))
We propose to add §  155.410(h) to require all Exchanges to permit consumers to provide eligibility information to Exchanges for the upcoming plan year prior to the beginning of the OEP each year. We propose that all Exchanges make this process available beginning on August 1, 2027, for the 2028 Plan Year and August 1 of each subsequent year.
