6. Overall Impact of the Proposed Exchange Eligibility Verification Provisions
We anticipate that the provisions of this proposed rule, although severable, may work in concert with each other and affect many of the same individuals seeking coverage through the individual health insurance market. Therefore, the overall impact of this proposed rule would likely be less than the simple accumulation of the individual provisions' impact analyses. To the best of our ability, we provide overall impact estimates of these provisions for enrollment, APTC, and premiums that minimize the overlap of individuals affected. These estimates consider the enrollment, APTC, and premium impact due to the provisions in this proposed rule, if finalized, compared to what would occur if these proposals were not finalized.
We propose to amend current regulations to align with section 71303(a) of the WFTC legislation amendments to section 36B of the Code. The proposed updates specify changes to processes that all Exchanges would be required to use following the actions taken to confirm applicants' eligibility for APTC and CSRs, as applicable.
Proposed updates at sections III.A.7. of this proposed rule would increase the number of individuals who need to update their information annually and therefore would increase the number of individuals who receive DMIs, which younger and healthier consumers often do not resolve. This would result in a decrease in enrollment and the amount of APTC paid out, while affecting the risk pool so that premiums would increase due to younger individuals dropping coverage.
Additionally, proposed updates in section III.A.4.b of this proposed rule would increase verification-related barriers to enrollment with APTC/CSRs by requiring eligibility verification be complete prior to providing APTC/CSRs to enrollees rather than providing them during the inconsistency period.
We expect this to result in fewer enrollees due to delays in receiving APTC so that many enrollees will receive APTC for fewer months. Younger and healthier consumers would be less incentivized to complete this process since they have lower perceived need for health care and would opt out when faced with administrative barriers, leading to less APTC being paid out as well as increased premiums as these consumers leave the risk pool.
Overall, more individuals may lose coverage because they are unlikely to be able to afford to enroll in a full-price QHP while they complete the verification process, leading to an increase in the rate of uninsurance. This increase may impose greater burdens on the health care system as treatment may shift to under-prepared emergency departments, additional costs to the Federal Government and to States to provide Medicaid coverage limited to the treatment of an emergency medical condition and cause an overall reduction to labor productivity due to a reduction in preventative as well as readily available care for illness.
We do expect these updated verification processes to decrease the occurrence of fraudulent activity by agents, brokers, and web-brokers in the Exchanges. These changes could help prevent fraudulent behavior by agents, brokers, and web-brokers who intentionally provide incorrect application attestations. By not providing APTC and CSRs until the resolution of all DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information, agents, brokers, and web-brokers that have historically participated in fraudulent behavior, especially those who mislead consumers into believing they are eligible for more APTC than they may actually be eligible for, would have to work with consumers to submit documents and resolve those DMIs before the consumers receive APTC or CSRs. Agents, brokers, and web-brokers are incentivized to engage in fraudulent behavior because current rules let them collect commissions for the duration a consumer is enrolled with financial assistance, even after that assistance is revoked. Requiring eligibility verification to be completed before APTC or CSRs are issued would eliminate this avenue for collecting unearned commissions on ineligible consumers.

a. Enrollment
We estimate that the proposed updates to the eligibility and verification process would result in a decrease in enrollment volume for all Exchanges. A large portion of this decrease in enrollment can be attributed to the decrease in improper enrollments we expect to occur because of additional eligibility verification standards. The 2028-2030 baseline enrollment estimates account for this decrease in enrollment due to WFTC legislation that is expected to reduce improper enrollments. Not accounted for in the baseline estimates is the expected decrease in enrollment due to the additional barriers to enrollment for properly enrolled consumers that will result from the additional eligibility verification standards proposed by this rule. This additional expected decrease in enrollment is discussed in this section.
The withholding of APTC during the inconsistency period and increased manual documentation verification would reduce the number of consumers who enroll in a QHP. Consumers whose information cannot be verified upon application submission will not be determined eligible for APTC/CSRs until the relevant information can be verified through the DMI process per proposed updates in section III.A.4.b. of this proposed rule. Therefore, consumers would have to make plan choices with less certainty about their APTC/CSRs and either enroll in a full-price QHP during the inconsistency period or select a plan that would be released to the issuer upon DMI resolution per proposed updates in section III.A.8.b. of this proposed rule.
It is unlikely that many consumers would be able to afford to enroll in a full-price QHP while they complete the verification process, so the proposed updates in section IIIA.8.b. of this proposed rule may mitigate some enrollment decrease. Additionally, the proposed updates in sections III.A.4.c. and III.A.4.d. of this proposed rule that would allow for exceptions to withholding APTC during the inconsistency period would also mitigate some enrollment decrease. However, we estimate overall that fewer eligible consumers would be enrolled and those who are eventually enrolled through a pended plan selection following the DMI process would be enrolled for fewer months compared to current requirements and processes.
The requirements to provide or confirm eligibility verification information on an annual basis per proposed updates in sections III.A.4.b. and III.A.7. of this proposed rule would increase the amount of consumers who receive DMIs and must submit documentation to verify their information and therefore, would negatively impact eligible consumers' ability to enroll in a QHP due to the proposed requirement to withhold APTC/CSRs during inconsistency periods for DMIs related to the applicable enrollment information. Eligible consumers who are unable to complete the verification process will not be eligible to receive APTC or may also be ineligible to enroll in a QHP because they were unable to submit sufficient documentation. Consumers who remain eligible to enroll in a QHP are unlikely to be able to afford to enroll in a full-price QHP and may choose not to enroll. However, overall, we estimate that the increase in the number of consumers who must return on an annual basis combined with the increase in the number of consumers who will be required to submit documentation will decrease enrollment due to administrative barriers.
For Exchanges on the Federal platform, we estimate an annual decrease of approximately 237,500 enrollees (11,840,500 enrollees in baseline estimates−11,603,000 enrollees in estimates that account for this proposed rule). For State Exchanges, we estimate an annual decrease of 95,000 enrollees (5,074,500 enrollees in baseline estimates−4,979,500 enrollees in estimates that account for this proposed rule). Together, 332,500 fewer individuals in all Exchanges (237,500 enrollees for Exchanges on the Federal Platform + 95,000 enrollees for State Exchanges) would enroll in QHP coverage per year as a result of the proposed updates to the previously mentioned regulations. These estimates are made in comparison to the enrollment projections presented in the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, HHS Notice of Benefit and Payment Parameters for 2027; and Basic Health Program final rule (

b. APTC
We estimate that the proposed updates to the verification process would reduce the amount of APTC payments for all Exchanges. If this rule is finalized, assuming that individuals who do not maintain or enroll in coverage would otherwise be subsidized QHP enrollees, we expect savings to the Federal Government in the form of reduced APTC payments.
Additionally, withholding APTC during the inconsistency period would result in enrollees receiving APTC for fewer months compared to current rules, under which APTC is paid out during the inconsistency period.
Consumers who cannot receive APTC during their inconsistency period may either choose to enroll in a full-price QHP during that time or may choose to select a plan where they would only be enrolled in such plan once they are deemed eligible for APTC per proposed updates in section III.A.8.b. of this proposed rule. For consumers who choose to pend their plan selection until their information is verified, APTC will be provided either on the 1st of the current month or 1st of the next month depending on when the information is verified per proposed effective dates in sections III.A.9.b. and III.A.10. of this proposed rule. Therefore, we estimate these consumers would receive APTC for 1.5 fewer months on average, because they may receive APTC later in the plan year than would currently be provided. The proposed updates would result in more eligible enrollees being required to complete the manual verification process. Younger and healthier consumers are less incentivized to complete this process since they have lower perceived need for healthcare and would opt out when faced with administrative barriers. We have estimated a 0.4 percent increase in premiums assuming 332,500 enrollees leave the market. These premium impact estimates assume the 332,500 exiting enrollees have average claims expenses that are 80 percent of the average claims experience for the overall risk pool. If the average claims PMPM is 86 percent of the premium PMPM (0.86 × $838.48 = $721.09), we estimate the 332,500 exiting enrollees have claims costs of $576.87 PMPM (0.8 × $721.09 = 576.87), and the remaining 16.583 million enrollees have an average claims cost of $723.98 (332,500/16,915,000 × $576.87 + 16,582,500/16,915,000 × $723.98 = 721.09). Comparing the new claims PMPM of $723.98 to the prior claims PMPM of $721.09 shows a 0.4 percent increase in average claims (723.98/721.09−1 = 0.004).
We anticipate the provisions in this proposed rule could reduce enrollment and APTC while increasing premiums each year beginning in 2028. We note that variables impacting enrollment, premiums, and APTC have changed over time and may continue to fluctuate. When considering the overall impact of this proposed rule, if all provisions are finalized as proposed, we also recognize that the degree of impact from the individual provisions working in concert with each other may vary more than what we estimate due to the inherent uncertainty in predicting enrollment trends. Therefore, it is possible that the overall impact of this proposed rule could be outside of the estimates provided in this section. We seek comment on the expected effects of this proposed rule on total enrollment. Likewise, we request comments on potential secondary effects of this proposed rule. These could, for example, include effects on premiums, burdens on the healthcare system, and effects on Federal spending due to shifts from individual market coverage to Medicaid coverage or uncompensated care. Finally, we request comment on any effects that this proposed rule might have on labor productivity.

E. Regulatory
                        
                         Alternatives Considered
In developing the proposals contained in this rule, we considered a number of regulatory alternatives. The following discussion describes the alternatives we considered and explains why we did not adopt them.
1. Eligibility Redeterminations During the Plan Year (§ 155.315(f)(4)(iii))
In developing our proposal at § 155.315(f)(4)(iii) regarding the treatment of APTC when a mid-year change results in a DMI related to the applicable enrollment information, we considered several alternatives. First, in cases when an enrollee reports a change that would result in a decrease in APTC, such as an increase in income, we considered proposing to require Exchanges to maintain the enrollee's higher, previously verified APTC amount during their inconsistency period. However, we did not propose this approach because it could expose consumers to large excess APTC repayment obligations at tax time, a concern that is particularly acute following the WFTC legislation's elimination of repayment caps.
We also considered proposing to require Exchanges to provide the higher APTC amount during the inconsistency period while encouraging consumers to voluntarily select a lower APTC amount. We did not propose this alternative because we determined that this would create consumer confusion, impose additional burden on enrollees who would need to manually adjust their APTC, and still create a risk of significant repayment obligations if consumers do not understand the downstream tax implications of failing to reduce APTC.
Finally, we considered proposing to remove APTC entirely during inconsistency periods arising from mid-year changes. We did not propose this approach because it would render coverage unaffordable for many enrollees during the inconsistency period, potentially leading to mid-year losses of coverage. We also determined that this alternative could increase adverse selection, as individuals with greater health needs would be more likely to maintain enrollment in unsubsidized coverage during their inconsistency period. Finally, we determined that this alternative would have a chilling effect on consumers' willingness to report changes in their
(
printed page 67711)
circumstances, undermining the ability of Exchanges to make accurate eligibility determinations.

We chose to propose this exception because permitting cross-year retroactive APTC would create significant complications for tax administration, including the need for certain enrollees to file amended Federal income tax returns. Accordingly, we are proposing to limit retroactive APTC eligibility to the current coverage year only, which we have determined appropriately balances consumer access to financial assistance while minimizing tax administration burdens.
Regarding the effective dates related to eligibility redeterminations due to enrollee-reported changes proposed at § 155.330(f)(1), we considered proposing that Exchanges be required or permitted to make such redeterminations effective immediately. While this may have improved the timeliness of eligibility determinations, we reasoned that immediate, mid-month adjustment of APTC and CSRs would be more difficult for Exchanges and issuers to implement.
In considering our proposal to maintain the current effective date rules for eligibility redeterminations following the expiration of an inconsistency period or following periodic data matching that results in a decrease in APTC or the level of CSRs, we considered whether to instead to propose to require Exchanges always to implement such redeterminations on the first of the following month. However, we reasoned that there were compelling reasons to maintain the current policy, including ensuring that enrollees were provided sufficient notice of the upcoming changes to their eligibility. We also are of the view that maintaining the current policy is operationally less burdensome for Exchanges than updating the current rules.
Finally, when developing our proposals at §§ 155.410(f)(5) and 155.420 regarding effective dates for consumers who elect to pend their plan selections, we considered a number of alternatives. Specifically, we considered proposing to allow effective dates to extend retroactively back to the effective date that a consumer could have qualified for, absent their choice to pend their plan selection. However, we elected not to propose this alternative due to the risk of increased adverse selection, given that under this policy, consumers would be able to wait to decide whether to submit documents to resolve their DMI until they incurred medical bills and would be assured that their coverage would retroactively extend to cover such claims. We also considered whether section 36B(c)(5)(C) of the Code requires coverage effective dates retroactive to the effective date that a consumer would have qualified for, absent their choice to pend their plan selection. However, we read the Code to mean that months prior to verification must be treated as coverage months if they would otherwise be considered coverage months under the requirements prescribed in 36B(c) of the Code, including the requirement that an individual be enrolled in a QHP as of the first of the month.
We also considered proposing that plan selections become effective on the day that all DMIs are resolved. Like our proposal, this approach would balance the benefits of immediate coverage availability with the harms imposed by requiring consumers to pay premiums for past periods of coverage and would limit risks of adverse selection. However, we chose not to propose this alternative because we have determined that requiring mid-month effective dates would be administratively challenging for issuers and Exchanges.
3. Notice of Annual Open Enrollment Period
We considered proposing to add a new, separate notification requirement for the pre-OE period for all Exchanges rather than modifying the existing notice of annual OEP requirement. As described in section III.A.9.a. of this proposed rule, we determined it was preferable to permit Exchanges to send the notice of annual OE earlier than currently allowed to support Exchanges in determining the best communication strategy for their enrollees. A new notification requirement separate from the notice of annual OE would presuppose the optimal strategy for Exchanges with unique communications infrastructure and operational capabilities. Instead, this proposed amendment to the regulation would enable Exchanges to send the notice of annual OE earlier, with information about the pre-OE verification period, if they determine that approach is appropriate for their enrollee population, or to notify enrollees through a separate mechanism if they prefer.
4. Annual Pre-Open Enrollment Verification Period (§ 155.410(h))
In developing our proposal at § 155.410(h) regarding the pre-OE verification period, we considered expanding the information that Exchanges would be required to permit applicants and enrollees to provide and verify during the pre-OE period beyond the minimum specified in the statute. Specifically, we considered requiring Exchanges to additionally provide a process for applicants to provide information regarding their eligibility for or enrollment in other MEC, in addition to the household income and other information required under section 71303(b) of the WFTC legislation. We decided, however, that it would be preferable to provide flexibility for Exchanges to collect additional information while establishing a minimum standard that does not exceed the statutory requirement. Accordingly, our proposal at § 155.410(h)(2)(i) sets forth the minimum information specified in the statute, while § 155.410(h)(2)(ii) specifies that Exchanges retain the flexibility to collect additional information during the pre-OE period if they choose to do so.
We also considered proposing detailed operational guidelines for the pre-OE period in rulemaking, including notice requirements and a requirement for Exchanges to provide a streamlined electronic re-enrollment form for existing enrollees seeking to confirm information for the upcoming coverage year. We decided not to adopt this approach to prioritize operational flexibility for Exchanges, enabling them to build a pre-OE process in a manner that is most efficient given their existing systems and processes. We are of the view that this approach reduces the risk of noncompliance, given the short timeframe for implementation. Finally, we have determined that this approach would enable Exchanges to enhance their implementation of the pre-OE process over time as they gain operational experience.

We anticipate that small issuers could be impacted by the provisions in this proposed rule. For example, under proposed revisions to § 155.315(f)(4)(iv), Exchanges would be required to ensure both retroactive and prospective coverage effective dates, as applicable, based on the timing of DMI resolution. This may impact current enrollment operations for small issuers.
We are unable to quantify the direct impact of these changes on small issuers due to uncertainty regarding their market share, market participation, membership in larger holding groups, enrollment and risk mix, and premium receipts, but we discuss possible indirect impacts on small issuers. A reduction in APTC payments means the consumers would be responsible for the balance of the premium not covered by APTC, not the issuers. However, we expect that many of the consumers who would be responsible for these balances are unlikely to be able to afford a QHP without APTC and that this group would exit the Exchanges rather than pay premiums not covered by APTC. We also anticipate that due to the small reduction in enrollment anticipated to result from the policies in this proposed rule, issuers may experience a reduction in premium revenue. However, we anticipate this could be balanced by a reduction in claims experience, and we are unable to quantify this indirect impact on small issuers due to uncertainty and a lack of data. For more information about the proposed overall impacts on enrollment, APTC, and premiums that minimize the overlap of individuals who may be affected by multiple provisions in this proposed rule, please see section VI.C.6. Additionally, we have determined that the following provisions could impact smaller agent, broker, and web-broker firms. We have determined that small agents, brokers, and web-brokers will be classified under NAICS code 524210 (Insurance Agencies and Brokerages) that have annual receipts of $15 million or less. According to SBA size standards, there are 120,434 firms in the Insurance Agencies and Brokerages Industry, of which 119,114 or approximately 99 percent, had annual receipts below the $15 million size standard.

]
In addition, the 2023 Nonemployer Statistics (NES) from the Census Bureau
[
48
]
indicate there are an additional 305,281 nonemployer firms within the 524210 NAICS code, and the Departments anticipate that the vast majority of these nonemployer firms had annual receipts below the $15 million size standard. Nearly all agents, brokers, and web-brokers affected by this proposed rule would therefore be small entities.
The proposed changes to annual eligibility redetermination and re-enrollment (§ 155.335) described in section III.A.7. of this proposed rule would require consumers who were previously automatically re-enrolled in a plan with APTC and CSRs to return to the Exchange and confirm certain eligibility information prior to receiving APTC or CSRs for the following plan year. This may change the current business model of agents, brokers, and web-brokers that currently do not engage a subset of their clients annually who are relying on automatic re-enrollment with APTC and CSRs. We expect agents, brokers, and web-brokers may experience increased consumer outreach efforts and interactions as they will likely need to communicate with more clients more frequently to verify and confirm their eligibility information to enroll them in a QHP with APTC or CSRs.
The proposed changes to the annual pre-OE verification period (§ 155.410) as described in section III.A.9.c. of this proposed rule would create a requirement for Exchanges to provide a verification period beginning August 1 of each year preceding the plan year, allowing consumers to update or provide information for verification for the upcoming plan year. Agents, brokers, and web-brokers assisted 76 percent of Exchange enrollments in PY 2026. The proposed amendments may change how agents, brokers, and web-brokers interact with their clients on an annual basis, potentially resulting in more frequent communications with their clients (for example, once during the pre-OE period and again during the OEP to select a plan for enrollment).
We seek comment on these proposed assumptions and impacts on small entities.
For regulatory alternatives considered regarding the provisions in this proposed rule, please see section VI.E. of this proposed rule.
In addition, section 1102(b) of the Social Security Act requires us to prepare a regulatory impact analysis if a rule may have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals. This analysis must conform to the provisions of section 603 of the RFA. For purposes of section 1102(b) of the Social Security Act, we define a small rural hospital as a hospital that is located outside of a metropolitan statistical area and has fewer than 100 beds. While this proposed rule is not subject to section 1102 of the Social Security Act, we have determined that this rule would not affect small rural hospitals. Therefore, we anticipate this proposed rule would not have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals.

Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA)
(
printed page 67713)
also requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule whose mandates require spending in any 1 year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. In 2026, that threshold is approximately $193 million. Although we have not been able to quantify all costs, we expect that this proposed rule would not impose a mandate that would result in the expenditure by State, local, and Tribal Governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of more than $193 million in any 1 year.
H. Federalism
In compliance with the requirement of
Executive Order 13132
that agencies examine closely any policies that may have Federalism implications or limit the policy making discretion of the States, we have engaged in efforts to consult with and work cooperatively with affected States, including participating in conference calls with and attending conferences of the NAIC, State Exchanges, and consulting with State insurance officials on an individual basis.
While developing this proposed rule, we attempted to balance the States' interest in administering their Exchanges with HHS' interest in ensuring that the statutory requirements of the WFTC legislation and the Affordable Care Act are implemented in ways that promote clarity, consistency, and market stability. By doing so, we complied with the requirements of
Executive Order 13132
.
Because States have flexibility in designing their Exchanges and Exchange-related programs, State decisions will ultimately influence both administrative expenses and overall premiums. States are not required to establish an Exchange. For States that elected previously to operate an Exchange, those States had the opportunity to use funds under Exchange Planning and Establishment Grants to fund the development of their programs. Accordingly, some of the initial cost of creating programs was funded by Exchange Planning and Establishment Grants. After establishment, Exchanges must be financially self-sustaining, with revenue sources at the discretion of the State. Current State Exchanges charge user fees to issuers.
In our view, this regulation has Federalism implications due to system and operational costs that State Exchanges will incur to implement the proposals in this rule. States will incur costs, including one-time implementation costs and ongoing operational costs, related to the proposals described in section IV.B. regarding DMIs, the proposals described in section IV.C. of this proposed rule regarding annual eligibility redeterminations, the proposals described in section IV.D. of this proposed rule allowing consumers to pend plan selections during an inconsistency period, and the proposals described in section IV.E. of this proposed rule requiring Exchanges to establish a pre-OE verification period. However, these federalism implications are mitigated in part by the fact that certain provisions, such as the proposal at § 155.315(f)(4)(ii) to no longer allow APTC or CSRs during certain inconsistency periods, are statutorily required under section 71303 of the WFTC legislation. These federalism implications are further mitigated by HHS' interest in promoting clear and consistent rules for the implementation of new statutory requirements. Finally, these federalism implications are mitigated by HHS' deference to State Exchanges regarding many aspects of the implementation of the proposals in this rule, including timing and methods for communicating with consumers, methods for collecting required information from consumers, and overall user experience and design.

Department of Transportation
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
[Docket No. NHTSA-2026-1717]
AGENCY:
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of intent to establish a Negotiated Rulemaking Advisory Committee for Tire Safety; request for comments; solicitation of nominations for membership.
SUMMARY:
NHTSA announces its intent to form a Negotiated Rulemaking Advisory Committee for Tire Safety. The committee will advise the Secretary on tire safety matters through a negotiated rulemaking process. The committee will terminate when its stated objectives have been accomplished (
i.e.,
the committee submits its recommendations to the Secretary) or upon the expiration of a period not to exceed two years, unless the charter is renewed by the Secretary. This notice seeks public comment on the proposed establishment of this committee and its proposed membership. This notice also requests nominations for membership on the committee.
DATES:
Comments on the intent to establish the committee and the proposed membership must be received by November 27, 2026. Applications for membership must be received by NHTSA on or before 5 p.m. ET November 27, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments to the docket number identified in the heading of this document by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the online instructions for submitting.
Mail:
Docket Management Facility, M-30, U.S. Department of Transportation, West Building, Ground Floor, Rm. W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
If you wish to apply for membership, your application should be submitted to:
Email:
tiresfac@dot.gov
. Mail: Use overnight mail only and send to:
U.S. Department of Transportation, National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Office of Rulemaking, Attn: Negotiated Rulemaking Committee for Tire Safety, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590. The committee charter can be found in the docket to this notice.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For committee-related issues, please contact Hisham Mohamed, Chief, Vehicle Dynamics Division, Office of Crash Avoidance, National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590; email:
hisham.mohamed@dot.gov
.
For legal questions, please contact Ella Hood, Attorney-Advisory, Office of the Chief Counsel, National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590; email:
ella.hood@dot.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background:
NHTSA announces its intent to establish a Negotiated Rulemaking Committee for Tire Safety in accordance with the Negotiated Rulemaking Act,
5 U.S.C. 561
,
et seq.
and the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA), as amended,
5 U.S.C. ch. 10
. In a negotiated rulemaking, an agency invites representatives of interested parties likely to be significantly affected by a regulation to work with each other and the agency on an advisory committee to seek to reach consensus recommendations on the appropriate resolution of the issues before the committee. If a consensus is reached, the Department will issue a proposed rule consistent with that consensus for public comment under established rulemaking procedures.
This committee would be formed to assist NHTSA, an operating administration of the Department, with the development of consensus recommendations to inform a rulemaking proposal to modernize existing tire requirements and test procedures under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act (
49 U.S.C. 30101
et seq.
) and the Transportation Recall Enhancement, Accountability, and Documentation Act (TREAD),
Public Law 106-414
. Specifically, the committee would be tasked with developing a detailed term sheet consisting of consensus recommendations to inform the agency's rulemaking proposal.
Consistent with its authority, NHTSA has determined that establishing a negotiated rulemaking committee is necessary and in the public interest based on agency regulatory review activities and stakeholder feedback. Previous actions included a prior request for comments concerning existing rules and agency actions that are candidates for repeal, replacement, suspension, or modification. Specifically, NHTSA issued an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) seeking public comment on the continued necessity and effectiveness of current Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards for tires.
[
1
]
In response, the agency received comments from stakeholders highlighting the need to lower regulatory burdens and increase safety effectiveness by addressing existing and longstanding performance requirements, such as the tire strength (plunger energy) tests, bead unseating resistance tests, and tire
(
printed page 67648)
endurance tests currently found in FMVSS Nos. 109, 119, and 139.
[
2
]
Furthermore, NHTSA has received official requests for interpretation—such as a recent inquiry from Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co. regarding the marking and testing of “Extra Load” passenger tires with a maximum inflation pressure of 350 kPa—demonstrating ambiguities in applying current load classification standards to modern tire designs.
[
3
]
These comments and requests underscore the limitations of the existing regulatory framework.
The agency initiated a rulemaking action (RIN 2127-AL96) in the Spring 2018 Unified Agenda of Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions (“Unified Agenda”). As detailed in the Unified Agenda abstract for this RIN, the scope of the potential rulemaking and committee discussions would focus on tire testing as well as other tire-related issues.
[
4
]
Through this negotiated rulemaking process, NHTSA would work collaboratively with interested stakeholders to address various topics of modernization. For tire testing, committee discussions would focus on the continued necessity and effectiveness of the tire strength test (plunger energy), the bead unseating resistance test, and the tire endurance test (chunking). For other tire-related issues, the committee would evaluate broader regulatory topics, including the incorporation of non-pneumatic tires, modernization of tire markings, and a specific petition from the Tire and Rim Association (TRA) regarding the inclusion of Load Range F light truck tires in FMVSS No. 139.
[
5
]
Prior comments received from the public have also allowed the agency to identify interested stakeholders that might participate in the negotiated rulemaking process.
[
6
]
Proposed Agenda and Schedule:
The committee would establish a working schedule to develop a rulemaking proposal within its chartered duration. In accordance with FACA, the charter shall terminate two years after the date on which the charter is filed, unless it is renewed by the Secretary. To ensure the committee timely completes its work within its two-year duration, NHTSA intents to publish a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) promptly after the committee submits its consensus recommendations, the Secretary approves them either as submitted or in modified form, and after appropriate consultation with the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs. The Agency expects that the committee will finalize its deliberations and provide its detailed term sheet within the active period of its charter.
The proposed agenda would include the drafting of a consensus report recommending specific regulatory updates. The committee would meet approximately four times per year with additional meetings as necessary to meet assigned tasks. Committee members would be provided with advance notice of any need to increase meeting frequency, and all meeting dates would be published in advance in the
Federal Register
in accordance with FACA requirements. Meetings would be open to the public and held virtually (or in a hybrid forum that does not require additional use of Federal funds), unless otherwise approved by the Secretary.
Administrative Support:
NHTSA would provide the necessary administrative support for the committee. This would include meeting facilities, virtual meeting access capabilities, technical assistance, and document management. In addition, NHTSA would procure the services of a neutral facilitator to manage the committee meetings and assist the members in reaching consensus. Committee members would not receive pay or other compensation for their committee service.
Interests Significantly Affected and Membership:
NHTSA has determined that establishing a negotiated rulemaking committee is in the public interest and that there are identifiable interests that would be significantly affected by the rulemaking. These groups include those that manufacture and sell tires in the United States, as well as groups that focus on engineering, safety, and general standard setting. To ensure a range of views among these groups, the agency proposes that the committee would consist of up to 18 members qualified to serve based on their expertise, training, experience, and ability to represent one of the identified categories. In general, appointments would reflect a balance of views and professional backgrounds.
Due to the various groups identified and the desired number of representatives from each, no single group would have a controlling stake in the committee, and the approach would be to achieve consensus on any topic discussed or recommendation produced. The Secretary of Transportation would appoint each member for a single term of two years or until the completion of committee activities, whichever is sooner, unless otherwise renewed in accordance with FACA. All members serve at the pleasure of the Secretary, who may appoint a member or terminate any member's tenure at his discretion. The Secretary also may extend appointments and may appoint replacements for members who resign outside a stated term, as necessary.
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 564(a)(4)
, NHTSA proposes representation from the following groups to reflect the interests significantly affected by this rulemaking:
Four representatives from tire manufacturers or tire retailers;
Two representatives from national motor vehicle manufacturers;
Four representatives from national motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment manufacturing associations;
Two representatives from national motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment safety organizations;
Three representatives from educational or research institutions, or testing organizations within the United States; and
Three representatives from national professional engineering associations or standard-setting associations.
Anyone who feels these categories do not fully represent their interests should detail their reasoning in their comment or membership application. NHTSA requests comments and suggestions regarding its tentative list of significantly affected stakeholder categories from which potential members of the committee may be selected.
Consistent with the Negotiated Rulemaking Act, the committee will also include a representative from NHTSA who will participate fully in the committee's deliberations and is authorized to represent the agency in discussions and negotiations. (
5 U.S.C. 566(b)
).
Process and Deadline for Submitting Comments and Nominations:
As part of establishing the committee, NHTSA is seeking public feedback. NHTSA welcomes public reviews of all aspects of the negotiated rulemaking committee described in this Notice, and requests comments specifically on (1) the
(
printed page 67649)
proposed scope of the committee and (2) the proposed balance of representation on the committee. NHTSA will consider the comments and information received in establishing its Negotiated Rulemaking Advisory Committee for Tire Safety.
Applications from interested individuals.
To be considered for appointment, qualified applicants are invited to self-nominate or be nominated by any stakeholder or stakeholder organization by submitting the following information:
Name, title, and relevant contact (including phone, fax (if available), and email address) of the nominee and a description of the interests the applicant or nominee shall represent;
A letter of support from a company, association, academic or nonprofit organization on letterhead authorizing the applicant or nominee to represent parties related to the interest the person proposes to represent;
Short biography of the nominee, including professional and academic credentials; and
A written commitment that the applicant or nominee shall actively participate in good faith in the development of the rule under consideration.
Each applicant must identify the category that he or she seeks to represent. Members should be senior level officials who are authorized to participate on the committee by their organizations and who either are experts on vehicle lighting with respect to the topics of interest to their organizations or who have access to such experts. Individuals applying for membership should keep in mind that committee members are representing a class of interests based on the sector identified and should be prepared to participate in committee activities from that perspective.
Materials submitted should total two pages or less. An applicant should include his or her full legal name and date of birth in the application. Evaluations will be based on publicly available information and the materials submitted. Submissions must be sent to the location listed in the
ADDRESSES
section by the deadline listed in the
DATES
section. Applicants selected for appointment to the committee will be notified by return email and by letter of appointment.
Authority:
Issued under authority in
49 CFR 1.95
.
Jonathan Morrison,
Administrator.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; closure.
SUMMARY:
NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for Pacific cod by vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA). This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of Pacific cod allocated to vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA.
DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 23, 2026, through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Adam Zaleski, 907-586-7228.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA exclusive economic zone according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the Gulf of Alaska (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of
50 CFR part 600
and
50 CFR part 679
.
The 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA is 3,080 metric tons (mt) as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (
91 FR 11902
, March 11, 2026) and reallocations (
91 FR 64807
, October 13, 2026 and
91 FR 66531
, October 21, 2026).
(
printed page 67529)
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (Regional Administrator) has determined that the 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA will be or has been reached. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(i) and 679.20(d)(1)(ii)(B), the Regional Administrator is establishing a directed fishing allowance of 2,480 mt and is setting aside 0 mt as incidental catch because it is not necessary to support other anticipated groundfish fisheries. The Regional Administrator finds that this directed fishing allowance will be or has been reached. Consequently, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(iii), NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for Pacific cod by vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA to prevent exceeding this sector's annual allocation of Pacific cod TAC.
While this closure is effective the maximum retainable amounts at § 679.20(e) and (f) apply at any time during a trip.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by
50 CFR part 679
, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under
Executive Order 12866
.
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data on Pacific cod catch in a timely fashion and would delay the closure of directed fishing for Pacific cod by vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data on Pacific cod catch by vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA only became available as of October 22, 2026.
There is good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
to establish an effective date less than 30 days after the date of publication. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.
Authority:
16 U.S.C. 1801
et seq.
Dated: October 23, 2026.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Section 106 of the Department of Housing and Urban Development Reform Act of 1989 (the HUD Reform Act) requires HUD to publish quarterly
Federal Register
notices of all regulatory waivers that HUD has approved. Each notice covers the quarterly period since the previous
Federal Register
notice. The purpose of this notice is to comply with the requirements of section 106 of the HUD Reform Act. This notice contains a list of regulatory waivers granted by HUD during the period beginning on January 1, 2026 and ending on March 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For general information about this notice, contact Amanda Wahlig, Acting Associate General Counsel for Legislation and Regulations, Department of Housing and Urban Development, 451 7th Street SW, Room 10282, Washington, DC 20410-0500, telephone 202-708-3055 (this is not a toll-free number). HUD welcomes and is prepared to receive calls from individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, as well as individuals with speech or communication disabilities. To learn more about how to make an accessible telephone call, please visit:
https://www.fcc.gov/​consumers/​guides/​telecommunications-relay-service-trs
.
For information concerning a particular waiver that was granted and for which public notice is provided in this document, contact the person whose name and address follow the description of the waiver granted in the accompanying list of waivers that have been granted in the first quarter of calendar year 2026.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 106 of the HUD Reform Act added a new section 7(q) to the Department of Housing and Urban Development Act (
42 U.S.C. 3535(q)
), which provides that:
1. Any waiver of a regulation must be in writing and must specify the grounds for approving the waiver;
2. Authority to approve a waiver of a regulation may be delegated by the Secretary only to an individual of Assistant Secretary or equivalent rank, and the person to whom authority to waive is delegated must also have authority to issue the particular regulation to be waived;
3. Not less than quarterly, the Secretary must notify the public of all waivers of regulations that HUD has approved, by publishing a notice in the
Federal Register
. These notices (each covering the period since the most recent previous notification) shall:
a. Identify the project, activity, or undertaking involved;
b. Describe the nature of the provision waived and the designation of the provision;
c. Indicate the name and title of the person who granted the waiver request;
d. Describe briefly the grounds for approval of the request; and
e. State how additional information about a particular waiver may be obtained.
Section 106 of the HUD Reform Act also contains requirements applicable to waivers of HUD handbook provisions that are not relevant to the purpose of this notice.
This notice follows procedures provided in HUD's Statement of Policy on Waiver of Regulations and Directives issued on April 22, 1991 (
56 FR 16337
). In accordance with those procedures and with the requirements of section 106 of the HUD Reform Act, waivers of regulations are granted by the Assistant Secretary with jurisdiction over the regulations for which a waiver was requested. In those cases in which a General Deputy Assistant Secretary granted the waiver, the General Deputy Assistant Secretary was serving in the absence of the Assistant Secretary in accordance with the office's Order of Succession.
This notice covers waivers of regulations granted by HUD from January 1, 2026 through March 31, 2026. For ease of reference, the waivers granted by HUD are listed by HUD program office (for example, the Office of Community Planning and Development, the Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity, the Office of Housing, and the Office of Public and Indian Housing, etc.). Within each program office grouping, the waivers are listed sequentially by the regulatory section of
title 24 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) that is being waived. For example, a waiver of a provision in
24 CFR part 58
would be listed before a waiver of a provision in
24 CFR part 570
.
Where more than one regulatory provision is involved in the grant of a particular waiver request, the action is listed under the section number of the first regulatory requirement that appears in 24 CFR and that is being waived. For example, a waiver of both § 58.73 and § 58.74 would appear sequentially in the listing under § 58.73.
Waiver of regulations that involve the same initial regulatory citation are in time sequence beginning with the earliest-dated regulatory waiver.
Should HUD receive additional information about waivers granted during the period covered by this report (the first quarter of calendar year 2026) before the next report is published (the second quarter of calendar year 2026), HUD will include any additional waivers granted for the first quarter in the next report.
(
printed page 67599)
Accordingly, information about approved waiver requests pertaining to HUD regulations is provided in the Appendix that follows this notice.

Nature of Requirement:
The ESG regulation at
24 CFR 576.203 (b)

All of the recipient's grant must be expended for eligible activity costs within 24 months after the date HUD signs the grant agreement with the recipient. Granted By:
Ronald J. Kurtz, Assistant Secretary for Community Planning and Development.
Date Granted:
March 17, 2026.
Reason Waived:
On July 10, 2025, DHS submitted a request for the Department to waive the ESG Program requirement at
24 CFR 576.203 (b)
for its Rapid Unsheltered Survivor Housing grant. DHS requested that the original expenditure deadline of November 23, 2025, be extended to December 31, 2026. On November 21, 2025 HUD provided a response, stating that:
1. The 24-month expenditure deadline would limit the State's ability to strategically use RUSH funding to address the needs of individuals affected by the Maui Wildfires.
2. Requiring that rental assistance expenditures end on the original period of performance end date of November 23, 2025, could result in program participants returning to homeless situations in a community still recovering from the natural disaster.
In that memorandum, the Department granted a one-month extension through December 31, 2025, requiring DHS to submit a spending plan to HUD on or before December 31, 2025, for consideration of a full-year extension. DHS submitted the spending plan to HUD on December 23, 2025, showing projected monthly expenditures by subrecipient through December 31, 2026. The spending plan provided detailed accounting of upcoming expenditures, giving a strong indication that this disaster response funding is greatly needed to continue street outreach activities and prevent currently housed program participants from returning to homeless situations in the wake of the Maui Wildfires. Based on the circumstances described above, pursuant to waiver authority provided at
24 CFR 5.110
, that there is good cause to waive, the waiver of
24 CFR 576.203 (b)
of the ESG Program regulations was granted, so long as the State complies with the expenditure deadline of December 31, 2026.

Reason Waived:
HUD grants the waivers on the basis of good cause, citing that EHA has demonstrated the monthly two-bedroom Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) Gross Rent is less than 30% of the monthly income of a family of four at the midpoint between the Very Low Income (VLI) HUD Income Limit and Extremely Low Income (ELI) HUD Income Limit for the area in which the Covered Projects are located through the following calculation: The applicable VLI limit is $68,550 and the ELI limit is $41,150 for a four-person household in the Bergen-Passaic, NJ HUD Metro Fair Market Rent Area in which the Covered Projects are located. AGENCY:
U.S. International Trade Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that on October 20, 2026, the presiding administrative law judge (“ALJ”) issued an Initial Determination on Violation of Section 337 and Recommended Determination on Remedy and Bond. The Commission is soliciting submissions on public interest issues raised by the recommended relief should the Commission find a violation. This notice is soliciting comments from the public and interested government agencies only.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Joelle Justus, Esq., Office of the General Counsel, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, telephone (202) 205-2593. Copies of non-confidential documents filed in connection with this investigation may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov
.
For help accessing EDIS, please email
EDIS3Help@usitc.gov
.
General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server at
https://www.usitc.gov
.
Hearing-impaired persons are advised that information on this matter can be obtained by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on (202) 205-1810.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930 provides that, if the Commission finds a violation, it shall exclude the articles concerned from the United States unless, after considering the effect of such exclusion upon the public health and welfare, competitive conditions in the United States economy, the production of like or directly competitive articles in the United States, and United States consumers, it finds that such articles should not be excluded from entry. (
19 U.S.C. 1337(d)(1)
). A similar provision applies to cease and desist orders. (
19 U.S.C. 1337(f)(1)
).
The Commission is soliciting submissions on public interest issues raised by the recommended relief should the Commission find a violation. The recommended relief includes a limited exclusion order directed to vaporizer devices, cartridges used therewith, and components thereof imported, sold for importation, and/or sold after importation by respondents Glas, Inc. and Glas, LLC that infringe claims 1, 5, 7, 15-16, and 18-21 of U.S. Patent No. 11,134,722 and claims 1, 5, and 8 of U.S. Patent No. 11,606,981. The recommended relief also includes a cease and desist order directed to the Glas respondents. Parties are to file public interest submissions pursuant to
19 CFR 210.50(a)(4)
.
The Commission is interested in further development of the record on the public interest in this investigation. Accordingly, members of the public and interested government agencies are invited to file submissions of no more than five (5) pages, inclusive of attachments, concerning the public interest in light of the ALJ's Recommended Determination on Remedy and Bonding issued in this investigation on October 20, 2026. Comments should address whether issuance of the recommended remedial orders in this investigation, should the Commission find a violation, would affect the public health and welfare in the United States, competitive conditions in the United States economy, the production of like or directly competitive articles in the United States, or United States consumers.
In particular, the Commission is interested in comments that:
(i) Explain how the articles potentially subject to the recommended remedial orders are used in the United States;
(ii) Identify any public health, safety, or welfare concerns in the United States relating to the recommended orders;
(iii) Identify like or directly competitive articles that complainant, its licensees, or third parties make in the United States which could replace the subject articles if they were to be excluded;
(iv) Indicate whether complainant, complainant's licensees, and/or third-party suppliers have the capacity to replace the volume of articles potentially subject to the recommended orders within a commercially reasonable time; and
(v) Explain how the recommended orders would impact consumers in the United States.
Written submissions must be filed no later than by close of business on November 19, 2026.
Persons filing written submissions must file the original document electronically on or before the deadlines stated above pursuant to
19 CFR 210.4(f)
. Submissions should refer to the investigation number (“Inv. No. 337-TA-1464”) in a prominent place on the cover page and/or the first page. (
See
Handbook for Electronic Filing Procedures,
https://www.usitc.gov/​secretary/​documents/​handbook_​on_​filing_​procedures.pdf
). Persons with questions regarding filing should contact the Secretary (202-205-2000).
Any person desiring to submit a document to the Commission in confidence must request confidential treatment by marking each document with a header indicating that the document contains confidential information. This marking will be deemed to satisfy the request procedure set forth in Rules 201.6(b) and 210.5(e)(2) (
19 CFR 201.6(b)
,
210.5(e)(2)
). Documents for which confidential treatment by the Commission is properly sought will be treated accordingly. Any non-party wishing to submit comments containing confidential information must serve those comments on the parties to the investigation pursuant to the applicable Administrative Protective Order. A redacted non-confidential version of the document must also be filed simultaneously with any confidential filing and must be served in accordance with Commission Rule 210.4(f)(7)(ii)(A) (
19 CFR 210.4(f)(7)(ii)(A)
). All information, including confidential business information and documents for which confidential treatment is properly sought, submitted to the Commission for purposes of this investigation may be disclosed to and used: (i) by the Commission, its employees and Offices, and contract personnel (a) for developing or maintaining the records of this or a related proceeding, or (b) in internal investigations, audits, reviews, and evaluations relating to the programs, personnel, and operations of the Commission including under 5 U.S.C. Appendix 3; or (ii) by U.S. government employees and contract personnel, solely for cybersecurity purposes. All contract personnel will sign appropriate nondisclosure agreements. All nonconfidential written submissions will be available for public inspection on EDIS.
This action is taken under the authority of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (
19 U.S.C. 1337
), and in Part 210 of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure (
19 CFR part 210
).
By order of the Commission.

AGENCY:
Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, Department of Energy.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The United States (U.S.) Department of Energy (DOE) is issuing this notice to advise the public that DOE added helium to the DOE Critical Material List. This notice also provides the link to the assessment that forms the justification for including helium on the Critical Material List. Helium is non-substitutable for multiple critical energy functions, including: semiconductor manufacturing, leak testing natural gas infrastructure, and quantum computing, along with being essential to key medical/scientific applications. Demand for helium is also growing as it enables advanced semiconductor manufacturing, which is essential for SI and data center supply chains.
ADDRESSES:
The assessment that forms the justification for including helium on the Critical Material List can be found on DOE's website:
https://www.energy.gov/​cmm/​what-are-critical-materials-and-critical-minerals
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Questions may be addressed to Jacob Ward, U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, Office of Analysis and Strategy, Forrestal Building, Room CM-1, 1000 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20585; (202) 430-2229;
jacob.ward@doe.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 7002(a)(2) of the Energy Act of 2020 (
Pub. L. 116-260
, div. Z, 134 Stat. 2418) defines “critical materials” to be: any non-fuel mineral, element, substance, or material that the Secretary of Energy determines has high risk for supply chain disruption and serves an essential function in one or more energy technologies, including technologies that produce, transmit, store, and conserve energy (referred to here as a critical material for energy) or a critical mineral (as designated by the Secretary of the Interior).
[
1
]
On August 4, 2023, DOE published its Notice of Final Determination on 2023 DOE Critical Materials List (“Critical Materials List”).
[
2
]
The Critical Materials List includes the following:
Critical materials for energy:
aluminum, cobalt, copper*, dysprosium, electrical steel* (grain-oriented electrical steel, non-grain-oriented electrical steel, and amorphous steel), fluorine, gallium, iridium, lithium, magnesium, natural graphite, neodymium, nickel, platinum, praseodymium, terbium, silicon*, and silicon carbide*.
[
3
]
Critical minerals:
The Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Director of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), published a 2022 final list of critical minerals that includes the following 50 minerals: Aluminum, antimony, arsenic, barite, beryllium, bismuth, cerium, cesium, chromium, cobalt, dysprosium, erbium, europium, fluorspar, gadolinium, gallium, germanium, graphite, hafnium, holmium, indium, iridium, lanthanum, lithium, lutetium, magnesium, manganese, neodymium, nickel, niobium, palladium, platinum, praseodymium, rhodium, rubidium, ruthenium, samarium, scandium, tantalum, tellurium, terbium, thulium, tin, titanium, tungsten, vanadium, ytterbium, yttrium, zinc, and zirconium.
The critical materials for energy included on the Critical Material List are based on the criticality assessed in the short- and medium-term. A detailed description of DOE's methodology can be found in its Critical Minerals Assessment published on its website in July 2023.
[
4
]
On May 22, 2025, metallurgical grade coal for steelmaking was added to DOE's list of critical materials for energy.
[
5
]
By this notice, the Secretary of Energy advises the public of the addition of helium to DOE's Critical Material List. The assessment that forms the justification for including helium on the Critical Material List can be found on DOE's website:
https://www.energy.gov/​cmm/​what-are-critical-materials-and-critical-minerals
.
The assessment concludes that helium is needed globally for semiconductor manufacturing and other key energy applications. Meeting the policy goal of building U.S. SI infrastructure will require expansion of semiconductor production and thereby supports the determination that helium is a DOE critical material.
Furthermore, this action directly supports the President's policy goal of “Winning the AI Race: America's AI Action Plan”
[
6
]
and “Advancing United States Leadership in Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure”.
[
7
]

This document of the Department of Energy was signed on October 21, 2026, by Audrey Robertson, Assistant Secretary, Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, pursuant to delegated authority from the Secretary of Energy. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DOE. For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DOE Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of the Department of Energy. SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is soliciting nominations for the position of an Interventional Radiologist on the Advisory Committee on the Medical Uses of Isotopes (ACMUI). Nominees should currently be practicing as an Interventional Radiologist.
DATES:

Nomination Process:
Submit an electronic copy of resume or curriculum vitae, along with a cover letter, to Ms. Sarah Hoenig,
Sarah.Hoenig@nrc.gov
.
The cover letter should describe the nominee's current duties and responsibilities and express the nominee's interest in the position. Please ensure that the resume or curriculum vitae includes the following information, if applicable: education; certification(s); professional association and committee membership activities; duties and responsibilities in current and previous clinical, research, and/or academic position(s).
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Sarah Hoenig, U.S Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards; 301-415-3284;
Sarah.Hoenig@nrc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
ACMUI members possess the medical and technical skills needed to address evolving issues. The current membership is comprised of the following professionals: (a) nuclear medicine physician; (b) nuclear cardiologist; (c) two radiation oncologists; (d) diagnostic radiologist; (e) therapy medical physicist; (f) nuclear medicine physicist; (g) nuclear pharmacist; (h) radiation safety officer; (i) patients' rights advocate; (j) Food and Drug Administration representative; (k) Agreement State representative; and (l) interventional radiologist (vacant). http://www.nrc.gov/​about-nrc/​regulatory/​advisory/​acmui/​membership.html

Abstract:
The STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program was authorized through the Violence Against Women Act of 1994 (VAWA), amended and reauthorized in 2000, 2005, 2013 and 2022. The STOP (Services, Training, Officers, and Prosecutors) Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program provides funding to states and territories for use by state, local, and Indian Tribal governments, courts, and victim service providers. This program enhances the capacity of local communities to develop and strengthen effective law enforcement and prosecution strategies to combat domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault and stalking and to develop and strengthen comprehensive, holistic victim services. The grant funds must be distributed by STOP state administrators to subgrantees according to a statutory formula.
Each state and territory must allocate 25 percent for law enforcement, 25 percent for prosecutors, 30 percent for victim services (of which at least 10 percent must be distributed to culturally specific community-based organizations), 5 percent to state and local courts, and 15 percent for discretionary distribution. VAWA provides for a 25 percent match requirement imposed on grant funds under the STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program. Thus, a grant made under this program may not cover more than 75 percent of the total costs of the project being funded. The state is exempted from matching the portion of the state award that goes to a victim service provider for victim services or that goes to a tribe. Territories are also exempted in full. States can apply to have the match requirement waived by submitting a petition to OVW and a demonstrating financial need. At the time of closeout, OVW will look at the entities and purposes of funds and determine the required match amount.
The purpose of this information collection is to provide a worksheet for documenting the amount of matching funds required at the closeout of a specific fiscal year award under the STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program. The type of questions on the worksheet will include award number, award amount and amount of funds sub-awarded to victim service providers for victim services or to tribes.
