Department of Homeland Security
AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection, DHS.
ACTION:
General notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice announces the decision of the Secretary of Homeland Security (Secretary) to suspend the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) Economic Vitality & Security Travel Authorization Program (EVS-TAP). EVS-TAP allows prescreened nationals of the People's Republic of China (PRC) to travel to the CNMI without a visa for temporary visits under specified conditions. Pursuant to the Immigration and Nationality Act and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) regulations, the Secretary has broad authority to suspend the program for good cause, including threats to national security, law enforcement interests, and immigration enforcement. The Secretary has determined that there is good cause to suspend EVS-TAP, while DHS, in consultation with the Secretary of State and the Secretary of the Interior, evaluates the program.
DATES:
Suspension of the CNMI EVS-TAP is effective at 1400 EDT on October 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Melanie Mataxas, Traveler Authorization and Communications Program Management Office, Office of Field Operations, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, at (202) 325-1372, or via email at
melanie.d.mataxas@cbp.dhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Generally, under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA),
8 U.S.C. 1101
et. seq.
, aliens seeking admission to the United States, including nonimmigrants visiting temporarily for business or pleasure, must obtain a visa before traveling to the United States.
See
section 212(a)(7)(B)(i) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(7)(B)(i)
. In 2008, Congress enacted the Consolidated Natural Resources Act of 2008 (CNRA),
Public Law 110-229
, 122 Stat. 754, which generally applied the INA, including the standard visa requirements, to Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI).
See
48 U.S.C. 1806(a)
; sections 212 and 214 of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182
and
1184
. Under the standard visa application process, nonimmigrant visitors must complete an application, submit fingerprints and certain biometrics, and participate in an interview at a U.S. Consulate or Embassy, subject to certain exceptions.
See
section 222 of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1202
;
8 CFR 103.2
;
22 CFR part 42
.
As a part of the CNRA, however, Congress also authorized the creation of a specific visa waiver program for travel specific to Guam and the CNMI.
[
1
]
Section 212(l) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)
, as amended by the CNRA, sets forth the general parameters of this specific visa waiver authority. The
(
printed page 67596)
statute authorizes the Secretary of Homeland Security (the Secretary), in consultation with the Secretary of the Interior and the Secretary of State, to designate countries whose nationals can seek admission to Guam or the CNMI as nonimmigrant visitors for business or pleasure for a period up to 45 days without first obtaining a nonimmigrant visa if certain conditions are met.
See
section 212(l)(1) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)(1)
. The statute also provides for a consultation process that allows the Governors of Guam and the CNMI to request that certain countries be added to the list of countries whose nationals are eligible for admission without a visa.
See
section 212(l)(6) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)(6)
.
Importantly, section 212(l)(5) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)(5)
, directs the Secretary to monitor the admission of nonimmigrant visitors admitted under the Guam-CNMI Visa Waiver Program (G-CNMI VWP), and mandates suspension of participation, on a country-by-country basis, if admissions lead to an unacceptable number of visitors from a country remaining unlawfully in Guam or the CNMI, unlawfully obtaining entry to other parts of the United States or seeking asylum or withholding of removal, or such visitors pose a risk to U.S. security, law enforcement, or immigration enforcement interests. Additionally, the statute further authorizes the Secretary to suspend the program at any time, on a country-by-country basis, for other good cause.
See
section 212(l)(5) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)(5)
. And it also provides that the Secretary, after consultation with the Secretary of the Interior and the Secretary of State, may discontinue the G-CNMI VWP on a country-by-country basis entirely after considering relevant factors.
See
section 212(l)(3), (4) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)(3)
, (4).
As required by statute, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has issued a series of regulations and regulatory actions to create and implement the G-CNMI VWP and the above discussed statutory framework.
See
section 212(l)(3),
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)(3)
(directing DHS to issue “all necessary regulations” to implement the G-CNMI visa waiver authority);
8 CFR 212.1(q)
,
(r)
. In January 2009, DHS issued an interim final rule (IFR) amending DHS regulations to, among other things, set forth the requirements and procedures for an authorized country's nationals to participate in G-CNMI VWP.
See
74 FR 2824
(Jan. 16, 2009) (2009 IFR). The 2009 IFR also codified in DHS's regulations the Secretary's authority to suspend or terminate that participation on a country-by-country basis.
See
74 FR 2825-29
.
At the time, the 2009 IFR announced the Secretary's determination, after appropriate consultations, that the nationals of several countries were eligible for participation in the G-CNMI VWP.
74 FR 2827
;
see also
8 CFR 212.1(q)(2)(ii)
. DHS determined that PRC nationals would not be eligible to participate in the G-CNMI VWP due to political and security concerns.
74 FR 2826-27
. However, in recognition of the economic significance of visitors from the PRC to the CNMI, the then-Secretary also announced that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) would favorably consider eligible PRC nationals for parole into the United States, on a case-by-case basis, pursuant to INA 212(d)(5),
8 U.S.C. 1182(d)(5)
, rather than requiring these individuals to obtain nonimmigrant visas.
See
89 FR 3299
,
3302
.
In 2024, DHS published an IFR updating the G-CNMI-VWP, requiring, among other things, that nationals from authorized countries must seek electronic travel authorization under the G-CNMI VWP, and creating a restricted sub-program for PRC nationals seeking visa-exempt travel to the CNMI only.
89 FR 3299
(Jan. 18, 2024) (2024 IFR). This sub-program is known as the CNMI EVS-TAP. EVS-TAP regulations, codified at
8 CFR 212.1(r)
, were developed following consultations between the Federal Government of the United States and the Government of the CNMI, and were structured to balance the importance of the PRC tourism industry to the CNMI with national security, public safety, and immigration concerns related to PRC nationals traveling visa-exempt to the CNMI.
See
89 FR 3302-3304
,
3306
. To that end, EVS-TAP regulations include additional restrictions that do not currently pertain to the rest of the G-CNMI VWP. For example, under EVS-TAP, travel authorizations are granted for a period of one year; travelers from the PRC are allowed to enter only the CNMI without a visa, are not permitted to enter Guam, the mainland, or any other U.S. location, and are generally authorized to remain in the CNMI for a maximum of 14 days per visit.
See
8 CFR 212.1(r)(2)
,
(9)
. In creating this regulatory program, DHS also explicitly preserved the Secretary's broad statutory authority in section 212(l)(5) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)(5)
, to suspend EVS-TAP. The applicable DHS regulation,
8 CFR 212.1(r)(3)(i)
, authorizes the Secretary to suspend EVS-TAP for good cause, including where the admission of PRC national visitors to the CNMI under EVS-TAP creates unacceptable risks to U.S. security interests, law enforcement, or immigration interests.
At the time these programs were established, to fully integrate the two automated systems in an efficient and cost-effective manner, DHS determined that EVS-TAP should be implemented after the system for G-CNMI VWP automation became fully operational.
See
89 FR 3303
,
3310
and
8 CFR 212.1(r)(11)
. The G-CNMI VWP automation became fully operational in November 2024 after a transition period provided by the IFR.
See
90 FR 658
,
659
(Jan. 6, 2025). On January 6, 2025, DHS published the required notice in the
Federal Register
,
90 FR 658
, announcing implementation of EVS-TAP with an effective date of February 20, 2025.
[
2
]
Concurrently, the previous parole policy for PRC nationals seeking to enter the CNMI was discontinued on February 20, 2025.
See id.
Suspension of EVS-TAP
After careful consideration, and consistent with the authorities provided under section 212(l)(5) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)(5)
, and the CNRA, as well as the DHS regulations at
8 CFR 212.1(r)
establishing EVS-TAP and giving the Secretary broad authority to suspend the program,
see
8 CFR 212.1(r)(3)
, the Secretary has determined there is good cause to suspend the EVS-TAP. This suspension is effective at 1400 EDT on October 30, 2026 for potential new applicants to EVS-TAP as well as previously approved travelers with an existing EVS-TAP travel authorization.
[
3
]
PRC nationals already admitted under EVS-TAP and legally present in the CNMI on the effective date of this notice will be permitted to remain for their current authorized period of stay, however, these travelers will need to
(
printed page 67597)
obtain a visa for any future travel to the CNMI.
The Secretary has found good cause for the suspension because the United States is facing evolving and sophisticated threats which, combined with a significant number of PRC nationals entering the CNMI under EVS-TAP, creates a significant risk to the security and law enforcement interests of the United States. In Fiscal Year (FY) 2025, more than 3,000 PRC nationals utilized EVS-TAP to enter the CNMI under the streamlined travel authorization process.
[
4
]
These PRC nationals are vetted through CBP instead of by a State Department consular officer. While the program was intended to facilitate economic travel and enhance security over the prior parole policy, this volume of visa-exempt entries presents unacceptable security and law enforcement risks. DHS judges that PRC nationals are almost certainly exploiting EVS-TAP. Prior incidents involving PRC nationals who used the former parole process or other streamlined travel to the CNMI demonstrate an enduring vulnerability involving unauthorized onward travel and activity near sensitive military installations. EVS-TAP continued to permit travel without the additional screening associated with a nonimmigrant visa and therefore did not eliminate this underlying vulnerability.
One significant national security concern is that EVS-TAP may be exploited to facilitate PRC espionage and intelligence collection directed against sensitive U.S. defense infrastructure in the region. The Indo-Pacific region and the security of Guam and the CNMI are of vital strategic importance to the United States. In the CNMI, the Department of War (DOW) is restoring the Tinian Air Base to support U.S. military strategic interests in the Indo-Pacific. Additionally, neighboring Guam is also home to several DOW military installations critical to homeland defense and U.S. military interests. Despite the strict regulatory prohibition against PRC nationals traveling beyond the CNMI, PRC nationals have the ability to illegally travel from the CNMI to Guam aboard smuggling vessels.
For example, prior to the implementation of EVS-TAP, in March 2024, the United States Attorney for the Districts of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, announced sentencing of a PRC national for conspiring to transport illegal aliens. In this case, the PRC national smuggler was engaged in smuggling nine other PRC nationals from CNMI to Guam.
[
5
]
Similarly, in February 2025, the United States Attorney for the Districts of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands in Saipan and Guam announced sentencing of a PRC national who had engaged in conspiracy to transport illegal aliens, by smuggling seven other PRC nationals from CNMI to Guam. Most of these PRC nationals were later encountered in or near sensitive military installations. As the United States Attorney at the time stated, these aliens “took advantage of unique federal immigration regulations that permit certain foreign nationals to visit the CNMI as tourists. Any local economic benefits from these provisions are lost when those persons later attempt to unlawfully enter another part of the United States” and linger around sensitive military installations.
[
6
]
DHS believes that circumventing onward travel restrictions, potentially exposing critical U.S. military installations, present unacceptable risks to U.S. national security interests, which DHS must take action to prevent.
In addition to espionage, EVS-TAP may create immigration enforcement challenges by aliens who seek to exploit EVS-TAP to engage in birth tourism and secure U.S. citizenship for children with no lasting ties to the United States. While birth tourism has long been an issue in the CNMI, the availability of visa-exempt travel and reduced vetting under EVS-TAP may lower barriers to this practice. Birth tourism can strain medical infrastructure in the CNMI and harm local citizens. Additionally, birth tourism may also be utilized to facilitate long-term intelligence or espionage activities. Suspending EVS-TAP allows DHS to evaluate measures to mitigate this threat.
Furthermore, the CNMI's history of PRC-linked criminal activity demonstrates the risks that must be considered when assessing streamlined, visa-exempt travel under EVS-TAP. The CNMI has previously experienced criminal activity, including significant money laundering and labor abuses from enterprises operated by PRC-linked entities, most notably the development of a casino gaming operation in Saipan. While a permanent casino was under construction, a PRC company opened a temporary casino that was linked to money laundering and labor abuses. This temporary facility, located in a former shopping mall, reported more than $2 billion monthly in VIP bets, rivaling Macau.
[
7
]
Meanwhile, the construction of the permanent facility was plagued by labor violations resulting in millions of dollars in fines. The executives of the operating company were eventually indicted on Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act charges.
[
8
]
Yet, open-source reporting indicates that individuals linked to the prior operators have since purchased and resumed construction on the permanent casino.
[
9
]
Given these developments, DHS believes that facilitating visa-exempt access to the CNMI for PRC nationals contributes to an unacceptable risk of fueling organized criminal networks, financial crimes, and labor abuses in the CNMI.
Consideration of Potential Reliance Interests
Section 212(l)(5) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)(5)
, and
8 CFR 212.1(r)(3)(i)
authorize suspension for good cause based on risks to national security, law enforcement, and immigration enforcement. These provisions do not require the Secretary to balance national security or law enforcement interests, including immigration, against any economic or other reliance interests that may be impacted by a suspension. Rather, the statute and regulation commit the evaluation of good cause to the broad and sole discretion of the Secretary, focusing squarely on whether the admission of PRC nationals threatens the security and law enforcement interests of the United States and its territories, including the CNMI.
Although the suspension standard does not prescribe a separate economic balancing test, the Secretary has considered the potential reliance interests of CNMI businesses and affected travelers. DHS acknowledges that certain businesses in the CNMI may have developed business plans based on tourism and commercial travel from EVS-TAP or the prior parole policy that
(
printed page 67598)
EVS-TAP replaced. Similarly, DHS recognizes that prospective travelers from the PRC may be inconvenienced or face financial loss from this suspension and revocation of travel authorizations. DHS believes, however, that any such impacts are mitigated by the fact that bona fide visitors for business or pleasure from the PRC remain able to obtain a nonimmigrant visa to travel to the CNMI.
See
8 CFR 212.1(r)(9)(vi)(B)
. In any event, DHS has determined that the identified acute risks to the national security, immigration, and law enforcement interests of the United States outweigh any countervailing personal or economic interests.
Notice of Suspension of EVS-TAP
For the above discussed reasons, and in accordance with section 212(l)(5) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(l)(5)
, and
8 CFR 212.1(r)(3)
, the Secretary is suspending EVS-TAP, which includes both future applicants for EVS-TAP travel authorization as well as any currently active EVS-TAP travel authorizations, except that PRC nationals already admitted under EVS-TAP and legally present in the CNMI on the effective date of this notice will be permitted to remain for their authorized period of stay. This suspension is effective at 1400 EDT on October 30, 2026.
As of 1400 EDT on October 30, 2026, PRC nationals seeking to travel to the CNMI for a temporary visit for business or pleasure must obtain an appropriate nonimmigrant visa before traveling to the CNMI unless another lawful exception applies. This suspension does not reinstate the prior parole policy for PRC nationals seeking to enter the CNMI, which was discontinued on February 20, 2025.
See
90 FR 658
.

SUMMARY:
The Department of Justice (DOJ), Office on Violence Against Women, will be submitting the following information collection request to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. The proposed information collection was previously published in the
Federal Register
on August 20, 2026, allowing a 60-day comment period.
DATES:
Comments are encouraged and will be accepted for 30 days until November 27, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have comments especially on the estimated public burden or associated response time, suggestions, or need a copy of the proposed information collection instrument with instructions or additional information, please contact: Tiffany Watson, Office on Violence Against Women, at 202-307-6026 or
Tiffany.Watson@usdoj.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Written comments and suggestions from the public and affected agencies concerning the proposed collection of information are encouraged. Your comments should address one or more of the following four points:
—Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility;
—Evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
—Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and/or
—Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.
, permitting electronic submission of responses.
Written comments and recommendations for this information collection should be submitted within 30 days of the publication of this notice on the following website
www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
. Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function and entering either the title of the information collection or the OMB Control Number 1122-0003. This information collection request may be viewed at
www.reginfo.gov
. Follow the instructions to view Department of Justice, information collections currently under review by OMB. If you submit a public comment, please send a copy to Tiffany Watson at
tiffany.watson@usdoj.gov
.
DOJ seeks PRA authorization for this information collection for three (3) years. OMB authorization for an ICR cannot be for more than three (3) years without renewal. The DOJ notes that information collection requirements submitted to the OMB for existing ICRs receive a month-to-month extension while they undergo review.
Abstract:
The STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program was authorized through the Violence Against Women Act of 1994 (VAWA), amended and reauthorized in 2000, 2005, 2013 and 2022. The STOP (Services, Training, Officers, and Prosecutors) Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program provides funding to states and territories for use by state, local, and Indian Tribal governments, courts, and victim service providers. This program enhances the capacity of local communities to develop and strengthen effective law enforcement and prosecution strategies to combat domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault and stalking and to develop and strengthen comprehensive, holistic victim services. The grant funds must be distributed by STOP state administrators to subgrantees according to a statutory formula.
This information collection is necessary for the Attorney General and STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program grantees and subgrantees to comply with federal statutory reporting requirements. The information will be used for reports to Congress on the use of appropriated funds in support of the STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program. There are two sets of respondents—the STOP state administrators who allocate the STOP
(
printed page 67612)
funds and the subgrantees who may include law enforcement agencies, prosecutors' offices, courts, and victim services organizations.
Overview of This Information Collection
1.
Type of Information Collection:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
2.
Title of the Form/Collection:
Annual Progress Report for the STOP Formula Grants Program.
3.
Agency form number, if any, and the applicable component of the Department of Justice sponsoring the collection:
Form Number: 1122-0003. U.S. Department of Justice, Office on Violence Against Women.
4.
Affected public who will be asked or required to respond, as well as a brief abstract:
Affected Public- State, local and Tribal governments. The affected public includes the 56 STOP state administrators (from 50 states, the District of Columbia and five territories and commonwealths (Guam, Puerto Rico, American Samoa, Virgin Islands, Northern Mariana Islands)) and their subgrantees.
5.
An estimate of the total number of respondents and the amount of time estimated for an average respondent to respond:
It is estimated that it will take the 56 respondents (STOP administrators) approximately one hour to complete an annual progress report. It is estimated that it will take approximately one hour for roughly 1,960 subgrantees
[
1
]
to complete the relevant portion of the annual progress report. The Annual Progress Report for the STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program is divided into sections that pertain to the different types of activities that subgrantees may engage in and the different types of subgrantees that receive funds,
i.e.
, law enforcement agencies, prosecutor offices, courts, victim services agencies, etc.
6.
An estimate of the total annual burden (in hours) associated with the collection:
The total annual hour burden to complete the annual progress report is 2,016 hours.
7.
An estimate of the total annual cost burden associated with the collection, if applicable:
The annualized costs to the Federal Government resulting from the OVW staff review of the progress reports submitted by grantees are estimated to be $3,278.80.

On August 30, 2024, Erie Boulevard Hydropower, L.P. filed an application to relicense the 29.14-megawatt Black River Hydroelectric Project No. 2569. The project is located on the Black River in Jefferson County, New York.
In accordance with the Commission's regulations, on August 4, 2026, Commission staff issued a notice that the project was ready for environmental analysis (REA notice). Based on the information in the record, including comments filed on the REA Notice, staff does not anticipate that licensing the project would constitute a major federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human environment. Therefore, staff intends to prepare an environmental assessment (EA) on the application to relicense the project.

Department of Energy
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
[Docket No. RC11-6-022]
Commission staff coordinated with the staff of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) to conduct the annual oversight of NERC's Find, Fix, Track and Report (FFT) program, as outlined in the Commission's March 15, 2012 order,
[
1
]
and the Compliance Exception (CE) Program, as proposed by NERC's September 18, 2015 annual compliance filing and accepted by delegated order.
[
2
]
Commission staff reviewed a sample of 29 of 206 FFTs and 34 of 1,619 CEs submitted by NERC between October 2024 and September 2025.
Commission staff found that the FFT and CE programs are meeting the Commission's expectations in accordance with FFT Order, with limited exceptions. Specifically, Commission staff identified one instance of an FFT in which the original description was incomplete. Staff also noted in two instances of CEs that the originally posted description had an inaccurate noncompliance start or end date. All 63 FFTs and CEs have been adequately remediated, and the root cause of each noncompliance was clearly identified. Commission staff also reviewed the supporting information for these FFTs and CEs and agreed with the final risk determinations for all 63 noncompliances, which clearly identified the factors affecting the risk prior to mitigation (such as potential and actual risk) and actual harm. Further, no FFTs or CEs sampled contained any material misrepresentations by the registered entities. Commission staff found that the Regional Entities appropriately identified all 63 of the sampled noncompliances as appropriate to be processed as FFTs and CEs.

Department of Energy
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
[Docket No. CP26-578-000]
The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) will prepare an environmental document that will discuss the environmental impacts of the Phase IX Project (Project) involving construction and operation of facilities by Florida Gas Transmission Company, LLC (FGT) in Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida. The Commission will use this environmental document in its decision-making process to determine whether the project is in the public convenience and necessity.
This notice announces the opening of the scoping process the Commission will use to gather input from the public and interested agencies regarding the project. As part of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review process, the Commission takes into account concerns the public may have about proposals and the environmental impacts that could result from its action whenever it considers the issuance of a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity. This gathering of public input is referred to as “scoping.” The main goal of the scoping process is to focus the analysis in the environmental document on the important environmental issues. Additional information about the Commission's NEPA process is described below in the
NEPA Process and Environmental Document
section of this notice.
By this notice, the Commission requests public comments on the scope of issues to address in the environmental document. To ensure that your comments are timely and properly recorded, please submit your comments so that the Commission receives them in Washington, DC on or before 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 23, 2026. Comments may be submitted in written form. Further details on how to submit comments are provided in the
Public Participation
section of this notice.
Your comments should focus on the potential environmental effects, reasonable alternatives, and measures to avoid or lessen environmental impacts. Your input will help the Commission staff determine what issues they need to evaluate in the environmental document. Commission staff will consider all written comments during the preparation of the environmental document.
If you submitted comments on this project to the Commission
before
the opening of this docket on September 9, 2026, you will need to file those comments in Docket No. CP26-578-000 to ensure they are considered as part of this proceeding.
This notice is being sent to the Commission's current environmental mailing list for this project. State and local government representatives should notify their constituents of this proposed project and encourage them to comment on their areas of concern.
If you are a landowner receiving this notice, a pipeline company representative may contact you about the acquisition of an easement to construct, operate, and maintain the proposed facilities. The company would seek to negotiate a mutually acceptable easement agreement. You are not required to enter into an agreement. However, if the Commission approves the project, the Natural Gas Act conveys the right of eminent domain to the company. Therefore, if you and the company do not reach an easement agreement, the pipeline company could initiate condemnation proceedings in court. In such instances, compensation would be determined by a judge in accordance with state law. The Commission does not subsequently grant, exercise, or oversee the exercise of that eminent domain authority. The courts have exclusive authority to
(
printed page 67561)
handle eminent domain cases; the Commission has no jurisdiction over these matters.
FGT provided landowners with a fact sheet prepared by the FERC entitled “An Interstate Natural Gas Facility On My Land? What Do I Need To Know?” which addresses typically asked questions, including the use of eminent domain and how to participate in the Commission's proceedings. This fact sheet along with other landowner topics of interest are available for viewing on the FERC website (
www.ferc.gov
) under the Natural Gas, Landowner Topics link.
Public Participation
There are three methods you can use to submit your comments to the Commission. Please carefully follow these instructions so that your comments are properly recorded. The Commission encourages electronic filing of comments and has staff available to assist you at (866) 208-3676 or
FercOnlineSupport@ferc.gov
.
(1) You can file your comments electronically using the eComment feature, which is located on the Commission's website (
www.ferc.gov
) under the link to FERC Online. Using eComment is an easy method for submitting brief, text-only comments on a project;
(2) You can file your comments electronically by using the eFiling feature, which is located on the Commission's website (
www.ferc.gov
) under the link to FERC Online. With eFiling, you can provide comments in a variety of formats by attaching them as a file with your submission. Summary of the Proposed Project
FGT proposes to expand its existing pipeline system by constructing and operating a 42-inch-diameter mainline pipeline, lateral pipelines, compressor stations, and other aboveground facilities in Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida. The Phase IX Project would provide about 508 million cubic feet per day of additional firm natural gas transportation capacity on FGT's interstate pipeline system. According to FGT, its project would meet growing transportation needs resulting from population growth, economic development, and expansion of local distribution company loads, while maximizing the use of and expanding FGT's existing transmission infrastructure.
The Phase IX Project would consist of the following facilities:
9 mainline looping
[
1
]
pipeline segments with varying diameters, totaling 94.6 miles;
modifications to 13 existing compressor stations;
construction of two new compressor stations in Lake and De Soto Counties, Florida;
construction of valves and pig
[
2
]
launchers/receivers; and
8 pig receiver station relocations.
The general location of the project facilities is shown in appendix 1.
[
3
]
A detailed summary of the project facilities is in appendix 2.
Land Requirements for Construction
Construction of the proposed facilities would disturb about 2,245 acres of land for the aboveground facilities and the pipeline. Following construction, FGT would maintain about 727 acres for permanent operation of the project's facilities; the remaining acreage would be restored.
NEPA Process and the Environmental Document
Any environmental document issued by the Commission will discuss impacts that could occur as a result of the construction and operation of the proposed project under the relevant general resource areas:
geology and soils;
water resources and wetlands;
vegetation and wildlife;
threatened and endangered species;
cultural resources;
socioeconomics;
land use, recreation, and visual resources;
air quality and noise; and
reliability and safety.
Commission staff will also evaluate reasonable alternatives to the proposed project or portions of the project and make recommendations on how to lessen or avoid impacts on the various resource areas. Your comments will help Commission staff identify and focus on the issues that might have an effect on the human environment and potentially eliminate others from further study and discussion in the environmental document.
Following this scoping period, Commission staff will determine whether to prepare an Environmental Assessment (EA) or an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS). The EA or the EIS will present Commission staff's independent analysis of the issues. If Commission staff prepares an EA, a
Notice of Schedule for the Preparation of an Environmental Assessment
will be issued. The EA may be issued for an allotted public comment period. The Commission would consider timely comments on the EA before making its decision regarding the proposed project. If Commission staff prepares an EIS, a
Notice of Intent to Prepare an EIS/Notice of Schedule
will be issued, which will open up an additional comment period. Staff will then prepare a draft EIS which will be issued for public comment. Commission staff will consider all timely comments received during the comment period on the draft EIS and revise the document, as necessary, before issuing a final EIS. Any EA or draft and final EIS will be available in electronic format in the public record through eLibrary

Background and Purpose

(“Administrative Procedure Act”),
46 U.S.C. 70110

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain The Boeing Company Model 757-200 and -300 series airplanes. This AD was prompted by a report that some passenger service unit (PSU)-mounted video monitors became detached from the PSU rails during a hard landing. This AD requires replacing PSU-mounted video monitors that do not have secondary retention lanyards. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
This AD is effective December 1, 2026. The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference of certain publications listed in this AD as of December 1, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2025-0003; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule, any comments received, and other information. The address for Docket Operations is U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
Material Incorporated by Reference:
For the material identified in this AD, contact Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Attention: Contractual & Data Services (C&DS), 2600 Westminster Blvd., MC 110-SK57, Seal Beach, CA 90740-5600; telephone 562-797-1717; website
myboeingfleet.com
.
You may view this material at the FAA, Airworthiness Products Section, Operational Safety Branch, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA. For information on the availability of this material at the FAA, call 206-231-3195. It is also available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2025-0003.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Julie Linn, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA 98198; phone: 206-231-3584; email:
julie.linn@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
by adding an AD that would apply to certain The Boeing Company Model 757-200 and -300 series airplanes. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on January 17, 2025 (
90 FR 5754
). The NPRM was prompted by a report that some PSU-mounted video monitors became detached from the PSU rails during a hard landing that did not exceed the emergency load requirements for the PSUs. In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require replacing PSU-mounted video monitors that do not have secondary retention lanyards. The FAA is issuing this AD to address PSU-mounted video monitors that could become fully detached or be held at an unsafe height, which, if not addressed, could result in injury to passengers and impede passenger and crew egress during emergency evacuation.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received a comment from one commenter, an individual, who supported the NPRM without change.
The FAA received additional comments from four commenters, including Aviation Partners Boeing, Delta Air Lines (Delta), Panasonic Avionics Corporation (Panasonic), and Precision Conversions, LLC (Precision). The following presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to each comment.
Request To Clarify Method for Determining Applicability
Delta requested that the FAA clarify that they can accomplish either a physical inspection for the existence of PSU-mounted video monitors or accomplish a review of Delta's PSU Layouts (Delta's PSU drawing configuration) to determine if this AD applies.
The FAA agrees to clarify that operators can determine if their airplanes are equipped with PSU-mounted video monitors by performing a physical inspection or a records check, provided the presence of PSU-mounted video monitors can be conclusively determined from that review; either method is acceptable to determine if this AD applies. The FAA did not change this AD in response to this comment.
Request To Revise Applicability
Precision requested that the FAA revise the applicability of the proposed AD to exclude Boeing Model 757-200 series airplanes that have been converted from passenger to freighter in accordance with a certain supplemental type certificate (STC). Precision STC ST01529SE, which converts Model 757-200 series airplanes from passenger to freighter airplanes, removes all PSU-mounted video monitors to convert the main deck into a cargo compartment, thus eliminating the unsafe condition referenced in the NPRM.
The FAA acknowledges that this AD does not apply to Model 757-200 airplanes converted to freighter in accordance with STC ST01529SE. This AD applies to Model 757-200 and -300 series airplanes equipped with PSU-mounted video monitors. Since Model 757-200 series airplanes converted to freighter in accordance with STC ST01529SE no longer have PSU-mounted video monitors installed, this AD does not apply. The FAA did not change this AD in response to this comment.
Effect of Winglets on Accomplishment of the Proposed Actions
Aviation Partners Boeing stated that the installation of blended or scimitar blended winglets per STC ST01518SE does not affect compliance with the mandated actions in the proposed rule.
The FAA agrees with the commenter that STC ST01518SE does not affect compliance with this AD. Therefore, the installation of STC ST01518SE does not affect the ability to accomplish the actions required by this AD. The FAA did not change this AD in response to this comment.
(
printed page 67443)
Request To Revise Paragraph (e) To Clarify Safety Concerns
Panasonic requested that the FAA revise paragraph (e) of the proposed AD to include the statement, “Although some models of PSU-mounted video monitors have not become detached under such landings, we have determined that this AD is warranted due to relative motion between the PSUs rails that drive forces exceeding the approved emergency landing conditions for the attached PSU-mounted monitors.” Panasonic asserted that the improvement action for Panasonic monitors involves an enhancement to its fail-safe design and is not a result of correcting any defect or noncompliance in the PSU-mounted monitor assemblies themselves. Panasonic requested this change to avoid potentially misleading operators that Panasonic monitors have become detached because they did not meet the existing emergency landing requirements they were designed to meet.
The FAA acknowledges the commenter's concern. The FAA is unaware of Panasonic monitors that have become detached during hard landings that did not exceed emergency landing requirements. However, paragraph (e) of this AD specifies that some, not all, PSU-mounted video monitors became detached. The FAA did not change this AD in response to this comment.
Requests To Include Panasonic Service Bulletins as an Accepted Method of Compliance
Delta requested that the FAA allow the use of Panasonic Service Bulletin RDAA902940-01-44-07 Revision 5, dated December 5, 2024, or RDAA902941-01-44-07 Revision 6, dated December 13, 2024, to meet the requirements of the proposed AD. Delta stated that the affected part numbers (P/Ns) installed on their fleet are P/N RD-AA902940-01 and P/N RD-AA902941-01, which are addressed by the Panasonic service bulletins noted, and requested the FAA add these service bulletins as a method of compliance for the requirements of the proposed AD.
Panasonic requested that the FAA include Panasonic Service Bulletin SB141908-44-002 as an accepted corrective action for the proposed AD but did not provide the specified service bulletin to the FAA. Panasonic asserted that the effectivity of Boeing Special Attention Requirements Bulletin 757-25-0321 RB does not include airplanes with STC alterations that would be affected by the NPRM and suggested that adding this service bulletin as an accepted method of compliance would reduce the FAA's efforts to support alternative methods of compliance (AMOC) requests to address airplanes installed with FAA STC ST03183NY.
The FAA disagrees. Paragraph (g)(3) of this AD already requires airplanes not identified in the effectivity paragraph of either Boeing service bulletin to perform the required actions with an approved AMOC. At this time, the FAA does not have enough data to approve Panasonic Service Bulletin RDAA902940-01-44-07 Revision 5, dated December 5, 2024, RDAA902941-01-44-07 Revision 6, dated December 13, 2024, or Panasonic Service Bulletin SB141908-44-002 as an accepted method of compliance for this AD. The FAA did not change this AD in response to these comments.
Additional Changes to the Final Rule
Since the FAA issued the NPRM, Boeing published Boeing Special Attention Requirements Bulletins 757-25-0320 RB, Revision 1, and 757-25-0321 RB, Revision 1, both dated August 6, 2025. The revised service information specifies an additional inspection of the inboard PSU rail to determine rail lightening hole configuration and applicable on-condition actions, because the original issue could not be complied with to address the unsafe condition. The revised service information adds instructions for installing lanyard retention brackets at locations that do not have 1.0-inch diameter holes in the PSU rail to support secondary retention lanyard installation and at locations that have temperature sensors installed in the inboard PSU rail area, where the existing holes do not allow for correct lanyard installation.
The FAA has revised this AD to mandate Boeing Special Attention Requirements Bulletin 757-25-0320 RB, Revision 1, dated August 6, 2025, and Boeing Special Attention Requirements Bulletin 757-25-0321 RB, Revision 1, dated August 6, 2025. The FAA has revised paragraph (i) of this AD to add credit for previous actions for airplanes that completed Boeing Special Attention Requirements Bulletin 757-25-0320 RB, dated January 19, 2024, and redesignated subsequent paragraphs accordingly.
The revised service information also provides updated cost information. The FAA has revised the cost estimate in this final rule to reflect the updated cost information.
Conclusion
The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, and any other changes described previously, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM.

SUMMARY:
The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain The Boeing Company Model 737-8, 737-9, and 737-8200 airplanes. This AD was prompted by a leak through the form-in-place (FiP) gasket found during a leak check. This AD requires a detailed inspection of the FiP gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for correct sealant installation, or a detailed inspection at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for any damage on the preformed seal, depending on configuration; a fluid leak test of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for any leak; and applicable on-condition actions. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
by adding an AD that would apply to certain The Boeing Company Model 737-8, 737-9, and 737-8200 airplanes. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on March 23, 2026 (
91 FR 13791
). The NPRM was prompted by a leak through the FiP gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel found during a leak check, completed as part of a nonconformance disposition for the Boeing Company Model 737-8, 737-9, and 737-8200 airplanes. An investigation found that the fairing requirements of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel caused thin regions of the FiP gasket, which caused the manufacturer to apply non-permitted sealant after the initial FiP gasket had cured, resulting in an uneven sealing surface on the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel and a fuel leak. In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require a detailed inspection of the FiP gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for correct sealant installation, or a detailed inspection at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for any damage on the preformed seal, depending on configuration; a fluid leak test of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for any leak; and applicable on-condition actions. The FAA is issuing this AD to address incorrect or missing sealant installation. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in fuel leaking onto the engine exhaust nozzle and a possible fire on the ground.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received a comment from the Air Line Pilots Association, International (ALPA) who supported the NPRM without change.
The FAA received additional comments from American Airlines (American) and Southwest Airlines (Southwest). The following presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to each comment.
Request To Combine Proposed ADs
American requested that the FAA revise the proposed AD by incorporating the affected airplanes and proposed requirements from another proposed AD (Docket No. FAA-2026-2725, Project Identifier AD-2025-00999-T) and then rescind that other proposed AD. American noted, although the proposed ADs reference different service information and different airplane models, both proposed ADs would mandate similar corrective requirements. American stated consolidating these actions into a single NPRM would improve clarity and enhance compliance management without changing the technical intent of the inspection or impacting airplane airworthiness.
The FAA disagrees with this request. The FAA acknowledges that some operators may prefer to address the unsafe condition with a single AD; however, other operators may prefer that the FAA issue two separate ADs. Additionally, when the manufacturer develops two separate service bulletins to address an unsafe condition on different airplane models, proceeding with two separate ADs, in general, allows the FAA to address the unsafe condition on all airplane models in a timely manner. For example, if development of one service bulletin is delayed, the rulemaking process would be delayed for all affected airplane models.
Request To Remove Exceptions to Service Information Instructions
American requested that the FAA remove the exceptions in paragraphs (h)(3), (5), and (6) from the proposed AD and instead adopt the instructions in the compliance tables and appendices of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1358 RB, dated November 17, 2025 (the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin). American stated that the language in the service information sufficiently defines the corrective action by referencing figure 4, and that retaining this information helps maintain consistency and minimizes the potential for misinterpretation.
The FAA notes that the exceptions in paragraph (h)(3) are necessary because the “on-condition corrective action(s)” in tables 1 and 2 of the Compliance and Accomplishment Instructions of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin are not defined in that bulletin. Similarly, the exceptions in paragraphs (h)(5) and (6) are necessary because Appendices A and B of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin do not explicitly specify to replace the FiP gasket if the fluid leak
(
printed page 67453)
test fails. Therefore, the exceptions in paragraphs (h)(3), (5), and (6) are necessary to clarify what on-condition corrective actions must be taken after a fluid leak test failure. The FAA has not revised this AD in response to this comment.
Request To Clarify Post-AD Requirements
Southwest asked if the FAA agrees that, after completing the actions required by this AD, an alternative method of compliance (AMOC) is not required to maintain the airplane per the Boeing aircraft maintenance manual (AMM). Southwest stated a certain task in the Boeing AMM provides instructions that vary subtly from the procedures in the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin.
The FAA agrees that an AMOC is not needed to maintain the airplane after complying with the requirements of this AD if the airplane is maintained per the Boeing AMM. The FAA notes that the unsafe condition was introduced during airplane production through the application of non-permitted sealant after the initial FiP gasket had cured. Since the FAA has not received any reports of in-service events where anomalies were introduced during maintenance based on AMM instructions, the FAA considers the relevant AMM tasks to be appropriate. Further, Boeing has updated the AMM task to include notes to prevent sealant touch-up after the initial sealant application. Boeing has also updated the AMM procedures for the fluid leak test to match the procedures in the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin. Those updates in the AMM instructions are expected to support operators for improved maintenance of the FiP gasket or preformed seal installed at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel.
Conclusion
The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1358 RB, dated November 17, 2025. This material specifies procedures for a detailed inspection of the FiP gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel of the left and right wing for correct sealant installation, or a detailed inspection at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel of the left and right wings for any damage on the preformed seal, depending on configuration; a fluid leak test of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for any leak; and applicable on-condition actions. On-condition actions include replacing the FiP gasket, repairing damage to the preformed gasket, and repeating the leak test until no leak is found.

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain The Boeing Company Model 737-700, -700C, -800, and -900ER series airplanes. This AD was prompted by a leak through the form-in-place (FiP) gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel found during a leak check. This AD requires a detailed inspection of the left- and right-side FiP gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for correct sealant installation, a fluid leak test of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panels for any leak, and applicable on-condition actions. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
This AD is effective December 1, 2026.
The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference of a certain publication listed in this AD as of December 1, 2026.

AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at

under Docket No. FAA-2026-2725; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule, any comments received, and other information. The address for Docket Operations is U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
by adding an AD that would apply to certain The Boeing Company Model 737-700, -700C, -800, and -900ER series airplanes. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on March 26, 2026 (
91 FR 14654
). The NPRM was prompted by a leak through
(
printed page 67449)
the FiP gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel found during a leak check, completed as part of a nonconformance disposition for the Boeing Company Model 737-8, 737-9, and 737-8200 airplanes. An investigation found that the fairing requirements of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel caused thin regions of the FiP gasket, which caused the manufacturer to apply non-permitted sealant after the initial FiP gasket had cured, resulting in an uneven sealing surface on the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel and leak. In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require a detailed inspection of the left- and right-side FiP gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for correct sealant installation, a fluid leak test of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panels for any leak, and applicable on-condition actions. The FAA is issuing this AD to address incorrect or missing sealant installation. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in fuel leaking onto the engine exhaust nozzle and a possible fire on the ground.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received comments from an anonymous commenter who supported the NPRM without change.
The FAA received additional comments from four commenters, including Aviation Partners Boeing (APB), American Airlines (American), Southwest Airlines (Southwest), and United Airlines (United). The following presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to each comment.
Request To Combine Proposed ADs
American requested that the FAA rescind the proposed AD and instead add the affected airplanes and proposed requirements to another proposed AD (Docket No. FAA-2026-2716, Project Identifier AD-2025-00990-T). American noted, although the proposed ADs reference different service information and different airplane models, both proposed ADs would mandate similar requirements. American stated consolidating these actions into a single NPRM would improve clarity and enhance compliance management without changing the technical intent of the inspection or impacting airplane airworthiness.
The FAA disagrees with this request. The FAA acknowledges that some operators may prefer to address the unsafe condition with a single AD; however, other operators may prefer that the FAA issue two separate ADs. Additionally, when the manufacturer develops two separate service bulletins to address an unsafe condition on different airplane models, proceeding with two separate ADs, in general, allows the FAA to address the unsafe condition on all airplane models in a timely manner. For example, if development of one service bulletin is delayed, the rulemaking process would be delayed for all affected airplane models.
Effect of Winglets on Accomplishment of the Proposed Actions
APB stated that the blended or split scimitar winglets installed per Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) ST00830SE does not affect compliance with the proposed requirements.
The FAA agrees that the installation of STC ST00830SE does not affect the ability to accomplish the actions required by this AD. The FAA has not changed this AD in this regard.
Request To Clarify Applicability Difference
United requested the FAA clarify why the applicability of the proposed AD was expanded beyond the effectivity of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, dated October 3, 2025 (original issue of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin). United stated this clarification would assist operators in understanding the unsafe condition and ensure consistent implementation across the affected fleet.
The FAA expanded the applicability of the AD based on a report from the manufacturer indicating that certain airplanes were incorrectly excluded from the effectivity of the original issue of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin. The missed airplanes are associated with the service information mandated by AD 2013-08-18, Amendment 39-17435 (
78 FR 25377
, May 1, 2013). Those airplanes had the FiP gasket incorporated in production, but a fluid leak test was not required as part of AD 2013-08-18 and its associated service information. Since the same non-conformance may have been introduced in production on those airplanes, the FAA concluded those airplanes must be included in the applicability of this AD.
Further, after issuance of the NPRM, Boeing issued Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, Revision 1, dated June 25, 2026 (Revision 1 of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin), to include the additional airplane serial numbers referenced in the applicability of the proposed AD. Therefore, the FAA has updated paragraph (c) of this AD to reference Revision 1 of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin.
Request To Remove Exceptions to Service Information Instructions
American requested that the FAA remove the exceptions in paragraphs (h)(2), (3), and (4) from the proposed AD and instead adopt the instructions in the compliance tables and appendices of the original issue of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin. American stated that the language in the service information sufficiently defines the corrective action, and that retaining this information helps maintain consistency and minimizes the potential for misinterpretation.
The FAA notes that the exception in paragraph (h)(2) is necessary because the “on-condition corrective action(s)” specified in tables 1 and 2 of the Compliance and Accomplishment Instructions of the original issue of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin are not defined in that bulletin. Similarly, the exceptions in paragraphs (h)(3) and (4) are necessary because Appendices A and B of the original issue of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin do not explicitly specify to replace the FiP gasket if any leak is found during the fluid leak test. However, the FAA reviewed Revision 1 of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin and determined that Revision 1 negates the need for the exceptions in paragraphs (h)(2), (3), and (4) of the proposed AD. Therefore, the FAA has revised paragraph (g) of this AD to require accomplishing all the applicable actions in Revision 1 of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin. Additionally, the FAA has added paragraph (i) to this AD to provide credit for accomplishing the actions in paragraph (g) of this AD before the effective date of this AD using the original issue of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin, except as provided by the exceptions in paragraphs (i)(1) through (3) of this AD.
Request To Clarify Post-AD Requirements
Southwest asked if the FAA agrees that, after completing the actions required by this AD, an alternative method of compliance (AMOC) is not required to maintain the airplane per the Boeing aircraft maintenance manual (AMM). Southwest stated a certain task in the Boeing AMM provides instructions that vary subtly from the procedures in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB.
(
printed page 67450)
The FAA agrees that an AMOC is not needed to maintain the airplane after complying with the requirements of this AD if the airplane is maintained per the Boeing AMM. The FAA notes that the unsafe condition was introduced during airplane production through the application of non-permitted sealant after the initial FiP gasket had cured. Since the FAA has not received any reports of in-service events where anomalies were introduced during maintenance based on AMM instructions, the FAA considers the relevant AMM tasks to be appropriate. Further, Boeing has updated the AMM task to include notes to prevent sealant touch-up after the initial sealant application. Boeing has also updated the AMM procedures for the fluid leak test to match the procedures in the required service information. Those updates in the AMM instructions are expected to support operators for improved maintenance of the FiP gasket installed at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel.
Conclusion
The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, Revision 1, dated June 25, 2026. This material specifies procedures for a detailed inspection of the FiP gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel of the left- and right-side wing for correct sealant installation, a fluid leak test of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panels for any leak, and applicable on-condition actions. On-condition actions include replacing the FiP gasket, repairing any leaks, and repeating the leak test until no leak is found.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the

section.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
by adding an AD that would apply to certain Airbus SAS Model A330-941 airplanes. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on August 19, 2026 (
91 FR 53542
). The NPRM was prompted by EASA AD 2025-0208, dated September 24, 2025 (EASA AD 2025-0208) (also referred to as the MCAI), issued by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. The MCAI states an occurrence was reported of a triple “PRIM FAULT” at touchdown, leading to the loss of ground spoilers, thrust reversers, and autobrake. An investigation determined the root cause was an undue triggering of the rudder order “COM/MON” monitoring in the three FCPCs. This condition, if not corrected, could result in the loss of autobrake and thrust reversers, possibly resulting in reduced control of the airplane. Airbus issued instructions for the installation of a new FCPC standard.
In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require the installation of a new FCPC standard and applicable concurrent modifications as specified in EASA AD 2025-0208. The NPRM also proposed to prohibit the installation of certain parts, as specified in EASA AD 2025-0208. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-8782.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received a comment from Air Line Pilots Association, International (ALPA) who supported the NPRM without change.
Conclusion
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
EASA AD 2025-0208 specifies procedures for the installation of a new FCPC standard by replacing the FCPCs, replacing the FCPC on board replaceable module (OBRMs), or reprogramming the FCPC OBRMs. EASA AD 2025-0208 further specifies that applicable concurrent modifications to the FCPC must be done (
i.e.,
FCPC, flight management, guidance and envelope computer (FMGEC), flight warning computer (FWC), and electronic instrument system (EIS) standard upgrades). EASA AD 2025-0208 also specifies parts installation restrictions allowing installation of only a serviceable FCPC.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
This AD will not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This AD will not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.

The full text of the Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) is available on the Agency website.
Section 1001(b)(4) of the American Rescue Plan Act (
Pub. L. 117-2
) authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to “ . . . make loans and grants and provide other assistance to maintain and improve food and agricultural supply chain resiliency.” Given this authority, and appropriation provided for this purpose in Section 1001, Paragraph (a), at least $5 billion in loan level is being made available for the SPUR Guaranteed Loan Program beginning in FY 2027. SPUR is designed and implemented in a manner similar to the Business and Industry (B&I) Guaranteed loan program with minor changes to meet the needs of the American beef industry and ranchers, and guaranteed loans made under this program are administered under
7 CFR part 5001
(OneRD Guaranteed Loan Program), as amended or supplemented by the NOFO.
The primary purpose of SPUR is to support the American Meat, Poultry, and Seafood Processing Industries by increasing processing capacity and promoting more competition in the sector, which is particularly vulnerable to disruption, consolidation, and concentration. SPUR funds will help the American protein processing industries diversify the Meat, Poultry, and Seafood supply chains and open local market opportunities. The intent is to diversify processing with value-added streams of business to increase resiliency and sustainability.
SPUR will provide financial assistance through loan guarantees designed to facilitate access to affordable capital through lenders providing loans to entities seeking to establish, reopen, retrofit, expand, or improve a Meat, Poultry, or Seafood Processing facility in America's rural or urban areas, as there are no geographic restrictions for the program.
As set forth in
7 CFR part 5001
, the Agency is authorized to charge a guarantee fee, a periodic guarantee retention fee, a fee for the issuance of the loan note guarantee prior to construction completion and establish a loan guarantee percentage for guaranteed loans made under this rule. The guaranteed loan guarantee fee, annual guarantee service fee, and fee for the issuance of the Loan Note Guarantee prior to completion of construction will correspond to the fees in effect for the Business & Industry (B&I) Guaranteed Loan Program under OneRD. The lender must hold a minimum of 10 percent of the total loan amount.
