Information Collection Request Title:
Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network Board of Directors and Committee Member Applications and Forms, OMB No. 0906-New.
Abstract:
The Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) is a public-private partnership that links professionals involved in the U.S. donation, procurement, and transplantation system. The OPTN focuses on promoting long, healthy, and productive lives for people with organ failure. The OPTN also aims to increase opportunities for transplants, optimize organ use, enhance efficiency, and prioritize patient care. The OPTN Board of Directors (BOD) is authorized by section 372 of the National Organ Transplant Act of 1984 (NOTA) (
see
42 U.S.C. 274(b)(1)(B)
), and the operation composition of the OPTN BOD are further codified in federal regulation under the regulations implementing NOTA (
see
42 CFR 121.3(a)
). These regulations also provide that the OPTN BOD shall “establish committees as are necessary to perform the duties of the OPTN” and describe the composition of these committees (see
42 CFR 121.3(a)(4)
). As part of the ongoing OPTN Modernization Initiative (
https://www.hrsa.gov/​optn-modernization/​learn-more-about-modernization
), HRSA seeks OMB approval of applications to be completed by candidates interested in volunteering to serve on the OPTN BOD and/or on the committees that support the BOD. Members of the OPTN BOD and committees do not receive payment for this work. HRSA also seeks approval of conflict-of-interest (COI), code of conduct, confidentiality, and attestation forms to be completed by the selected/confirmed members of the OPTN BOD, committees, and review boards on an annual, tri-annual, or ad hoc basis. The OPTN BOD consists of 35 members who serve 2 to 3-year terms and are supported by 21 committees with a total of approximately 419 members with the same term limits. Select members of the BOD also serve on committee(s) as Visiting Board Members. In addition, there are ad hoc committees or BOD workgroups that may be established to work on time-limited issues, and these members (approximately 20 a year) would fill out the annual COI form as well. Given some committee turnover, there are approximately 505 committee and BOD members filling out the annual COI form, code of conduct form, confidentiality form, and attestation form every year. In addition, approximately 841 members of OPTN Review Boards will fill out the annual COI form, confidentiality agreements, and code of conduct forms.
A 60-day Notice was published in the
Federal Register
on August 6, 2026, Vol. 91, No. 150, FR pp. 50861. HRSA received comments from one entity, the Association of Organ Procurement Organizations. The commenter recognized the important role of volunteers within the OPTN and provided recommendations intended to clarify and improve the proposed Board of Directors and Committee Volunteer Interest Forms and the COI disclosure forms. The commenter recommended revisions to the forms related to questions concerning applicant disciplinary history, Organ Procurement Organization (OPO) roles and transplant programs, living and deceased donor experience, social media information, prior OPTN volunteer service, financial interests, and the frequency of recurring COI disclosures.
On Form 1, the commenter asked for the justification for requesting social media handles and expressed concern that they would be used to screen out applicants with divergent views.
HRSA Response:
HRSA removed an optional open-ended question regarding social media handles.
On Form 1, the commenter expressed concern that a question asking about an applicant's employer facing regulatory discipline could require an applicant to disclose confidential information.
HRSA Response:
HRSA revised the question concerning criminal, ethics, or regulatory disciplinary matters. The revised question no longer requests information concerning disciplinary matters involving an applicant's employer and separates the remaining inquiry into two yes/no questions addressing prior actions and currently pending matters regarding the applicant and not the employer.
On Form 1, the commenter also asked, for clarification purposes, to list “organ donor” as “living donor” and allowing for OPO experience to be marked as OPO-administrative versus OPO-clinical.
HRSA Response:
HRSA revised Form 1 and accepted both changes.
On Form 1, the commenter expressed concern that questions asking patient and family members about their advocacy and outreach experience may discourage people from applying if they lack this experience.
HRSA Response:
Regarding the comment that the questions may discourage applicants who lack outreach or advocacy experience, the form also asks for other background experience in areas such as finance, governance, and ethics. The nominating committee considers all applicants, and inclusive language will be included in outreach materials for these roles.
On Forms 1 and 2, the commenter suggested some questions did not appear to apply to the procurement side because they only mentioned transplantation experience.
HRSA Response:
On Forms 1 and 2, HRSA broadened “transplant” language throughout to “transplant, donation, or procurement” in order to be more inclusive to applicants on the donation or procurement side.
Based on feedback from leadership of the OPTN Board of Directors, on Forms 1 and 2, HRSA added two employment-related questions regarding the applicant's current employment status and whether the applicant's employer is aware of the application. These questions require only selection from predefined response options and are expected to require negligible time to complete.
On Form 3, the commenter suggested the financial question in the COI form was overly broad and should be more limited.
HRSA Response:
HRSA clarified in the COI form (the annual COI form as well as the tri-annual COI form) that financial conflicts should exclude salary from current employers and exclude investments in broadly diversified funds. However, HRSA is not adopting the proposed 5 percent threshold. The question intentionally reaches the broader concept of an individual's or family member's “ownership or beneficial interest.” A 5 percent threshold could exclude financial interests that might still create an actual, potential, or perceived COI in the OPTN context.
On Form 3, the commenter expressed concern that disclosing information in the COI form could be used to screen applicants with diverse views from serving.
HRSA Response:
HRSA appreciates the commenter's concern. As noted in the instructions, answering “Yes” to any question does not automatically
(
printed page 67591)
preclude an individual from serving. Rather, the information provided is used to assist in assessing the relevant circumstances.
On Form 3 and Form 4, the commenter suggested an annual filing with reminders to file any changes in the interim as they occur rather than the tri-annual cadence between annual filings.
HRSA Response:
The OPTN has members fill out the form proactively with updates on a tri-annual basis to ensure the most recent COI information is collected to uphold the strongest governance standards. However, volunteers are also asked to submit updates every time a change takes place between filings, so COI information is up to date ahead of every meeting.
Need and Proposed Use of the Information:
HRSA and the OPTN anticipate collecting committee and BOD applications on an annual basis for committee and board openings. Resumes are requested and required for Board applicants and requested but not required for committee applicants. To ensure applicants to the OPTN BOD and committees have the appropriate expertise, the proposed applications will collect information including candidates' professional background, expertise, experience in organ donation and transplantation, and areas of interest. The OPTN and its Nominating Committee, with HRSA oversight, will evaluate the applications to analyze qualifications and support a structured nomination and selection process. The application information will help ensure the OPTN governance bodies are composed of individuals with the necessary knowledge, skills, and perspectives to effectively oversee and support the nation's organ donation and transplantation system.
In addition, annual COI disclosures will be collected from BOD, committee members, and will be used to review board members upon their election/selection or annual anniversary. The BOD and Membership and Professional Standards Committee members will also submit COI updates on a tri-annual basis as well as fill out an ad hoc COI form when needed. HRSA and the OPTN will use information collected via the selected BOD and committee members' COI forms to routinely identify, monitor, prevent, and address actual, potential or appearances of COI relating to the operation of the OPTN. HRSA will use this information to strengthen oversight and accountability within the OPTN to enhance trust and confidence among stakeholders and the public. Without access to this information, HRSA and the OPTN would be less able to prevent potential conflicts of interest, which could jeopardize the independence and objectivity of the OPTN BOD and committees that inform national organ procurement and transplantation policy. Upon committee election or appointment and volunteer orientation, BOD and committee members will complete and submit an attestation form, confidentiality agreement, as well as the code of conduct. The code of conduct and confidentiality agreement, and attestation are collected to ensure that OPTN BOD and committee members annually acknowledge their obligations to act in the best interests of the OPTN, comply with applicable ethical and conduct requirements, protect confidential information, and uphold the standards necessary to maintain good standing and public trust in OPTN governance.
Likely Respondents:
Respondents completing the application forms will be individuals who express interest in serving in volunteer governance or committee roles within the OPTN. This includes a broad and diverse group of stakeholders involved in or connected to organ donation and transplantation, such as transplant professionals (
e.g.,
physicians, surgeons, coordinators, administrators), OPO personnel, histocompatibility experts, researchers, patients, living donors, family members, caregivers, and members of the public with relevant expertise (
e.g.,
ethics, finance, governance, public policy, or operations). Respondents may be employed or unaffiliated individuals and will represent a wide range of professional disciplines, lived experiences, and geographic regions across the United States, helping to support a more dynamic and representative governance process. Respondents completing the COI forms, code of conduct, confidentiality, and attestation forms will be individuals who have been elected or appointed to committee, review board, and BOD positions for the OPTN.
Burden Statement:
Burden in this context means the time expended by persons to generate, maintain, retain, disclose, or provide the information requested. This includes the time needed to review instructions; to develop, acquire, install, and utilize technology and systems for the purpose of collecting, validating, and verifying information, processing and maintaining information, and disclosing and providing information; to train personnel and to be able to respond to a collection of information; to search data sources; to complete and review the collection of information; and to transmit or otherwise disclose the information. The total annual burden hours estimated for this ICR are summarized in the table below.
HRSA calculated estimated burden hours based on internal testing for completing each form. The estimated total annual burden for this information collection is 2,110.84 hours across all respondents on an annual basis, including for both tri-annual and annual responses. HRSA made minor revisions to several forms, and in the annual and tri-annual conflict-of-interest forms consolidated eight conflict questions down to two. In addition, since two questions were added to the application forms, the time increased slightly for the committee application but remained the same for the board application as two questions were removed. HRSA also increased the total volume of respondents by adding 841 review board member volunteers to receive the COI, confidentiality, and code of conduct forms annually. Thus, the total number of responses increased from the 60-day FRN to the 30-day FRN from 5,160 to 7,683, and the total burden hours increased from 1,870.39 to 2,110.84.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for all Airbus Helicopters Model AS350B2, AS350B3, AS355N, AS355NP, and EC130B4 helicopters. This AD was prompted by a report of a release of the load on the cargo hook without manual release initiation by the pilot. This AD requires inspecting the load dropping control system, inspecting the manual release lever for free play, and, depending on the results, performing corrective actions. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
This AD is effective November 12, 2026.
The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference of a certain publication listed in this AD as of November 12, 2026.
The FAA must receive comments on this AD by December 11, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may send comments, using the procedures found in
14 CFR 11.43
and
11.45
, by any of the following methods:

regulations.gov
. Follow the instructions for submitting comments.

U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
Hand Delivery:
Deliver to Mail address above between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-11816; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The street address for Docket Operations is listed above.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written data, views, or arguments about this final rule. Send your comments using a method listed under
ADDRESSES
. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-11816; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00790-R” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the final rule, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend this final rule because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to
regulations.gov
, including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this final rule.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this AD contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this AD, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this AD. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Anthony Kenward, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590. Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union, has issued EASA AD 2026-0146, dated July 24, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0146) (also referred to as “the MCAI”), to correct an unsafe condition on all Airbus Helicopters Model AS 350 B2, AS 350 B3, AS 355 N, AS 355 NP, and EC 130 B4 helicopters. The MCAI states a report was received of a loss of a collapsible bucket during water pickup when the load released from the cargo hook without manual release initiation by the pilot. Subsequent investigation revealed that the release mechanism could not be properly adjusted due to the poor condition of the release activation cable, which appeared to be twisted and, therefore, no longer met the tolerances for the cable length.
The FAA is issuing this AD to prevent unintended loss of the load on the cargo hook. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in in-flight loss of a cargo load and cause injury to persons on the ground.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-11816.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2026-0146, which specifies procedures for inspecting the load dropping control of the cargo swing installation without removal from the helicopter. EASA AD 2026-0146 also requires repetitively inspecting the required free play of the manual release lever and the correct functioning of the dropping control of the mechanical emergency release system of the cargo swing installation. Depending on the results of the inspections, EASA AD 2026-0146 further specifies procedures for removing the load dropping control from the helicopter and visually inspecting the dropping control, adjusting the cargo swing emergency release control or replacing the dropping control.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority (CAA) of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this AD after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
AD Requirements
This AD requires accomplishing the actions specified in EASA AD 2026-0146, described previously, as incorporated by reference, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this AD. See “Differences Between this AD and the MCAI” for a discussion of the general differences included in this AD.
Differences Between This AD and the MCAI
The MCAI specifies the “check” for free play of the manual release lever may be accomplished by a pilot (owner/operator), whereas this AD refers to that action as an “inspection” and requires those inspections to be accomplished by persons authorized under
14 CFR 43.3
.
Interim Action
The FAA considers that this AD is an interim action. If final action is later identified, the FAA might consider further rulemaking.
Explanation of Required Compliance Information
In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD process, the FAA developed a process to use some CAA ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with requirements for corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, EASA AD 2026-0146 is incorporated by reference in this AD. This AD requires compliance with EASA AD 2026-0146 in its entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this AD. Using common terms that are the same as the heading of a particular section in EASA AD 2026-0146 does not mean that operators need comply only with that section. For example, where the AD requirement refers to “all required actions and compliance times,” compliance with this AD requirement is not limited to the section titled “Required Action(s) and Compliance Time(s)” in EASA AD 2026-0146. Material required by EASA AD 2026-0146 for compliance will be available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-11816 after this AD is published.
Justification for Immediate Adoption and Determination of the Effective Date
Section 553(b) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (
5 U.S.C. 551
et seq.
) authorizes agencies to dispense with notice and comment procedures for rules when the agency, for “good cause,” finds that those procedures are
(
printed page 67447)
“impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” Under this section, an agency, upon finding good cause, may issue a final rule without providing notice and seeking comment prior to issuance. Further, section 553(d) of the APA authorizes agencies to make rules effective in less than thirty days, upon a finding of good cause.
An unsafe condition exists that requires the immediate adoption of this AD without providing an opportunity for public comments prior to adoption. The FAA has found that the risk to the flying public justifies forgoing notice and comment prior to adoption of this rule because the unintended in-flight loss of the load on the cargo hook could result in injury to persons on the ground. Specifically, the inspections must be accomplished within 50 sling cycles or within 30 days, whichever occurs first after the effective date of this AD. Additionally, the compliance time of this AD is shorter than the time necessary for public comment and for publication of the final rule. Accordingly, notice and opportunity for prior public comment are impracticable and contrary to the public interest pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)
.
In addition, the FAA finds that good cause exists pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)
for making this amendment effective in less than 30 days, for the same reasons the FAA found good cause to forgo notice and comment.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The requirements of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) do not apply when an agency finds good cause pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553
to adopt a rule without prior notice and comment. Because the FAA has determined that it has good cause to adopt this rule without prior notice and comment, RFA analysis is not required.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
This AD will not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This AD will not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.

(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by a report of a release of the load on the cargo hook without manual release initiation by the pilot. The FAA is issuing this AD to prevent the unintended loss of the load on the cargo hook. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in in-flight loss of cargo load and cause injury to persons on the ground.
(f) Compliance

(g) Required Actions
(1) Except as specified in paragraphs (h) and (i) of this AD: Comply with all required actions and compliance times specified in, and in accordance with European Union Aviation Safety Agency AD 2026-0146, dated July 24, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0146).
(2) For purpose of this AD, a “sling cycle” is defined as one landing with or without stopping the rotor or one external load-carrying operation; an external load-carrying operation occurs each time a helicopter picks up an external load and drops it off.
(h) Exceptions to EASA AD 2026-0146
(1) Where EASA AD 2026-0146 refers to its effective date, this AD requires using the effective date of this AD.
(2) Where paragraph (1) of EASA AD 2026-0146 specifies “a `visual check”, this AD requires replacing that text with “an `inspection”.

title: Airworthiness Directives; Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Helicopters
abstract: The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Model EC135P1, EC135P2, EC135P2+, EC135P3, EC135T1, EC135T2, EC135T2+, EC135T3, EC635T2+, MBB-BK 117 C-2, and MBB-BK 117 D-2 helicopters. This AD was prompted by reports of cracks on the cable drum of the rescue hoist assembly. This AD requires repetitively inspecting the cable drum of certain rescue hoist assemblies for cracks and, depending on the results, replacing or repairing the cable drum of the rescue hoist assembly. This AD also prohibits the operation and the installation of an affected rescue hoist assembly on a helicopter, unless certain requirements are met. SUMMARY:
The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Model EC135P1, EC135P2, EC135P2+, EC135P3, EC135T1, EC135T2, EC135T2+, EC135T3, EC635T2+, MBB-BK 117 C-2, and MBB-BK 117 D-2 helicopters. This AD was prompted by reports of cracks on the cable drum of the rescue hoist assembly. This AD requires repetitively inspecting the cable drum of certain rescue hoist assemblies for cracks and, depending on the results, replacing or repairing the cable drum of the rescue hoist assembly. This AD also prohibits the operation and the installation of an affected rescue hoist assembly on a helicopter, unless certain requirements are met. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
by adding an AD that would apply to certain AHD Model EC135P1, EC135P2, EC135P2+, EC135P3, EC135T1, EC135T2, EC135T2+, EC135T3, EC635T2+, MBB-BK 117 C-2, and MBB-BK 117 D-2 helicopters. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on February 13, 2026 (
91 FR 6795
). The NPRM was prompted by an MCAI, issued by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued EASA AD 2025-0055, dated March 11, 2025 (EASA AD 2025-0055) (also referred to as the MCAI). The MCAI states that cracks were reported on a cable drum installed on certain part-numbered Goodrich rescue hoist assemblies. Additionally, the material referenced in the MCAI states that Goodrich determined that this occurrence was isolated to a batch of cable drums made from a plate material, which was determined to have increased susceptibility to corrosion-induced fatigue. This unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in corrosion-induced fatigue of the cable drum, and consequent injuries to human load or individuals on the ground.
In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require repetitively inspecting the cable drum of certain rescue hoist assemblies for cracks and depending on the results, replacing or repairing the cable drum of the rescue hoist assembly. Additionally, in the NPRM the FAA proposed to prohibit the operation and the installation of an affected rescue hoist assembly on a helicopter, unless certain requirements are met. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
Additionally, since the FAA issued the NPRM, it was determined that the special flight permit restriction specified in paragraph (j) of the proposed rule is no longer needed. Accordingly, the FAA has revised this final rule by removing the special flight permit paragraph.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received comments from three commenters. The commenters were AHD, Onboard Systems Hoist and Winch, and an individual commenter. The following discussion presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to these comments.
Request To Clarify Affected Parts
An individual commenter requested that the FAA specify the affected part by serial number, part number, and manufacturing batches that have the highest risk. The commenter also stated that by including this information, it will avoid unnecessary repeated inspections which may delay rescue missions.
The FAA disagrees with specifying or limiting this final rule by adding the serial number, part number, or manufacturing batch information. The AD already incorporates this information by reference, and the serial numbers associated with a subset of the affected part numbers are identified in the incorporated MCAI. Additionally, manufacturing batch information is not necessary to determine the affected parts, and all of the identified part numbers present an equivalent level of risk; none represent a “highest risk” category as suggested by the commenter. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
(
printed page 67458)
Request To Revise Inspection Requirements
One individual commenter requested that the FAA clarify why only visual inspections are required and not other forms of testing or inspections. The commenter stated that visual inspections may not detect small, undetectable cracks that are caused by corrosion, which may grow faster than expected. The commenter further stated that by including this information, it will help determine how often inspections must occur to ensure safe cable drums.
The FAA infers the commenter is requesting the inspection methods increase to other forms of inspections and not just visual inspections alone. The FAA disagrees with revising the inspection method outside of the requirements that were proposed in the NPRM. EASA, the State of Design authority for these helicopters, determined the appropriate inspection methodology and criteria for the required inspections. The FAA agrees with EASA. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Revise the Inspection Requirements
AHD and Onboard Systems Hoist and Winch (Onboard Systems) both requested that the FAA revise or remove the inspection requirements of paragraphs (h)(3) and (4) of the proposed AD.
Onboard Systems requested the FAA revise paragraph (h)(3) of the proposed AD by allowing maintenance personnel a limited compliance time to confirm indications of a crack with personnel at Airbus Helicopters or Onboard Systems Hoist and Winch prior to repairs. Onboard Systems stated the inspection process was carefully considered to ensure that cracks are detected well before they pose any risk of fracture, while also preventing the removal of essential search and rescue assets from service for misidentified indications. Additionally, Onboard Systems stated that they would have the operator send detailed images of the indication and if the indication could not be identified as benign, then they would require removing the part from the helicopter. AHD stated the proposed inspection as specified in paragraph (h)(3) of the proposed AD implies further changes to the inspection process, which could eliminate the 3mm minimum crack size criteria.
The FAA disagrees with Onboard System request to revise the compliance time to confirm indications because the FAA may prioritize immediate action upon detection of potential safety concerns, such as cracks, to eliminate any risk of fracture that could compromise safety. However, the FAA agrees to revise paragraph (h)(3) of this AD by removing the criteria for contacting the Manager, International Validation Branch, or Airbus Helicopters' Design Organizational Approval if any cracks or suspected cracks longer than 3mm in length are found.
Onboard Systems requested the FAA remove paragraph (h)(4) of the proposed AD. Onboard Systems stated if using more than 6X magnification and no minimum threshold, the risk of false indications increases exponentially. AHD requested the FAA remove paragraph (h)(4) of the proposed AD or revise by removing the words “or higher.” AHD stated the use of such high magnification could increase misidentifications or surface cracks, leading to false-positive indications. AHD stated this inspection deviations could lead to false-positive indications and the unnecessary grounding of search and rescue assets.
The FAA acknowledges the commenter's concern to prevent unnecessary actions that may remove important resources essential to rescue missions and the FAA has determined that a crack length of 3 mm is too small to accurately detect with the unaided eye (1x magnification). However, the FAA agrees that a 4X-6X magnification is sufficient. Accordingly, the FAA has revised paragraph (h)(4) of this AD to specify that 4X-6X magnification is required for the visual inspection.
Conclusion
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, and any other changes described previously, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2025-0055, which specifies procedures for repetitively inspecting the cable drum installed on the rescue hoist assembly for cracks longer than 3 mm and, depending on the results, contacting the manufacturer for approved repair instructions. Additionally, the MCAI allows the installation of an affected rescue hoist assembly on a helicopter if it meets certain requirements. Finally, the MCAI prohibits the operation of an affected rescue hoist assembly after a certain effective date as specified in the MCAI.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
Differences Between This AD and the MCAI
The MCAI applies to AHD Model EC635 P2+, EC635 P3, EC635 T1, and EC635 T3 helicopters, whereas this AD does not because those models do not have an FAA type certificate.
Where the MCAI specifies to contact the manufacturer for repair instructions, this AD requires repairing an affected rescue hoist assembly in accordance with a method approved by the Manager, International Validation Branch; EASA; or Airbus Helicopters' Design Organization Approval.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
This AD will not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This AD will not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.

,

Amendment 39-23498; Docket No. FAA-2026-1326; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-00312-R.
(a) Effective Date
This airworthiness directive (AD) is effective December 1, 2026.
(b) Affected ADs
None.
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Model EC135P1, EC135P2, EC135P2+, EC135P3, EC135T1, EC135T2, EC135T2+, EC135T3, and EC635T2+ helicopters, certificated in any category, all serial numbers (S/N) up to 1999; and Model MBB-BK 117 C-2 and MBB-BK 117 D-2 helicopters, certificated in any category, all S/Ns.
Note 1 to paragraph (c):
Helicopters with an EC135P3H designation are Model EC135P3 helicopters. Helicopters with an EC135T3H designation are Model EC135T3 helicopters.
Note 2 to paragraph (c):
Helicopters with an MBB-BK 117 C-2e designation are Model MBB-BK 117 C-2 helicopters.
(d) Subject
Joint Aircraft System Component (JASC) Code 2500, Cabin equipment/furnishings.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by reports of cracks on the cable drum of the rescue hoist assembly. The FAA is issuing this AD to detect and correct cable drums installed on certain rescue hoist assemblies that have been manufactured with a certain plate material that could result in corrosion-induced fatigue of the cable drum. This unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in failure of the cable drum and injuries to human load or individuals on the ground.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Requirements
Except as specified in paragraphs (h) and (i) of this AD: comply with all required actions and compliance times specified in, and in accordance with, European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AD 2025-0055, dated March 11, 2025 (EASA AD 2025-0055).
(h) Exceptions to EASA AD 2025-0055
(1) Where EASA AD 2025-0055 refers to its effective date, this AD requires using the effective date of this AD.
(2) Where EASA AD 2025-0055 requires compliance in terms of flight hours, this AD requires using hours time-in-service.
(3) Where paragraph (2) of EASA AD 2025-0055 and the material referenced in EASA AD 2025-0055 specifies to contact a manufacturer for repair instructions, for this AD repair an affected rescue hoist assembly in accordance with a method approved by the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA; EASA; or Airbus Helicopters' Design Organization Approval (DOA). If approved by the DOA, the approval must include the DOA-authorized signature.
(4) Where the material referenced in EASA AD 2025-0055 specifies “magnifying glass 6X maximum,” this AD requires replacing that text with “4X-6X magnification”.
(5) This AD does not adopt the “Remarks” section of EASA AD 2025-0055.
(i) No Reporting Requirement
Although the material referenced in EASA AD 2025-0055 specifies to submit certain information to the manufacturer, this AD does not require that action.

Background
EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union, has issued EASA AD 2026-0029, dated February 12, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0029) (also referred to as the MCAI), to correct an unsafe condition on all Airbus Helicopters Model SA 365 N helicopters. The MCAI states that occurrences were reported of a tightening torque loss on the input flange nut, due to circular wear on the faces of the flange, the slip ring, and the input flange. This condition, if not addressed, could lead to degradation or jamming of the input roller bearings and loss of yaw control of the helicopter. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-11815.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2026-0029, which specifies procedures for repetitive functional checks (inspections) of the tail gear box part number 365A33500000 for non-displacement of the tail gear box (TGB) input flange and, depending on the results of the inspections, corrective actions. These corrective actions include gauging the non-displacement of the input flange with a comparator gauge and contacting Airbus Helicopters for a repair solution before resuming flights if the comparator gauge confirms a value more than or equal to 0.1 millimeters (.0039 inches), as specified in the service material referenced in EASA AD 2026-0029.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority (CAA) of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this AD after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
AD Requirements
This AD requires accomplishing the actions specified in EASA AD 2026-0029, described previously as incorporated by reference, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this AD. See “Differences Between this AD and the MCAI” for a discussion of the general differences included in this AD.
Differences Between This AD and the Referenced Material
Where EASA AD 2026-0029 and the material referenced in EASA AD 2026-0029 specify to contact Airbus Helicopters if the comparator gauge confirms a value more than or equal to 0.03 mm, or after completing an oil sample analysis, this AD requires corrective actions to be done in accordance with a method approved by the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA; EASA; or Airbus Helicopters Design Organization Approval (DOA). If approved by the DOA, the approval must include the DOA-authorized signature.
Explanation of Required Compliance Information
In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD process, the FAA developed a process to use some CAA ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with requirements for corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, EASA AD 2026-0029 is incorporated by reference in this AD. This AD requires compliance with EASA AD 2026-0029 in its entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this AD. Using common terms that are the same as the heading of a particular section in EASA AD 2026-0029 does not mean that operators need comply only with that section. For example, where the AD requirement refers to “all required actions and compliance times,” compliance with this AD requirement is not limited to the section titled “Required Action(s) and Compliance Time(s)” in EASA AD 2026-0029. Material required by EASA AD 2026-0029 for compliance will be available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-11815 after this AD is published.
Justification for Immediate Adoption and Determination of the Effective Date
Section 553(b) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (
5 U.S.C. 551
et seq.
) authorizes agencies to dispense with notice and comment procedures for rules when the agency, for “good cause,” finds that those procedures are “impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” Under this section, an agency, upon finding good cause, may issue a final rule without providing notice and seeking comment prior to issuance. Further, section 553(d) of the APA authorizes agencies to
(
printed page 67441)
make rules effective in less than thirty days, upon a finding of good cause.
There are currently no domestic operators of these products. Accordingly, notice and opportunity for prior public comment are unnecessary, pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)
. In addition, for the foregoing reason(s), the FAA finds that good cause exists pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)
for making this amendment effective in less than 30 days.
Regulatory Flexibility Act

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Pursuant to section 111.96 of
title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) (
19 CFR 111.96(c)
), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) assesses an annual user fee for each customs broker permit granted to an individual, partnership, association, or corporation. The CBP regulations provide that this fee is payable each calendar year for a national permit held by a customs broker and must be paid by the due date published annually in the
Federal Register
. See
19 CFR 24.22(h)
and
(i)
;
19 CFR 111.96(c)
.
Section 24.22 of
title 19 of the CFR
(
19 CFR 24.22
) sets forth the terms and conditions for when fees for certain services, including specific customs user fees, are required. The specific customs user fee amounts that appear in
19 CFR 24.22
are not the actual fees but represent the base year amounts that are subject to adjustment each fiscal year in accordance with the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act (FAST Act) (
Pub. L. 114-94
, December 4, 2015). Section 32201 of the FAST Act amended section 13031 of the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA) of 1985 (
19 U.S.C. 58c
) by requiring the Secretary of the Treasury to adjust certain customs COBRA user fees and corresponding limitations to reflect certain increases in inflation. Paragraph (k) of section 24.22 of
title 19 of the CFR
(
19 CFR 24.22(k)
) sets forth the methodology to adjust fees for inflation and to determine the change in inflation, including the factor by which the fees and limitations will be adjusted, if necessary.
Customs brokers are subject to an annual customs broker permit user fee calculated using the base year amount in Appendix A to 19 CFR part 24, as adjusted by the terms in
19 CFR 24.22(k)
.
See
19 U.S.C. 58c(a)(7)
and
19 CFR 24.22(h)
. In accordance with
19 CFR 24.22
, CBP determines annually whether an adjustment to the fees and limitations is necessary and publishes a
Federal Register
notice specifying the amount of the fees and limitations for each fiscal year. On July 31, 2026, CBP published a
Federal Register
notice, entitled Customs User Fees To Be Adjusted for Inflation in Fiscal Year 2027 (CBP Decision 26-14), which announced, among other fee adjustments, that the annual customs broker permit user fee will increase to $190.88 for calendar year 2027.
See
91 FR 48398
.
Thus, as required by
19 CFR 24.22
, CBP provided notice in the
Federal Register
of the annual fee amount at least 60 days prior to the date that the payment is due for each customs broker national permit. This document notifies customs brokers that, for calendar year 2027, the due date for payment of the annual customs broker permit user fee is January 29, 2027. If a customs broker fails to pay the annual customs broker permit user fee by January 29, 2027, the national permit is revoked by operation of law.
See
19 CFR 111.45(b)
and
111.96(c)
.
Customs brokers are strongly encouraged to submit the payment electronically via the eCBP portal located at
https://e.cbp.dhs.gov/​brokers/​#/​home
.
Customs brokers who are first-time users of the eCBP portal must create a
Login.gov
account. Instructions and training resources—such as user and quick reference guides for customs brokers on how to create a
Login.gov
account and how to use the eCBP portal—can be found on CBP's website at
https://www.cbp.gov/​trade/​eCBP
.
CBP will also accept payments at the processing center as defined in
19 CFR 111.1
, in accordance with the remittance procedures in
19 CFR 24.22(i)
.

SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to adopt a new airworthiness directive (AD) for all CFM International, S.A. (CFM) Model CFM56-7B engines. This proposed AD was prompted by an event involving a CFM Model CFM56-7B26/3 engine where a fan blade separated and resulted in an engine in-flight shutdown (IFSD) with debris penetrating the fuselage, which caused a loss of pressurization and prompted an emergency descent. This proposed AD would require a visual inspection of the fan blades for findings considered not serviceable and, depending on the results of the inspection, replacement with a serviceable part and additional fan blade inspections. This proposed AD would also require sending the inspection results to CFM if any finding considered not serviceable is found. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed under the

Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Alexei Marqueen, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 2200 South 216th Street, Des Moines, WA 98198. Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
The FAA received a report that a Boeing 737-800 Model airplane powered by CFM56-7B26/3 engines experienced a fan blade separation during flight that resulted in an engine IFSD with debris penetrating the fuselage, which caused a loss of pressurization and prompted an emergency descent. The manufacturer investigation into the root cause of the fan blade failure is ongoing, but preliminary investigation indicates deformation to the fan blades induced a localized vibratory response in the failed blade. This condition, if not addressed, could result in debris penetrating the fuselage and cause a loss of pressurization and prompt an emergency descent.
On April 17, 2018, a Southwest Airlines flight experienced a CFM56-7B engine failure due to a fractured fan blade that led to the engine inlet cowl
(
printed page 67533)
disintegrating and debris penetrating the fuselage. The FAA has received no factual information that indicates that the April 17, 2018 incident on a Southwest Airlines flight is related to the unsafe condition addressed by this proposed AD. It is noted here for completeness only.
The FAA is providing a 30-day comment period for this NPRM instead of the standard 45-day comment period. This shortened timeframe is necessary to align the effective implementation of this safety action with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union, and in consideration of the recent in-service engine event. The FAA has determined that a 30-day comment period provides sufficient opportunity for public input while ensuring harmonization with EASA.
FAA's Determination
The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed CFM Service Bulletin CFM56-7B S/B 72-1119, dated September 8, 2026, which specifies procedures for visual inspection of the fan blades for findings considered not serviceable (cracks, tears, tip curls, local distortion on leading edge), and additional inspections of adjacent (forward looking aft) fan blades. This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require a visual inspection of the fan blades for findings considered not serviceable (cracks, tears, tip curls, local distortion on leading edge) and, depending on the results of the inspection, replacement with a serviceable part and additional fan blade inspections. This proposed AD would also require sending the inspection results to CFM if any unserviceable finding is found.
Interim Action
This AD is considered to be interim action. The inspection reports that are required by this AD will enable the manufacturer to obtain better insight into the nature, cause, and extent of the fan blade failure, and eventually allow the manufacturer to develop final action to address the unsafe condition. Once final action has been identified, the FAA might consider further rulemaking.

(b) Affected ADs

This AD applies to all CFM International, S.A. (CFM) Model CFM56-7B20, CFM56-7B20/2, CFM56-7B20/3, CFM56-7B20E, CFM56-7B22, CFM56-7B22/2, CFM56-7B22/3, CFM56-7B22/3B1, CFM56-7B22/B1, CFM56-7B22E, CFM56-7B22E/B1, CFM56-7B24, CFM56-7B24/2, CFM56-7B24/3, CFM56-7B24/3B1, CFM56-7B24/B1, CFM56-7B24E, CFM56-7B24E/B1, CFM56-7B26, CFM56-7B26/2, CFM56-7B26/3, CFM56-7B26/3B1, CFM56-7B26/3B2, CFM56-7B26/3B2F, CFM56-7B26/3F, CFM56-7B26/B1, CFM56-7B26/B2, CFM56-7B26E, CFM56-7B26E/B1, CFM56-7B26E/B2, CFM56-7B26E/B2F, CFM56-7B26E/F, CFM56-7B27, CFM56-7B27/2, CFM56-7B27/3, CFM56-7B27/3B1, CFM56-7B27/3B1F, CFM56-7B27/3B3, CFM56-7B27/3F, CFM56-7B27/B1, CFM56-7B27/B3, CFM56-7B27A, CFM56-7B27A/3, CFM56-7B27AE, CFM56-7B27E, CFM56-7B27E/B1, CFM56-7B27E/B1F, CFM56-7B27E/B3, and CFM56-7B27E/F engines.
(d) Subject

(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by an event involving a CFM Model CFM56-7B26/3 engine, which experienced a fan blade separation that resulted in an in-flight engine shutdown and debris penetrating the fuselage, causing a loss of pressurization and prompting an emergency descent. The FAA is issuing this AD to prevent failure of the fan blade. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in debris penetrating the fuselage and cause a loss of pressurization and prompt an emergency descent.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Definition
For the purpose of this AD, a “serviceable fan blade” is a new, zero-hour fan blade or a fan blade that has passed the inspections required by paragraph (h)(1) of this AD.
(h) Required Actions
(1) Perform a visual inspection of the fan blades in accordance with the Accomplishment Instructions, paragraph 3.C., of CFM Service Bulletin (SB) CFM56-7B S/B 72-1119, dated September 8, 2026 (CFM56-7B S/B 72-1119), as follows:
(i) For engines installed on aircraft as of the effective date of this AD, within 400 flight cycles or within 90 days after the effective date of this AD, whichever occurs first.
(ii) For engines not installed on aircraft as of the effective date of this AD, before further flight.
(2) If any findings considered not serviceable are detected, before further flight, do the following:
(i) Remove the fan blade from service and replace with a serviceable fan blade.
(ii) Perform an inspection of the adjacent clockwise (forward looking aft) fan blade for findings considered not serviceable in accordance with the Accomplishment Instructions, paragraph 3.D.(2), of CFM56-7B S/B 72-1119.
(iii) If any unserviceable finding is found during the inspection required by paragraph (h)(2)(ii) of this AD, before further flight, remove the fan blade from service and replace with a serviceable fan blade.
(i) Credit for Previous Actions

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The National Mediation Board (NMB) is issuing this final rule; technical amendment to amend its regulations to reflect a change in address for its Washington, DC headquarters office. This technical amendment is a nomenclature change that replaces outdated addresses with the NMB's current headquarters address. Additionally, this final rule amends the NMB's regulations to eliminate references to the NMB Chief of Staff position, a position that no longer exists in the agency's organization. This action is administrative, technical, and editorial in nature; is necessary to provide accuracy and clarity to the NMB's Rules; and does not alter the rights, duties, or obligations of the public.
DATES:
The final rule is effective October 27, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The NMB maintains regulations in title 29, parts 1201-1209 of the Code of Federal Regulations, a number of which identify the agency's Washington, DC headquarters address and/or a staff position that no longer exists in the agency's organization. On August 1, 2026, NMB's Washington, DC headquarters office relocated from 1301 K St. NW, Suite 250-E, Washington, DC 20005 to 445 12th St. SW, Suite 2500, Washington, DC 20024. This final rule updates NMB's regulations at
29 CFR 1203.1

1203.3(a)

1208.2(a)

1208.2(b)(6)(ii)
,

1209.07(f)
, and
1209.08(d)
to reflect the NMB's current headquarters address and eliminate references to the non-existent staff position. The NMB has already notified the public of the address change on its website and through other means of communication.
Regulatory Analysis
A. Administrative Procedure Act
This action is taken under NMB's authority, at
5 U.S.C. 552
, to publish regulations in the
Federal Register
. Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), at
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(3)(B)
, statutory procedures for agency rulemaking do not apply “when the agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefore in the rules issued) that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” The NMB finds that such notice and public procedure are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest, on the grounds that: (1) These amendments are technical and non-substantive; and (2) the public benefits from timely notification of a change in the official agency headquarters address, and further delay is unnecessary and contrary to the public interest. Similarly, because this final rule makes no substantive changes and merely reflects, in existing regulations, a change of address and the removal of references to a staff position that no longer exists in the agency, this rule is not subject to the effective date limitation of
5 U.S.C. 553(d)
.
B. Congressional Review Act
As this is a rule of agency organization, procedure, or practice that does not substantially affect the rights and obligations of non-agency parties, it is not a “rule” covered by the Congressional Review Act,
5 U.S.C. 804(3)(C)
.
C. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995
This rule will not result in the expenditure by state, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million or more in any one year, and it will not significantly or uniquely affect small governments. Therefore, no actions were deemed necessary under the provisions of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
Pub. L. 104-4
).
D. Executive Orders 12866, 14192, and 13563
This rule is “not significant” under
Executive Order 12866
; therefore, the rule is exempt from the provisions of
Executive Order 14192
. The benefit of the rule in providing clarity to the public on the current address of the
(
printed page 67481)
agency's Washington, DC headquarters office and eliminating references in the NMB's regulations to a position that no longer exists within the agency outweighs any costs to the public, which are minimal or non-existent.
E. Regulatory Flexibility Act: Small Business
The NMB certifies that this rule will not have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA),
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.,
as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (SBREFA) (
Pub. L. 104-121
). The RFA applies only to rules for which an agency publishes a general notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)
of the APA. Consistent with section 553(b)(3)(B) of the APA, and as noted above, the NMB has determined for good cause that general notice and opportunity for public comment is unnecessary because the rule makes only technical changes to its regulations and does not alter any substantive standard, and, therefore, the NMB is not issuing a notice of proposed rulemaking. Accordingly, the NMB has concluded that a regulatory flexibility analysis under the RFA is not required. We are taking this action to ensure our Rules reflect updated and accurate information for the public.
This action is not a major rule as defined by section 804 of the SBREFA. This rule will not result in an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more; a major increase in costs or prices for consumers, individual industries, federal, state or local government agencies, or geographic regions; or significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or on the ability of U.S.-based companies to compete with foreign-based companies in domestic and export markets.
F. Paperwork Reduction Act
This rule does not contain information collection requirements, and a submission to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995,
44 U.S.C. 3501
,
et seq.,
is not required.

AGENCY:
Forest Service, Agriculture; Office of Subsistence Management, Interior.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule revises regulations for hunting and trapping seasons, harvest limits, and methods and means related to taking of wildlife for subsistence uses during the 2026-27 and 2027-28 regulatory years. The Federal Subsistence Board (hereafter referred to as “the Board”) is on a schedule of completing the process of revising subsistence taking of wildlife regulations in even-numbered years and subsistence taking of fish and shellfish regulations in odd-numbered years; public proposal and review processes take place during the preceding year. The Board also addresses customary and traditional use determinations during the applicable cycle. This final rule revises the existing subsistence wildlife taking regulations, the general regulations on subsistence taking of fish and wildlife, customary and traditional use determinations, and addresses a deferred proposal regarding eulachon harvest in District 1 from the last fish cycle and a deferred proposal regarding brown bear hide sales from the last wildlife cycle. This final rule also makes administrative corrections to the regulations and corrects errors discovered since the last rulemaking.
DATES:
This rule is effective October 27, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The comments received in response to the proposed rule are available at
https://www.regulations.gov
in Docket No. DOI-2024-0011. Federal Subsistence Board meeting transcripts are available for review on the Office of Subsistence Management (OSM) website (
https://www.doi.gov/​subsistence
); and at
https://www.regulations.gov
in Docket No. DOI-2024-0011.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Chair, Federal Subsistence Board, c/o Office of Subsistence Management, Attention: Crystal Leonetti, Director; (907) 786-3888 or
subsistence@ios.doi.gov
.
For questions specific to National Forest System lands, contact Gregory Risdahl, Regional Subsistence Program Leader, USDA, Forest Service, Alaska Region; (907) 302-7354 or
gregory.risdahl@usda.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Under title VIII of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) (
16 U.S.C. 3111-3126
), the Secretary of the Interior and the Secretary of Agriculture (hereafter referred to as “the Secretaries”) jointly implement the Federal Subsistence Management Program (hereafter referred to as “the Program”). The Program provides a priority for take of fish and wildlife resources for nonwasteful subsistence uses on Federal public lands and waters in Alaska. Only Alaska residents of areas identified as rural are eligible to participate in the Program. The Secretaries published temporary regulations to carry out the Program in the
Federal Register
on June 29, 1990 (
55 FR 27114
), and final regulations on May 29, 1992 (
57 FR 22940
). Program officials have subsequently amended these regulations many times. Because the Program is a joint effort between the Departments of the Interior and Agriculture, these regulations are located in two titles of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR): The Agriculture regulations are at title 36, “Parks, Forests, and Public Property,” and the Interior regulations are at title 43, “Public Lands: Interior,” at
36 CFR 242.1-28
and
43 CFR 51.1-28
, respectively. Consequently, to indicate that identical changes are proposed for regulations in both titles 36 and 43, in this document we will present references to specific sections of the CFR as shown in the following example: § __.24.
The Program regulations contain subparts as follows: Subpart A, General Provisions; Subpart B, Program Structure; Subpart C, Board Determinations; and Subpart D, Subsistence Taking of Fish and Wildlife. Consistent with subpart B of these regulations, the Secretaries established the Board to administer the Program. The Board comprises:
A Chair appointed by the Secretary of the Interior with concurrence of the Secretary of Agriculture;
Five public members appointed by the Secretary of the Interior with concurrence of the Secretary of Agriculture;
The Alaska Regional Director, Bureau of Indian Affairs;
The Alaska State Director, Bureau of Land Management (BLM);
The Alaska Regional Director, National Park Service (NPS);
The Alaska Regional Director, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS); and
The Pacific Geographic Area Regional Forester, U.S. Forest Service.
Through the Board, these agencies and public members participate in the development of regulations for subparts C and D. Subpart C sets forth important Board determinations regarding program eligibility (
i.e.,
which areas of Alaska are considered rural and which species are harvested in those areas as part of a “customary and traditional use” for subsistence purposes). Subpart D sets forth specific seasons, limits, and other harvest parameters and requirements.
In administering the Program, the Secretaries divided Alaska into 10 subsistence resource regions, each of which is represented by a Federal Subsistence Regional Advisory Council (Council). The Councils provide a forum for rural residents with personal knowledge of local conditions and resource requirements to have a meaningful role in the subsistence management of fish and wildlife on Federal public lands in Alaska. The Council members represent varied geographical, cultural, and user interests within each region.
The Board conducts rulemaking for the Program on a biennial schedule with the process of revising the fish and shellfish regulations and the process for revising the wildlife regulations occurring during opposite years. The Board addresses “customary and traditional use” determinations during the applicable biennial cycle. The regulations at § __.4 define “customary and traditional use” as “a
(
printed page 67483)
long-established, consistent pattern of use, incorporating beliefs and customs which have been transmitted from generation to generation.” Since establishment of the Program regulations in 1992, the Board has made a number of customary and traditional use determinations at the request of affected subsistence users. These determinations have resulted in revisions to the regulations at § __.24. Those modifications, along with some administrative corrections, were published in the
Federal Register
as follows:
Current Rulemaking Action
The Departments published a proposed rule, Subsistence Management Regulations for Public Lands in Alaska—2026-27 and 2027-28 Subsistence Taking of Wildlife Regulations, on January 21, 2025 (
90 FR 6922
), to amend the regulations in subparts C and D of
36 CFR part 242
and
50 CFR part 100
for seasons, harvest limits, and methods and means related to taking of wildlife for subsistence uses. Since the Department of the Interior Federal subsistence regulations were subsequently relocated from
50 CFR part 100
(
90 FR 34148
, July 18, 2025), the regulations referenced in the remainder of this document will be
36 CFR part 242
and
43 CFR part 51
.
The proposed rule opened a comment period that closed on April 4, 2025. The Departments advertised the proposed rule on the Program's web page and social media, and it was sent via email. The Councils met between February 19 and April 2, 2025, and in addition to other business, received suggestions for proposals from the public. The Board received a total of 84 proposals, 1 of which was classified as invalid. The invalid proposal requested a change to the Unit 2 black bear harvest limit for nonresidents, which is outside of the Board's authority. The Board received 7 valid proposals for changes to subpart C (customary and traditional use determinations) and 76 valid proposals for changes to subpart D regulations (which are specific provisions regarding the take of fish and wildlife). In addition, 18 wildlife closure reviews were presented for comment as required
(
printed page 67484)
by Board policy that specifies a review of each closure at least every 4 years. The Board also addressed one request for reconsideration submitted in response to the Board changing the status of Ketchikan from nonrural to rural, and one deferred proposal from the previous fish and shellfish regulatory cycle (
90 FR 34152
, July 18, 2025).
The public submitted twelve general comments, which are available for review at
https://www.regulations.gov
in Docket No. DOI-2024-0011. Most of these comments supported some combination of the proposed rule and the Title VIII rural priority and conservation mandate. Another comment expressed concern for effects on wildlife populations but supported the Board's holistic decision-making process. The remaining comment supported including proposed meeting dates to maximize participation. We provided fall and winter meeting dates and locations for the ten Councils. We did not provide specific dates for the Board meeting because the dates were unknown. The remaining public comment was outside the scope of this rulemaking action.
After the comment period closed, the Board posted the proposals on the Program website and distributed a news release notifying the public on May 7, 2025. The public then had 55 days, until June 30, 2025, to comment on the proposed regulatory changes.
The 10 Councils met again between September 16, 2025, and March 13, 2026, received public comments, and formulated their recommendations to the Board on proposals and closure reviews for their respective regions. The public also had an opportunity to comment at the Board meeting. Therefore, the public received extensive opportunity to review and comment on all changes.
The Councils had a substantial role in reviewing the proposed rule and making recommendations for the final rule. Moreover, a Council Chair, or a designated representative, presented each Council's recommendations at the Board's public meeting held April 21-24, 2026.
Summary of Board Actions on Proposals and Closure Reviews
The Board's actions on each proposal and closure review are listed in table 2 below. When making decisions, the Board may consider, among other factors, whether a proposal:
provides a subsistence priority on public lands;
is supported by substantial scientific evidence and traditional ecological knowledge (TEK);
recognizes principles of fish and wildlife conservation;
provides opportunity; and
would not be detrimental to or place undue burden on rural Alaskan subsistence users.
The Board considered 83 wildlife proposals and 18 wildlife closure reviews during the 2026-28 wildlife regulatory cycle. The Board adopted 51 of the proposals, deferred 5, approved the withdrawal of 3 (WP26-27 and WP26-41/42), rejected 12, and took no action on 12. The Board acted on 18 wildlife closure reviews, voting to retain status quo on 13 of them, rescind 3, and take no action on 2. The Board adopted deferred fisheries proposal FP25-02 as modified by the Southeast Alaska Subsistence Regional Advisory Council and determined the requests for reconsideration of Ketchikan's rural status (RFR25-01) do not meet the threshold for further consideration.
Consensus agenda:
The consensus agenda is made up of proposals and closure reviews for which there is agreement concerning a proposed regulatory action among the affected Councils, a majority of the Interagency Staff Committee members, and the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G). Anyone may request that the Board remove a proposal or a closure review from the consensus agenda and place it on the non-consensus agenda. Proposals or closure reviews may be taken off the consensus agenda following the agreement of at least one Board member; such proposals or closure reviews then follow the Board's process for non-consensus items and are deliberated and voted on individually. Wildlife proposals WP26-22 regarding trapping setbacks in Unit 7, WP26-62b regarding establishing a muskox hunt in Unit 22A, and WP26-66 regarding wolf hunting in Unit 23 were moved from the consensus agenda to the non-consensus agenda at the request of the public and agreement by the Board. Of the proposals and closure reviews being considered, 39 were on the consensus agenda. The Board votes
en masse
on the consensus agenda after deliberation and action on all other proposals.
Of the proposals on the consensus agenda, the Board adopted 17 as they were written, adopted 3 with modifications, rejected 8, and took no action on 5. Of the closure reviews on the consensus agenda, the Board retained the status quo on four and rescinded two. Analysis and justification for the action taken on each proposal on the consensus agenda can be found in the Board meeting book and transcripts for the meeting that occurred April 21-24, 2026 in Anchorage, AK.

Administrative Procedure Act Compliance
The Board has provided extensive opportunity for public input and involvement in compliance with the Administrative Procedure Act (
5 U.S.C. 551
et seq.
), including publishing a proposed rule in the
Federal Register
, participation in multiple Council meetings, additional public review and comment on all proposals for regulatory change, and opportunity for additional public comment during the Board meeting prior to deliberation. Additionally, an administrative mechanism exists to request reconsideration of the Board's decision on any proposal for regulatory change (
36 CFR 242.20
and
43 CFR 51.20
). Therefore, the Board believes that sufficient public notice and opportunity for involvement have been given to affected persons regarding Board decisions.
The administrative correction to the Unit 3 moose season start date was not identified as a proposed change in the proposed rule. We find that there is good cause to make this change without notice and comment under the Administrative Procedure Act at
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
. First, we find that notice and comment is unnecessary because the change merely fixes an inadvertent error in the publication process and thus would not have benefitted from public input. In addition, it is impractical to make this correction with notice and comment because such notice and comment would delay making the correction until after September 1, 2026 and thus likely lead to continued confusion as to when hunting can begin.
The notice and comment process is also unnecessary for the remaining administrative changes not identified in the proposed rule, which include correcting a spelling error, removing closures no longer in effect, and making changes to Board-adopted language that improve regulatory clarity. In these cases, we find good cause that the notice and comment process is unnecessary because the changes are of a technical nature, are not substantial, and are unlikely to be of interest to the public.
In the more than 30 years that the Program has been operating, no benefit to the public has been demonstrated by delaying the effective date of the subsistence regulations. A lapse in regulatory control could affect the continued viability of fish or wildlife populations and future subsistence opportunities for rural Alaskans and would generally fail to serve the overall public interest. Therefore, the Board finds good cause pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
to make this rule effective upon the date set forth in
