National Environmental Policy Act
A draft environmental impact statement that described four alternatives for developing a Federal Subsistence Management Program was distributed for public comment on October 7, 1991. The final environmental impact statement (FEIS) was published on February 28, 1992. The Record of Decision (ROD) on Subsistence Management for Federal Public Lands in Alaska was signed April 6, 1992. The selected alternative in the FEIS (Alternative IV) defined the administrative framework of an annual regulatory cycle for subsistence regulations.
A 1997 environmental assessment dealt with the expansion of Federal jurisdiction over fisheries and is available at the office listed under
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
. The Secretary of the Interior, with concurrence of the Secretary of Agriculture, determined that expansion of Federal jurisdiction does not constitute a major Federal action significantly affecting the human environment and, therefore, signed a Finding of No Significant Impact.
DOI conducted a Determination of NEPA Adequacy of the 1992 and 1997 documents and determined that there were no changes that warrant a new NEPA review in accordance with DOI NEPA Manual Section 3.1.
Section 810 of ANILCA
An ANILCA section 810 analysis was completed as part of the FEIS process on the Program. The intent of all Federal subsistence regulations is to accord subsistence uses of fish and wildlife on public lands a priority over the taking of fish and wildlife on such lands for other purposes, unless restriction is necessary to conserve healthy fish and wildlife populations. The final section 810 analysis determination appeared in the April 6, 1992, ROD and concluded that the Program, under Alternative IV with an annual process for setting subsistence regulations, may have some local impacts on subsistence uses, but will not likely restrict subsistence uses significantly.
During the subsequent 1997 environmental assessment process for extending fisheries jurisdiction, an evaluation of the effects of the subsistence program regulations was conducted in accordance with section 810. That evaluation also supported the Secretaries' determination that the regulations will not reach the threshold that would require notice and hearings under ANILCA section 810(a).

printed page 67516)

(i) Unit 25 consists of the Yukon River drainage upstream from but not including the Hamlin Creek drainage, and excluding drainages into the south bank of the Yukon River upstream from the Charley River:
(A) Unit 25A consists of the Hodzana River drainage upstream from the Narrows, the Chandalar River drainage upstream from and including the East Fork drainage, the Christian River drainage upstream from Christian, the Sheenjek River drainage upstream from and including the Thluichohnjik Creek, the Coleen River drainage, and the Old Crow River drainage.
(B) Unit 25B consists of the Little Black River drainage upstream from but not including the Big Creek drainage, the Black River drainage upstream from and including the Salmon Fork drainage, the Porcupine River drainage upstream from the confluence of the Coleen and Porcupine Rivers, and drainages into the north bank of the Yukon River upstream from Circle, including the islands in the Yukon River.
(C) Unit 25C consists of drainages into the south bank of the Yukon River upstream from Circle to the Subunit 20E boundary, the Birch Creek drainage upstream from the Steese Highway bridge (milepost 147), and then following the Steese Highway to the northeast staying on the north side of the road from the Steese Bridge at milepost 147 to Circle; the Preacher Creek drainage upstream from and including the Rock Creek drainage, and the Beaver Creek drainage upstream from and including the Moose Creek drainage.
(
printed page 67525)
(D) Unit 25D consists of the remainder of Unit 25.
(ii) In the following areas, the taking of wildlife for subsistence uses is prohibited or restricted on public land:
(A) You may not use firearms, snowmobiles, licensed highway vehicles or motorized vehicles, except aircraft and boats in the Dalton Highway Corridor Management Area, which consists of those portions of Units 20, 24, 25, and 26 extending 5 miles from each side of the Dalton Highway from the Yukon River to milepost 300 of the Dalton Highway, except as follows: Residents living within the Dalton Highway Corridor Management Area may use snowmobiles only for the subsistence taking of wildlife. You may use licensed highway vehicles only on designated roads within the Dalton Highway Corridor Management Area. The residents of Alatna, Allakaket, Anaktuvuk Pass, Bettles, Evansville, and Stevens Village, and residents living within the Corridor may use firearms within the Corridor only for subsistence taking of wildlife.
(B) The Arctic Village Sheep Management Area consists of that portion of Unit 25A north and west of Arctic Village, which is bounded on the east by the East Fork Chandalar River beginning at the confluence of Red Sheep Creek and proceeding southwesterly downstream past Arctic Village to the confluence with Crow Nest Creek, continuing up Crow Nest Creek, through Portage Lake, to its confluence with the Junjik River; then down the Junjik River past Timber Lake and a larger tributary, to a major, unnamed tributary, northwesterly, for approximately 6 miles where the stream forks into two roughly equal drainages; the boundary follows the easternmost fork, proceeding almost due north to the headwaters and intersects the Continental Divide; the boundary then follows the Continental Divide easterly, through Carter Pass, then easterly and northeasterly approximately 62 miles along the divide to the headwaters of the most northerly tributary of Red Sheep Creek then follows southerly along the divide designating the eastern extreme of the Red Sheep Creek drainage then to the confluence of Red Sheep Creek and the East Fork Chandalar River.
(iii) Unit-specific regulations:
(A) You may use bait to hunt black bear between April 15 and June 30 and between August 1 and September 25; in Unit 25D you may use bait to hunt brown bear between April 15 and June 30 and between August 1 and September 25; you may use bait to hunt wolves on FWS and BLM lands.
(B) You may take caribou and moose from a boat moving under power in Unit 25.
(C) The taking of bull moose outside the seasons provided in this part for food in memorial potlatches and traditional cultural events is authorized in Unit 25D west provided that:
(
1
) The person organizing the religious ceremony or cultural event contacts the Refuge Manager, Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge, prior to taking or attempting to take bull moose and provides to the Refuge Manager the name of the decedent, the nature of the ceremony or cultural event, number to be taken, and the general area in which the taking will occur.
(
2
) Each person who takes a bull moose under this section must submit a written report to the Refuge Manager, Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge, not more than 15 days after the harvest specifying the harvester's name and address, and the date(s) and location(s) of the taking(s).
(

AGENCY:
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of public meeting.
SUMMARY:
This notice announces a meeting of the National Emergency Medical Services Advisory Council (NEMSAC).
DATES:
This meeting will be transmitted via virtual interface and is scheduled to be held on November 4, 2026, from 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. ET. Pre-registration is required to attend the meeting. Once registered, a link permitting access to the meeting will be distributed to registrants by email. If you wish to speak during the meeting, you must submit a written copy of your remarks to DOT by October 26, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
General information about the Council is available on the NEMSAC internet website at
www.ems.gov
.
The registration portal and meeting agenda will be available on the NEMSAC internet website at
www.ems.gov
at least one week in advance of the meeting.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
The Office of Emergency Medical Services, National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation is available by email at
NEMSAC@dot.gov
.
Any committee-related requests should be sent to the email address listed in this section.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
NEMSAC is authorized under Section 31108 of the Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act of 2012, codified at
42 U.S.C. 300d-4
as a Federal Advisory Committee. The purpose of NEMSAC is to serve as a nationally recognized council of emergency medical services (EMS) representatives to provide advice to and consult with:
a. The Federal Interagency Committee on Emergency Medical Services (FICEMS) on matters relating to EMS issues; and
b. The Secretary of Transportation on matters relating to EMS issues affecting DOT.
NEMSAC provides an important national forum for the non-Federal deliberation of national EMS issues and serves as a platform for advice on DOT's national EMS activities. NEMSAC also provides advice and recommendations to the FICEMS.
II. Agenda
At the meeting, the agenda will cover the following topics:
NHTSA Initiatives
Updates from Federal Partners
FICEMS Strategic Plan for National Implementation of Prehospital Blood Transfusion
Request for Consultation and Advice
General Informational Sessions
Strategic Planning for NEMSAC
Public Comment Period
III. Background on FICEMS Strategic Plan for National Implementation of Prehospital Blood Transfusion
Severe bleeding is the leading cause of preventable death in trauma patients. Evidence demonstrates that prompt prehospital blood transfusion can save an estimated 37 percent of trauma patients experiencing severe bleeding, whereas every minute of delay increases mortality risk by 11 percent. The draft FICEMS Strategic Plan for National Implementation of Prehospital Blood Transfusion (2026-2028) aims to prevent 10,000 deaths annually and achieve a 5 percent reduction in overall trauma mortality from severe bleeding by 2028.
The Council will deliberate on a letter from the Designated Federal Officer requesting consultation and advice on the FICEMS Strategic Plan for National Implementation of Prehospital Blood Transfusion. The Council will also deliberate on the Request for Information (RFI) published in the
Federal Register
on October 5, 2026. The RFI solicits public comments on feasibility, operational challenges, data linkage, and logistics associated with meeting the following national targets (key performance indicators or KPIs) across three core pillars:
Goal 1: Integrated Informatics
Pediatric Pre-Arrival Instructions:
Increase the percentage of children with life-threatening bleeding post-crash receiving 911 pre-arrival instructions from a calendar year (CY) 2025 baseline of 20 percent to a 2028 target of 25 percent.
Overall Pre-Arrival Instructions:
Increase the percentage of all patients with life-threatening bleeding post-crash receiving 911 pre-arrival instructions from a CY 2025 baseline of 20 percent to a 2028 target of 25 percent.
Goal 2: Systems Innovation
Ground EMS Agency Programs:
Expand the total number of ground EMS
(
printed page 67650)
agencies with operational prehospital blood transfusion programs from a CY 2026 baseline of 450 agencies to a 2028 target of 2,028 agencies.
Goal 3: Clinical Excellence
Pediatric Prehospital Transfusion:
Increase the percentage of pediatric patients with life-threatening bleeding post-crash receiving prehospital blood transfusion from a CY 2025 baseline of 7 percent to a 2028 target of 28 percent.
Overall Prehospital Transfusion:
Increase the percentage of all patients with life-threatening bleeding post-crash receiving prehospital blood transfusion from a CY 2025 baseline of 4 percent to a 2028 target of 16 percent.
IV. Public Participation
This meeting will be open to the public. We are committed to providing equal access to this meeting for all participants. People with disabilities who need accommodation should send a request to the individual in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this notice no later than October 26, 2026.
A period of time will be allotted for comments from members of the public attending the meeting. Members of the public may present questions and comments to the Council using the live chat feature available during the meeting. Members of the public may also submit materials, questions, and comments in advance to the individual listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this notice.
Members of the public wishing to reserve time to speak directly to the Council during the meeting must submit a request. The request must include the name, contact information (address, phone number, and email address), and organizational affiliation of the individual wishing to address NEMSAC; it must also include a written copy of prepared remarks and must be forwarded to the individual listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this notice no later than October 26, 2026.
All advance submissions will be reviewed by the Council Chairperson and Designated Federal Officer. If approved, advance submissions shall be circulated to NEMSAC representatives for review prior to the meeting. All advance submissions will become part of the official record of the meeting.

II. Statutory Standard for Registration as a Clearing Agency
Clearing agencies are broadly defined under the Exchange Act and undertake a variety of functions,
[
10
]
including providing the services of a CCP.
[
11
]
Pursuant to Section 17A of the Exchange Act and Rule 17Ab2-1 thereunder, an entity that meets the definition of a clearing agency must register with the Commission.
[
12
]
Section 17A(b)(1) also states that, upon the Commission's motion or upon a clearing agency's application, the Commission may conditionally or unconditionally exempt a clearing agency from any provisions of Section 17A or the rules or regulations thereunder if the Commission finds that such exemption is consistent with the public interest, the protection of investors, and the purposes of Section 17A, including the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and the safeguarding of securities and funds.
[
13
]
In addition to the requirements set forth in Rule 17Ab2-1, Section 19(a)(1) of the Exchange Act establishes the standard for Commission review of an application for registration as a clearing agency. Pursuant thereto, the Commission shall grant registration of a clearing agency if it finds that the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder with respect to the applicant are satisfied.
[
14
]
The Commission shall deny such registration if it does not make such finding.
[
15
]
The requirements of the Exchange Act applicable to clearing agencies are set forth in Section 17A and the rules and regulations thereunder.
[
16
]
Accordingly,
(
printed page 67625)
to grant CCUS's Application for registration as a clearing agency, the Commission must find that the Application satisfies the requirements of Section 17A(b) of the Exchange Act and rules and regulations thereunder, including the determinations set forth in paragraphs (A) through (I) of Section 17A(b)(3) of the Exchange Act.
[
17
]
Pursuant to Rule 17Ab2-1(c), the Commission, upon the request of a clearing agency, may grant registration of the clearing agency but exempt the registrant from one or more of the requirements as to which the Commission is directed to make a determination pursuant to Section 17A(b)(3) of the Exchange Act, provided that any such registration shall be effective only for eighteen months from the date the registration is made effective (or such longer period as the Commission may provide by order).
[
18
]
After a clearing agency's application for registration is granted, the clearing agency must continue to satisfy the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder. In the context of temporary registration, the clearing agency must satisfy the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder, except as to requirements, rules, or regulations to which an exemption has been provided. The Commission has explained that “[a]n approval of clearing agency registration does not mean that no further modifications of the applicant's rules, systems, procedures, or practices are needed.”
[
19
]
Rather, the Commission stated that a registered clearing agency's obligation to continue to satisfy the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder means that “[t]he self-regulatory obligations of [a] fully registered clearing agenc[y] cannot end” after registration.
[
20

To ensure such compliance, the Commission stated that it “will continue to use its oversight, inspection, and enforcement authority as necessary and appropriate to further the purposes of the [Exchange] Act.”

A. Organization and Capacity
1. Statutory Standard: Section 17A(b)(3)(A)
Section 17A(b)(3)(A) of the Exchange Act states that a clearing agency shall not be registered unless the Commission determines that such clearing agency is so organized and has the capacity to be able to facilitate the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and derivative agreements, contracts, and transactions for which it is responsible, to safeguard securities and funds in its custody or control or for which it is responsible, to comply with the provisions of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder, to enforce (subject to any rule or order of the Commission pursuant to Section 17(d) or 19(g)(2) of the Exchange Act) compliance by its participants with the rules of the clearing agency, and to carry out the purposes of Section 17A of the Exchange Act.

B. Participation Standards
1. Statutory Standard: Section 17A(b)(3)(B)
Section 17A(b)(3)(B) of the Exchange Act states that a clearing agency shall not be registered unless the Commission determines that the rules of the clearing agency provide that any (i) registered broker or dealer, (ii) other registered clearing agency, (iii) registered investment company, (iv) bank, (v) insurance company, or (vi) other person or class of persons as the Commission, by rule, may from time to time designate as appropriate to the development of a national system or the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions may become a participant in such clearing agency.
[
154
]
Section 3(a)(24) of the Exchange Act defines a “participant” with respect to a clearing agency as any person who uses a clearing agency to clear or settle securities transactions or to transfer, pledge, lend, or hypothecate securities, and further states that the term does not include a person whose only use of a clearing agency is (i) through another person who is a participant or (ii) as a pledgee of securities.
[
155
]
2. Summary of Application
The CCUS Rules specify the entities that can become clearing members. The definition of “clearing member” is “an FCM Clearing Member, a BD Clearing Member, or Direct Clearing Member. . . .”
[
156
]
A BD clearing member is defined as a “Person that (i) is registered as a broker dealer under Section 15(b) of the Securities Exchange Act; (ii) has completed a Clearing Member Application; and (iii) has been granted clearing privileges by Cboe Clear US specifically with respect to Securities Contracts.”
[
157
]
As previously discussed in Part III.A.2.a), in its Application CCUS “acknowledges that the Rules do not at this time reference all of the categories of participants enumerated in Section 17A(b)(3)(B) of the Exchange Act.”
[
158

To become a clearing member, an applicant must execute the Clearing Member Agreement and satisfy CCUS's eligibility criteria. As a general matter, a clearing member must consent to abide by CCUS Rules, agree that CCUS Rules are part of the terms and conditions of every contract or transaction that it may make or have with CCUS, and agree to maintain adequate controls to ensure continued satisfaction of financial and operational obligations of itself and its customers, as applicable. Currently, CCUS has established that a clearing member must be either a registered futures commission merchant (“FCM”) or a registered broker-dealer.
[
159
]
In Exhibit S, CCUS also explains that with the exception of Direct Clearing Members, clearing members eligible to clear securities products, either for their own accounts or the account of a customer, must be registered broker-dealers . . .”

As noted above, CCUS also provides in the CCUS Rules for participation by “Direct Clearing Members.” That is defined as an entity that is registered under the Exchange Act and submits trades for clearing at CCUS only on behalf of its own accounts, has completed a Clearing Member Agreement, and has been granted clearing privileges by CCUS. CCUS Rules provide, for the avoidance of doubt, that a Direct Clearing Member may not carry customer accounts, submit customer transactions for clearing, or otherwise facilitate access to CCUS for customers or other participants.
[
161

In Exhibit O, CCUS explains that Direct Clearing Members are legal entities (not individuals) that trade exclusively for their own proprietary accounts and may include proprietary trading firms, commercial firms, corporations, institutional investors, or other market participants that seek direct access to CCUS's clearing services. (
printed page 67633)

Because CCUS has not provided for all categories of participants enumerated in Section 17A(b)(3)(B) of the Exchange Act, including registered clearing agencies, registered investment companies, banks, insurance companies, or other classes of persons designated as appropriate by the Commission, CCUS is requesting temporary registration as a clearing agency and an exemption from the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(B) for a period of 18 months. Accordingly, the Commission is not, at this time, making a determination as to whether CCUS's Application satisfies the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(B) of the Exchange Act. C. Fair Representation
1. Statutory Standard: Section 17A(b)(3)(C)
Section 17A(b)(3)(C) of the Exchange Act states that a clearing agency shall not be registered unless the Commission determines that the rules of the clearing agency assure a fair representation of its shareholders (or members) and participants in the selection of its directors and administration of its affairs.
[
162
]
2. Summary of Application and Analysis
Under Section 17A(b)(3)(C) of the Exchange Act, the Commission considers whether the Application provides fair representation both to shareholders (or members) and to participants in the selection of directors and the administration of affairs. In doing so, the Commission undertakes an analysis of the documents in the Application that govern or otherwise affect the selection of directors by the clearing agency and the administration of its affairs. Such documents include, for example, the constitution, articles of incorporation, bylaws, rules, and written policies or procedures. Such analysis considers both qualitative and quantitative factors, including the number of board positions that a clearing agency may reserve for shareholders or to represent participants, as well as the existence of provisions in governing documents that may impede representation in the selection of directors or the administration of affairs. The Commission also considers the overall organization of the clearing agency, the nature of the products it clears, and the structure of the market it serves, including the nature of existing clearing and settlement arrangements in the market served, the existence of other clearing agencies that offer comparable services and how they are structured, and the size of the market served by the applicant, to evaluate whether the representation proposed by the applicant is consistent with the requirements of the Exchange Act.
[
163
]
Finally, because CCUS will operate the KPI Options Business in the same existing legal entity where it provides futures clearing services, the Commission considers CCUS's existing arrangements to the extent they indicate whether CCUS, as an entity, would provide fair representation to shareholders and participants of its KPI Options Business.
Under Section 3(a)(7) of the Exchange Act, the term “director” is defined as “any director of a corporation or any person performing similar functions with respect to any organization, whether incorporated or unincorporated.”
[
164
]
When an applicant is not organized as a corporation, the Commission assesses whether the directors under its business form are performing functions similar to the directors of a corporation. CCUS is organized as a member-managed LLC, which places control over CCUS with the LLC Member. This organizational and management structure differs from registered clearing agencies that are organized as corporations,
[
165
]
or organized as LLCs but operate as manager-managed LLCs.
[
166
]
As a result, below the Commission considers whether the role of director as set forth in CCUS's LLC Agreement is consistent with the statutory definition of director, in order to assess whether shareholders and participants have fair representation in its selection consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(C) of the Exchange Act.
Under the proposed LLC Agreement, CCUS is managed by, and with some decisions regarding CCUS reserved to, the LLC Member. The LLC Member has delegated its authority over the business and affairs of CCUS to the Board, but as described in Part III.A.3 above regarding the Applicant's organization, the LLC Agreement makes the Board's exercise of many business decisions contingent upon the sole written approval of the Member. However, the LLC Agreement makes clear that, “[f]or purposes of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder, each Director shall constitute a `director' within the meaning of Section 3(a)(7) of the Exchange Act.”
[
167
]
Additionally, the proposed LLC Agreement states that, “notwithstanding anything to the contrary in [the LLC Agreement], the Member shall not exercise any consent right or other authority reserved to it under [the LLC Agreement] in a manner that: impairs the board's authority to direct the operations of [CCUS] consistent with Section 17A of the Exchange Act; denies or impairs the fair representation of participants of [CCUS] contemplated by Section 17A(b)(3)(C) of
(
printed page 67634)
the Exchange Act; or prevents the Board from being composed or operating in a manner required by the Exchange Act or applicable SEC regulations, including Rule 17Ad-25.
[
168
]
These provisions in the LLC Agreement make clear that the Member's reserved authority would not prevent the Board from performing those functions necessary for CCUS to meet the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules thereunder, including the requirements as to board composition and governance under Rule 17Ad-25. These above-described provisions of the proposed LLC Agreement make clear that the role of a Director on the Board is intended to perform similar functions—such as serving as the governing body, responsible for oversight—as performed by a “director” as defined in Section 3(a)(7) of the Exchange Act on the board of directors of an incorporated corporation.
Having concluded that the Board under the proposed LLC Agreement would perform similar functions as the board of directors of a corporation, the Commission next evaluates fair representation consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(C) of the Exchange Act.
With respect to the fair representation of the shareholders (or members), under the proposed LLC Agreement, as described above, CCUS is managed by, with some decisions regarding CCUS reserved to, the LLC Member. The Board will consist of between three and eleven Directors. The LLC Member appoints all Directors, and also designates which Director serves as Chair of the Board. The LLC Member is also able to remove any Director with or without cause. The LLC Member's ability to retain or delegate all decision-making authority for CCUS, and to appoint and remove all Directors, demonstrates that the LLC Member has meaningful representation in the selection of directors and administration of CCUS's affairs.
With respect to fair representation of participants, CCUS's parent is the LLC Member, and under the structure set forth in the draft LLC Agreement, the Application includes no provision to make CCUS voting stock available for purchase to participants.
[
169
]
Two positions on the Board, however, are reserved for Directors who are market participants as defined and determined by the Board.
[
170
]
In defining and determining who are “market participants” eligible to serve as Directors, the LLC Agreement makes clear, as previously discussed that (i) “Director” has the same meaning as “director” in Section 3(a)(7) of the Exchange Act and (ii) the Member shall not exercise any consent right or other authority reserved to it under [the LLC Agreement] in a manner that: impairs the board's authority to direct the operations of [CCUS] consistent with Section 17A of the Exchange Act; denies or impairs the fair representation of participants of [CCUS] contemplated by Section 17A(b)(3)(C) of the Exchange Act; or prevents the Board from being composed or operating in a manner required by the Exchange Act or applicable SEC regulations, including Rule 17Ad-25. In addition, although the number of positions on the Board for market participants is fixed at two, currently the two participant-representatives constitute approximately 29 percent of Directors on the Board, suggesting that the Board provides representation for participant-representatives in the administration of the affairs of the clearing agency.
[
171
]
As previously discussed, Section 17A(b)(3)(B) also requires that participants have fair representation in the selection of directors. Accordingly, it is important to consider the role of the Nominating Committee in the selection of directors. As discussed above, the Nominating Committee is constituted by a majority of Independent Directors and tasked with considering the views of participants and other relevant stakeholders regarding material developments in CCUS's risk management and operations on a recurring basis, including whether a potential nominee's appointment would reflect the range of different business strategies, models, and sizes across participants, as well as the range of customers and clients the participants serve. The Nominating Committee's composition requirement for a majority of Independent Directors (which can include participant-representatives), and requirement to consider participant views when evaluating potential candidates to serve as a Director, provides meaningful representation to participants in the selection of Directors.
Taken together, the above discussed provisions clarifying the ways in which the LLC Member's reserved authority will not interfere with Board functioning consistent with the Exchange Act, providing representation on the Board for Directors to represent market participants, and directing the Nominating Committee to consider participant viewpoints in the evaluation of all candidates for Director provide for fair representation to CCUS's participants in the selection of directors and the administration of CCUS's affairs, consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(C) of the Exchange Act.
For the reasons discussed directly above, the Commission determines that the rules of CCUS assure fair representation in the selection of its directors and administration of its affairs consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(C) of the Exchange Act.

Section 17A(b)(3)(D) of the Exchange Act states that a clearing agency shall not be registered unless the Commission determines that the rules of the clearing agency provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its participants.

172

CCUS's Application includes a fee schedule that sets forth the fees CCUS will charge as clearing fees in connection with its plans to clear Binary KPI Options listed and traded on Cboe Exchange.

As CCUS describes in its response letter, the Application identifies CCUS's proposed fee schedule and the rules governing any fees that it will assess on its clearing members, as described above. With respect to allocating the fees equitably, CCUS's per contract fees are based on each clearing member's usage. With respect to the reasonableness of such fees, the per contract basis for each fee is a common approach to applying fees among registered clearing agencies to clearing members, as it enables clearing members and their customers to determine the appropriate volume of transactions to execute and submit for clearing with CCUS and, in so doing, to anticipate the precise costs they will incur for such activity. E. Rules Designed To Promote Prompt and Accurate Clearance and Settlement and the Safeguarding of Securities and Funds
1. Statutory Standard: Section 17A(b)(3)(F)
Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Exchange Act states that a clearing agency shall not be registered unless the Commission determines that the rules of the clearing agency are designed to promote the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and, to the extent applicable, derivative agreements, contracts, and transactions, to assure the safeguarding of securities and funds which are in the custody or control of the clearing agency or for which it is responsible, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in the clearance and settlement of securities transactions, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a national system for the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. It also states that a clearing agency shall not be registered unless the Commission determines that the rules are not designed to permit unfair discrimination in the admission of participants or among participants in the use of the clearing agency, or to regulate by virtue of any authority conferred by the Exchange Act matters not related to the purposes of this section or the administration of the clearing agency.
2. Summary of Application and Analysis
The Commission's rules for clearing agencies provide for the safeguarding of securities and funds and promote prompt and accurate clearance and settlement by establishing specific requirements for a clearing agency's rules, policies and procedures related to operations and risk management. Specifically, these requirements address rules and procedures for the collection of margin, the composition of the guaranty fund, default management and loss allocation, and the management of other risks associated with the custody, clearing, and settlement of securities.
[
183
]
To analyze under Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Exchange Act an application seeking to provide CCP services, the Commission considers a clearing agency's rules concerning its account structures, margin system, guaranty fund, default management, and loss allocation processes.
In the context of this Application, CCUS has requested temporary registration with an exemption from certain requirements under Section 17A(b)(3)(F) for a period of 18 months, as discussed further in Part IV. Accordingly, below the Commission analyzes the Application under Section 17A(b)(3)(F) only with respect to the rules of the clearing agency for BD Clearing Members (
i.e.,
registered broker-dealers and Direct Clearing Members, each as set forth in the CCUS Rules.
(a) Account Structure and Safeguarding of Securities and Funds
The Rules provide for several types of accounts. All funds deposited by a clearing member with CCUS on behalf of the clearing member's own account shall be held in a Member Property Account or a Market-Maker Account, as applicable.
[
184
]
All funds and assets held by CCUS on behalf of Securities Customers of a BD Clearing Member shall be maintained in a Securities Customer Account, segregated from Futures Customer Accounts and from the BD Clearing Member's proprietary
(
printed page 67636)
accounts.
[
185
]
All funds and assets held by CCUS in a PAB Account will be segregated from funds and assets held in Customer Accounts, Member Property Accounts, and Market Maker Accounts and will be treated as belonging to the carried broker-dealer.
[
186
]
Each clearing member shall establish and maintain account(s), including any customer segregated accounts, at an Approved Depository Institution for the payment of Initial Margin, Variation Margin, and any other Obligations due to the CCUS pursuant to the Rules.
[
187
]
Guaranty Fund Deposits must be made in cash and will be held in a settlement bank approved for the purpose by CCUS.
[
188
]
(b) Margin System
According to the Rules, each clearing member shall deposit Initial Margin in the quantity not less than the applicable Initial Margin Requirement as determined by CCUS at the times prescribed by CCUS.
[
189
]
The Rules also require each clearing member to establish Initial Margin Requirements for its Customers at a level that is not less than 100% of CCUS's Initial Margin Requirements with respect to each product and portfolio and commensurate with the risk presented by each customer account and in such amount as is communicated by CCUS from time to time.
[
190
]
(c) Guaranty Fund
The Rules provide that CCUS will establish and maintain a Guaranty Fund to collateralize financial exposures.
[
191
]
The Guaranty Fund is comprised of Guaranty Fund Deposits by clearing members to satisfy any Guaranty Fund Requirements and has two components: a Minimum Guaranty Fund Requirement and an Exposure-Based Guaranty Fund Requirement.
[
192
]
clearing members must satisfy a Minimum Guaranty Fund Requirement of $100,000.00 per clearing member.
[
193
]
Clearing members will be required to meet the Exposure-Based Guaranty Fund Requirement if the CCUS's Default Financial Resources Requirement exceeds the Corporate Contribution amount plus the total combined Minimum Guaranty Fund Requirement provided by all clearing members.
[
194
]
The Default Financial Resources Requirement is the amount of financial resources required to enable CCUS to meet its obligations to clearing members notwithstanding the default of the two clearing members, including any affiliates, generating the largest financial exposures for CCUS in extreme but plausible market conditions.
[
195
]
(d) Default Management and Loss Allocation
In the Rules, the “Default Management Plan” is the plan set forth by CCUS for the management of a Clearing Member Default.
[
196
]
If a clearing member is in Default, Collateral held with respect to such clearing member's Member Property Accounts or Market-Maker Accounts, and any other of such Clearing Member's assets held by, pledged to or otherwise available CCUS, may be applied to discharge the Obligations of such clearing member to CCUS.
[
197
]
The Rules further state Guaranty Funds Deposits from a Defaulting Clearing Member will be applied to mitigate the Default Loss prior to applying CCUS capital contributed as Default Financial Resources.
[
198
]

[
199
]
Assessments on clearing members to replenish the Guaranty Fund shall not exceed the thresholds set forth in the Default Management Plan.
[
200
]
The Rules state that CCUS may use Default Financial Resources to fund Non-Default Losses, which are defined as “a Clearing Member's collateral losses due to the failure or insolvency of an Approved Depository Institution.”
[
201
]

[
202
]
(e) Conclusion
With respect to its rules as applied to BD Clearing Members, the Application describes a comprehensive risk management framework consistent with Commission rules that help ensure CCUS will collect sufficient margin to cover its exposures, maintain an appropriately sized Guaranty Fund, and be able to manage a default and allocate losses appropriately, if or when needed. CCUS's risk management framework is designed to address the particular features of CCUS's proposed structure,
i.e.,
to manage the risks presented by BD Clearing Members and Direct Clearing Members submitting Binary KPI Options for clearing. For these reasons and as discussed in more detail above in Parts III.E.2.a) through d), the Commission determines that CCUS Rules as to the BD Clearing Members and Direct Clearing Members are designed to promote the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions, assure the safeguarding of securities and funds which are in its custody or control or for which it is responsible, and protect investors and the public interest as set forth in Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Exchange Act. The Commission also determines that CCUS Rules as to the BD Clearing Members and Direct Clearing Members do not regulate by virtue of any authority conferred by the Exchange Act matters not related to the purposes of Section 17A of the Exchange Act or the administration of the clearing agency.
The Commission is not, at this time, making a determination regarding the CCUS Rules under Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Exchange Act for the types of participants set forth in the Exchange Act other than registered broker-dealers—namely, clearing agencies, registered investment companies, banks, or insurance companies. Because the Application does not address the other types of participants, the Commission is not, at this time, making a determination as to whether CCUS Rules foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in the clearance and settlement of securities transactions, or remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a national system for the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions. The Commission also is not, at this time, making a determination that CCUS Rules are not designed to permit unfair discrimination in the admission of
(
printed page 67637)
participants or among participants in the use of the clearing agency. As discussed further below in Part IV, pursuant to Rule 17Ab2-1(c), the Commission is granting CCUS's request for temporary registration with an exemption from requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Exchange Act for a period of 18 months.
F. Participant Discipline
1. Statutory Standard and Analysis: Section 17A(b)(3)(G)
Section 17A(b)(3)(G) of the Exchange Act states that a clearing agency shall not be registered unless the Commission determines that the rules of the clearing agency provide that (subject to any rule or order of the Commission pursuant to Sections 17(d) or 19(g)(2) of the Exchange Act) its participants shall be appropriately disciplined for violation of any provision of the rules of the clearing agency by expulsion, suspension, limitation of activities, functions, and operations, fine, censure, or any other fitting sanction.
With respect to discipline and sanctions, the CCUS Rules provide that CCUS can restrict, suspend, or terminate clearing privileges and fine clearing members. Under CCUS Rule 607(a), CCUS states it has the authority to take any actions it deems in the best interest of CCUS or the clearing members.
[
203
]
CCUS Rule 607(b) and (c) further state that CCUS shall have the power to suspend or revoke clearing privileges or authorize the assessment of fines or charges against clearing members for engaging in conduct inconsistent with just and equitable principles of trade or engaging in acts detrimental to the interest or welfare of CCUS.
[
204
]
Specifically, CCUS Rule 601(a) provides situations under which CCUS may summarily suspend any clearing member, including default, statutory disqualification, failing to meeting clearing member eligibility, the discovery of false or misleading representations made by the clearing member, breach or material violation of the CCUS Rules, or if CCUS determines that suspension is necessary for the protection of CCUS, clearing members, customers, or the general public.
[
205
]
Additionally, CCUS Rule 606 lays out the circumstances in which CCUS can restrict or terminate clearing privileges.
[
206
]
CCUS also has the power to assess fines against clearing members that fail to make timely and accurate submission to CCUS of notices, report, or other information required under the CCUS Rules.
[
207
]
Under CCUS Rule 604(a), CCUS may publish a schedule of fines for clearing members that fail to make timely and accurate submissions to CCUS of notices, reports, or other information required under the CCUS Rules and other minor violations of the CCUS Rules.
[
208
]
CCUS has procedures for enforcing rules and disciplining clearing members that are consistent with the requirements of the Exchange Act. The CCUS Rules provide CCUS with authority to discipline clearing members for rule violations and to impose each of the sanctions enumerated in the Exchange Act. Accordingly, the Commission determines that the CCUS Rules provide that CCUS's clearing members shall be appropriately disciplined for violation of any provision of the rules consistent with the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(G) of the Exchange Act.
2. Statutory Standard and Analysis: Section 17A(b)(3)(H)
Section 17A(b)(3)(H) of the Exchange Act states that a clearing agency shall not be registered unless the Commission determines that the rules of the clearing agency, in general, provide a fair procedure with respect to the disciplining of participants, the denial of participation to any persons seeking participation therein, and the prohibition or limitation by the clearing agency of any person with respect to access to services offered by the clearing agency.
[
209
]
(a) Application for Participation
When a participant application is submitted to CCUS, CCUS states it shall have the sole discretion to determine whether any applicant meets the clearing privileges qualifications as detailed in Rule 301 under the CCUS Rules, and CCUS shall disapprove an application and deny the grant of clearing member status where an applicant has failed to meet any requirements.
[
210
]
Additionally, CCUS states it shall have no liability to any applicant who is denied clearing member status.
[
211
]
Upon completion of the application process, CCUS states it shall determine whether to approve or disapprove the application and will promptly give the applicant written notice of the decision. If CCUS denies an application to become a clearing member, CCUS shall give the applicant notice of its decision, setting forth the grounds for the denial, and notes that the decision shall be the final action of CCUS. Any applicant to become a clearing member who has been denied clearing privileges pursuant to this Rule 302 shall not be eligible for re-application during the six months immediately following such denial.
[
212
]
Under CCUS Rules, Rule 301 further states that the notification of the written decision can be delayed if for example an applicant is the subject of an inquiry, investigation, or proceeding conducted by an SRO or governmental authority that involves the applicant's fitness to be a clearing member and CCUS will defer acting on the application until the matter is resolved.
[
213
]
(b) Clearing Member Discipline
Once an entity is a participant, CCUS Rules outline the process CCUS will follow when imposing sanctions on clearing members. CCUS Rule 608 outlines the authority of the Chief Compliance Officer, the Compliance Department, the Chief Regulatory Officer and the Regulatory Division. The Chief Compliance Officer and the Compliance Department will be assisted by the Chief Regulatory Officer and the Regulatory Division, with respect to disciplinary proceedings.
[
214
]
Under the direction of the Chief Regulatory Officer, the Regulatory Division will determine the nature and scope of CCUS's inquiries and investigations and will perform its regulatory functions, including conducting disciplinary proceedings. The Regulatory Division will have the authority to: (i) initiate inquiries; (ii) request that participants appear for an interview, which may be conducted under oath; (iii) request documents and/or other tangible evidence; (iv) review other transaction activity; (v) gather any additional information the Compliance Department it deems necessary; (vi) prepare investigative reports, make determinations as to whether reasonable cause exists to believe that a rule violation has been committed, and make recommendations as to what charges should be brought; (vii) recommend the commencement of a disciplinary proceeding pursuant to Chapter 6 of the CCUS Rules; (viii) prosecute alleged violations of CCUS Rules; (ix) represent
(
printed page 67638)
the Regulatory Division before the Business Conduct Committee during the phases of the disciplinary process consisting of settlement offers and hearings; (x) issue and serve statements of charges on clearing members; (xi) review denials of access to CCUS for disciplinary reasons; and (xii) issue appearance and document requests as provided in CCUS Rules.
[
215
]
If CCUS decides to impose a suspension on a clearing member, CCUS Rules require CCUS to send a notice to the clearing member that will state in general terms how pending transactions, open positions, and other pending matters will be affected and what steps are to be taken.
[
216
]
If a clearing member defaults under CCUS Rules,
[
217
]
receives a suspension, or CCUS determines that the financial or operational condition of a clearing member could adversely affect CCUS or cleared markets, CCUS may take certain action to restrict or terminate clearing privileges.
[
218
]
Additionally, CCUS may also impose protective measures related to a clearing member's clearing activity such as increasing initial margin requirements, prohibiting excess margin withdraws, imposing additional capital, margin, financial reporting or other requirements, or “take any other actions it deems proper or in the best interest” of CCUS or its clearing members.
[
219
]
If CCUS imposes a fine against a clearing member which is included in the schedule of fines, CCUS will give notice for such fines to the clearing member that specifies (1) the rule(s) violated; (2) the act or omission constituting each such violation; (3) the fine imposed for each violation; and (4) the date by which such determination becomes final and such fine must be paid or contested as provided below, which date shall be not less than 30 days after the date of service of such written statement.
[
220
]
The maximum fine imposed on the schedule of fines shall not exceed $5,000 per violation.
[
221
]
(c) Hearing and Appeals Process
Under CCUS Rules, applicants who have been denied approval to become a clearing member and clearing members who have received a sanction including fines, suspensions, and restrictions or terminations of clearing member services may appeal such decisions. For appeals of fines under CCUS Rule 604, a clearing member may appeal the fine in writing to CCUS. The matter will then be referred to the Chief Regulatory Officer and the Regulatory Division and will be subject to review by the Business Conduct Committee (“BCC”) Panel.
[
222
]
For appeals of disciplinary actions under CCUS Rule 603(a), the clearing member has 15 days to submit a petition for review to which CCUS has an opportunity to respond and then the clearing member has the opportunity submit a final reply.
[
223
]
The review will be conducted by the Board or a committee of the Board composed of at least three directors whose decision must be ratified by the Board.
[
224
]
Any Director who participated in the matter before the BCC Panel or other committee may not participate in any review of that matter by the Board.
[
225
]
The review shall be based solely on the record including the petition for review and any subsequent responses, unless the introduction of new information is allowed by the Board.
[
226
]
The Board may affirm, reverse or modify, in whole or in part, the decision of the BCC Panel in a written final decision.
[
227
]
Additionally, the Board may initiate a review of a decision made by the BCC Panel and such review will follow the procedures outlined in this paragraph.
[
228
]
For appeals of application denials, suspensions, or restrictions or terminations of clearing member services, the aggrieved party must file an application for review within 30 days of the notice of action.
[
229
]
If they party needs additional time to produce the application for review, they can submit an application for the extension of time which will be decided by the Chairman of the Appeals Committee and shall be final.
[
230
]
The CCUS Appeals Committee that is responsible for the review of such appeals will be appointed by the Chairman of the Board of Directors with the approval of the Board on an annual basis as well as when there are changes to the composition of the committee during the year.
[
231
]
Members of the appeals committee serve a one-year term until the next annual reappointment of the committee, or the individual resigns or is removed by the Board.
[
232
]
Once a application for a hearing is sent to the Appeals Committee, it will appoint a hearing panel of no less than three persons.
[
233
]
All relevant materials for the hearing will be provided to the parties at least 72 hours prior to the date of the hearing.
[
234
]
The applicant is entitled to be represented by counsel at the hearing.
[
235
]
Each of the parties will be permitted to make an opening statement, present witnesses and documentary evidence, cross- examine opposing witnesses and present closing arguments orally or in writing as determined by the panel.
[
236
]
The panel will also have the right to question all parties and witnesses to the hearing.
[
237
]
The panel's decision will be made in writing and will include the reasons supporting the conclusions of the panel.
[
238
]
The decision of the panel of the Appeals Committee can be subject to review by the Board either on its own motion within 30 days after issuance, upon written request submitted by the applicant, by the President of CCUS or by the Chairman of the committee whose action was subject to the prior review of the Appeals Committee, within 15 days after issuance of the decision.
[
239
]
The petition must be in writing and specify the findings and conclusions to which exceptions are taken together with the reasons for such
(
printed page 67639)
exceptions.
[
240
]
Parties may petition to submit a written argument to the Board and may request an opportunity to make an oral argument before the Board. The Board, or a committee of the Board, will have sole discretion to grant or deny either request.
[
241
]
As described above, the CCUS Rules address the discipline of clearing members, denial of applications, and prohibitions or limitations imposed by the clearing agency with respect to access to services offered by the clearing agency. CCUS has established rules and procedures that describe in detail the process taken by CCUS both when reviewing applications to become clearing members and when disciplining existing clearing members. The CCUS Rules ensure that written notification with reasoning is provided to any applicant whose application has been denied and to any clearing member who is being sanctioned for a violation of the CCUS Rules. Once the appropriate notification is provided, the affected party is afforded an opportunity to appeal the denial or sanction by requesting a hearing at which the affected party may be represented by counsel. The Commission therefore determines that the CCUS Rules provide a fair procedure consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(H) of the Exchange Act.
G. Burden on Competition
1. Statutory Standard: Section 17A(b)(3)(I)
Section 17A(b)(3)(I) of the Exchange Act states that a clearing agency shall not be registered unless the Commission determines that the rules of the clearing agency do not impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Exchange Act. In addition, Section 17A(a)(2) of the Exchange Act directs the Commission, having due regard for the maintenance of fair competition among brokers, dealers, clearing agencies, and transfer agents, to use its authority under the Exchange Act to facilitate the establishment of a national system for the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of transactions in securities (“National System”) and to facilitate the establishment of linked or coordinated facilities for the clearance and settlement of transactions in securities.
[
242
]
2. Summary of Application and Analysis
As described throughout this order, CCUS proposes to operate a registered clearing agency that provides CCP services for binary options that are securities. In assessing whether the rules of a clearing agency impose or do not impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Exchange Act under Section 17A(b)(3)(I) of the Exchange Act, the Commission considers the impact of the Applicant's rules on competition among brokers, dealers, clearing agencies, and transfer agents, and on competition between the Applicant and these entities.
[
243
]
Where there is a burden on competition, the Commission must determine if that burden is necessary or appropriate consistent with the determination required by Section 17A(b)(3)(I) of the Exchange Act.
[
244
]
In the context of impacts on competition among clearing agencies, one commenter—while generally supportive of CCUS's request for temporary registration as a time-limited bridge that allows innovative, investor-protective products to reach the market—is “fully opposed” to CCUS becoming a “permanent fixture” of the listed options market, as a second, fully registered clearing agency alongside the Options Clearing Corporation (“OCC”).
[
245
]
While acknowledging that its concern is “structural rather than a comment on [CCUS's] present intentions,” the commenter opposes adding to the National System for Clearance and Settlement a “vertically integrated clearing structure” such as characterizes the U.S. futures market, where, as the commenter describes, each major exchange group operates its own clearinghouse.
[
246
]
The commenter supports instead a central, industry utility clearing model, of the kind OCC has provided for listed options as a registered clearing agency.
The commenter states that the Commission should consider the broader market structure implications of this Application before granting permanent registration, explaining its view that a vertically integrated “monopolistic market structure “is the kind of structure Section 17A of the Exchange Act was designed to avoid.
[
247
]
The commenter explains that the pool of firms capable of serving as clearing members in the listed options market is limited due to the substantial capital, operational, and risk management infrastructure that clearing membership requires. In the commenter's view, a more fragmented structure with multiple clearing agencies would add to the costs of clearing membership among this limited group—and therefore the associated costs borne by market participants as their clients—through the potential for higher clearing fees, capital inefficiencies that result from holding positions that could offset but for multiple clearing agencies, and the loss of portfolio margining benefits.
[
248
]
The commenter also argues that, in addition to increased costs, an additional clearing agency introduces structural risk into the market ecosystem for listed options. The commenter states that the structural change associated with a second clearing agency will require routing new product categories through less proven exchange-affiliated clearing agencies rather than an industry utility. Nonetheless, the commenter explains that its members are “frustrated with OCC's pace of innovation” and that OCC is unable to currently provide clearing services for Binary KPI Options.
[
249
]
The commenter also acknowledges that the binary options to be cleared by CCUS have a comparatively simple risk profile relative to conventional options, which may mitigate the potential for procyclicality, wrong-way risk, model risk, and concentration risk.
[
250
]
The Commission acknowledges PTG's comments as outlined above. Currently pending before the Commission however, is an application for temporary registration. PTG's points relate to permanent registration and therefore are more appropriately addressed in any future Commission order related to permanent registration. That said, the risks and costs associated with changes to the structure of the listed options market will be evaluated during the period of CCUS's temporary registration by the Commission and market participants alike.
CCUS's clearing model and its ability to quickly bring to market clearing services for innovative product types for which there is market demand supports both innovation and competition in the market for clearing services, consistent
(
printed page 67640)
with the purposes of Section 17A of the Exchange Act. And, more broadly, CCUS's Application does not impose any burden not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Exchange Act. As CCUS states, its clearing infrastructure “has been built specifically with open-access clearing top of mind,” and CCUS intends to pursue cross-margining arrangements that may benefit investors and citing the experience of its European affiliate.
[
251
]
The Commission, has long viewed cross-margining arrangements between separately registered clearing agencies as a well-established mechanism for achieving margin efficiencies and facilitating the purposes of Section 17A of the Exchange Act. In other markets including the U.S. Treasury market, the Commission has approved applications for registration by new clearing agencies to help bring innovative products to market that serve investors and the public interest. The Commission agrees, as CCUS contends, that new clearing agencies, structured consistently with the requirements of Section 17A and Commission rules thereunder, can bring enhancements to market resilience by expanding access to central clearing and promoting effective risk management.
[
252
]
Accordingly, for the reasons discussed above, and based on the facts and circumstances presented by this Application, the Commission determines, pursuant to Section 17A(b)(3)(I) of the Exchange Act, that the Application does not impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of Section 17A of the Exchange Act.
[
253
]
IV. Temporary Registration and Exemption
CCUS has requested, pursuant to Rule 17Ab2-1(c), that the Commission grant CCUS temporary registration as a clearing agency with an exemption from certain requirements as to which the Commission is directed to make a determination under Sections 17A(b)(3)(B) and (F) of the Exchange Act for a period of 18 months.
[
254
]
With respect to Section 17A(b)(3)(B), as discussed in Part III.B.2, CCUS has not provided in its Application for participation standards addressing all categories of participants enumerated in Section 17A(b)(3)(B) of the Exchange Act, including registered clearing agencies, registered investment companies, banks, insurance companies, or other classes of persons designated as appropriate by the Commission. Relatedly, as discussed in Part III.E.2, CCUS has not provided CCUS Rules under Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Exchange Act addressing these same categories of participants. For the reasons discussed below, pursuant to Section 17A(b) of the Exchange Act and Rule 17Ab2-1(c) thereunder, the Commission is granting CCUS's request for temporary registration as a clearing agency and finds that an exemption from the above-described requirements of Sections 17A(b)(3)(B) and (F) of the Exchange Act is consistent with the public interest, the protection of investors, and the purposes of Section 17A, including the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and the safeguarding of securities and funds.
[
255
]
CCUS explains that its request for temporary registration would enable CCUS to meet market demand for Binary KPI Options in a regulated securities trading environment while other securities clearing agencies are not prepared or able to provide clearing agency services for these products. In its request, CCUS explains that its Application would not affect existing standardized securities options products traded on national securities exchanges and cleared by OCC, and that CCUS and its affiliates have a long history of close, successful, and productive relationships with other option exchanges and OCC. One commenter also expressed support for CCUS's request for temporary registration, as previously discussed in Part III.G.2, because it would serve as a “time-limited bridge” that allows innovative products to reach the market sooner than would be possible through the existing registered clearing agency that serves the listed options market.
[
256
]
CCUS states that not establishing participation standards for these other categories of participants listed in Section 17A(b)(3)(B) is appropriate, citing “the nature of the product, the categories of market participants who have indicated an interest in clearing Binary KPI Options, CCUS's risk management and liquidity framework, the broker-dealer customer protection framework and other factors.”
[
257
]
In Exhibit S, CCUS explains that it would be prepared to consider the feasibility and appropriateness of the other types of participants enumerated in Section 17A(b)(3)(B) during the period of its temporary registration,
[
258
]
and reiterates in its response letter that it would demonstrate compliance with all applicable clearing agency requirements within 18 months of its approval for temporary registration.
[
259
]
With respect to these requests for exemptive relief from Section 17A(b)(3)(B) and (F) of the Exchange Act, made in connection with its request for temporary registration, the Commission finds such relief is consistent with the public interest, the protection of investors, and the purposes of Section 17A of the Exchange Act for two reasons. First, providing clearing services only to BD Clearing Members is an appropriate, and incremental step, for bringing to the securities market Binary KPI Options. The Application establishes a comprehensive framework for the management of risk surrounding binary options that are securities, and commenters agree Second, CCUS has represented that it will consider including other entities during the period of temporary registration. Providing relief from Section 17A(b)(3)(B), which the Commission has granted before, allows prospective clearing agencies to develop their participation standards on an incremental basis because the financial and operational membership standards for such market participants depends, in part, on the extent and manner in which the clearing agency allocates losses resulting from member defaults, and the development of such participation standards will inform the overall risk profile and risk management framework of the registered clearing agency.
[
260
]
In the absence of such participation standards, the Commission cannot assess under Section 17A(b)(3)(F) whether clearing agency rules implementing participation standards for the categories of participants enumerated in Section 17A(b)(3)(B) are designed to promote the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and to assure the safeguarding of securities and funds.
[
261
]
Further, in the absence of such participation standards and associated rules, the Commission cannot assess whether the CCUS Rules foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in the clearance and settlement of securities transactions, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a national system for the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions,
(
printed page 67641)
and are not designed to permit unfair discrimination in the admission of participants or among participants in the use of the clearing agency because these requirements are primarily directed to assessing how the Application addresses the different categories of participation in its rules.
[
262
]
Accordingly, assessment of these provisions of Section 17A(b)(3)(F) requires that CCUS Rules incorporate the other enumerated categories of participants. With respect to the participation categories provided (
i.e.,
BD Clearing Members and Direct Clearing Members), the Commission has assessed and found that CCUS Rules do promote the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and assure the safeguarding of securities and funds. In so doing, the Application and CCUS Rules demonstrate consistency with the purposes of Section 17A of the Exchange Act (including the protection of investors and the public interest). Therefore, the Commission is providing exemptive relief from requirements under Section 17A(b)(3)(F) on a temporary basis to enable CCUS time to develop its rules, policies, and procedures as to the other participation categories enumerated and ensure such rules, policies and procedures are consistent with the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(F). Temporary relief is appropriate and consistent with the public interest and the protection of investors because existing CCUS Rules, as applied to BD Clearing Members and Direct Clearing Members, are consistent with promoting the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and the safeguarding of funds and securities.
[
263
]
Specifically, the reasons discussed in Part III.E.2, CCUS rules provide a comprehensive risk management framework for BD Clearing Members and Direct Clearing Members consistent with the purposes of Section 17A of the Exchange Act. Granting exemptive relief from this provision permits CCUS to operate on a temporary basis with respect to BD Clearing Members and Direct Clearing Members, is in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors because it enables CCUS to evaluate its risk management framework as to registered broker-dealers and participants that meet the definition of Direct Clearing Members while it considers how best to incorporate the other categories of participants enumerated in Section 17A(b)(3)(B) and whether its risk management standards need to be adjusted to account for the way the other categories might interact with the clearing agency and the risks they would bring via their participation.
Furthermore, such exemptive relief is consistent with the public interest, the protection of investors and purposes of 17A because while CCUS operates under temporary registration, CCUS must continue to satisfy its obligations under Rule 17Ab2-1 and Form CA-1, including submission of any amendments to its Form CA-1 application. As a registered clearing agency and self-regulatory organization, CCUS also will be obligated to file changes to its rules, policies, and procedures pursuant to Section 19(b) and Rule 19b-4 under the Exchange Act.
[
264
]
CCUS also would be subject to recordkeeping requirements, Commission supervision as a registered clearing agency, and examinations under the Exchange Act.
For the reasons described above, the Commission is granting CCUS's request for temporary registration with an exemption from the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(B) and (F) described above for a period of 18 months from the date of this order.
[
265
]
V. Conclusion
For the reasons discussed above, pursuant to Section 17A(b) of the Exchange Act and Rule 17Ab2-1(c) thereunder, the Commission is exempting CCUS from certain of the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(B) and (F) as described in this order and has determined that CCUS's Application otherwise satisfies the requirements of Section 17A of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder. Accordingly, the Commission is granting CCUS's request for temporary registration for a period of 18 months.
[
266
]
It is therefore ordered,
pursuant to Sections 17A and 19(a) of the Exchange Act and Rule 17Ab2-1(c) thereunder, that the application for temporary registration as a clearing agency filed by Cboe Clear U.S., LLC (File No. 600-47) be, and hereby is,
approved,
and that CCUS is granted exemptions from certain of the requirements in Section 17A(b)(3)(B) and (F) of the Exchange Act for the reasons described in this order and subject to the terms and other qualifications set forth in the Application, to be effective for not more than 18 months from the date of this order.

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Notice of availability.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is announcing
(
printed page 67566)
the availability of the latest major release of the MOtor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES) model, MOVES6. MOVES6 is the latest version of the EPA's state-of-the-science modeling tool for estimating emissions from cars, trucks, buses, and motorcycles based on the latest data and regulations. MOVES6 is available for use in State Implementation Plans (SIPs) and transportation conformity analyses. This notice starts a two-year grace period before MOVES6 will be required for use in transportation conformity determinations, both in new regional emissions analyses and in new hot-spot analyses.
DATES:
The EPA's announcement of the MOVES6 emissions model for SIPs and transportation conformity determinations in States other than California is effective October 27, 2026. This announcement starts a two-year transportation conformity grace period that ends on October 27, 2028. After this date, MOVES6 will be required for use as the latest EPA emissions model for new transportation conformity analyses other than California in both regional emissions analyses and in hot-spot analyses.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For technical model questions regarding the use of MOVES6, please email
moves@epa.gov
. For questions about SIPs, contact Kaitlyn Leffert at
leffert.kaitlyn@epa.gov
. For questions about transportation conformity, contact Aaron Letterly at
letterly.aaron@epa.gov
.

I. General Information
A. Does this action apply to me?
Entities potentially impacted by the approval of MOVES6 are those that adopt, approve, or fund transportation plans, transportation improvement programs (TIPs), or transportation projects as defined in
40 CFR 93.101
and those that develop and submit SIPs to the EPA. Regulated categories and entities potentially affected by this action include:
Category
Examples of regulated entities
Local government
Local air quality and transportation agencies, including metropolitan planning organizations (MPOs).
State government
State air quality and transportation agencies.
Federal government
U.S. Department of Transportation (Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) and Federal Transit Administration (FTA)).
This table is not intended to be exhaustive but rather provides a guide for readers regarding entities likely to be affected by the release of MOVES. Other entities not listed in the table could also be affected. To determine whether your organization is affected by this action, you should carefully examine the transportation conformity applicability requirements in
40 CFR 93.102
. If you have questions regarding the applicability of this action to a particular entity, consult the persons listed in the preceding
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section.
B. How can I get copies of MOVES6 and other related information?
The official version of the MOVES6 model and supporting documentation are available on the EPA's MOVES website at:
https://www.epa.gov/​moves
. Individuals who want to receive EPA announcements related to the MOVES6 model can follow instructions linked from the MOVES website at:
https://www.epa.gov/​moves/​latest-version-motor-vehicle-emission-simulator-moves
to receive EPA email announcements related to MOVES and MOVES guidance.
Available guidance on how to apply MOVES6 for SIPs and transportation conformity purposes can be found on the EPA's transportation conformity website,
https://www.epa.gov/​state-and-local-transportation/​policy-and-technical-guidance-state-and-local-transportation
