AGENCY:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Notice of Agency Order.
SUMMARY:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a component of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), announces it is issuing an Order under Sections 361, 365, 368, and 369 of the Public Health Service Act, and associated implementing regulations, prohibiting the boarding of any passenger who is not otherwise subject to an exemption on any aircraft destined to the United States from a foreign country unless the passenger presents a signed attestation confirming the passenger has not been present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States. This Order was issued on October 22, 2026, to become effective at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time (EST) on November 3, 2026, and shall remain in effect through 11:59 p.m. EST on December 18, 2026. This Order may be amended or rescinded prior to that time at the discretion of the Secretary or his designee.
DATES:
This action will take effect November 3, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EST. For individuals intending to travel to the United States by air, the Order will apply to flights departing at or after 11:59 p.m. EST on November 3, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Mina Zadeh, Acting Chief of Staff, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1600 Clifton Road NE, MS V18-2, Atlanta, GA 30329. Phone: 404-639-7000. Email:
cdcregulations@cdc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
On October 22, 2026, the Assistant Secretary for Health (ASH), HHS, signed an Order prohibiting the boarding of any passenger on any aircraft destined to the United States from a foreign country unless the passenger presents a signed attestation in paper or digital format confirming that the passenger has not been present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States. This includes any flight arriving in the United States, regardless of whether the United States is its final destination or the flight is connecting through the United States en route to another country. The airline or aircraft operator must retain a copy of the completed version of the signed attestation for at least 42 days after the passenger's flight departs for the United States from a foreign country and provide the attestation to the U.S. Government upon request.
This Order is effective for a period of 45 days. This Order may be amended or rescinded prior to that time at the discretion of the Secretary or his designee. Any amendment or extension of this Order will be based on the current outbreak metrics, including case counts, geographic spread, community-transmission indicators, and containment capacity in affected countries.

42 U.S.C. 268
, the U.S. customs officers and U.S. Coast Guard officers will assist in implementation of this Order. Other federal departments and agencies, including the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Department of Transportation, may also cooperate and assist with implementation of this Order consistent with their own legal authorities.

.

.

Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
Notice and Order Under Sections 361, 365, 368, & 369 of the Public Health Service Act (
42 U.S.C. 264
,

,

, & 71.32(b)
Requirement for Attestation for all Airline or Other Aircraft Passengers Arriving in the United States From any Foreign Country and Controlled Free Pratique for Airlines Confirming That Such Passengers Have Not Been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the Past 21 Days
Summary
Pursuant to
42 CFR 71.20
,
71.31(b)
, and
71.32(b)
, and as set forth in greater detail below, this Notice and Order prohibit the boarding of any passenger who is not otherwise subject to an exemption on any aircraft destined to the United States from a foreign country unless the passenger presents:
A signed attestation in paper or digital format confirming that the passenger has not been present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States.
(
printed page 67583)
This includes any flight arriving in the United States, regardless of whether the United States is its final destination or the flight is connecting through the United States en route to another country. This Order does not apply to overflights that do not land at any airport in the United States.
Further, pursuant to
42 CFR 71.31(b)
and as set forth in greater detail below, this Notice and Order operates as a controlled free pratique requiring an airline or other aircraft operator with an aircraft arriving into the United States to confirm to the U.S. Government that every passenger onboard the aircraft has completed and signed an attestation confirming that the passenger has not been in the DRC during the 21 days prior to boarding the flight to the United States as a condition of the airline or aircraft operator being granted permission to enter a U.S. port of entry, disembark passengers, and begin operations with respect to arriving at a U.S. airport.
A parent or other authorized individual may complete and sign the required attestation on behalf of a passenger under 18 years of age. An authorized individual may also act on behalf of any passenger who is unable to act on their own behalf (
e.g.,
by reason of age, or physical or mental impairment).
The passenger must provide the airline or aircraft operator with a paper or digital copy of the completed attestation reflecting that the passenger has not been present in the DRC in the past 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States. The airline or aircraft operator must retain the paper or digital copy of each passenger's completed and signed attestation for at least 42 days after the passenger's flight departs for the United States from a foreign country and provide the attestation to the U.S. Government upon request.
CDC encourages airlines and aircraft operators to incorporate the attestation into paperless check-in processes. An airline or aircraft operator may use a third party (including a third-party digital application) to provide translations. However, an airline or aircraft operator has sole legal responsibility to ensure the accuracy of any translation and to comply with all other obligations under this Order. An airline or aircraft operator is responsible for any failure to comply with its responsibilities as set forth in this Order, including for actions of a third party used to help effectuate its compliance with this Order. As between the airline or aircraft operator and the U.S. Government, the airline or aircraft operator remains responsible for compliance with this Order regardless of the involvement of any third party.
Pursuant to
42 U.S.C. 268
, customs officers and U.S. Coast Guard officers will assist in the implementation of this Order. Other federal departments and agencies, including the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Department of Transportation, may also cooperate and assist with implementation of this Order consistent with their own legal authorities.
The U.S. Department of Justice may seek to prosecute individuals who knowingly and willfully submit false attestations in violation of
18 U.S.C. 1001
.
Relationship to Other Orders
This Order operates in addition to, and does not supersede, modify, or replace, other CDC orders currently in effect concerning Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, including the Order Suspending the Right to Introduce Certain Persons from Countries Where a Quarantinable Communicable Disease Exists issued pursuant to
42 U.S.C. 265
,
268
and
42 CFR 71.40
, as most recently continued. Nothing in this Order limits the authority of CDC, the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Transportation, or any other federal department or agency to take additional measures under their own separate legal authority.
Statement of Intent
This Order shall be interpreted and implemented to achieve the following paramount objectives:
Preservation of human life;
Preventing the introduction, transmission, and spread of the Ebola virus into the United States; and
Preserving the health and safety of crew members, passengers, airport personnel, and communities.
Definitions
21 days
for purposes of the passenger attestation means a 21-day waiting period based on calendar days. Day 0 is the day the individual departed the DRC. Day 1 is the first full calendar day the individual is outside the DRC. An individual who was present in the DRC may board a flight to the United States on day 22.
Aircraft
shall have the same definition as under
49 U.S.C. 40102(a)(6)
. “Aircraft” includes, but is not limited to, commercial, general aviation, and private aircraft destined for the United States from a foreign country.
Aircraft Operator
means an individual or organization causing or authorizing the operation of an aircraft.
Airline
shall have the same definition as under
42 CFR 71.1(b)
.
Attest/Attestation
means completion and signature of the attestation in Attachment A. Such attestation may be completed and signed in paper or digital form, including through electronic signature. The attestation is a statement, writing, entry, or other representation made under
18 U.S.C. 1001
.
Foreign country
means anywhere that is not a state, territory, or possession of the United States.
Present/Presence
in the DRC means any physical presence, including entering or traveling through the country by air (excluding overflights), land, or sea. Presence also includes connecting through an airport in the DRC, even if the passenger did not disembark the plane or leave the airport.
United States
has the same definition as “United States” in
42 CFR 71.1(b)
, meaning “the 50 States, District of Columbia, and the territories (also known as possessions) of the United States, including American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.”
Exemptions
The following are exempt from the requirements of this Order:
Aircraft operators transporting passengers with Ebola disease pursuant to U.S. Government authorization and in accordance with CDC guidance.
Individuals for whom the CDC has issued an exemption based on humanitarian or other important government considerations,
e.g.,
emergency medical evacuations. Additional conditions may be placed on individuals granted such exemptions, including but not limited to, observing precautions during travel, providing consent to post-arrival monitoring, and/or self-quarantine after arrival in the United States, as may be directed by federal, state, territorial, tribal or local public health authorities to reduce the risk of disease transmission.
Background
A. Ebola Disease
Viral hemorrhagic fever refers to a group of severe illnesses caused by certain viruses that damage the body's blood vessels and affect the ability of the blood to clot properly. Viral hemorrhagic fevers include diseases such as Ebola, Marburg, and Lassa fever.
Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe and often fatal illness caused by
(
printed page 67584)
one of the viruses in the Ebola family. Ebola disease outbreaks occur mainly in parts of sub-Saharan Africa and can spread rapidly in communities with limited healthcare resources. Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus is a rare form of Ebola first identified during an outbreak in Bundibugyo District, Uganda, in 2007. BVD is one of several species within the orthoebolavirus family and causes symptoms similar to other forms of Ebola, including fever, weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, and, in severe cases, hemorrhagic complications and organ failure. The disease spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids or contaminated materials.
The incubation period for BVD is typically between 2 and 21 days, with most people developing symptoms within 4 to 10 days after exposure. During this incubation period, infected individuals do not spread BVD until symptoms begin.
Screening for BVD focuses on identifying symptoms and possible exposure history, such as recent travel to affected areas or contact with infected individuals. Patients with suspected BVD are evaluated for symptoms including fever, weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, and bleeding, and laboratory confirmation is performed using specialized tests such as PCR (polymerase chain reaction) to detect the virus in blood and other body fluid samples. Health authorities also use temperature checks and contact tracing to identify suspected cases, and quarantine and isolation procedures, as applicable, to prevent transmission.
There are currently no widely approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments for BVD. Treatment mainly consists of supportive care, including intravenous fluids, electrolyte replacement, oxygen support, pain and fever management, and treatment of secondary infections. Early medical care significantly improves survival chances. Robust public health measures such as early detection, rapid isolation, strong infection prevention measures (
i.e.,
use of personal protective equipment [PPE]), and monitoring of contacts are critical to controlling outbreaks and reducing deaths. Clinical trials of monoclonal antibodies and of an existing vaccine approved for use to prevent disease caused by the Ebola Zaire virus are presently underway in the DRC.
[
1 2
]
However, experts expect it will be several months before these therapeutics are potentially available for wider use.
B. Ongoing Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak
The confirmed ongoing outbreak of BVD in the DRC continues to escalate in intensity. The outbreak remains centered in eastern DRC's Ituri Province, although cases have been identified in North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Bas-Uélé, Tshopo, North Ubangi, and South Ubangi provinces. This geographic expansion is concerning, particularly given that response efforts are still not at the scale required for outbreak containment. As of October 18, 2026, the DRC reports 9,455 confirmed cases and 4,561 deaths in 66 health zones across eight provinces.
The World Health Organization has reported substantial under-ascertainment of cases and persistent challenges with contact tracing. As of its most recent assessment, only approximately 20 percent of BVD cases were identified through follow-up of listed contacts, and approximately 40 percent were ultimately linked to a known chain of transmission, indicating substantial undetected transmission.
[
3
]
Surveillance challenges persist in the most heavily affected areas, with conflict and insecurity, weak health infrastructure, and relatively porous borders in the region complicating containment efforts. Although contact tracing efforts are underway, they remain insufficient and the daily follow-up necessary to rapidly detect symptomatic individuals and ensure their prompt isolation has not been achieved.
Travelers who have unknowingly been infected with BVD may travel before becoming symptomatic. Such travelers may spread the virus beyond DRC and ultimately reach the United States. The DRC is connected to the global aviation network through a series of regional and international transit hubs that provide pathways into the United States. These international transportation corridors support continuous movement of travelers between Central and East Africa and major U.S. metropolitan centers, increasing the likelihood that travelers exposed to Ebola disease could enter the United States before symptoms become apparent. Complex multi-leg itineraries and the rapid pace of international travel create substantial challenges for identifying potentially infected travelers before arrival.
The risk of BVD introduction into the United States is heightened by the virus's incubation period, which can extend up to 21 days, allowing infected persons to travel internationally while asymptomatic and therefore unlikely to be detected through routine symptom-based screening measures. The current outbreak has demonstrated this risk: for example, a physician infected while providing patient care in the DRC traveled internationally before becoming ill and was diagnosed only after arriving in France.
[
4
]
That case required extensive public health coordination, including federal, state, and local government efforts to identify, notify, and monitor potentially exposed U.S. citizens, demonstrating that a single infected traveler can impose significant cross-border public health response demands even without onward transmission occurring within the United States. Additionally, on October 6, 2026, the Kenya Ministry of Health announced the country's first BVD case and death in an individual who had traveled from DRC to Uganda, flown from Kampala to Nairobi on October 2, and was hospitalized before dying on October 5, 2026.
[
5
]
By October 19, 2026, Kenya had announced another seven cases had been confirmed in previously identified close contacts, reaching a total of eight BVD cases in Kenya, including the initial case that resulted in a death.
[
6
]
The interconnected nature of global air travel presents a credible pathway for BVD importation into the United States, underscoring the importance of aggressive surveillance, traveler monitoring, airport public health screening, healthcare preparedness, and rapid containment capabilities.
(
printed page 67585)
The ongoing outbreak has also demonstrated that substantial U.S. public health resources may be required to respond to an Ebola exposure or infection in any U.S. citizen. On July 10, 2026, CDC announced that an additional U.S. citizen working for a humanitarian organization in the DRC had tested positive for BVD.
[
7
]
The individual, who was not involved in direct patient care,
[
8
]
prompted an extensive U.S. public health response. CDC, in coordination with the humanitarian organization, initiated contact tracing, exposure risk assessments, and monitoring activities to identify high-risk contacts and evaluate potential exposures among humanitarian personnel who had recently returned to, or are planning to return to, the United States. The Department of State arranged medical evacuation outside of the DRC for treatment. This incident demonstrates that even when an infected U.S. citizen remains overseas, the outbreak can require substantial U.S. public health resources to identify, assess, and monitor potentially exposed individuals associated with international humanitarian operations.
Travelers utilizing air transit pathways originating in the DRC include U.S. and non-U.S. citizens, regional migrants, foreign contract workers, humanitarian personnel, business travelers, students, refugees, and third-country nationals moving through international aviation hubs in Africa, the Middle East, and Europe. Many travelers entering U.S.-bound itineraries from these pathways may do so under temporary visas, refugee or asylum processing mechanisms, international organizational travel, or multi-country itineraries that obscure their original point of departure. As a result, public health screening and border security systems face heightened operational complexity in identifying travelers with recent exposure histories linked to Ebola-affected regions, particularly when travelers transit through multiple jurisdictions prior to arrival at major U.S. metropolitan airports.
CDC has issued Travel Health Notices (THN) for affected countries and regions. Currently, there is a Level 4 THN for Ituri and Nord-Kivu Provinces of DRC (avoid all travel); a Level 3 THN for Haut-Uélé and Tshopo Provinces of DRC (reconsider nonessential travel); a Level 2 THN (practice enhanced precautions) for the remainder of the DRC and Uganda; and a Level 1 THN (practice usual precautions) for Nairobi, Kenya.
[
9
]
CDC modeling indicates that, absent rapid and sustained public health interventions, the outbreak could become one of the largest Ebola epidemics ever recorded.
[
10
]
The analysis further demonstrates that early identification of cases, contact tracing, isolation, and treatment of symptomatic persons, community engagement, and safe burial practices are critical to reducing transmission and mitigating outbreak growth.
[
11
]
CDC has concluded that the current outbreak is already the largest known outbreak of BVD and that large-scale, temporary public health measures are necessary to prevent further international spread of the disease and to reduce the risk of introduction of infected persons into the United States.
[
12
]
Commensurate with the deterioration of the epidemiological situation in the DRC, CDC escalated its response to the outbreak to a Level 1, the highest level within the agency's Graduated Response Framework.
[
13
]
CDC has determined that the risk profile presented by the DRC is materially distinct from that of other affected countries. The DRC remains the epicenter of the outbreak, with an estimated 80 percent of newly confirmed cases in Ituri Province not linked to known contacts, indicating substantial undetected community transmission. Contact tracing, surveillance, and containment capacity in the DRC are impaired by conflict, insecurity, weak health infrastructure, and porous borders. CDC has therefore determined that a categorical temporary measure directed at travelers with recent presence in the DRC is appropriately tailored to the elevated importation risk presented by that country. CDC will continue to monitor conditions in the DRC and other affected countries and may modify the scope of this Order accordingly.
Statement of Good Cause Under the Administrative Procedure Act
This Order is not a rule within the meaning of the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”) but rather is an action taken under the existing authority of
42 U.S.C. 264(a)
and
42 CFR 71.20
,
71.31(b)
, and
71.32(b)
, which were promulgated in accordance with the APA after full notice and comment rulemaking and a delayed effective date. If this Order qualifies as a new rule under the APA, notice and comment and a delayed effective date are not required because there is good cause to dispense with prior public notice and comment and a delay in effective date.
See
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, (d)(3).
Based on the foregoing, I have determined that Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a highly transmissible quarantinable communicable disease designated as such by
Executive Order 13295
, as amended, is confirmed present in the DRC. I have also determined that Ebola disease if introduced into the United States would constitute a public health emergency. I have considered other alternatives, including reliance on airport-based public health screening, voluntary questioning, and expansion of the existing federal public health travel restrictions process, and have determined that these alternatives, standing alone or in combination, would not adequately address the identified risk given the disease's incubation period of up to 21 days, the substantial proportion of asymptomatic transmission-window travel, and the demonstrated capacity of a single infected traveler to consume substantial U.S. public health resources. Finally, I determine that requiring airline passengers to submit an attestation confirming that they have not been present in the DRC during the 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States, combined with a conditioning of controlled free pratique on airline confirmation of such attestations, is a necessary public health measure to protect the public health and prevent the introduction, transmission, and spread of Ebola disease into the United States. In making these determinations I have considered the prevalence of Ebola disease in the DRC, that country's limited ability to screen for the disease and engage in other mitigation measures, and the potential for spread in the United States. Accordingly, I find that any delay in issuing this Order beyond the minimum necessary for operationally feasible implementation would be contrary to the public's health
(
printed page 67586)
in the United States and therefore the public's interest.
Any delay in the effective date, would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest for the additional reason that the outbreak in the DRC continues to expand, the 21-day incubation period of Ebola disease means that each additional day of pre-effective delay materially increases the risk that infected persons will board flights bound for the United States while asymptomatic, and public notice of a forthcoming attestation requirement could prompt individuals presently in the DRC to accelerate their travel to the United States before the requirement takes effect, defeating the purpose of this Order.
If any provision of this Order, or the application of any provision to any carriers, persons, or circumstances, shall be held invalid, the remainder of the provisions, or the application of such provisions to any carriers, persons, or circumstances other than those to which it is held invalid, shall remain valid and in effect.
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, and for the reasons stated above, I hereby conclude that notice-and-comment rulemaking would defeat the purpose of the Order and endanger the public health, and is, therefore, impracticable and contrary to the public interest. For the same reasons, I have determined, consistent with
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
, that there is good cause to make this Order effective immediately following the minimum delay necessary for the Order's implementation to be operationally feasible.
Action
For the reasons outlined above, I hereby determine that passengers covered by this Order are at risk of transmitting Ebola disease and requiring passengers to attest that they have not been present in the DRC during the 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States is needed as a public health measure to protect the health of other travelers and U.S. communities.
This Order shall remain in effect until rescinded or modified based on specific public health or other considerations, or until December 17, 2026, whichever occurs first. Any amendment or extension of this Order will be based on a review of then-current outbreak metrics, including case counts, geographic spread, community-transmission indicators, and containment capacity in affected countries.
1. Requirements for Airlines  Other Aircraft Operators
This Order conditions the grant of controlled free pratique on the airline compliance measures specified below. This Order does not regulate landing rights, airspace access, or aircraft certification, which remain within the jurisdiction of the Department of Transportation, the Federal Aviation Administration, and other agencies exercising their respective legal authorities.
Any airline or other aircraft operator with passengers who are not otherwise exempt from the requirements of this Order boarding a flight to the United States from a foreign country, shall:
A. Confirm to the U.S. Government, at or before the time of boarding, that all passengers boarding or onboard the aircraft have completed and signed an attestation in paper or digital format confirming that they have not been present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the 21 days preceding their boarding a flight to the United States. For purposes of this requirement, “confirm” means that the airline or aircraft operator has reviewed the completed attestation from each covered passenger prior to boarding and has determined, based on the face of the attestation, that the attestation is complete and signed; and
B. Not board any passenger who has failed to complete and present such an attestation.
C. Retain a paper or digital copy each passenger's completed and signed attestation for at least 42 days after the passenger's flight departs for the United States from a foreign country and provide the attestation to the U.S. Government on request.
Any airline or other aircraft operator that fails to comply with section 1, “Requirements for Airlines  Other Aircraft Operators,” may be subject to criminal penalties under,
inter alia,
42 U.S.C. 270
and
271
and
42 CFR 71.2
, in conjunction with
18 U.S.C. 3559
and
3571
(providing for fines of up to $100,000 for individuals and $200,000 for organizations, and/or imprisonment of up to one year). CDC anticipates that separate compliance mechanisms may be established by the Transportation Security Administration pursuant to its own statutory authorities.
Any airline or other aircraft operator that fails to provide the U.S. Government the confirmation of completed attestations of all passengers as outlined above will not receive controlled free pratique to enter a U.S. port of entry, disembark passengers, and begin operation with respect to arriving at an airport in the United States.
2. Requirements for Aircraft Passengers Who Are Not Otherwise Exempt
A. Complete and sign the attestation under penalty of law as provided by
18 U.S.C. 1001
which provides criminal penalties for knowingly and willfully submitting false statements to the U.S. government; and
B. Provide for confirmation the completed and signed attestation to the airline or other aircraft operator confirming that they have not been present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the 21 days preceding their boarding a flight to the United States.
The required attestation text is attached to this Order as Attachment A. Unless otherwise permitted by law, a parent or other authorized individual may present the required documentation on behalf of a passenger under 18 years of age. An authorized individual may act on behalf of any passenger who is unable to act on their own behalf (
e.g.,
by reason of age, or physical or mental impairment).
Any passenger who fails to provide this attestation, or submits false or misleading information, may face a delay of travel, denial of boarding, or denial of boarding on future travel.
Any passenger who fails to comply with the requirements of section 2, “Requirements for Aircraft Passengers,” may be subject to criminal penalties under,
inter alia,
42 U.S.C. 271
and
42 CFR 71.2
, in conjunction with
18 U.S.C. 3559
and
3571
. Willfully giving false or misleading information to the government may result in criminal penalties under,
inter alia,
18 U.S.C. 1001
. This Order shall be enforceable through the provisions of
18 U.S.C. 3559
,
3571
;
42 U.S.C. 243
,
268
,
270
,
271

AGENCY:
National Assessment Governing Board, Department of Education.
ACTION:
Notice of open and closed meetings.
SUMMARY:
This notice sets forth the agenda, time, and instructions to access the National Assessment Governing Board's (hereafter referred to as the Board or Governing Board) standing committee meetings and quarterly Governing Board meeting. This notice provides information to members of the public who may be interested in attending the meetings and/or providing written comments related to the work of the Governing Board. The meetings will be held either in person and/or virtually, as noted below. Members of the public, whether participating in person or virtually, must register in advance. A registration link will be posted on the Governing Board's website,
www.nagb.gov
,
no later than five (5) business days prior to each meeting.
DATES:
The Quarterly Board Meeting and Standing Committee meetings will be held on the following dates:
Quarterly Board Meeting
November 19, 2026, from 9:05 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., EST
November 20, 2026, from 10:40 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. EST
(
printed page 67556)
Standing Committee Meetings
Executive Committee
November 19, 2026, from 8:15 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. (EST)
Assessment Development Committee
November 20, 2026, from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. (EST)
Committee on Standards, Design and Methodology
November 20, 2026, from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. (EST)
Reporting and Dissemination Committee
November 20, 2026, from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. (EST)
ADDRESSES:
TBD.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Angela Scott, Designated Federal Officer (DFO) for the Governing Board, 400 Maryland Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20202; telephone: (202) 245-6234; email:
Angela.Scott@ed.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Statutory Authority and Function:
The Governing Board is established under the National Assessment of Educational Progress Authorization Act (
20 U.S.C. 9621
). Information on the Governing Board and its work can be found at
www.nagb.gov
.
Notice of the meetings is required under section 1009(a)(2) of
5 U.S.C. chapter 10
(commonly known as the Federal Advisory Committee Act). The Governing Board formulates policy for the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) administered by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES). The Governing Board's responsibilities include:
(1) selecting the subject areas to be assessed; (2) developing appropriate student achievement levels; (3) developing assessment objectives and testing specifications that produce an assessment that is valid and reliable, and which are based on relevant, widely accepted professional standards; (4) developing a process for review of the assessment, which includes the active participation of teachers, curriculum specialists, local school administrators, parents, and concerned members of the public; (5) designing the methodology of the assessment to ensure that assessment items are valid and reliable, in consultation with appropriate technical experts in measurement and assessment, content and subject matter, sampling, and other technical experts who engage in large-scale surveys; (6) measuring student academic achievement in grades 4, 8, and 12 in the authorized academic subjects; (7) developing guidelines for reporting and disseminating results; (8) developing standards and procedures for regional and national comparisons; (9) taking appropriate actions needed to improve the form, content, use, and reporting of results of an assessment; and (10) planning and executing the initial public release of NAEP results.
Standing Committee Meetings
The Governing Board's standing committees will meet to conduct regularly scheduled work. Standing committee meeting agendas and meeting materials will be posted on the Governing Board's website,
www.nagb.gov
,
no later than five (5) business days prior to the meetings. Members of the public may attend the open sessions and may register via the website. Minutes of prior standing committee meetings are available at
https://www.nagb.gov/​governing-board/​quarterly-board-meetings.html
.
Standing Committee Meetings
Thursday, November 19, 2026
Executive Committee (In-Person).
8:15 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. (EST), Closed Session.
The Executive Committee will meet in closed session on Thursday, November 19, 2026, from 8:15 a.m. to 9:00 a.m., to discuss the NAGB budget and receive updates on the Board's strategic priorities. This session must be closed because the discussion may impact current and future NAEP contracts and budgets and must be kept confidential to maintain the integrity of the Federal budgeting and acquisition processes. Public disclosure of this information would significantly impede implementation of the NAEP assessment program if conducted in open session. Such matters are protected by exemption 9(B) of the Government Sunshine Act,
5 U.S.C. 552b(c)
.
Friday, November 20, 2026
Assessment Development Committee (In-Person).
8:30 a.m. to 9:50 a.m. (EST), Open Session.
9:50 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. (EST), Closed Session.
The Assessment Development Committee will convene in open session on Friday, November 20, 2026, from 8:30 a.m. to 9:50 a.m., and in closed session from 9:50 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. From 8:30 a.m. to 8:35 a.m., the committee will review the agenda. From 8:35 a.m. to 9:35 a.m., the committee will receive an update on the NAEP Civics Framework. From 9:35 a.m. to 9:50 a.m., the committee will discuss a process for evaluating the 2026 NAEP Contextual Questionnaires. The committee will transition to closed session from 9:50 a.m. to 10:30 a.m., to discuss the plans for the NAEP Long-Term Trend content documentation. This meeting will be closed to the public because it will involve discussion of unreleased assessment information and confidential budget and procurement information. Public disclosure of this information would reveal unreleased assessment content, and proprietary contract costs of the current NAEP contractors, independent government cost estimates for future assessments, and would have an adverse financial effect and significantly impede the implementation of future assessments if conducted in open session. These matters are protected from public disclosure under exemption 9(B) of the Government Sunshine Act,
5 U.S.C. 552b
.
Committee on Standards, Design and Methodology (In-Person).
8:30 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. (EST), Closed Session.
10:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. (EST), Open Session.
The Committee on Standards, Design and Methodology will meet in closed session on Friday, November 20, 2026, from 8:30 a.m. to 10:00 a.m., followed by an open session from 10:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. From 8:30 a.m. to 9:20 a.m., the committee will discuss plans for multi-stage testing (MST), and from 9:20 a.m. to 10:00 a.m., the committee will receive updates on 2026 evaluations and methodology in progress. This meeting will be closed to the public because it will involve discussion of unreleased and preliminary assessment data. Public disclosure of this information would reveal unreleased assessment data and content and impede the implementation of future assessments if conducted in open session. These matters are protected from public disclosure under exemption 9(B) of the Government Sunshine Act,
5 U.S.C. 552b
. From 10:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m., the committee will meet in open session to discuss the committee's priorities for 2027 and beyond.
Reporting and Dissemination Committee (In-Person).
8:30 a.m. to 9:20 a.m. (EST), Open Session.
9:20 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. (EST), Closed Session.
The Reporting and Dissemination Committee will meet on Friday, November 20, 2026. The committee will convene in open session from 8:30 a.m. to 9:20 a.m., and in closed session from 9:20 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. The chair will welcome the committee from 8:30 a.m. to 8:40 a.m., followed by a strategic communications update from 8:40 a.m.
(
printed page 67557)
to 9:00 a.m. The committee will then discuss the evaluation of the 2026 NAEP Contextual Questionnaires from 9:00 a.m. to 9:20 a.m. The committee will meet in closed session from 9:20 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. to discuss the release plan for the 2026 NAEP results. This session must be closed because the results have not been released to the public. Public disclosure of this confidential information would significantly impede implementation of the NAEP assessment program if conducted in open session. These matters are protected from public disclosure under exemption (9)B of the Government Sunshine Act,
5 U.S.C. 552b
.
Quarterly Governing Board Meeting
The plenary sessions of the Governing Board's November 2026 quarterly meeting will be held on the following dates and times:
Thursday, November 19, 2026
9:05 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. (EST), Hybrid Meeting.
9:05 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. (EST), Open Session.
12:45 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. (EST), Closed Session.
2:30 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. (EST), Open Session.
3:30 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. (EST), Closed Session.
On Thursday, November 19, 2026, the Board will meet in open session from 9:05 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. The open session will begin at 9:05 a.m. with welcome remarks from Mark White, Chair of the Governing Board, followed by approval of the November 2026 agenda, and the August 2026 meeting minutes. At 9:15 a.m. to 9:45 a.m., U.S. Assistant Secretary of Elementary and Secondary Education Kirsten Baesler, will deliver remarks and administer the oath of office to new and reappointed members. From 9:45 a.m. to 10:00 a.m., newly appointed and reappointed members will deliver remarks.
At 10:00 a.m. to 10:45 a.m., Lesley Muldoon, Executive Director of the Governing Board, will provide updates on the Board's work. From 10:45 a.m. to 11:00 a.m., Matthew Soldner, Acting Commissioner, NCES, will report on key activities at NCES. The Board will receive updates on the NAEP Civics Framework from 11:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Following a 15-minute transitional break to closed session, the Board will receive a briefing on embargoed data for the 2026 NAEP Grades 4 and 8 Reading and Mathematics from 12:45 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. This session must be closed because the presentation and discussion will include information on the budget and the federal acquisition process, as well as data which cannot be released to the public at this time. Public disclosure of this confidential information would significantly impede the implementation of the NAEP assessment program if conducted in open session. Such matters are protected by exemption 9(B) of the Government Sunshine Act,
5 U.S.C. 552b
.
The board will meet in open session from 2:30 p.m. to 3:15 p.m., to discuss and take action on the NAEP Achievement Level Descriptions for Reading and Mathematics Grades 4 and 8. Following a 15-minute transitional break, the Board will meet in closed session to discuss State Trends in Test Accommodations from 3:30 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. This session must be closed because disclosure of this confidential information would significantly impede implementation of the NAEP assessment program if conducted in open session. Such matters are protected by exemption 9(B) of the Government in the Sunshine Act,
5 U.S.C. 552b
.
The Board will continue in closed session from 4:30 p.m. to 5:00 p.m., for a member discussion on board governance matters and strategic priorities going forward. This discussion pertains to information of a personal nature and disclosure would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy. This session will be closed pursuant to exemption 6 of the Government Sunshine Act,
5 U.S.C. 552b(c)(6)
.
The Thursday, November 19, 2026, session will adjourn at 5:00 p.m.
Friday, November 20, 2026
10:40 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. (EST), Hybrid Meeting.
10:40 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. (EST), Open Session.
On Friday, November 20, 2026, the Board will meet in open session from 10:40 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. From 10:40 a.m. to 11:00 a.m., the Board will discuss and take action on the release plan for NAEP 2026 Reading and Mathematics results. From 11:00 a.m. to 11:30 a.m., the Board will receive a briefing on opportunities for members to contribute to communications about NAEP results and Board policies. The Board will hear reports from its standing committees from 11:30 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. The November 20, 2026 Governing Board meeting will adjourn at 12:00 p.m.
Instructions for Accessing and Attending the Meetings
Registration:
Members of the public may attend open sessions of the standing committee meetings in person only and may attend the full Governing Board on November 19-20, 2026, either in person or virtually. Attendance at closed sessions is limited to individuals approved to participate. A link to the final meeting agenda and information on how to register for the open and closed sessions will be posted on the Governing Board's website,
www.nagb.gov
,
no later than five (5) business days prior to the meeting. Registration is required to attend the meeting, whether in person or virtually.
Public Comment:
Written comments related to the work of the Governing Board and its standing committees may be submitted to the attention of the DFO, either via email to
Angela.Scott@ed.gov
,
or in hard copy to the address listed above in the For Further Information Contact section. Written comments related to the standing committee meetings and the full Governing Board meeting should be submitted no later than close of business five (5) days prior to each meeting and should reference the relevant agenda item.
Access to Records of the Meeting:
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 1009
, the public may inspect the meeting materials and other Governing Board records at 500 D Street SW, Washington, DC 20024, by emailing
Angela.Scott@ed.gov
to schedule an appointment. The official verbatim transcripts of the open meeting sessions will be available for public inspection no later than thirty (30) calendar days following each meeting. Requests for the verbatim transcriptions may be made via email to the DFO.
Reasonable Accommodations:
The meeting location is accessible to individuals with disabilities. If you need auxiliary aid or service to participate in the meeting (for example, an interpreter, assistive listening device, or materials in alternate format), notify the DFO listed in this notice by close of business on November 12, 2026.

AGENCY:
Consumer Product Safety Commission.
ACTION:
Notice of information collection; request for comment.
SUMMARY:
As required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC or Commission) announces that the Commission has submitted to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) a request for extension of approval of information collection requirements associated with the Standard for the Flammability of Mattresses and Mattress Pads and the Standard for the Flammability (Open Flame) of Mattress Sets. OMB previously approved the collection of information under control number 3041-0014. OMB's most recent extension of approval will expire on October 31, 2026. On June 18, 2026, CPSC published a notice in the
Federal Register
to announce the agency's intention to seek extension of approval of the collection of information. The Commission received four public comments. By publication of this notice, the Commission announces that CPSC has submitted to OMB a request for extension of approval of that collection of information.
DATES:
Submit comments on the collection of information by November 27, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Submit comments about this request by email:
OIRA_submission@omb.eop.gov
or fax: 202-395-3888. Comments by mail should be sent to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, Attn: OMB Desk Officer for the CPSC, Office of Management and Budget, Room 10235, 725 17th Street NW, Washington, DC 20503. Written comments that are sent to OMB also should be submitted electronically at
http://www.regulations.gov
under Docket No. CPSC-2010-0055.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Cynthia Gillham, Consumer Product Safety Commission, 441 G Street NW, Washington, DC 20548; (301) 504-7791, or by email to:
pra@cpsc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
CPSC seeks to renew the following currently approved collection of information:
Title:
Standard for the Flammability of Mattresses and Mattress Pads (
16 CFR part 1632
) and Standard for the Flammability (Open Flame) of Mattresses (
16 CFR part 1633
).
OMB Number:
3041-0014.
Type of Review:
Renewal of collection.
Frequency of Response:
On occasion.
Affected Public:
Manufacturers and importers of mattresses and mattress pads.
General Description of Collection:
The Standard for the Flammability of Mattresses and Mattress Pads,
16 CFR part 1632
, was issued and amended under section 4 of the Flammable Fabrics Act (FFA),
15 U.S.C. 1193
, to reduce unreasonable risks of burn injuries and deaths from fires associated with mattresses and mattress pads. The standard prescribes requirements to test whether a prototype mattress or mattress pad will resist ignition from a smoldering cigarette. The standard also requires recordkeeping of all prototype test results. Manufacturers and importers must maintain these records for three years. Also, under
16 CFR part 1632
, each mattress or mattress pad must be permanently labeled with the month and year of manufacture and the location of the manufacturer. Mattress pads treated with a chemical flame
(
printed page 67553)
retardant must also be labeled prominently with the letter “T” and instructions on how to protect the pads from agents or treatments that can cause deterioration of their flame resistance.
The Commission promulgated the Standard for the Flammability (Open Flame) of Mattress Sets,
16 CFR part 1633
, under section 4 of the FFA, to reduce deaths and injuries associated with mattress fires by limiting the size of the fire generated by a mattress set during a thirty minute test. The standard requires manufacturers and importers to maintain certain records to document compliance with the standard, including maintaining records concerning prototype testing, pooling, and confirmation testing, and quality assurance procedures and any associated testing. The required records must be maintained for as long as mattress sets based on the prototype are in production and must be retained for three years thereafter.
16 CFR part 1633
also includes labeling requirements for each mattress set to bear a permanent, conspicuous, and legible label containing specified information.
See
16 CFR 1633.2
.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
CPSC estimates there are 80 respondents annually to part 1632 for mattress pads and 403 respondents for mattresses. For part 1633, CPSC estimates 403 respondents annually.
Estimated Time per Response:
On average, a mattress pad producer will respond for three prototypes annually and a mattress producer will respond for eight prototypes annually for both parts 1632 and 1633. CPSC estimates that each respondent will spend five hours for labeling and five hours for recordkeeping, annually.
Total Estimated Annual Burden:
If a mattress pad producer responds to the collection three times annually and a mattress producer responds to the collection eight times annually, the estimated annual burden for mattress pads subject to part 1632 is 1,200 hours (80 respondents × 3 responses per year × 5 hours per response = 1,200 hours per year), and the estimated annual burden for mattresses subject to 1632 is 16,120 hours (403 respondents × 8 responses per year × 5 hours per response = 16,120). For mattresses subject to part 1633, based on an average of eight different qualified prototypes, the total estimated burden is about 16,120 hours annually (403 respondents × 8 responses annually × 5 hours per responses = 16,120 hours).
Total Estimated Annual Cost to Respondents:
The hourly compensation for the time required for record keeping for both parts 1632 and 1633 is estimated at $80.04 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, “Employer Costs for Employee Compensation,” December 2025, Total compensation of all management, professional, and related occupations in goods-producing industries:
https://www.bls.gov/​news.release/​archives/​ecec_​03202026.htm
). At this rate, the annualized cost to the respondents would be $2,676,538 (33,440 hours × $80.04 = $2,676,537.60). Therefore, CPSC estimates the total cost of the information collection burden to respondents, for
16 CFR 1632
and
16 CFR 1633
, is approximately $2.7 million, annually.
Response to Public Comments:
Comments:
CPSC received four public comments on the information collection. Two comments were out of scope. One commenter, a manufacturer and supplier of bedding goods, commented in support of the collection. An individual commenter also expressed support for the collection but provided suggestions to improve the burden estimates and suggestions to encourage secure electronic recordkeeping.
The individual commenter recommended that CPSC refine its burden analysis with current industry data, issue clearer compliance guidance, and promote voluntary electronic recordkeeping tools in order to better satisfy the PRA's goals of obtaining useful information while minimizing unnecessary paperwork burden. With regard to the burden estimate, the commenter stated that the five-hour estimate does not capture all the time spent maintaining electronic systems, training personnel, coordinating with laboratories and suppliers, reviewing material or design changes, responding to audits, or translating records for imported products. The commenter, however, noted that mature digital compliance systems may need less time for routine records. The commenter suggested requesting information from manufacturers and importers on burden estimates by activity and prototype type.
The commenter also provided suggestions to improve clarity and reduce unnecessary compliance costs by publishing a plain-language electronic recordkeeping guide, confirming that electronic records are acceptable, providing a voluntary standardized template for reporting, and clarifying how records for one product sold under multiple brands or channels should be organized. Lastly, the commenter suggested that the burden on small entities should be explained further, optional templates and guidance should be provided, and CPSC should solicit targeted small-entity feedback.
Response:
Prototype testing, records, and permanent labels are integral to reducing deaths and injuries associated with mattress safety and justify renewal under the PRA. CPSC's current estimate of 33,440 annual burden hours reflects these required functions. CPSC acknowledges the commenter's point that the actual time may vary based on firms' digital maturity, staff training, coordination with lab/suppliers, audits, translations, and product changes. In the June 2026
Federal Register
60-day notice, CPSC requested public comments on the estimated burden of the proposed collection of information.
91 FR 36811
. In response, CPSC did not receive any suggested revisions to the burden estimates.
CPSC recognizes that small businesses may have fewer dedicated compliance staff and less ability to absorb testing and documentation costs. CPSC provides compliance guidance that is available to the public at CPSC's Regulatory Robot:
https://www.cpsc.gov/​Business--Manufacturing/​Regulatory-Robot/​Safer-Products-Start-Here
.
In addition, exemplar labels are included in
16 CFR 1633
Figures 12-17. CPSC also provides helpful information on suggested record keeping formats at
https://cpsc.gov/​Business--Manufacturing/​Business-Education/​Business-Guidance/​Mattresses/​Suggested-Recordkeeping-Forms-for-16-CFR-1633
.
Small businesses can also receive guidance concerning CPSC regulations, including mattress flammability, to help them bring their products into compliance and resolve procedural issues. For more information, please see CPSC's Small Business Resources page at
https://cpsc.gov/​Business--Manufacturing/​Small-Business-Resources
.
Moreover, consistent with long-standing practices, firms may use any technology, including electronic recordkeeping, to compile and maintain required business records for both parts 1632 and 1633. CPSC does not prescribe how firms maintain their internal recordkeeping systems.
Alberta E. Mills,
Secretary, Consumer Product Safety Commission.

On the basis of the record

]
Background
The Commission instituted these reviews on April 1, 2026 (
91 FR 16229
) and determined on July 6, 2026 that it would conduct expedited reviews (
91 FR 51745
, August 11, 2026).
The Commission made these determinations pursuant to section 751(c) of the Act (
19 U.S.C. 1675(c)
). It completed and filed its determinations in these reviews on October 22, 2026. The views of the Commission are contained in USITC Publication 5803 (October 2026), entitled
Mattresses from Cambodia, China, Malaysia, Serbia, Thailand, Turkey, and Vietnam: Investigation Nos. 701-TA-645 and 731-TA-1495 and 1497-1501 (Review).
By order of the Commission.
